286:
## Commentary on Pācittiya
## 5. Pācittiya Section
## 1. Chapter on False Speech
## 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech
In the term "vādakkhitto," the three types of discourse known as argument (vāda), persuasion (jappa), and sophistry (vitaṇḍa) are simply referred to as "vāda" without distinction. Among these three, because of the phrase "together with heretics," it is said that one type of argument is excluded, and the remaining persuasion and sophistry are intended. Due to skill in the six grounds for rebuke (chalajātinigga hāṭṭhāna), a person sometimes denies and then admits something; likewise, having admitted a statement previously, he later denies it. In this way or another, he prevaricates. Having admitted to such deliberate lying (sampajānamusā) that has arisen, he acts falsely, makes an appointment, and speaks deceptively. Thus, being one who has cast away his word (vādakkhitto), he wanders about fulfilling the grounds for a Pācittiya offense; this is the intended meaning.

In the phrase "in his own view," regarding his own view first undertaken as "All phenomena are non-self" (sabbe dhammā anattā), he holds the view: "Whatever is suffering, that is non-self." When it is said "all phenomena," Nibbāna is also included. However, because it is said "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness," that Nibbāna is not suffering (dukkha). There is no possibility of it being suffering. Thinking that an opponent (paravādī) might point to the sutta "Whatever is suffering, that is non-self," confuse his conclusion, and charge him with the fault "the contradictory view is wrong," he might perceive some fault in that first view. Whether a fault is charged or not, he denies his view saying, "This is not my view." Later, seeing a sutta such as "Nibbāna alone is permanent" or "It is concluded as non-self," and noticing the faultlessness of that first argument, he later admits it again, saying, "This is indeed my view."

Reflecting on the benefits mentioned in that view and having admitted it, if all phenomena were non-self, they could not even be phenomena (dhamma). This is because they are called "dhamma" as they bear a nature (sabhāva). This word "atta" (self) also denotes nature (sabhāva). Thus, whether a fault is charged or not, perceiving it as a fault, he later denies that first argument again, saying, "This is not my view." Then, that opponent prohibits his own side's view...
287:
Withdrawing an admission (paṭijānanattāpanayana). According to the statement "He admits, it would be to him," it is said, "Your being rebuked is called an admission." With the intention of denying a meaning that exceeds the true nature (sabhāva), he says: "My statement of admission 'All phenomena are non-self' referred to the self imagined by fools (bālaparikkappita) which exceeds the true nature. Since that admission only referred to that imagined state, there is no withdrawal of my admission." His denial "This is not my view" was made with the intention: "I do not say 'All phenomena are non-self' referring to the self known as nature (sabhāva)." By this other reason, he conceals the reason for withdrawing what was previously admitted. Based on the reason "Because the word 'atta' denotes nature, it should not be said 'All phenomena are non-self'," he withdrew his previous admission. The meaning is that he conceals that reason with another reason shown later.

Since he does not only deny and admit the meaning in the manner shown, but also the words, it is said in the Commentary: having first stated the reason "because it is to be known (jānitabbato)," when the opponent (paravādī) says, "If it is impermanent because it is to be known, then your Nibbāna would also be impermanent," he says, "I did not state the reason 'because it is to be known'; I said 'because it has the nature of arising (jātidhammato).' You noted it differently because of your deafness," and so on. This is the intended meaning. It is said that after saying "because it is to be known," he again says "because it has the nature of arising," etc. It is written that one who admits after denying is said to conceal that denial with this admission. The two meanings "having known" or "while knowing" are shown.

Furthermore, "included in false speech" (micchāvācāpariyāpanna) means included in the four types of false speech. Some say it has reached the distinction of names such as Sīhaḷa. Therefore, both the speech of one who speaks thus and the intention (cetanā) that originates it are mentioned because both are included in the Matika. In the Vibhaṅga, since that speech cannot exist without intimation (viññatti), "vocal intimation" (vācasikā viññatti) is also shown. Although it is said in worldly parlance as "the speech of one who speaks thus," to show it in the ultimate sense, it is also said "the intention that originates it." "Grossly" (oḷārikena) means that since the speech originating from intention is subtle, it is treated only by way of its object. In the place "diṭṭhassa hoti," it should be understood that the words are to be split as "diṭṭho assa." I do not know that this monk does not strive by the power of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). "I do not see the white cloth..."
288:
In the phrase "Diṭṭhassa hoti," the words should be analyzed as "Diṭṭho assa." If a monk says "I do not know" regarding something he did not attend to by the power of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), or if he says "I did not see the clean cloth," etc., or if he says "I see neither woman nor man" based on ultimate emptiness (paramattha-suññatā), it does not constitute a lie (musāvāda).

In the passage "āpattiṃ āpajjativeva," it is said to be an "offense of wrong speech" (dubbhāsita). Why? Because it is stated as "acting in jest." Although it directly refers to "speech, utterance... vocal intimation (vacasika-viññatti)," the body is not upright.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Lying (Musāvāda-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 2. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Insulting Speech (Omasavāda-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā)

"Puna are patte" means when it rolls back to that place and reaches another spoke (ara). "Patiṭṭhitārappadesaṃ" refers to the ground. Regarding "puna are," some say it means reaching the ground at that same spoke again, but that does not seem correct. "Jāpito" means defeated; there is also a variant reading "parājito." "Pāpesī" means to overcome or oppress. Regarding the heavy burden of the Brahmin who speaks pleasant words, "udabbahī" means he pulled or dragged it; or it is a genitive case in the sense of disregard (anādara). "Dhanañca naṃ alābhesī" means he acted in such a way that the Brahmin did not obtain the wealth.

"Pubbe" means in the origin story (nidāna). "Avakaṇṇaka" is the name "Cut-ear." "Javakaṇṇaka" is the name "Crooked-ear." "Dhaniṭṭhaka" is a name meaning "Wealth-increaser," and "Siriwaḍḍhaka" is just a name for one who increases the family (Kulawaḍḍhaka). "Tacchakakamma" is the work of carpenters who perform digging and carving; some say it is the work of stone-masons. "Muddā" is the art of counting by finger joints, and "gaṇanā" is the art of large-scale calculation, as stated in the Ancient Glossary (Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada). It is written as "madhumehaṃ omehaṃ." Some say it refers to the increase of flesh in a person with a large body. The word "yabha" occurs in the sense of sexual intercourse. It is said by some that even one who insults by saying "one free from lust" (vītarāga), etc., is indeed insulting by way of the defilements; likewise, one who insults by saying "Stream-enterer" (sotāpanna) is indeed insulting by way of an offense. Because it is connected to appearance (liṅga), extreme whiteness, etc., are also considered as appearance.

The word "sabbattha vadeti" is the summary (uddesa), and the word "bhaṇati" is the detailed explanation (vitthāra). Alternatively, the word "vadeti" indicates making another person understand.
289:
In the sections on indirect speech (aññāpadesavāra), however, it is said "he speaks thus" (evaṃ vadeti). Why? To point out the order of the summary (uddesa) shown previously. Even previously, the word "evaṃ" (thus) is used to point out the order of the summary shown in four ways for each category such as birth (jāti): "a low person by a low person, a high person by a low person, a low person by a high person, and a high person by a high person." The intention is that when it is said "he speaks thus" in the very place where it was said "he speaks a low person by a low person," that manner is pointed out. Otherwise, it would follow that such a manner is not possible through indirect speech. If one asks, "Is it really not possible?" No, it is because there is no special reason, because it would lead to the contingency of no offense in that indirect speech, and because the indefinite meaning is possible through an indefinite (aniyama) designation. The intention is that the indefinite meaning—that an offense is incurred for one who speaks with reference to either a Caṇḍāla or a non-Caṇḍāla through an indefinite designation such as "There are some Caṇḍālas here"—is possible.

If it is so, one might say that only this much should be said, as the pointing out of the previously shown summary order is accomplished by that much. No, because without being joined with the word "vadeti," it cannot be directly understood that the word "evaṃ" points out this particular manner. Alternatively, it should be understood that the word "vadeti" has the purpose of being a rule (niyama), just as in the method of indirect speech, a dukkaṭa or pācittiya occurs only when making another person understand.

Another way: if one, standing near another monk, commands him to speak of a low birth by a low birth, he incurs a pācittiya offense. If he himself is a low person and speaks of a low Caṇḍāla... or Pukkusa as "a Pukkusa" by a low birth, he incurs a pācittiya offense for every word. It should be understood that this method also applies in the sections on indirect speech. This meaning should be sought in the words "duṭṭhadosa." Otherwise, one of the words "vadeti" or "bhaṇati" would be redundant in both the direct and indirect speech sections, or especially in the indirect speech sections, because the smoothness of the speech is possible even without it. It should be understood that because it is not directly stated in the Pali text, it is called "sāṇattika" (by command) here. In that context, "vadetīti" is the junction of "vada" and "iti."

For one who speaks in the absence (of the person), there is a dukkaṭa offense. This is because it is stated in the Andhaka Commentary: "But for one who speaks in the presence with the seven classes of offenses, there is a dukkaṭa offense." The desire to play (davakamyatā) means jesting; to show that manner, it is said "because of the desire to laugh" (hasādhippāyatā). The teachers say: "Even in the absence, for one who speaks with the desire to laugh, there is only an offense of wrong speech (dubbhāsita)." It should be understood that for one who speaks out of anger, wishing to blame evil, there is a dukkaṭa offense; but in the absence, there is no offense.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Insulting Speech (Omasavāda-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
290:
## 3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Slander (Pesuññasikkhāpada)

36-7. There is the text: "Having heard from this one [to tell] that one." The phrase "Having heard from these" is not good (incorrect). In the word *bhedāyapi*, *bhedāya* means for the sake of causing division. Because the three persons involved exist only in the status of monks, the plural form "in the slandering of monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ pesuññe*) is used.

38-9. The construction is: saying, "The venerable so-and-so is a Caṇḍāla... p... a Pukkusa," he conveys slander. Otherwise, it would lead to the state of merely saying, "He says he is a Pukkusa." In this section, although the *anupasampanna-vāra* (the section concerning the unordained) could be obtained, it is not explicitly extracted and shown, either because the method has already been shown in the *Omasavāda* training rule, or because of the desire to show it briefly at the end. Indeed, at the end, three types of *dukkaṭa* offenses are shown. The Blessed One, in showing those *dukkaṭa* offenses, considered that a *pācittiya* offense is incurred through the reversal of either one or both of the two terms stated as "Having heard from an ordained one, he conveys slander to an ordained one." Desiring to show both those terms together, He said first of all: "An ordained one, having heard from an ordained one, conveys slander to an ordained one; there is an offense of *pācittiya*."

Regarding these two terms, some teachers say: "Because a monk who has committed a *pārājika* offense is still [technically] an ordained one, if he insults such an ordained one with the desire to revile him, or having heard the words of such an ordained one, conveys slander to such an ordained one, there is an offense of *pācittiya*; therefore, this initial term '*upasampanno*' is stated in all places." That statement is not appropriate, because it is impossible for an offense to occur again for one who has already committed an absolute *pārājika* offense. Therefore, it should be understood that the initial term "*upasampanno*" is stated only because there is no subject term "*bhikkhu*" in the *mātikā*, and without it, it is impossible to indicate the doer (*kattu-kāraka*) of the words "speaks" and "conveys."

This training rule is *anāṇattika* (incurring an offense only if committed by oneself) because there is no mark of command in the Pali. The phrase "not for the sake of being loved, not with the intention of causing division" is a possessive case (*sāmivibhat*) that depends on the action of conveying slander (*upasaṃharaṇa*); this is because there is no purpose in speaking to one who remains silent. Therefore, it is said: "There is no offense for one who speaks with the desire to condemn evil."

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Slander is finished.
291:
## 4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Teaching Dhamma Word by Word (Padasodhammasikkhāpada)

45-6. In the phrase "All this is called Dhamma word by word," the term "Dhamma" should be connected as "spoken by the Buddha" (*buddhabhāsita*). "Collection of syllables" (*akkharasamuha*) occurs in an incomplete word. Words spoken by Paccekabuddhas should also be included within the words spoken by the Buddha. It should be understood that words spoken by laypeople who are not lay followers (*anupāsaka-gahaṭṭha*) are included in the words spoken by seers (*isibhāsita*) and so on. In some books, the term "spoken by deities" (*devatābhāsita*) does not exist; where it does exist, that text itself is the Pali.

This method also applies to verse compositions (*gāthābandha*); it is indeed permissible to stop after reciting only a single syllable. When making someone recite a sutta such as "*Evaṃ me sutaṃ*," if one stops after reciting the syllable "*E*," there is a *pācittiya* offense by way of syllable (*anvakkhara*). If one stops after reciting an incomplete word, there is a *pācittiya* offense by way of articulation (*anubyañjana*). Among the words, if the first word is defective, there is a *pācittiya* offense by way of word (*anupada*). "Based on the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathānissita*) means words that stand by way of depending on the commentary. This refers to the commentary spoken in the original language (Sinhalese) in ancient times. "Based on the Pali" (*pāḷinissita*) means words that appear only in the Pali Canon. There are also treatises such as the *Maggakathā*.

The vicinity (*upacāra*) is twelve cubits. It is written that "*opāteti*" means reciting together or arriving simultaneously. Although the sutta on the taming of the dragon Apalāla and the *Sīlupadesa Sutta* arose during the time of the Blessed One, in order to make it known that only whatever is extracted and spoken from the Buddha's words in those suttas becomes a basis for an offense, the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* expressed it loosely with the words "they say" (*vadanti*). Because the portions extracted from the Buddha's words are numerous, the offense in those suttas is stated by way of that majority; therefore, the meaning is that the intention of that *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* is clarified in the *Mahāpaccari* commentary.

It is said: "Others say it is the speech of all disciples." If a teacher stands and gives the text (*pāṭha*) to students who are sitting, some teachers say he does not incur the offense stated as "I will not teach Dhamma to one who is sitting while I am standing." That statement is not appropriate because their giving of the text is nothing other than teaching the Dhamma; otherwise, it would lead to the contingency of no offense in giving the text to those holding umbrellas and so on, whereas the existence of an offense is established. For it has been said:

"Both do not know the meaning,
Both do not see the Dhamma,
He who teaches the mantra,
And he who learns it unrighteously."

In this verse, "*adhīyati*" means learning; therefore, giving the text is also teaching the Dhamma. In the *Sekhiya* commentary, it is said: "The definition of Dhamma here should be understood according to the method stated in the *Padasodhammasikkhāpada*."
292:
"The chaplain priest teaches the mantra; the king learns the mantra unrighteously; both the priest and the king do not know the benefit (or the meaning); both do not see the cause (or the Pali text)." This has been stated. In this verse, the meaning of "adhīyati" is bad (unrighteous). Therefore, giving the Pali is also the preaching of the Dhamma. In the Sekhiya Commentary, it is stated: "The distinction of the Dhamma should be understood by the method stated in the Padasodhamma training rule." Therefore, this principle should be understood in all training rules related to the Dhamma. If it were the case that no offense is incurred by a monk who preaches the profound Dhamma through the power of the language of formations (saṅkhāra-bhāsā) and so forth, by the power of the Sekhiya training rule, then it would contradict the Chappaka Jātaka. In that Chappaka Jātaka, would one say there is no offense because the mantras are external texts (bāhiraka)? No, because that is not understanding the intention of that Jātaka. The intention in that Jātaka is this: "O monks, I do not even like the teaching of mantras, which are called external texts, to one sitting on a high seat; how much less would I like the preaching of the Dhamma?" Indeed, this Pali: "O monks, even then, I did not like sitting on a low seat and teaching mantras to one sitting on a high seat; what need is there to say about preaching the Dhamma now?" shows only the aforementioned intention and no other. For that very reason, a distinction in wording was made: "teaching the mantra" and "preaching the Dhamma." Otherwise, in both cases, it should have been said only as "preaching the Dhamma."

However, in the phrase beginning with "Do not speak with me," it is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: "If a monk wishes to speak together with a novice, and likewise the novice wishes to speak together with the monk, and they speak together suddenly—as in the case of 'reciting together with one who is reciting a text that is mostly familiar'—there is no offense. For by this much, it does not mean the monk is teaching the novice." Since this is not in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is appropriate to say there is no offense. If it were investigated and rejected in the Mahāpaccari and so forth, an offense would be incurred. However, it does not reach the state of kiriyā-akiriyā (action/non-action). Why? Because there is the intention to speak together with the mind. Even while having such an intention, if he forbids the novice, saying "Do not speak together," and yet speaks together, he incurs an offense. For a monk who speaks together by mistake suddenly without the intention to speak, there is no offense. Therefore, it is said: "If he speaks even though it was said 'Do not speak with me,' there is no offense." Even so, following the opinion of the teachers, one should practice in such matters according to the method already stated. Why? Because it is not in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, an offense is incurred simply because of its absence. If the statement "no offense" is not possible in that Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, this is because it is not the right place and is inappropriate.

In this matter, there is this investigation: "If he speaks together even though it was said 'Do not speak with me,' there is no offense for the monk"—this statement is appropriate because of the monk's lack of intention to speak, and even if there is an intention, because there is no offense in the three cases such as chanting (sajjhāya). If the novice, being skillful, says "Do not speak with me," and the monk, being unskillful, speaks, an offense is indeed incurred because the intention to speak is evident. If he speaks suddenly, there is no offense because of the absence of that intention. If the monk himself speaks together with that novice even though it was said "Do not speak with me," an offense is indeed incurred. In fact, this training rule is not kiriyā-akiriyā. If this training rule were kiriyā-akiriyā, the statement in the Mahāpaccari and so forth that "there is no offense" would be appropriate. Why? In the Mahāpaccari, with this meaning, "With me..."
293:
If one says "Do not speak with me" and then speaks with that novice himself, it is indeed an offense. This is because this training rule is not kiriyā-akiriyā (an offense arising from both action and non-action). If this training rule were kiriyā-akiriyā, then the statement of "no offense" in the Mahāpaccariya and other commentaries would be appropriate. This is the meaning. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is likely said with this very intention: "Do not speak with me." This is because here, the action of the novice is not the standard (measure). If said with this intention, it is very appropriate. Akkharattha (meaning of the letter) is the same as byañjanattha (meaning of the articulation).

Although it is said, "Whatever is a word (pada), a subsequent word (anupada), a subsequent letter (anvakkhara), or a subsequent articulation (anubyañjana), all this is called padasodhamma," yet only these two are applied: "He teaches by the word; for every word, there is an offense of pācittiya. He teaches by the letter; for every letter, there is an offense of pācittiya." Why is that? Because anupada and anubyañjana are included within the term pada. For it is said: "Anupada is the second foot (of a verse). Anubyañjana is the subsequent articulation similar to the preceding articulation." Therefore, it is established that only a portion of anupada is anubyañjana.

If it is asked: "Since it is said that the collection of letters and articulations is called a word (pada), and since the three types starting with anupada are taken by that word, should only the word be mentioned?" It should not be so mentioned because of the distinction in phrasing (vacana-visesa). For one who teaches by the word incurs an offense in the word, the subsequent word, or the subsequent articulation, but not in the letter. One who teaches by the letter incurs an offense in any one of the words, etc. For in words such as "Varo varaññū varado varāharo," if one teaching the first va-sound finishes at the second va-sound, or teaching the first ro-sound finishes at the second ro-sound, or teaching the first ra-sound finishes at the second ra-sound, then it is possible that a pācittiya offense occurs.

If it is asked: "Is it possible because it follows the sequence of articulations (anubyañjana)?" No, because it contradicts the Pali: "For every word, there is an offense of pācittiya." This statement shows that there is one offense for one word. If it is asked: "Based on the statement 'When Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ is being said, he finishes at Rū', it is established that for one teaching the whole foot, an offense occurs when only the first letter is spoken together?" No, because it contradicts the Pali: "For every letter, there is an offense of pācittiya." Therefore, because it is impossible to say "he finishes at Rū", and because the Rū-sound is established as being included in the aforementioned Dhamma, without saying that meaning, the phrase "When Rūpaṃ aniccaṃ is being said" is stated to show the status of the letter as being included in the aforementioned Dhamma for one teaching purely by the letter. Alternatively, it should be understood like the word vedanā in anubyañjana for the sake of smooth phrasing.

## The Explanation of the Padasodhamma Training Rule is finished.
294: ## 5. Explanation of the First Sahaseyya Training Rule. The phrase "Na sahaseyyaṃ kappetabbaṃ" is stated by way of the verb (kiriya). In some Pāḷi versions, there is the reading "Na sahaseyyā kappetabbā". It means that the Buddha prescribed that a monk should not practice sleeping together [with an unordained person]. In the context of "apassenaṃ vā", it is written that it refers only to a couch woven with cane. One should fill in the remaining text as: "Thinking that whatever training rule is not allowable for those monks is also not allowable for those novices (sāmaṇeras), he might practice sleeping together without going to the presence of the preceptor (upajjhāya) and so forth." Because it is said, "An unordained person (anupasampanna) means the rest excluding a monk," other teachers say that on the fourth night, a woman is an unordained person; therefore, she causes both sahaseyya offenses. It is also said, "Excluding a monk... an unordained person refers to a male animal which is a basis for a Pārājika offense." Both of these statements should be scrutinized. In the second training rule, "mātugāmo nāma" (a woman) refers only to a human woman, and female yakkhas, female petas, and female animals which are bases for Pārājika should not be included, because in the case of those who are not human women, only a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing) offense occurs. It is also said, "If a dukkaṭa occurs in one's own training rule, why should it be called a pācittiya in the first training rule?" There is a statement in the Sinhalese Commentary (Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā): "Apariikkhitte pamukhe anāpatti" (There is no offense in an unenclosed porch). To explain the meaning of that statement, it is said in the Andhaka Commentary: "It is said with reference to a porch located on a terrace (jagati) other than the ground." Furthermore, "vasati" means staying on the fourth day. "Bhikkhu nipanne" means when the monk has lain down. "Sannipatita-maṇḍapaṃ" refers to the assembly hall in the Mahāvihāra monastery. Some teachers say, "If one stays in a dukkaṭa area for three days and sleeps in a place sufficient for a sahaseyya offense on the fourth day, only a pācittiya occurs." That statement is not appropriate. ## The Explanation of the First Sahaseyya Training Rule is finished. ## 6. Explanation of the Second Sahaseyya Training Rule. There are readings "Atha kho te manussā" and "Te addhikā". There is also a reading "Ekarattaṃ", but that reading is not good. Since a dukkaṭa offense is mentioned in the Pāḷi regarding a pandaka (eunuch), they say, as it is said regarding a hermaphrodite (ubhatovyañjanaka), "It seems a root offense (mūlāpatti) occurs in hermaphrodites," and "Women without signs (animitta) and so forth are just women." Although a dead woman is a basis for Pārājika, she does not cause an offense in this training rule because she stands on the side of the non-living (anupādinna). In this context, the grounds for a Pārājika offense should not be considered. ## The Explanation of the Second Sahaseyya Training Rule is finished.
295:
## 7. Dhamma-desanā-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Because of the words "viññū paṭibalā" (wise and capable), there is no offense for a monk who teaches the Dhamma to a woman who is not wise (not clever). In this training rule, female spirits (yakkhī) and others are objects of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) because they are not as gross (oḷārika) as human women. Some teachers say that since it is stated that a female animal in human form is capable of receiving the Dhamma, other beings besides female spirits are also objects of dukkaṭa. The word "mātugāmāya" (to a woman) is spoken by way of gender transformation. It is written that, setting aside the Pali text of the Commentaries and so on, one is allowed to teach as one wishes in local languages such as Tamil (Damiḷa). If it is asked: "Just as female spirits and others are objects of dukkaṭa, why does one incur an expiation (pācittiya) instead of a dukkaṭa when teaching a woman who is staying with a male spirit (yakkha) who has taken a human form?" It is because such a being does not enter the category of a companion even slightly. If even a human woman cannot be a companion, how could a spirit and others be a companion? If it is argued that in the second Aniyata training rule, that woman is a companion and thus there is no offense; in that Aniyata rule, the companionship is not in consideration of lewd words (duṭṭhullā-vācā), but rather in consideration of sitting. In this training rule, it is not merely sitting, but teaching that is intended. And that teaching is more gross (significant) than sitting. Therefore, citing that Aniyata rule is an incomplete illustration.

## 1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Vegetation (Bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada)

It makes known the state shown by being unable to hold the axe. 90-92. Because of the words "bhavanti" and "ahuvuñca," the word "bhūta" occurs in two tenses (past and present). If the seed is shown by the vegetation (bhūtagāma) produced from the seed, that seed itself is the property. It is like the answer: "That very chicken is smeared with meat." In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathās) also, it is written: "one who perceives a seed as a seed." Whatever seed is called vegetation (bhūtagāma), it should be construed as "in that seed which is the seed of vegetation." It is said that because it lacks roots, it does not become a complete bhūtagāma; the reason given is "only that which has roots and leaves is called bhūtagāma." It is written in two ways: "it is called abhūtagāmamūla because it does not arise from bhūtagāma, or because the bhūtagāma has no root." The reason is that no other bhūtagāma arises from it. Piyaṅgu is the Asana tree, having a thick bark and edible fruit; it is also called "pītasāla." The statement that it is included in rootless vegetation refers to a young coconut tree. Because it grows on the back of a pot and because it conforms to the category of seed-born plants (bījagāma), it is a matter of a dukkaṭa offense. It is written: "It should not be used because it is badly practiced (durūpacinna)." It is said: "Because it is said that the branches of certain trees grow, it is understood that for those trees whose branches do not grow, there is no need for the act of making them allowable (kappiya-karaṇa)." Mudda-tiṇa is the name of that grass. It is written that there is a variant reading "muñja-tiṇa."

"By means of the samana-kappa" means by the allowable terms of recluses; therefore, a monk should say, "Make it allowable (kappiyaṃ karohi)." Even if a novice (sāmaṇera) or others do so by the command of that monk...
298:
It is clear that the act of making it allowable by fire should be done only after saying "kappiya" (allowable). Because they are permissible like those made allowable by fire, etc., seeds that are not born from seeds are also included here in the phrase "by the five allowable terms of recluses." Or, the recluse's word for making it allowable should be taken as it is obtained. It is said that if one intends to say "kappiya" but says "kappa," it is still "allowable." It is said that the word "kappiya" may also be said in one's own language. Because it is said "having said kappiya," a monk should say only "kappiya." However, others say that novices (sāmaṇeras) and others may speak in whatever language they are proficient in; this point should be investigated. The statement "intending to make the sugarcane allowable, he pierces the wood" means that he missed while intending to perform the act of making it allowable. Teachers, however, say: "If one says kappiya intending to have the act of making allowable performed, and has a lump of rice or such made, it is allowable." The reason they give for this is that even if it is done by piercing, it becomes allowable because it was done with the intention that it is proper to do so. If it were not allowable, it would not be allowable even when done to a lump of rice, etc.; this point should be reflected upon.

It is allowable to place a water pot with growing moss in the sun. If there is an intention to destroy it, it is like a dukkaṭa offense. It is said: "The string for tying flowers is like the vessel it is placed in; therefore it is not allowable. However, in a bundle of flowers tied to a flower stalk, even if it is done to the stalk, it is allowable, because the flowers are present on that stalk." In the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, it is said: "Vegetation (bhūtagāma) is shown by seed-born plants (bījagāma) for the purpose of including everything without exception."

98-99. It is called "aññavādaka" because one speaks something else (evasively). It is written: "One should not speak frivolous words." ## 3. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Inciting Grumbling (Ujjhāpanaka Sikkhāpada)
In the word "chandāya," it is spoken with a change of gender, like "akkharakkharāya" and so on; or it means for the purpose of desire (chandattha). It means for the purpose of making [the monks] follow his own desire, those for whom he prepares the lodgings.

In the words "anupasampannaṃ" and so on, the instrumental sense (karaṇattha) should be taken. "Aññaṃ anupasampannaṃ" means by another unordained person. It appears as if two Pācittiyas are stated, as in the case of cutting trees etc. in the preliminary effort (pubbapayoga), because an offense is incurred due to false speech; this should be investigated.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Inciting Grumbling is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the First Training Rule on Lodgings (Paṭhamasenāsana Sikkhāpada)
Because it is said, "Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks," and because it is said in the Parivāra, "One primary regulation (paññatti), one supplementary regulation (anupaññatti)," it is established that there is a supplementary regulation here. How is it established? Although the place of the regulation is not clear from such words as "Monks, you should recite this training rule in this way," it is only stated that "I allow you, monks, for eight months... to put it away." That...
300:
If it is asked why it is not stated, it is because it is to be stated in the same manner as mentioned in the first regulation, and because there is no distinction. If so, what is the supplementary regulation here? The word "ajjhokāse" (in the open air) is the supplementary regulation. If it is asked, "Is this supplementary regulation not also in the original regulation?" [The answer is] it is. However, the word "ākāsa" in that original regulation indicates only the place, while the word "ākāsa" in the second supplementary regulation indicates the time known as the four months of the rainy season. It should be understood that the Blessed One, wishing to show that both time and place are combined into one as "ajjhokāse," said, "I allow you, monks... to put it away."

For this very reason, it is said in the Mātikā Commentary: "Wherever and whenever it is not proper to spread [the bedding], all that is to be understood here as falling under the term 'ajjhokāsa' (open air)." Since the winter season is a time when there is no offense, it is established that this training rule is independent of the origin (nidāna). By the power of the word "ajjhokāse," this distinction is known: in the rainy season, it is not proper [to leave bedding] in a place where it rains, in the open air, or in a pavilion (maṇḍapa), etc. In the winter season, although it is not proper in the natural open air, it is proper in pavilions, etc., where the lodging is not wetted by frost or snow. In the summer season, it is proper even in the natural open air, provided that unseasonal rain clouds are not seen. This distinction is also established by the power of these two terms: "aṭṭha māse" (eight months) and "avassika-saṅkete" (the sign of the non-rainy season).

Furthermore, according to the distinction shown in the Commentary, a couch covered with leather, etc., or one newly woven, does not perish quickly. "Kāyānugatikatttā" means because it goes wherever the body goes. The Elder Dhammasiri says that it is not proper to stay touching the body to a communal (saṅghika) couch, etc. However, because it is stated in the Andhaka Commentary, "Venerable sirs, use the communal couch, etc., in the open air as you please," as offered by the donors, and because there is no prohibition here, it is proper. Others say, "It is also proper for other such types of bedding." "Pādaṭṭhānābhimukhā" is written as facing the place where the feet of the person sitting fall. The teachers' opinion is that it means facing the place where the feet of the person sweeping are.

"Pāduddhārena" is written as being because it stands in the outer precinct (upacāra). If one goes like a Dhamma-preacher, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Why is there no Pācittiya? Because it should be taken up after making the senior monks who arrive later rise. But for a Dhamma-preacher, since he should not be made to rise, [a Pācittiya is incurred]. Some say that among the group of six (chabbaggiya), they were senior monks (thera). 302:

For this reason, in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā (the commentary on the Anupakhajja training rule in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī), it is stated: "For one who is entering, the vicinity (upacāra) is from the foot-washing stone up to the bed or bench; for one who is going out, it is from the bed or bench up to the place of urination." Therefore, the reading found in some books—"for one who enters having washed the feet, and for one who goes out for the purpose of urinating, from the foot-washing stone placed at the door, and from the place of urination up to the bed or bench"—is a corrupted reading. Why? Because the vicinity of the beds and benches has been stated. The Teacher says that one should only accept the kind of reading that accords with this meaning: "For one who is entering, the vicinity is up to the beds and benches; for one who is going out, it is from there up to the place of urination, the place of defecation, and the cloister walk."

"Setting aside the vicinity (upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā)" means setting aside the vicinity mentioned in this training rule. It is written: "Even in the vicinity of sight and hearing, for one who spreads [the bedding]."

"Up to the doorpost (yāva dvārakoasā)" means from near the door "up to the wall (yāva bhittī)"; that statement is well-said. "The size of the width of the door-leaf (kavāṭavitthārappamāṇo)" means that because a forearm's length (hatthapāsa) is required, and because the vicinity (upacāra) measuring the width of the door-leaf all around is taken, it may also be an incomplete vicinity. However, the ancient teachers (porāṇā) say: "It is proper to determine three courses even at the first time; from the fourth course onwards, there is an offense of pācittiya; from the fourth plastering onwards, there is an offense." ## 1. Ovāda Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

"Kathanusārena" means that a monk who wishes to exhort bhikkhunīs asks and speaks in the order of conversation, such as "What is her virtue? What is her conduct? "Atthato" means by way of the meaning of the Pali. "Kāraṇato" means by way of logical reason, implying the meaning derived from the Commentary. Alternatively, "kāraṇato" means by way of the Dhamma (Pali), thus it means by way of meaning (atthato) and by way of Dhamma (dhammato). Alternatively, "atthato" means by way of the fruit (phala), and "kāraṇato" means by way of the cause (hetu). The Dhammapada is also written together with the Jātaka. "Pañhaṃ kathetunti" means in the context of "when a question is asked, he answers," one cannot remain without answering "I do not know" when asked by a bhikkhunī. There is a reading "na kho pana taṃ bhagavantaṃ." Some write "na kho panetaṃ," but that is not good. According to the phrase "kāsāyavatthavasanāya," it is not appropriate even for a bhikkhunī who has committed a Pārājika. Only physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggā) with a bhikkhunī is mentioned. By committing sexual intercourse, however, one becomes a defiler of bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunīdūsaka).

148-149. "Upasampannā" (ordained) in the presence of monks refers to those who have changed gender (parivattaliṅga) or the five hundred Sakyan ladies. By the term "bhikkhunī," however, "mātugāma" is included only in the Tiriyantaraṇa Sikkhāpada (Pācittiya 187-190) and not elsewhere. 305: The meaning is... "Osāretabba" is the Pāḷi of the Commentary. If one asks, "Since there is no fault in paying respects in one place, is it allowable if only one among many bhikkhunīs pays respects?", it is not allowable because there is no duty to be performed by the monks; it must be performed only by the bhikkhunī. "Sitting in any place" is said to refer to a bhikkhunī sitting within twelve cubits (hattha). The meaning is that monks who wish to go because they were invited are not intended here; only those who wish to enter the rains-retreat (vassa) are intended. "Yato pana" means from the bhikkhunīs' monastery. "Tattha" means in the bhikkhunīs' monastery. Although it is said that "because of the phrase 'monks who give exhortation', a residence with monks is only one with monks who give exhortation, and not with all monks," nevertheless, when there is no monk to give exhortation, one must definitely go to request for the sake of exhortation and communal living (saṃvāsa); therefore, a residence with other monks should also be known as a residence with monks. "That [rains-retreat] should be protected" means the offense of breaking the rains-retreat (vassaccheda) should be guarded against. Why? It is said starting with "In times of danger," etc. Although it is said, "One should ask if this Uposatha is the 14th day," such a question should be asked only on the 13th day. Nowadays, however, bhikkhunīs go only on the 14th day and ask, "Venerable sirs, when is the Uposatha?" It is said that this was spoken with the meaning of "wives or mistresses (jāriyo)". There is a reading "If one goes, there is an offense (gaccheyya ce, āpatti)". "Two or three" refers to two or three bhikkhunīs. The meaning is that the plural "they" (tāhi) is used because they come together. The detail of the statement "One bhikkhunī or many bhikkhunīs are sent from many bhikkhunī residences for the sake of exhortation" is stated starting with "The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and the noble bhikkhunīs," etc. It is written that "The Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and the noble bhikkhunīs," etc., is the speech of a bhikkhunī sent from various residences, and "Approaching five times is stated by way of the speech of an incomplete Saṅgha, an individual, various residences, and a companion bhikkhunī." In a residence where the recitation of the Pātimokkha does not take place, the monk who accepted the request should say on the following day, "There is not even one monk authorized (sammata) to give exhortation," and so forth. If there is an authorized monk, he should be pointed out. If he himself is the authorized monk, it is said that he should say, "It is I." If either the authorized monk or the one who accepted the exhortation recites the Pātimokkha, some say another person should inform [the bhikkhunīs]; others say it is allowable to inform them oneself. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, it is written "Invites the noble ones (ayyanam pavareti)"; if so, it should be said "I invite the noble one (ayyassa pavaremi)", but it is not in the manuscript. ## The Explanation of the Ovāda Training Rule is finished.
306:
## 2. Atthangata-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

The word 'munāti' should be understood to mean 'jānāti' (he knows). In the phrase 'antaradhāyatipi,' if there be a power more excellent than that, I shall see it. Whatever wonderful miracle there is, I shall also see that miracle which has such wonderful benefit. Truly, having performed that cause at that moment, immediately following the action, the individual performances occur. Having directed those miracles with the mind to whatever place is desired, the twin miracles also occur.

Look at the Blessed One, named the Arahant, who is as beautiful as a lotus that has risen from the water and stands in the morning. Indeed, not only like a lotus, but look at the radiant Blessed One, named the Arahant, who is as beautiful as the sun shining brightly in the sky—this is how the connection is made. Alternatively, look at the Blessed One, named the Arahant, as beautiful as a lotus; look at the Blessed One, named the Arahant, as radiant as the sun. Just as one sees a Kokanuda lotus, fully bloomed in the morning with unceasing fragrance, so look at the Blessed One named Angīrasa who is similarly beautiful. Since the Buddha's lovable virtues are shown through both metaphors, how could one worship that beautiful Buddha who possesses such demonstrated virtues? One should note that it should be surpassed even by special intention of worship or special objects of offering. The Pali text has 'Ekatō upasampannāya.' The Commentary version has 'Ekatō upasampannānaṃ.'

It appears that there is no offense for a monk who, out of compassion, expels a co-resident (saddhivihārika) from a communal monastery (saṅghika vihāra) by saying 'You are unfit,' etc. Indeed, it is not fitting for the Elder Mahāpanthaka to intentionally expel him [Cūḷapanthaka]. Some teachers say that in this matter, a suitable logic must be sought. My opinion is that the Elder Mahāpanthaka did this before the training rule was laid down.

## Atthangata-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā is finished.

## 3. Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Because of the statement 'They stay even for one night,' some say that it is allowable to go and exhort in a place where they do not stay at night. If that is so, it is established that it is allowable to go to a designated place to exhort. It should not be said that 'A residence with monks must be sought only within half a league.' If the exhorter of Bhikkhunīs wishes to go half a league to exhort, and the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha wishes to go half a league to listen, it should be said 'it is allowable.' Since that is not said, it is not allowable. However, by the lower limit, it is said 'even for one night.' From that one night's stay onwards, it is called a residence (upassaya). It means it does not become so merely by the appearance of a residence. Where
307:
Bhikkhunīs who have entered the rainy season stay, that place reaches the designation of a Bhikkhunī residence. One should not go to that residence to give exhortation. Some teachers say that it is allowable during the day in the same residence. Having investigated, one should accept what is most appropriate.

## Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā is finished.

## 4. Āmisa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā

Because of the Pali statement 'One ordained but not authorized by the Saṅgha,' and the Commentary statement 'Placed in charge by an authorized person or by the Saṅgha,' it is established that a person endowed with the eight qualities who is either authorized, or requested by one who wishes to be away, saying 'Until I return, let this burden be yours,' or if no such monk exists, a monk similarly placed in charge by the Saṅgha, is allowed to exhort with the eight Garudhammas (Heavy Rules), let alone with other teachings. It should be understood that this Pali text, 'If a monk not authorized by the Saṅgha exhorts Bhikkhunīs, it is a Pācittiya,' refers to a monk who was not previously placed in charge.

The view of the monks residing in the Abhayagiri Monastery is also the same. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, this method is rejected, stating, 'Currently, an exhorter who is not authorized is called an unauthorized Bhikkhunovādaka,' and it says, 'In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated: "Even if not authorized by the Saṅgha through a formal act (kammavācā), if the Bhikkhu Saṅgha requests, 'Please support the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, exhort the Bhikkhunīs, and provide comfort for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha,' and the Elder, having thus been requested and having informed the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, exhorts the Bhikkhunīs—such a monk is called one not authorized by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. The meaning should be taken according to the method stated there."' 

In the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, it is stated: 'An unauthorized monk who, hearing the words of Bhikkhunīs who have come to the village for the sake of exhortation, gives a reply with the consent of the Saṅgha (is considered authorized), but not by a formal motion with three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kammavācā).' This statement agrees with the view of the Anugaṇṭhipada. The statement in the Andhaka Commentary also agrees with that Gaṇṭhi statement. And that is indeed the Pali statement. In truth, one who receives the exhortation or recites the Pātimokkha does not become a Bhikkhunovādaka merely by saying 'May you fulfill it gracefully.' If it were so, even an unordained person (anupasampanna) should be called a 'Bhikkhunovādaka' by such words. If it were so, it is said in the Gaṇṭhipada and Anugaṇṭhipada: 'What is called an unauthorized person is, in the state of being unauthorized, "You are one of great learning..."'
308:
“Exhort” means a person who has been placed in charge by the Saṅgha. What is the benefit of great learning (bāhusacca) in this context? In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: “Having heard that a teacher living at Abhayagiri said so, the Elder Dhammasiri later acknowledged that one who is appointed (sammata) or commanded (āṇatta) by the Saṅgha receives the right to exhort.”

Why speak so much? By merely saying these words, “May you fulfill it in a pleasing manner,” one becomes an exhorter of bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovādaka). What is the benefit of the phrase “having placed in charge” in the Commentary? No one else is allowed to say even that much. If that were the case, it would contradict this Cūḷavagga Pali: “Monks, I allow you to receive exhortation from those remaining, except for the foolish, the sick, and those on a journey.”

How so? According to the words, “Monks, it is not that exhortation should not be brought back,” since there is no one who is either appointed or unappointed, one should say, “May you fulfill it in a pleasing manner.” One who says this would be made to undergo an offense according to the first training rule in this Dispensation. Let it be so, because of not being appointed and not being placed in charge. In this monk's status as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) would be incurred due to criticizing this monk. All these are undesirable things. Therefore, because it is not stated in the Commentary that “in this Dispensation, such a person is called an exhorter of bhikkhunīs,” the Teacher said that only a person so placed in charge by the Saṅgha receives the right to exhort, and no one else.

## The Explanation of the Āmisa Training Rule is finished.

“Will you accept?” is a question.

## The Explanation of the Cīvaradāna Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Cīvarasibbana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

“By deceiving” means not saying “for your relative bhikkhunī” but saying only this much: “for a bhikkhunī.” Having heard the words “for a (certain) bhikkhunī,” they sewed it thinking it belonged to a non-relative. In this training rule, “robe” means...
309:
“One of the six robes” — only this much is the Pali text. Therefore, it is said: “A robe is a garment to be worn or to be draped,” and so on. The writing “the last one suitable for assignment (vikappanūpagaṃ pacchimaṃ)” is merely a clerical error (pamādalekha).

## The Explanation of the Cīvarasibbana Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Saṃvidhāna Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

The meaning should be changed to “They corrupted those bhikkhunīs.”

182-4. “Sampadanti” means they go on foot. “In the same manner as stated” refers to the previously mentioned method, such as “It is called sampāta because they fall together in this place.” In walking on foot, the village precinct (upacāra) is not obtained; because it is very close, it is as if they are mixed. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is defined by the distance at which a cock's crow can be heard. It is written: “That word is also appropriate in common usage.” It is also said: “The Commentary states so because they are generally situated nearby; therefore, it is not a clerical error,” and “The Commentary speaks in terms of the maximum limit; if it exceeds that, it should be understood as possessing the characteristic of half a league (addhayojana).” It is said: “This place is a suitable ground... they do not say.” Here, the reason is difficult to see. What is that reason? It is said: “If they arrange, saying ‘Let's go,’ an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) is incurred.” There, the word “gacchāma” (let's go) is a word showing the present tense, and it is not possible in places like a bhikkhunīs' quarters which are not on the main road, because people travel by taking shortcuts through the village, and because it is a place where high couches (uccāsayana) and such arise. Or, it is not possible because the dwelling of heretics is the dwelling of those who have gone forth. The word “dvāre” (at the gate) is in the locative case (sattamī vibhatti) expressing proximity; therefore, to make that meaning clear, it is said again “rathikāya” (on the street). In the other commentaries, it does not agree because it says: “Even if they arrange in this interval, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) is incurred for the monk.” Because of the word “gāmantare” (between villages), the offense is incurred only upon entering the precinct of another village. Because of the word “addhayojane” (at half a league), it is appropriate that the offense occurs only upon exceeding it.

“Raṭṭhabhede” occurs in the sense of destruction (vilopa). In the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, it is said: “There are three kinds of agreements (saṅketa) by way of time, day, and route; therein, the offense is incurred only because of the last one, the route agreement.” The meaning is that if they arrange, saying “We will go by this route,” and then go by another route, an offense is indeed incurred.

## The Explanation of the Saṃvidhāna Training Rule is finished.
310:
## 8. Navābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
If it is asked, "Where is the interval between villages in a river?", the commentator said, "Yassā nadiyā," and so on. "By counting the interval between villages" means that when arriving at a village landing-place, excluding that landing-place and counting another village (is the basis for an offense). "In this training rule, mātugāma (woman) is also included" is the teacher's reasoning (takka). For that very reason, it was not stated, "When both attain higher ordination at the same time, there is an offense of dukkaṭa; there is no offense for sikkhamānās and sāmaṇerīs." This same method applies to other such training rules.

Because it is said, "Having made an arrangement with the aim of playing through intimacy with worldly gains," should an unwholesome mind be called lokavajja (a worldly fault)? It should not be so called. The phrase "with the aim of playing" is mostly said with a specific intention. In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is also said, "Three minds, three feelings." Alternatively, at the time of making an arrangement, the monk who aims at playing makes the arrangement. An offense occurs for the monk when entering the interval between villages or when exceeding half a league. When traveling while reflecting or when traveling while seeing a cetiya, etc., there is a wholesome mind. When sleeping due to exhaustion, there is an indeterminate mind (abyākata-citta). Thus, it should be understood that the three minds are taken.

## Navābhiruhanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.

## 9. Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
Ceṭaka refers to boys. Ancient teachers say they are young boys. "This training rule is prescribed to cut off the association of bad monks; therefore, it is written that an offense occurs only regarding the five kinds of staple food."

194-7. "Caused to be prepared" means it is not through requesting, but through roundabout talk (parikathā), etc. Therefore, there is no offense by this training rule. With reference to that lack of offense, it is said, "There is no offense in all places." Elder Dhammasiri said, "According to the sequence of the conversation, that person gives with faith; this is not food prepared by a bhikkhunī (paripācita), it is allowable," because it was said in the first training rule. However, Elder Upatissa said, "Other material food is also certainly allowable." In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is said, "Devadatta naturally eats alms-food prepared by a bhikkhunī there; therefore, this training rule was prescribed based on this incident (atthuppatti)."

## Paripācitasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.
311:
## 10. Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
There is the text: "Upanandassa catuttha-sikkhāpadena ca."

## Rahonisajjasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.

## The third chapter, the Ovāda-vagga, explained in order, is finished.

## 4. Bhojana-vagga

## 1. Āvasathapiṇḍasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
203-4. "Pūgassa" means by a group. "Kukkuccāyanto" (being scrupulous) is said because of making a decision that "there must be a way out (from the offense) here, but we do not know that way." Just as the Venerable Upāli, by grasping the method, said, "Friends, there is no offense because of a dream," why does the Elder (Ven. Sāriputta) not decide definitively, "There is no offense for one who is ill"? It is because the Vinaya prescription was not his own authority, because it was rejected as "this is not one's own opportunity," and because the training rule was not yet complete. For only after the first Pārājika training rule was fully prescribed did that Elder say, "There is no offense because of a dream," following the phrase "except for a dream" that had been stated. Because there is no harassment of the donors when consuming as much as desired without specifically designating them, it is said, "unspecified, as much as desired" (anodissa yāvadattho).

"One day in the middle of the journey" is said with reference to only one time; and "In this same way" is said to show the method already mentioned, starting with "one who goes and returns"; and "Being of pure mind, one is allowed to eat only when traveling normally"; and "It occurs through the body of a monk who is not ill but perceives himself as ill"—so it is written.

## Āvasathapiṇḍasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā is finished.

## 2. Gaṇabhojanasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
209-218. "Guḷhapaṭicchanno" means simply unmanifest. "Eko puttena" means for a single monk, regarding a single meal, it is not said, "I am invited by another." If together...
312:
Because it is stated (in the Pācittiya Commentary) that "they accept; it is a group meal (gaṇabhojana)," some teachers say that if four lay devotees invite four monks separately and offer to the monks standing within reach (hatthapāsa), such an offering also constitutes a group meal. This statement seems inappropriate. It is written: "If one accepts food arising from solicitation (viññatti) together as a group, there is an offense by this training rule; if accepted separately, however, there is an offense by the training rules on soliciting superior food (paṇītabhojana-viññatti) and curry and rice (supodana-viññatti)." The statement "Food arising from solicitation is permitted in the Commentary according to the incident (aṭṭhuppatti). There is an offense in that food arising from solicitation only by way of curry, rice, etc." is inappropriate. Why? Because both modes appear in the Parivāra itself. Therefore, the statement in the Commentary that "it is permitted" is poorly stated. Since it is clear only in the origin of the incident (aṭṭhuppatti), it should be said that "it is not mentioned in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana)."

"They accept together" means that even after receiving the food, if they wait until others have received it, such waiting is called accepting together. They say, "If they leave (without waiting), there is no offense."

In this context, it is said that "acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) alone is the standard in this training rule." If so, why is it stated in the Pali, "What is called a group meal is where four monks... eat; this is called a group meal"? The answer is: the locative case in "yattha" (in which place) is used in the sense of the accusative (upayogattha). "Cattāro" (four) is to show the lower limit of a group. "Pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ" (of the five types of food) is to show the food sufficient for an offense. "Aññatarena bhojanena nimantitā" (invited with one or another of the foods) is to show an invitation made in an improper way.

Since a group meal is spoken of only by way of invitation, it is said, "being invited, they eat." It is not said, "having solicited one or another of the foods, they eat," because this is clear in the origin of the incident (aṭṭhuppatti) itself. It should be understood by connecting it as "the food which they eat." In that Pali, the word "they eat" is a term that defines the acceptance. This is because monks do not eat food that has not been formally accepted. The meaning is: "A pācittiya offense is incurred because of consuming nutriment that has been accepted as a group."

They sew the hem (anuvāta) with a basting thread (moghasutta) and set it down. They rub it with their hands so that it becomes level at the hem of that robe. "Vaḷeti" means to roll (āvaṭṭeti). "Parivattanaṃ" means they turn the thread (suttaparivattana) to make it easy for those handling the thread to grasp, and they also turn the layer (paṭṭaparivattana) to make it easy for those sewing the layer to sew. In this robe-season, only one who is making a new robe is intended, not any other (one repairing an old robe). They say, "While the materials were being prepared after asking permission from King Bimbisāra, time passed; later, when the training rule on group meals was promulgated, he approached the Blessed One and inquired." Otherwise, it would contradict the Commentary.
313:
"Two or three together" means that by the opening statement "even those who consent to an improper invitation," it is shown that there is no offense due to an improper invitation, but there is an offense only due to solicitation (viññatti). When an uninvited monk is the fourth in that meal, that meal is called "animantita-catuttha" (a meal with an uninvited fourth). This method is the same in all groups of four. "Pavesetvā" means having seated them (arranging their seats). They obtain the group of four received during the time of robe-giving, the group of four received during the time of robe-making, and so on. "Tāni ca" refers to those foods for which there is no breach of agreement (visaṅketa). "Mahāthere" refers to one who has attained higher ordination (upasampanna). "Aṭṭhatvā" means showing a sign while standing. "Tattha tattha gantvā" means going near the monk in places such as the main road. In this training rule, in some manuscripts, the reading appears as: "Bhikkhus, I allow you to eat a group meal during the time of robe-giving. Thus was this [allowed] by the Blessed One to the monks." In some, after saying "to eat," the reading is: "And thus, bhikkhus, should you recite this training rule." This latter reading is better.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Group Meals is Finished.

## 3. Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

"Adhiṭṭhitā" refers to a meal that is constantly provided. "Badarasāḷavaṃ" is jujube jam prepared with jujube powder, sugar, etc. "Kirakammakārena" means by the worker of the householder named Kira.

Regarding the statement "Take it after performing assignment (vikappanā)," the ancient elders said: Without performing vikappanā in the presence of the Blessed One, one leaves the monastery and performs vikappanā in the presence of another monk on the street. The monk performing vikappanā should say, "I give my expectation of a meal to such-and-named person for assignment." The monk receiving the assignment should say, "Either consume what belongs to him, or do as is appropriate." Regarding "among the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika)," some say that if one wishes to perform vikappanā to a co-religionist who was in one's presence but cannot find that co-religionist, one should eat after saying either in the presence of a householder or by oneself, "Among the five classes of co-religionists, I assign this to such-and-named person." If this is so, the thought appears that Elder Ānanda, while sitting in that very place, uttered such words and accepted the gift. In the Mahāpaccari and other commentaries, however, only assignment in the absence (parammukhā vikappanā) is mentioned. That statement agrees with this: "Ānanda, if so, take it after performing assignment." Even though it so agrees, because it is said in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, "Therefore, whichever monk performs assignment, or performs assignment in the absence thus," only in the presence of a co-religionist...
314:
Among the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika), it is seen that [the assignment] should be spoken only in the presence of a co-religionist, not by oneself, because of the statement: "I give my expectation of a meal to you" or "I assign it to you"—thus in the presence; or "I give it to such-and-named person" or "I assign it to him"—thus in the absence. Since this latter method also agrees with the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada, the meaning in this matter should be understood according to the sequence of the Mātikāṭṭhakathā.

In this matter of invitation, although an improper invitation (akappiya-nimantana) is evident from the words "Those people... gave food," it should be understood that the Elder was invited with food because of the arising of remorse (kukkucca). Otherwise, it would contradict the later statement "He eats two or three invitations together" and the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra).

There is this investigation (vicāraṇā) here: Because of the statement "Another person takes the bowl, it should not be given," there is no benefit from an improper invitation in the later part, but only in the earlier part. Therefore, in the words "Venerable sir, please come tomorrow as well," which is the improper invitation? Thus, intention (adhippāya) is the standard (pamāṇa) here. It is not so; it is because of the statement "He eats food obtained by wandering for alms, there is an offense."

In that commentary, just as the meaning is taken according to the sequence of improper invitation without taking the mere words "Venerable sir, tomorrow as well," so too in the words "wandering for alms," the meaning should be taken as referring to food obtained through an intervening improper invitation. Indeed, food given by someone who, seeing a monk wandering for alms, says "Venerable sir, take food here," is also called food obtained by improper invitation. In common usage, however, it is called "food obtained by wandering for alms"; thus the completeness of the illustration should be understood.

Otherwise, it would contradict the statement in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: "By the method stated in the gaṇabhojana section, for one invited to the five kinds of food... in the food of subsequent donors." This statement explains the meaning as: having taken the first invited food from the one who first invited him, [eating] in the food of subsequent donors who invited and gave. Thus, it shows that an offense is incurred only by eating food obtained from an invitation. It also agrees with the statement "two or three invitations together." Otherwise, it should only have been said "in the food of a person subsequent to the food of the one by whom he was invited," or in the Pali, it should only have been said "he eats together by invitation." To prevent the contingency of an offense in the first food of a second invitation, "by whomsoever" etc., was said. If it is asked, "Is there not a Pali text saying he eats according to the order of invitation?" No, because it would contradict the Pali such as "no offense in permanent food (niccabhatta)."
315:
In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is written: "If it is asked why one does not get to eat food obtained by wandering for alms, it is because it is said: 'What is called paramparabhojana (out-of-turn eating) is when one is invited to one of the five kinds of food, and setting aside that food, one eats another of the five kinds of food; this is called paramparabhojana.'" If that were so, it would follow that permanent food (niccabhatta) etc., would also not be allowable. If it is said that permanent food etc., are designated (odissaka) food, that is not so. For it would lead to the contingency of unallowability for food other than that, such as food produced by one's own property, food received from the Sangha, or if the gruel cooked in the morning is thick, and also for permanent food to be obtained by way of alms-gathering for one residing depending on a village of only one house.

If it is said that among those, food obtained by alms-gathering is not allowable because it brings about lack of faith (appasāda) in the donors who invited, it is not so. Because it would be a contradiction of the statement: "Except for the five kinds of food, there is no offense in all places." Even if one eats the snacks (khādanīya) of another and does not eat the invited food, one certainly causes lack of faith. Therefore, bringing about lack of faith is not the standard. Thus, permanent food etc., cannot be designated (odissaka). Furthermore, some teachers' decision is that one should compare the method stated above with the method stated here and accept whichever decision is suitable. The teacher's own decision will become clear at the end. It is said: "The intention is that it is unmixed even for one drinking milk or juice." In the Gaṇṭhipada, it is written: "It stands above without being mixed with the boiled rice below."

"Great Lay Devotee" (Mahā-upāsaka) means the master of the house. The statement "there is an offense" in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā and the statement "it is allowable" in the Kurundī seem to be contradictory. It is written: "The intention of both was investigated in the Mahāpaccari." It is said: "Cārittato (by custom) is because of the Cāritta-sikkhāpada to be mentioned later: 'without asking a monk who is present.'" One should not specifically deliberate on the verbal act (vacīkamma).

In this matter, because it is said in the Commentary: "A great lay devotee invites monks... there is an offense for one who eats food obtained later. If he eats food obtained by wandering for alms, there is an offense"; and because of the Pali: "We have already eaten by wandering for alms early in the morning"; and because it is said in the Khandhaka: "Monks, except for an invitation, the food or gruel of another is not to be consumed; whoever should consume it, is to be dealt with according to the rule" (Mahāvagga 283); therefore, whether having invited or having informed without inviting, for a monk who has accepted a first invitation, any food belonging to another other than the first invited food causes an offense of paramparabhojana. Food belonging to oneself, or food received from the Sangha or a group which does not belong to a householder, is allowable. However, because they are permanently fixed prior to the invitation, permanent food (niccabhatta) etc., are allowable even if they belong to another.
316:
## Explanation of the Paramparabhojana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Kāṇamātā Sikkhāpada
31-3. 'Paṭiyāloka' means the western region. 'Pūvagaṇanāya' means by the count of excess cakes. If one accepts with the thought 'it is prepared for journey provisions, etc.', an offense is incurred even if there is no intention (acittaka) [due to mistake]. If one accepts an item whose consecration is lost (uggahita), one is certainly not free from offense. However, in the case of non-distribution, there is no offense because it is unallowable. Some teachers say that being 'acittaka' (without intention) occurs only through not knowing the regulation, not through not knowing the object. This statement should not be accepted because in the Mātikā Commentary, 'knowing that it is prepared for journey provisions, etc.' is not mentioned among the factors.

In the old Gaṇṭhipada, it is said: 'If a single monk or many monks have accepted cakes to fill two or three bowls, and then accept other cakes without informing those monks or knowing it themselves, that monk incurs a dukkaṭa offense. When three or four monks enter together, if one monk accepts cakes to fill two bowls, and while the second is accepting, the first does not forbid him, the first monk incurs a pācittiya offense. If he forbids him, there is no offense, and only the second monk incurs a dukkaṭa offense.' If one knows but does not speak, according to the method of the old Gaṇṭhipada, it is a pācittiya; according to the Mātikā Commentary, it is a dukkaṭa offense. In that Mātikā Commentary, 'accepting in excess' is stated as the fifth factor; therefore, because one does not accept in excess, there is no pācittiya, but a dukkaṭa is incurred for not doing what should be done. Otherwise, this training rule would fall into the category of 'action and non-action' (kiriyākirya), and 'not forbidding' or 'not informing' would have to be stated as a sixth factor.

Regarding 'monks of a single Nikāya': 'If monks living in a nearby monastery or monks who have come to the rest house know that if they do not accept the cakes brought by unrelated persons (visabhāga), they will give them only to the monastery attendants (ārāmika), etc., then it is allowable to give to those who will consume them.' Some who consider themselves experts in Vinaya (Vinayadhara) say that because of the phrase 'two or three bowlfuls of cakes,' there is no offense even if one takes in excess in baskets (pacchi), etc. Let that statement remain only with them (it is not to be accepted). Teachers, however, say: 'Even in baskets, etc., one should take only two or three bowlfuls according to the measure of the best bowl. This is a statement defining the maximum limit.'
