## 5. Explanation of the First Pavāraṇā Sikkhāpada

Although one invited by 'yāvadatthapavāraṇā' (invitation as much as desired) can be called 'pavāritā' (one who has finished eating) by way of the origin of the story (atthuppatti), in this context, only the final (pacchima) pavāraṇā is intended. Because it is said 'this is enough of all,' it is called 'atiritta' (leftover). For the monk, it means: 'This alms-food is also in excess for you; you will not get any alms-food other than this.'

238-9. By the phrase 'asanaṃ paññāyati' (food is evident) itself, the meaning of the word 'bhuttāvī' (having eaten) is accomplished; thus there is no separate accomplishment of meaning. If there were, it would lead to showing six factors. This statement also shows that there are five factors of pavāraṇā. 'Varaka' means any kind of bean or grain. Making clear water by separating rice grains does not constitute pavāraṇā. If a monk drinking gruel (yāgu) drinks the water first, it is allowable. It is written that the rice grains remaining at the bottom do not constitute pavāraṇā. Elder Upatissa says, 'It certainly constitutes pavāraṇā,' but the teachers do not accept that. 'Bhajjitapiṭṭha' is simply rice flour. A 'sattumodaka' is a cake made by combining roasted cakes.

Because it is said 'if one rejects... even two grains of rice in gruel, it does not constitute pavāraṇā,' Elder Dhammasiri said that if one is drinking mixed gruel containing 'paracaṅkama' etc., and rejects other such gruel, pavāraṇā does not occur. If one rejects something else, it is not pavārita. Why? Because there is no unfinished meal known as eating. If a monk eating in the refectory rejects a portion brought forward that has not yet reached him, it is not pavārita. Indeed, even if he rejects it, if the monastery attendant (ārāmika) pours it into the bowl, it is not allowable to eat that poured alms-food. This falls under improper seeking (anesanā) which is censured by the Buddha. For example, just as if a person of bad conduct gives alms-food taken from the Saṅgha's portion and one rejects it, it is not pavārita; this is similar to that example. Other teachers say: 'If a shameful person (lajjī) of a different practice gives, and one rejects it because of not wanting to share (sambhoga) with him, it is pavārita.'

'Parivesanāya' means in the refectory (bhattagga). Because 'māṃsarasa' applies to meat and juice, or meat and juice together, pavāraṇā occurs upon rejection when 'māṃsarasa' is mentioned. The analysis (viggaha) as 'juice of meat' is not intended.

'Māṃsakarambaka' means... it is allowable, meaning it is only pure gruel. Because it is only 'karambaka' mixed with food that does not suffice for pavāraṇā (appavāraṇa), it is not pavārita. Therefore, it is said later: 'This should not be compared with karambaka,' etc. Therefore, that...
318:
It is said: 'Even if one refuses when [porridge] is brought forward and it is said, "Take the rice porridge," it does not constitute a formal refusal (pavāraṇā).' This is because it was not said, 'Take the mixed porridge,' and because it was said, 'He gives the mixed food after separating it.' Since in these two words 'mixed with porridge' (yāgu-missaka), there is no mention of the name of the food that warrants pavāraṇā, therefore, in that mixture of porridge, whether the porridge is more or equal, it does not constitute pavāraṇā. Why? Because in that case, both the one who brings it and the one who refuses it perceive it as porridge. If the porridge is little and the boiled rice (bhatta) is more, it constitutes pavāraṇā. Why? Because both of them have a different perception (that it is food other than porridge) in that case—this is the teacher's opinion. In the case of being mixed with boiled rice, since the name of the food that warrants pavāraṇā is evident, it always constitutes pavāraṇā. In the case of a mixture, the reason should be stated according to the method mentioned. 'Giving after separating' means squeezing and filtering firmly with the hand so that the grains of rice do not fall.

Regarding 'made by one who is not allowable' (akappiyakata): 'Even if one has the remnant (atiritta) made together with bananas and such that have not yet been made allowable (kappiya), it is proper to set aside those bananas and eat the remaining food.' It is said that because the juices are not mixed, it is proper to have those bananas made allowable again, place them in another vessel, make them a remnant (atiritta), and eat them. Why? Because the disciplinary act (vinayakamma) has not yet been applied to those objects previously. From the statement, 'It is performed by one who has finished eating, has refused further food (pavārita), and has risen from his seat,' it is established that it should be performed by a monk who is still eating, has not yet refused further food, and has risen from his seat. Therefore, it is said: 'Of two monks traveling early in the morning, one has refused further food and remains sitting there without rising; the other monk, his companion, having gone for alms and received food, even if he has not yet eaten it himself, is allowed to make it a remnant (atiritta) by saying, "This is all enough."' This statement is established by the phrase in the 'bright side' (sukkapakkha): 'It is performed by one who has finished eating.' In that case, his seven factors (sattaṅgāni) are not complete. It should be understood that the seven factors are mentioned similarly in the 'dark side' (kaṇhapakkha). If it is performed by a monk who has finished eating, has not refused further food, whether he has risen from his seat or not, it is proper. To show this specific meaning, 'only by a monk who has refused further food and has not risen from his seat,' it is also proper to say, 'the seven factors are mentioned.' That monk is not allowed to perform it again, because it would follow that the disciplinary act already performed must be performed again by the same person. For it is said that only what has not been performed should be performed. If that first person wishes to perform it again, he is allowed to perform it on an object not previously performed in another vessel. The second monk is allowed to perform it even in the first vessel. For it is said, 'It should be performed by the one who has not performed it.' Referring to this very meaning: 'The object which a person has first made allowable (kappiya), that same person is not allowed to perform it again; another person...'
319:
...should perform it.' This is what is written. In that text, 'that' (taṃ) refers to the object upon which the disciplinary act was first performed. Regarding 'should have it performed by sending [someone]': if an unordained person (anupasampanna) has gone, one should have it received by one monk present there and have it performed by another. Therefore, it should be understood that a single monk is not allowed to perform it in this way. Because of the words, 'Whatever is intended for the sick,' etc., the portion due to a sick monk in monasteries and such is also called 'remnant for the sick' (gilānātiritta); therefore, it is proper—so they say. 'For the sake of nutriment' means only at the wrong time (after noon)—so some say.

Bodily action (kāyakamma) occurs because of swallowing. Verbal action (vacīkamma) should be understood as occurring because of not having it performed by saying, 'Venerable sir, please make this a remnant (atiritta).'

## 8. Sannidhikāraka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

Storing up (sannidhi) for the next day is the meaning. "Accepted today" refers not only to what is formally accepted but also to what is taken by oneself (where the formal acceptance is broken). Therefore, in the Commentary, it is stated starting with "He accepts, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)" that for a monk who takes any yāvakālika or yāmakālika that has been stored up, with the desire to swallow it, there is an offense of wrongdoing at the very moment of receiving it. If that kālika had already been formally accepted previously, it should not be said "at the very moment of receiving it." Therefore, it should be understood that "accepted today" means the kālika accepted within one's own proper time.

Here, an objector says: "Just as among the five medicines, those whose acceptance is broken are not intended, and even after seven days have passed, there is no offense because they are not to be swallowed, so too in this Sannidhi training rule, those whose acceptance is broken should not be intended." To this, it is replied: It is appropriate to say that in the Bhesajja training rule, those whose acceptance is broken are not intended. Why? Because in that Bhesajja training rule, one could fall into an offense merely by the passing of one's own time. In this Sannidhi training rule, however, it is not appropriate because there is no falling into an offense merely by the passing of one's own time. The intention is that the offense occurs only through swallowing. Therefore, according to the Anugaṇṭhipada, a monk who takes food today such that the acceptance is broken and eats it the next day commits two offenses.

In this matter, there is this investigation: If one takes food today such that the acceptance is broken with the desire to eat it oneself and eats it the next day, two offenses are committed. A monk who eats food that was taken (with broken acceptance) only for the sake of novices (sāmaṇeras) and the like, by having it formally accepted the next day, should not be punished with an offense (no offense is committed). In the phrase "He accepts, there is an offense of wrongdoing," the meaning is this: Like the Elder Belatthasīsa, if one accepts food today for the sake of the second or third day and gives it to novices etc. to be guarded, and then accepts it again for the sake of swallowing it the next day, it is possible that an offense of wrongdoing occurs. Or, if one guards that food oneself and, seeing dust fallen on it the next day, accepts it again due to doubt, an offense of wrongdoing occurs at the very moment of acceptance. If he does not accept it, there is no such wrongdoing. It is said: "Indeed, this decision is like the decision starting with 'He oversteps with one foot, there is an offense of thullaccaya (grave offense).'" Just as for a monk who oversteps with both feet at once, there is no such thullaccaya offense, so too this decision should be understood in the same way. Here, only for a monk who does not relinquish the state of having accepted...
322:
Although Elder Dhammasiri says (it causes sannidhi only for a monk who does not relinquish the state of having received it), this statement contradicts the Pāḷi which says, "If he accepts it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa." The oily residue of oil drunk from a bowl is merely negligible (abbhohārika). Even if the oily residue flows from the bowl because it was placed in the sun, it is said to be just as stated in the Bhesajja Sikkhāpada. Otherwise, there would be the fault that ghee and so forth drunk from a bowl would cause an offense when seven days have passed.

In this phrase "having accepted it himself," it is also according to the procedure mentioned previously. The statement regarding the bowl used for washing milk also seems to agree with this method. The phrase "for the purpose of food" can also be used in the morning. "Natural food (pakati-āmisa)" means allowable food. Regarding the statement that two offenses are incurred by a monk who swallows with a mouth containing food: "Two pācittiya offenses are incurred by a monk who, in the morning today, swallows yāmakālika accepted yesterday along with food in the mouth," so it is written. Even yāvakālika accepted today, if mixed with a drink that has passed its time (yāma), causes sannidhi (storing up). Among unallowable meats, if it is human flesh, a thullaccaya offense is incurred; if it is other [unallowable] meats, the dukkaṭa offense increases.

Some teachers say that even if one consumes sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika in the morning for the purpose of food, only a dukkaṭa offense is incurred because it does not reach the offense of sannidhi. If it is asked, "Is it allowable if one consumes a thing accepted on that day in the morning of that same day?", the answer is "It is not allowable." This is because there is no specific distinction mentioned in either the Pāḷi or the Commentary. If it is asked, "Is it not stated in the Bhesajja Sikkhāpada that one may consume as one pleases in the morning?", the teacher Upatissa says that since ghee and so forth are included in food, it is stated by way of being similar to that food, not by way of medicine.

With a "caruka" (a small ball of rice). In the phrase "even to one who is awake (jāgarantassapi)," it is written that "by the word 'api', even to one who is asleep." "Some (keci)" refers to the monks residing at Abhayagiri. Although it is written, "'By a weapon (satthaka)' means by an accepted weapon," that is a poor writing (dullikhita), because even if there is stain (rust), there is no need to accept it again.

In this context where it says "only the original acceptance is allowable," those teachers who say, "Because it is said to be for the purpose of warding off flies, it is allowable even when accepted and taken for the purpose of not eating," should be told: "If a monk accepts oil for anointing the head and, knowing 'this is oil for anointing the head,' neglects it and lets seven days pass, would it not be a nissaggiya?" and so forth. In the discussion on exchange (parivattanakathā), it is said: "Elder Upatissa said, 'If the thought arises in monks that when our rice is exhausted, we can be supported by these things belonging to the novice that are in our hands, then the exchange is meaningful.'" If that is so, it follows that it is meaningless for those with pure minds. Furthermore, it means that if one has the thought, "This novice is wise; he will perform the exchange of bowls and give it; we ourselves will ask and eat his food out of intimacy," then even if the exchange is made, it is not allowable to eat. What is the use of speaking much?...
324:
If there is the thought, "We shall ask and eat," it implies that it is not allowable to eat even if an exchange has been made; what more needs to be said? The teacher stated this to show that it should be taken only without attachment, and should not be taken if there is attachment. This very meaning is established by the statement: "If, however, one is able to purify the thought (vitakka), then it is allowable to eat what is obtained from that."

Placing the bowl on a stand is a state of being free from attachment (ālayā), just as it was accepted. (Washing, etc.) with unaccepted ocean water. Goat's milk is allowable simply because it is milk. It is stated to show that "there is no offense for a monk who drinks his own milk directly with his mouth." Although it is written that "here, the great elements (mahābhūta) dependent on the body are intended," both of those [statements] contradict the method stated as "allowable meat or milk," and so on.

Furthermore, if one puts one's own alms-food into another monk's unaccepted vessel, and says "it is too little" or for any other reason, it is not allowable for all. Why? Because it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) according to the Vinaya. The meaning is that it is a wrong-doing because one did not follow the Vinaya procedure of accepting it oneself before putting it in. If so, why does one not eat such alms-food? Because it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) that "it becomes handled (ugghitaka)." In the Anu-ganthipada, it is also stated: "Whether on the ground, in a vessel, a fruit, or any other material gift (āmisa), even if it is a life-long (yāvajīvika) item, if one touches it without knowing it is unaccepted, it is not allowable; it becomes handled (ugghitaka)." Therefore, according to this view of the Anu-ganthipada, if a monk places alms-food in another monk's unaccepted bowl, it is established that the alms-food is unallowable (akappiya) and handled (ugghitaka). This meaning should be stated in comparison with the words: "If in one's own or the monks' gruel-cooking vessel... it should be eaten after making it free from material gifts (nirāmisa)." The phrase "allowable meat or milk" is mentioned by way of context. Some teachers, however, say that the obtained curd is intended.

The three: "The act was not removed, the act was poorly removed, the act must not be removed again," are found in the legal question of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa). ## 4. Duṭṭhullasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
If it is asked, "How is it known that Pārājika offenses are shown by way of extracting the meaning?", it is known through the Parivāra Pali. For it is said there: "How many offenses are incurred because of the legal question of offenses? Four offenses are incurred because of the legal question of offenses. If a bhikkhunī knowingly conceals a Pārājika matter, it is a Pārājika offense. If she conceals it while in doubt, it is a Thullaccaya offense. If a bhikkhu conceals a Saṅghādisesa offense, it is a Pācittiya offense. For concealing a misconduct (ācāravipatti)..."

"...if one conceals it, it is a Dukkaṭa offense" (Parivāra 290). If it is said that a bhikkhu who conceals a Pārājika has no offense because it is not mentioned, that is not so. Because concealing with a defiled mind cannot occur without an offense. The Pārājika offenses mentioned in the Dukkaṭa section should be understood as not being repeated because they were already mentioned along with Saṅghādisesas by way of extracting the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "as long as the limit is not broken": even if one informs another for the sake of concealing, or does not inform, one incurs an offense by the mind of concealing alone. For that monk, the limit is not broken simply by not informing another for the sake of concealing. What benefit would there be in returning and speaking? The limit is not broken by not informing the last monk; it is broken only by not concealing. Therefore, for the sake of not concealing, one should inform someone who has not heard it before; from that point on, the limit is broken. If such informing does not occur, one should return and inform for the sake of not concealing; even so, the limit is broken—this is how it appears to us, says the teacher. In the phrase "to the second person by the third person," the claim by some that "the second is the first" is not good because it is forbidden to not mention the basis and the person. Informing another fourth person is also not good. Why? Because it was heard from the beginning and not informed to another. They say that by hearing, it should be informed to another.

If it is a thieving caravan and an ordinary woman, two offenses are committed. If they are nuns, the circumstance (samaya) protects them (they are treated the same). Some say that because they are protected by treating the case as a thieving caravan, the fellow-dhamma practitioners (sahadhammikas) are indeed protected. Others say that in the state of being thieves, there is no state of being a fellow-dhamma practitioner; therefore, they are not protected. If it is said that there is the state of being a fellow-dhamma practitioner when there is the state of being an undefeated thief, then in other cases, one falls into other offenses; therefore, because they are not released, one falls into an offense. If a monk is part of a thieving group, it is according to the object. It should also be understood as "having arranged together, being aware that the group is a thieving caravan." In some versions, the word "saddhiṃ" (together) is missing; that absence is inappropriate. It is the same in the second case.

There is also the reading "Tena kho pana samayena aññatarā itthī"; in some versions, it is not there. Some say that its absence is good because of the heading "Tena kho samayena". For these three, the circumstance protects them; this is the distinction between these three and an ordinary woman.

Furthermore, some say that because of the words "viññū paṭibalā" (wise and capable), a nun who is not capable has no grounds for an offense. That statement is not suitable because it is a matter of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). It is said, "The monk arranges, the woman does not arrange; an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is committed." ## 8. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Ariṭṭha

Even for a layman, the act of defiling a nun is an obstruction to liberation (mokkhantarāya, an obstruction to Nibbāna). Therefore, for such a person, even the state of a novice is prohibited. Because of rootless rebirth (ahetu-paṭisandhi), it is an obstruction to the result (vipākantarāyika). "Offenses committed in the past with the intention to transgress while knowing, indeed cause obstruction. Even for a monk who is mindful but thinks he is pure, they indeed cause obstruction." In the phrase "sesā", it means those of the same class (jātikā). In "rasena", it means by nature or function. In "adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhena", it means in the sense of cutting by making a base, in the sense of cutting off wholesome states; thus it is called "like a sword and a butcher's block" (asisūnūpamā). Ancient teachers say it is "like a spear and a spit" (sattisūlūpamā) because of the nature of piercing the mind. In the text on non-offense, the word "ādikammikassa" is written by virtue of oral recitation.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Ariṭṭha is finished.

## 8. Ariṭṭhasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

Even while a layman, the act of violating a nun is indeed an obstacle to liberation (mokkhantarāyika). Therefore, for such a person, even going forth (pabbajjā) is rejected. It is an obstacle to the result (vipākantarāyika) because of being rootless (ahetuka) at rebirth. For a monk who previously committed an offense intentionally, or who committed an offense through forgetfulness, or who committed an offense while perceiving it as pure, those offenses are indeed obstructive. "Sesā" means those of the same kind (jātikā). "Rasena" means by nature. "Adhikuṭṭanaṭṭhena" means in the sense of cutting by making a base. "Asisūnūpamā" (like a sword and a butcher's block) is so called because it cuts off wholesome states (kusaladhamma). "Sattisūlūpamā" (like a spear and a spit) is so called because it pierces the mind; thus say the ancient teachers. In the text on non-offenses (anāpattipāḷi), the word "ādikammikassa" is written by way of oral recitation.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule concerning Ariṭṭha is finished.

## 8. Sahadhammika Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Sahadhammika Training Rule

The Sahadhammika training rule has a clear meaning.

## 2. Commentary on the Vilekhana Training Rule

In the phrase 'āpattiñca satisammosāyā', the word 'ca' indicates that one also does not do what should be done; it means that one does not do only the four things. A part of a country is called a janapada. During the time of the Buddha, the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇṭaka were enemies of the Dispensation (Sāsana). By saying 'it is not able to cause an obstacle', they were indicating the Buddha's lack of omniscience (asabbaññuta). After the Buddha's Parinibbāna, the Vajjiputtaka monks who presented the ten points (dasavatthu) were enemies of the Vinaya Dispensation. Doctrines such as parūpahāra and so forth are enemies of the Sutta and Abhidhamma. Who are they? To show that it is not all but only some, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, the qualifying words 'parūpahārā... pe... vādā' were spoken.

Among those enemies of the Dispensation, those who are deceitful (kuhaka) and of evil desires (pāpiccha) speak of qualities they do not possess, and after eating excellent food obtained thereby, they fall into a lapse of mindfulness and experience an emission of semen while asleep. When others see this and ask, 'Does an Arahant have emissions of semen?', they deceive the people by saying, 'It was brought by the followers of Māra.' Some well-behaved and non-deceitful monks, upon hearing those words, also come to hold that view and develop overestimation (adhimāna). Even when they see their own emission of semen, they are unable to reflect properly and remain with the perception that they have attained what they have not yet attained. Similarly, the meaning should be understood by applying it as far as possible to the idea that an Arahant has ignorance and doubt regarding the Truths, just as they might regarding names, lineages, and so forth, or that dispelling the doubts of others is merely a name designated by others. At that time, a monk who is a master of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara), showing the Sutta passages such as 'Monks, there is no cause, there is no opportunity for an emission of semen to occur in an Arahant...',
336:
"Monks, there is no cause, there is no opportunity for an emission of semen to occur in an Arahant"—this meaning should be understood by applying it as appropriate. Regarding those enemies of the Dispensation, the Vinayadhara monk shows Sutta passages such as "Monks, there is no cause for an emission of semen to occur in an Arahant... even in the present life... without depending on others in the Teacher's Dispensation (he sees for himself)," and thus it means he rebukes what should be rebuked among those enemies of the Dispensation. Other teachers who hold the view that "Learning (pariyatti) is the root" say that the phrase "when the Pātimokkha is being recited" is spoken by way of the introduction (nidāna). The Buddha's Vibhaṅga sections are completed. If they are completed, what are the factors of this training rule? They are: the desire to criticize and the act of criticizing the training rule in the presence of a monk.

## The Commentary on the Vilekhana Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Mohana Training Rule
The Mohana training rule has a clear meaning.

## 4. Commentary on the Pahāra Training Rule
"Rattacitto" means having a mind affected by lust with the desire for bodily contact. If, upon seeing someone one wishes to harass, one thinks, "If I kill this person, there is no way out for me," and becoming angry, one strikes them while maintaining the perception of a living being (sattasaññā), that monk incurs an offense according to the object (the extent of the injury).

## The Commentary on the Pahāra Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Talasattika Training Rule
Because it is said, "either the body or something connected to the body," whichever limb among the limbs of the body one raises [to strike], that limb is called 'tala'. That tala itself is called 'talasattika'. Some teachers say it is called 'sattika' because of its capacity to strike. This talasattika is limited by the phrase "even if it is only a lotus petal." People who are angry in this way, by the power of their anger, do not consider their inability to strike and throw whatever is in their hand. Even if it is something pleasant to the touch, it is still a pācittiya offense. The reason is that if one strikes with the desire to strike, one incurs a pācittiya offense according to the previous training rule. By merely raising [the hand or an object] with the sole desire to raise it, one incurs a pācittiya offense according to this training rule. It is not because of the striking. However, if one does strike, and that act is not due to the desire to strike but happens as a result of the striking [motion], one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. If it is asked whether this dukkaṭa offense is due to the striking or due to the raising, it is only due to the striking that the dukkaṭa offense is incurred.
337:
If done by this training rule, a Pācittiya offense is committed. By this training rule, however, if one misses the target and strikes, it is a Dukkaṭa offense because it was given without the intention to strike (having missed the intended target). If it is asked: "Is this Dukkaṭa due to the strike or due to the raising of the hand?", it is a Dukkaṭa due to the strike only. Since it was said that a Pācittiya offense is committed due to the initial raising of the hand, a Pācittiya along with a Dukkaṭa is appropriate. This is because the initial raising of the hand occurs first, and the strike occurs later. The teacher says: "Our thought is that the initial raising of the hand should not become a non-offense based on the subsequent strike." Even by this text: "If any limb such as a hand is broken by that strike, it is only a Dukkaṭa," it is established that the Dukkaṭa is due to the strike. The raising of the hand remains according to the object; this should be well-considered. They say: "For a monk who, seeing the defecation of animals etc., becomes angry and raises his hand, his intention is only to drive them away."

## The Explanation of the Talasattika Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Amūlaka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the phrase "accusing with a groundless Saṅghādisesa offense while perceiving an ordained monk as unordained," it should be understood as accusing with the grounds of a Saṅghādisesa offense such as emission of semen (sukka-vissaṭṭhi) or bodily contact (kāya-saṃsaggi). This is because for an unordained person (novice), there is no such thing as a Saṅghādisesa offense.

## The Explanation of the Amūlaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Sañcicca Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the phrase "I think he is less than twenty years old," if a monk says "I think" for the purpose of causing remorse (kukkucca) without actually perceiving it so in his own mind, should he be charged with an offense of lying (musāvāda)? It would not be an offense because the factors (of lying) are not complete. The word "I think" alone does not necessarily complete the factors. The determination of meaning occurs only in certain places. In phrases like "I think the water is burning," whether another person feels remorse or not is not the measure; in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā, "causing remorse" is said to be according to the intention of that monk.

## The Explanation of the Sañcicca Sikkhāpada is finished.
338:
## 8. Upassuti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
In the phrase "having heard these," there is the remaining text "words" (vacanaṃ). "Of the same definition" (ekaparicchedāni) means they have the same decision in the manner of "it may be an act of commission (kiriya), it may be an act of omission (akiriya)." Here, even if the offense due to evasive speech (aññavādaka) is an act of commission and the offense due to harassing (vihesaka) is an act of omission, considering both as one training rule, that training rule called evasive speech should be understood as: some are commission by the power of the first (aññavādaka), and some are omission by the power of the second (vihesaka).

## The Explanation of the Upassuti Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Kammapaṭibāhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Because of the words "of legal acts" (dhammikānaṃ kammānaṃ), some monks say "I give consent" for legal acts and give their consent. Such giving is merely their wish, not the practice (according to Vinaya). If it is said: "If one criticizes based on illegality or overturns that illegal act, is it not a non-offense?" No, it is indeed a non-offense. Because it is taught in the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra) due to criticizing an illegal act later, without having done so at the time of giving consent. If it is said: "Because it causes release from an offense by performing an act for a monk who is not entitled to the act, whether illegally or by a faction, such a statement is merely general." This cannot be said. Because at the time of giving consent, there is no agreement to perform an illegal act, and the fault falls only on the performer. If it is said: "The group (gaṇa) incurs a Dukkaṭa." Only the monks who give consent for purity (pārisuddhi-chanda) incur a Dukkaṭa; the group does not incur a Dukkaṭa because the act is not valid. In the Kamma-vagga of the Parivāra, those who give consent for a valid act are mentioned separately. Even so, consent should not be given for an illegal act; if given, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to consenting to what is improper (akappiya). The teacher says: "Our thought is that they are not released from the Dukkaṭa offense in that improper act."

## The Explanation of the Kammapaṭibāhana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Chandaṃ adatvā gamana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Some teachers say there is no offense if one does not come to the assembly and does not give consent. Some teachers say a Dukkaṭa is incurred because of the intention to obstruct a legal act. For the purpose of giving consent in the midst of the Saṅgha...
339:
...some teachers say one obtains (the right to give consent in the midst of the Saṅgha). If it is said: "Even if one enters the midst of the Saṅgha after giving consent and leaves again, the consent does not lapse." (The answer is:) It does lapse. Why? Because it contradicts texts such as "One who is outside the forearm's length (hatthapāsa) is eligible to give consent." Some teachers say that in the Pali, it refers to a monk who, desiring to give consent, goes beyond the forearm's length.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on going without giving consent is finished.

## 11. Dubbala Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
484-5. "He gave" (adāsi) means he gave after asking permission. In the word "monks" (bhikkhū), those six-group monks (chabbaggiya), excluding themselves, said "monks" instead of "Saṅgha." "They divert" (pariṇāmeṇti) means they lead away (or cause to incline). In that text, the extraction of the word "gain" (lābho) is for the purpose of showing gain by extracting the meaning of any word, even if not intended here. Indeed, only robes are intended here; therefore, it is said: "If one criticizes the giving of other requisites, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred." The words "given" (dinnāṃ) and "requisite" (parikkhāraṃ) are in the accusative case with a locative sense.

## The Explanation of the Dubbala Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 12. Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
If one causes what is intended to be given to another, even to a relative, to be given to someone else, an offense is indeed incurred. In all matters, one who wishes to give after asking permission may manage it as they please.

## The Explanation of the Pariṇāmana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The eighth chapter, the Sahadhammika Vagga, is completed according to the order of explanation.

## 9. Ratana Vagga

## 1. Antepura Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
494-7. The meaning is: "In the manner that one attends upon the Blessed One, by that manner of attending, this man is not fit to be wicked, he is not wicked," or it has a causal meaning.
340:
The word "taṃ" is merely a particle, or it means "for which reason". "Hatthisammadda" means being crowded with elephants, trampling, or being crushed to powder.

500. A "jewel" (ratana) refers to the Chief Queen. Nevertheless, in this training rule, it does not protect other royal lineages because in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra), the statement "she is not a queen" is absent. The teacher says that if one is of royal lineage but not yet consecrated, or if one is consecrated but not of royal lineage, [the rule] protects them. Since it is stated as a factor in the Mātikā Commentary in the section on non-offense, being consecrated is the standard. Some teachers say the remaining words are the ultimate limit.

500-501. The three divisions of "no perception of a bedchamber in a bedchamber" can also be found here. What is not a bedchamber refers to things like the root of a tree without an enclosure.

## The Explanation of the Antepura Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 2. Ratana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

There are phrases such as "Let the householders accept the food" and "My householders".

According to the Kurundī commentary, if monks have doubts even in a house, it means they should stand there and inform [the residents]. Regarding the word "appropriate" (patirūpa), it is written: "taking as a discarded rag (paṃsukūla) an object considered a jewel, or going without concern for the jewel." They say, "One is not allowed to take an untouchable object (anāmāsa) even temporarily." "Samādapetvā" means by entreating, according to the method stated: "The Noble Ones stand with a purpose; this standing with a purpose is the entreaty of the Noble Ones."

## The Explanation of the Ratana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Vikālagāmappavisana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

511-2. In the case of a snake bite, that monk went without asking a monk who was present, and remorse arose in him. The phrase "by the method stated in the Adinnādāna [rule]" is said with reference to "the village and the vicinity of the village."

## The Explanation of the Vikālagāmappavisana Sikkhāpada is finished.
341:
## 4. Sūcighara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Taṃ" means breaking (bhedanaka). "Assa" is said because one must first break [the needle-case] for the Pācittiya offense and then confess it. This method also applies to the other training rules. "Vāsijaṭe" means in the handle of an adze (vāsidaṇḍaka).

## The Explanation of the Sūcighara Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Mañca Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
521-2. In some texts, there are the phrases "ucce mañce" and "uccā mañce". "Āyato" means in width (vitthato). "Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakaṃ" means the state of having legs (bhāvanapuṃsaka) or a leg of eight finger-breadths in measure.

## The Explanation of the Mañca Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Tūlonaddha Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
"Poṭakitūlaṃ" means any kind of grass-down (tiṇatūla). In the phrase "one should destroy it upon acquisition and confess a Pācittiya," although it seems as if a Pācittiya is incurred merely by acquisition, it should be understood that the offense is incurred only upon use. The statement "If one acquires and uses what was made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)" is the evidence in this matter.

## The Explanation of the Tūlonaddha Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 7. Nisīdana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā
Although the type (jāti) of the sitting cloth is not clear here, it should be known that its type is indeed the robe-type, because it is permitted in the Cīvarakkhandhaka and is included in the phrase "nine robes are to be determined (adhiṭṭhātabbāni)." By the phrase "spreading it like a rug," it is compared to the sitting cloth with a border mentioned previously, as it is a sitting-cloth rug. If obtained, a rug with a border; if not obtained...
342:
...some teachers say that even one without a border is allowable, but that is not proper. This is because the form of that sitting cloth is fixed by the statement "What is called a sitting cloth (nisīdana) is said to have a border."

## The Explanation of the Nisīdana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 8. Kaṇḍupaṭicchādi Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

If the cloth that covers the itch, sores, or boils occurring below the navel and above the kneecap is intended as the "itch-covering cloth" (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi), then this measure stated as four spans in length and two spans in width by the Sugata's span also appears to be an excessively large measure. This is because all men are seven spans tall by their own span, and one span of the Sugata is equal to three spans of an average man (majjhimapurisa). Therefore, the itch-covering cloth reaches the height of an ordinary man in width, and in length, it reaches twice that. Let it be so; if the ultimate limit of that itch-covering cloth is desired, it will indeed cover the whole body. A monk who wishes to wear it by making many layers, like the Saṅghāṭi worn on the whole body, will wear it—this might be the Blessed One's intention.

## The Explanation of the Kaṇḍupaṭicchādi Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

The rain-cloth (vassikasāṭika) is also permitted according to the ultimate limit. This might be the Blessed One's intention: "In the rainy season, some monks will use it only by using the Saṅghāṭi." Although they are permitted through such reasoning, it should be known that because it was prescribed in the case where [it was said], "They wear itch-covering cloths and rain-cloths of unlimited size," the permission for these rain-cloths was given with this specific limit, on the grounds that those monks of the group of six (chabbaggiya) wore those rain-cloths with a measure exceeding the full limit. This same method applies to the tenth training rule.

## The Explanation of the Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada is finished.
343:
## 10. Nandatthera Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In that tenth training rule, because of the statement "he makes a mattress or a pillow," this meaning is appropriate: "he makes it for the sake of common use by many monks in terms of length."

## The Explanation of the Nandatthera Sikkhāpada is finished.

## The Ninth Chapter on Jewels (Ratana Vagga) is finished in the order of explanation.

## The Explanation of the Pācittiya Section is finished.
344:
## 6. Pāṭidesanīya Section
## 1. Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
553-5. Because it is stated in the Commentary as "showing the manner of confession," the offense should be confessed only as it appears in the Pali, and not in any other way. One should also show the application of the other three triads (tika) in the same manner, such as "perceiving the inhabited area as an inhabited area," "perceiving what is edible or consumable as what is not edible or consumable," and "perceiving a bhikkhunī as not a bhikkhunī."

## The Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule
Regarding the phrase "being invited, they eat," even if it is said "being invited with any of the five kinds of food, they eat," in this training rule, the state of being invited with an improper invitation is not a factor. This is because there is no such intention in the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra) either in the Mātikā Commentary or in this commentary. Therefore, the meaning of the word "nimantitā" (invited) is stated only according to previous practice. It should be understood that the other three triads are also to be applied and shown as stated in the word-by-word analysis (padabhājanīya). Indeed, for monks who eat in any manner and do not stop such a bhikkhunī, there is a Pāṭidesanīya offense. There are two readings: "this bhikkhunī directs" (vosāsati) and "while directing" (vosāsantī). The singular form "Friends, [I have fallen into] a blameworthy matter" (gārayhaṃ āvuso dhammaṃ) contradicts the phrase "at every swallow." It is stated with reference to the offense incurred at the very first swallow; similarly, it appears in other places because of the word "āpajjimhā" (we have fallen into). Some teachers say it is also allowable for one person to confess for many; that statement is not good. My opinion is that it is because it is stated in the Pali as "by those monks" (tehi bhikkhūhi), etc. Along with one person, "I have fallen into" (ahaṃ āpajjiṃ) should also be said; since it is to be confessed by one, two, or three, it is allowable for all to say it this way. Some teachers say, "It should be said only together as 'āpajjimhā' (we have fallen into)." If one person is not stopped, "Friend, I have fallen into a blameworthy matter" should also be said.

## The Commentary on the Second Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule is finished.

562-570. The third and fourth training rules have clear meanings.

## The Commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya Section is finished.
345:
## 7. Sekhiya Section
## 1. Commentary on the Parimaṇḍala Group

"Sikkhitasikkhena" means one who has training (to be practiced) through the four paths. Because one who wears the robe hanging down eight finger-breadths finds it becomes four finger-breadths when sitting, both those views of the Commentary have the same limit. The phrase "two and a half cubits" refers to a thin or single-layered undergarment (antaravāsaka). This is because that (single-layered) one remains as it is placed. Elder Upatissa said that "even the measure of two cubits (is allowable)" is said with reference to a double-layered undergarment. It should be understood that "the measure of two cubits" is stated as the minimum limit for either a single or double-layered one. For it is said in the Nissaggiya Commentary, "even a width of two cubits is allowable," and that is said only in the case of unavailability: "when unavailable, even a width of two cubits is allowable." All these words are said with reference to a robe that has been determined (adhiṭṭhāna). If one sees it is worn wrongly, it should be corrected. If one does not correct it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Because it is said "on account of disrespect," it is an offense with intention (sacittaka) only with the mind that knows the regulation, not with the mind that knows the object; for even if one knows "this was done thus," there is no offense. The view of Elder Phussadeva is also suitable in one way. Likewise, the view of Elder Upatissa is also suitable.

Whether a training rule is laid down or not, that which is a fault by nature is called "worldly fault" (lokavajja). But this (Sekhiya) is a fault only when laid down, and not before it was laid down; therefore, because it is unlike other worldly faults, it is not a worldly fault. Because it is a fault starting from the regulation, it is called "fault by regulation" (paṇṇattivajja). Because the offense is incurred only with a mind of disrespect, it is "with intention" (sacittaka); because that mind can have all three feelings, it is "triple-feeling" (tivedana). Because the mind of disrespect is purely unwholesome, and that unwholesome is a fault by nature, this (Sekhiya) is a worldly fault. It should be understood that intentional transgression occurs only to one with a mind of displeasure, thus it is an offense with painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). However, in the Gaṇṭhipada it is written: "Elder Phussadeva says it is a fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja) because the fault of wearing [the robe] etc. is not blamed by the world like killing etc."

"Vihārepi" refers to times such as attending on the Buddha; therefore, the word "should be robed" (pārupitabba) is said by way of the duty regarding the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga). In the first and second training rules, it is allowable (not to be fully robed) due to reasons such as oppression by heat (pariḷāha); however, in those connected with the inhabited area, it is not allowable.
346:
Regarding the phrase "standing in one place," it is written: "Even while walking, it is indeed permissible to look to see if there are no dangers; likewise, it is permissible to look for offerings in the village." It should be understood that because it is said "standing in one place," that statement was made with reference to such dangers.

## The Commentary on the Pari-maṇḍala Chapter is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Ujjagghika Chapter

In the word "hasanīyasmiṃ," the locative case is used in the sense of cause (hetu); it means "because of a laughable matter." It is said that there is no offense for a monk who performs appreciation (anumodanā) and so forth with a loud voice inside a village. For this reason, the Elder Mahinda also preached the Dhamma to the multitude in elephant stables and such places.

Some monks say, "By merely placing one's requisites, one is considered to have entered the residence (staying there)." This is merely the opinion of those teachers. If Bhikkhunīs have entered and are staying at a place, that Bhikkhunī-monastery itself is a suitable ground (kappiyabhūmi). Because of the statement, "Wherever Bhikkhunīs stay even for a single night, this is called a Bhikkhunupassaya" (Pācittiya, 161), it is allowable for a monk to go as he pleases, thinking, "I will go to the vicinity of those Bhikkhunīs" or "to the residence occupied by them." Our teacher considers that by merely going to that house, it does not fall under the category of being "inside the village" (antaraghara), and thus it is allowable to go.

## The Commentary on the Ujjagghika Chapter is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Khambhakata Chapter

Sūpa (curry) is the type of mung bean curry mentioned in the explanation of the bowl's proportion. "Oloṇī" refers to a boiling liquid; it means being filled with milk and heaped up.

In the phrase "it decreases downwards," it is said, "Even if it is heaped up in one part while there is a decreasing amount, there is no offense." It is also said, "It is allowable to receive alms-food placed by covering the bottom and top of the bowl with lotus leaves and so forth." In this training rule, "Because the statement 'Alms-food should be received level with the rim' [indicates] alms-food and..."
347:
...shows that 'Alms-food should be received only level with the rim.' Therefore, when alms-food is being offered into the bowl already in one's hand, even if it becomes heaped up, it is shown to be allowable. The statement 'If one receives heaped-up alms-food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)' refers to a monk who receives alms-food that was already heaped up beforehand. If it becomes heaped up while being received with the bowl, it is allowable because it was received as non-heaped-up. There is no effort (payoga) other than the previous indication. It is also said that the word 'samatittikaṃ' is a gerundial neuter (adverb). Therefore, it should be accepted after consideration.

## The Commentary on the Khambhakata Chapter is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Sakkacca Chapter

In the training rule concerning requesting curry and rice, the reason "curry means two types of curry" is not stated is to include all other types of food besides the choice foods (paṇītabhojana) by the term "curry." In the non-offense section of that training rule, the phrase "for relatives, for those who have invited, for the sake of another, with one's own wealth" is redundant. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, it only says, "There is no offense if it is unintentional, through forgetfulness, unknowingly, when ill, or in times of danger." That is not appropriate. In the non-offense section of the training rule "I will eat alms-food with an equal amount of curry," it is written in some places "for the sake of another." That writing is also due to negligence. It is written, "For one who, after putting it in the mouth, regrets it and wishes to spit it out, if it enters [the throat] suddenly, this is called 'unintentional.' If one eats by taking something suddenly without reflecting, whether it was requested or not, while it is in the same place, it is called 'through forgetfulness'." In the non-offense section of some palm-leaf manuscripts, it is said that the term "rasarasa" is written and should be accepted.

## The Commentary on the Sakkacca Chapter is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Kabaḷa Chapter

Because of the phrase "the whole hand," some say there is no offense for a monk who puts a part [of the hand] into the mouth. Others say that because of the word "whole," even a part is not allowable. Since there is no specific distinction in the non-offense section, that [latter] statement is appropriate.
348:
In the word "sitthāvakārake," there are readings: "one who discards rubbish might discard a grain of rice" and "one who discards rubbish."

## The Commentary on the Kabaḷa Chapter is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Surusuru Chapter

There are readings "surusuru" and "surosuro." "Sītikato" means afflicted by cold (sītaṅko). It is written, "The word 'silakabuddho' is merely a joking word among the Noble Ones."

In the phrase "paṭikkūlavasena" (by way of loathsomeness), if it is rejected because it is loathsome, one should not say "like the enjoyers of sense pleasures." If it is argued that those people do not perform loathsome acts? No, because it is possible to hold it by way of the sign of authority. They tend to act disrespectfully. "Pattadhovana" refers to bowl-washing water associated with food.

There are readings "chattapādukāya" and "chattapāde."

"Cāpa" (bow) is a weapon that kills living beings. It is also written, "All other specific types of bows are included in the kodanda weapon." "Paṭimukka" means inserted or hung.

## The Commentary on the Surusuru Chapter is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Pāduka Chapter

Being in a vehicle oneself,
Just as one is able to speak to one who is in a vehicle,
In the same way, a monk with an umbrella,
Is not able to speak to one who has an umbrella in hand.

As in this case, it should be understood in other training rules as well.

In the Chappaka story, there is the reading "If I shall not get." There is also "If I shall not get ten." The phrase "to one who is not ill in the story" also appears. That phrase is not good; it is good only in the training rule itself. The word "thomito" [is used] with the words "I also know"...
349:
...is connected. There is that prosperity called the gain of wealth and the gain of fame. There is also that prosperity which exists apart from practicing unrighteousness. In the future life, it occurs because of the cause of ruin in the lower realms. Alternatively, in the word 'vinipātena', the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause, meaning it occurs because of falling into ruin. 'Adhammacaraṇena' means by practicing unrighteousness. They also recite 'asmā kumbhimiva'.

## The Explanation of the Footwear Chapter is finished.

## Miscellaneous Explanation

Thinking that they arise from the three—body, speech, and mind—they are said to 'have the origin of formal admonition (samannubhāsana-samuṭṭhāna)'. Formal admonition is an action. These actions have the origin of Dhamma teaching. If it is asked, 'In this context of speech and mind, because of the state of bodily and vocal intimation, should they be said to arise from body, speech, and mind, as in the case of loud laughter (ujjagghika) and loud noise (uccāsadda)?' The answer is: they should not be so called. While it is appropriate in those training rules where bodily intimation is evident, such as sitting, walking, and putting food into the mouth, it is not appropriate in the teaching of Dhamma because such bodily intimation is absent.

## The Miscellaneous Explanation is finished.

## The Explanation of the Sekhiya Section is finished.
