## Explanation of the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga

## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One

## 1. Pārājika Kaṇḍa Vaṇṇanā (Explanation of the Section on Defeat)

## Ganthārambha Vaṇṇanā (Introduction to the Text)

Just as the detailed arrangement was made in the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga, I shall now speak of the sequence of the word-commentary (ganthipada) for the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga without making a detailed arrangement. The meaning is that the sequence of the explanation for whatever Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga there may be has arrived.

## The Introduction to the Text is Finished.

## 1. Paṭhama Pārājika Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā (Explanation of the First Training Rule on Defeat)

656-7. The wisdom that knows the cause arising in various instances is called investigation (vīmaṃsā). "Padapaṭipāṭiyā eva" means only by the sequence of the matrix (mātikā) terms. In the word "stated" (vuttaṃ), it is written that it refers to the analysis of the elders who participated in the Council and who thought according to the Buddha's intention.

Some teachers say that this Pali, "She is a Bhikkhunī because of 'Come, nun' (Ehi-bhikkhunī), she is a Bhikkhunī because of being ordained by the three refuges," is stated by way of the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa). Some say it existed during the time of other Buddhas; that statement seems improper because it would imply the possibility of it occurring during our Buddha's time as well, and because a shadow of the prohibition of Ehi-bhikkhunī [ordination] is seen. As it is said in the Dhammapada in the story of Visākhā: "Due to the result of that gift of robes, she obtained this Great Creeper Ornament (Mahālatā-pasādhana). Indeed, for women, the gift of robes reaches its peak with the Great Creeper Ornament; for men, it reaches its peak with the robes and bowl created by psychic power." This is how it is. For a Bhikkhunī who is ordained by the three refuges...
352:
The arising of a nun (by 'ehi-bhikkhunī' or by the three refuges) might occasionally occur during the time of other Buddhas, but it certainly does not exist during the time of our Buddha. However, by way of the elegance of the teaching, the description of nuns is stated following the sequence of the teaching for monks. For that reason, although nuns ordained on one side (ekatoupasampanna) by the power of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha exist, they are not mentioned in that Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga. Their existence should be known by this Parivāra-kathā:

'Two nuns receive ordination together,
If one should receive a robe from the hands of both,
The offenses would be various;
This question is considered by those skilled in the Vinaya.' (Parivāra)

Alternatively, if a male monk who was ordained by the 'ehi-bhikkhu' formula or the three refuges while still a worldling (puthujjana) remains in the state of a nun due to the appearance of the female gender (itthilinga), he is reckoned as an 'ehi-bhikkhunī' or a 'nun ordained by the three refuges' based on the ordination received while a man. Some say that if it were not so, that statement would be contradictory; this should be accepted after investigation. The phrase 'a competent wise person' is stated because of the fulfillment of the state of oozing (avassava-bhāva, i.e., lust) in both men and women. In this matter, the fingertips of nuns receiving any material gift and the hands of men sometimes come into contact; or the heads of men who are bowing sometimes come into contact with the toes of nuns; or when shaving hair, the head comes into contact with the hands of men. This mind indeed seeks excessive attachment or is difficult to guard. Therefore, thinking 'Let not the offense of defeat (pārājika) occur too easily for nuns,' the Buddhas, out of compassion, taught the boundaries of the field of Pārājika and the field of Thullaccaya (grave offense) separately.

In the phrase 'It is stated mostly by that method,' the sequence of the sub-glossary (anugaṇṭhipada) composed by the Venerable Vajirabuddhi is as follows: It is called 'originating from action (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna)' because it mostly arises due to an action. However, because it is stated as 'should consent (sādiyeyya)' instead of 'should commit bodily contact (kāya-saṃsagga)', it should be known that it also arises from non-action (akiriya). Just as in this training rule, below also, after stating the origin from action by the method 'For a monk who practices sexual intercourse in the three paths of a human woman, there is an offense of defeat,' immediately after that, the origin from non-action is also stated by the method 'The enemies of a monk... etc... if that monk consents to the insertion, there is an offense of defeat.' Therefore, the first Pārājika should also be known as originating from action mostly by that method. Indeed, the origin from action is not evident in consenting to insertion (pavesana-sādiyana), etc. In this matter, the movement of the organ should not be regarded as the essence. Because in the case 'If that monk does not consent to the insertion... does not consent to the staying, but consents to the withdrawal, there is an offense of defeat,' the function of movement is naturally fulfilled even in the non-consenting to the staying. Here, the movement during the practice is also not evident except through consenting. Therefore, it should be taken as originating from action mostly. In various commentaries also, mostly that method is stated.
353:
“If one does not consent to the insertion [of the organ], does not consent to it having been inserted, does not consent to it remaining, but consents to the withdrawal, a Pārājika offense is committed.” In this Pārājika Pāḷi, even if there is no consent while it remains, it is because there is naturally a complete movement. Since the movement during indulgence due to consent is not clearly evident here, it should be understood as action-originated (kiriya-samuṭṭhāna) only by the general method (yebhuyya-naya).

If it is asked why the general method is not mentioned in various commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), it is because in the Matikā, which states, “Whatever monk should indulge in sexual intercourse,” the action-originated nature is explicitly stated. Therefore, in accordance with that Matikā and without considering the Vibhaṅga method, it is stated simply as “action-originated.” Just as the action-originated nature is stated by the general method in these training rules, likewise, liquor (surā) and such should be consumed only with an unwholesome mind (akusala citta), and not otherwise. When it is said, “That which one commits only with an unwholesome mind is a worldly fault (lokavajja); the rest are faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja),” the defining characteristics of worldly faults and faults by regulation are established. If it were not said so, but instead said, “In the aspect where there is intention for that training rule, the mind is only unwholesome; this offense is a worldly fault, and the rest are faults by regulation,” then the term 'worldly fault' would be meaningless, because even in the aspect of not knowing the object (vatthu), it is consumed only with an unwholesome mind.

Since there is no arising of an unwholesome mind in the transgression of drinking liquor when one does not know the object, it is stated in the Khandhaka Commentary: “In the case of drinking liquor, if a monk drinks it starting from the seed even without knowing, he commits a Pācittiya offense; a novice (sāmaṇera) breaks his virtue (sīla) only if he drinks it knowingly, not if he drinks it unknowingly.” It is not stated that “In the aspect of not knowing the object, even if there is an arising of mind similar to the unwholesome mind that accomplishes acts such as killing (pāṇātipāta), the novice does not reach the breaking of virtue.” The statement regarding the intention is because the drinking of liquor by novices is of the same nature as killing and so forth. For one who transgresses by way of drinking and so on, knowing the object as “these are liquor and such,” there is no possibility that an unwholesome mind does not arise. Therefore, it is said, “In the aspect where there is intention for that training rule,” and so forth.

In this sequence of words, if it is asked by way of logical argument: “Since Arahants do not enter [into such acts], what is the determination of unwholesomeness in both aspects of having intention and not having intention?” The answer is: No, because by the nature of things (dhammatā), even Learners (sekhas) do not enter [into such acts]. To show the absence of the determination of unwholesomeness in the aspect of not having intention, examples such as a drop of liquor should be cited, like a drop of water placed in the mouth of a sleeping person. If the meaning is taken by the general method, the earlier and later words in the Commentary are consistent. Other teachers say, “Because there is no difference in meaning along with the Pāḷi, it will become clear later.”

What should be considered here is: if there were drinking of liquor free from unwholesomeness in the aspect of knowing the object, why would it not pass through (not be swallowed) the middle of the throat of the Noble Ones (ariyas) who perceive it as a beverage and so forth? If it is argued that the transgression of the object of breaking virtue cannot happen to Noble Ones even without intention by their very nature, it is not that it cannot happen; it can indeed happen, as it would otherwise contradict stories such as that of Cakkhupāla Thera. Alternatively, if it is asked: “Just as drinking liquor occurs for a novice only when there is intention, why does it not occur for a monk only when there is intention?” If the answer is “Because it is improper,” it is also improper for novices. This is because those novices are also fellow practitioners (sahadhammika). If it is said “Because it is a great fault,” it is also a great fault for novices. If it is said that for novices, only the training rule with intention is a Pārājika, while other training rules without intention are objects for punishment (daṇḍakamma), then for monks, there is no Pārājika in drinking liquor. In this training rule, a Tika-Pācittiya would not occur. A Dukkaṭa offense should be prescribed for a monk who perceives it as not being liquor. If it is said that, like animal-novices, a monk’s Pācittiya object is a Pārājika for novices, then even the monk’s lack of intention in drinking liquor and so forth...
354:
It should be considered. If, in the aspect of knowing the object, the drinking of intoxicants were to occur without unwholesome intent, why does it not pass through the throats of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who perceive it as a beverage and so on? If it is said that the transgression of the object that causes the breach of virtue does not occur to the Noble Ones even without intention, simply by the power of their nature (dhammatā), it is not so, because it would contradict the story of Elder Cakkhupāla and others (where transgression occurs without intention).

Furthermore, why is it that for a monk, the drinking of intoxicants is only sacittaka (with intention), just as it is for a novice (sāmaṇera)? If it is said that it is because it is improper, it is also improper for novices. For they are indeed fellow-practitioners (sahadhammika). If it is said that it is because it is a great fault, it is also a great fault for novices. If it is said that for novices, it is a Pārājika only when it is sacittaka, and otherwise it is a matter for punishment (daṇḍakamma), then for monks also, there is no Pārājika in drinking intoxicants. In this training rule, there should not be a tika-pācittiya (the triad of pācittiya offenses). A dukkaṭa offense should be prescribed for a monk who perceives what is an intoxicant as a non-intoxicant. If it is said that a monk's pācittiya offense becomes a Pārājika for novices, like in the case of animal-like novices, then the acittaka (unintentional) act of monks should also be prescribed as a Pārājika for novices. If it is said that an acittaka act cannot be a Pārājika, it is not so, for a paṇṇattivajja (fault by regulation) can also be a Pārājika. In the views of other Nikāyas (sects), there is this fault. In our view, however, the drinking of intoxicants is only a lokavajja (worldly fault).

In this regard, why is it that only the drinking of intoxicants is not done by the Noble Ones by the power of their nature? It is not only the drinking of intoxicants that the Noble Ones do not do by the power of their nature; it should be understood that they also do not commit acts such as beheading while perceiving a being as a being through the power of anger, they do not transgress against the wives of others while perceiving them as their own wives, they do not speak lies that destroy benefits while perceiving them as causing harm, and they do not practice wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) while perceiving it as right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). The teachers also say that there is no absolute rule of unwholesomeness in the drinking of intoxicants. For that very reason, in the section on lokavajja and paṇṇattivajja in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā Gaṇṭhipada, it is written: "The statement that it is unwholesome in the aspect of being sacittaka is for the purpose of including the drinking of intoxicants and so on; otherwise, one would say it is only unwholesome."

The action-originated (kiriyā-samuṭṭhāna) nature of this training rule follows the method of 'mostly' (tabbahula-naya); it is not like in the first Pārājika. How? The training rule on bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga) has the same origin (samuṭṭhāna) as the first Pārājika. In this training rule, when there is bodily contact between a monk and a bhikkhunī, the bhikkhunī incurs an offense if she consents with her mind even without moving her limbs; it is not so for the monk. The monk incurs an offense only when he moves. Likewise, in the first Pārājika, one incurs an offense only when there is movement; if there is none, one does not. In the phrase "consents to the entry" (pavesanaṃ sādiyati), consenting to the entry means the arising of the thought of engaging in sexual intercourse. Even though this is so, it is stated that "it should be accepted after careful investigation."

## The explanation of the commentary on the first Pārājika training rule is finished.
355:
## 2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika Training Rule
Because of the statement, "Sister, why did you commit a Pārājika offense while knowing it?", and because of the statement, "She commits one of the eight Pārājikas" (Pācittiya 666), and because of the statement at the end, "Sisters, the eight Pārājika rules have been recited" (Pācittiya 677), and because of the statement in the Parivāra, "common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paṇṇatti), regulation for both orders (ubhato-paṇṇatti)" (Parivāra 201), when reaching the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, the Blessed One, regarding the common training rules shared with monks, in the very context of the arisen story, laid down the Mātikā (matrix) in both specific and non-specific ways, such as: "Whatever bhikkhunī, being filled with desire, should engage in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, she is one who is defeated (pārājika), no longer in communion." Then, in due order, He explained in detail the word-analysis (padabhājanī), the classification of offenses, the triads (tika), and the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra) without omission. It should be understood that the Elders who conducted the Recital (Saṅgīti) elaborated only the uncommon regulations (asādhāraṇa-paṇṇatti) here.

In that training rule, the phrase "of the eight Pārājikas" is a statement placed solely according to the method of the Elders of the Recital, because before this, the sixth, seventh, and eighth Pārājikas had not yet been prescribed. The Blessed One, however, referring to this first prescribed training rule, might have said "of the six Pārājikas." Some teachers say that the statement "of the eight Pārājikas," referring also to the training rules prescribed after this one, arose at a later time. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said: "This Pārājika was also prescribed later; therefore, it is said 'of the eight' in the Vibhaṅga." Thus, according to the opinion of the commentators, this point is established: they were recited exactly according to the order in which they were prescribed. The reading is "aññāsi" (she knew). It should not be taken as "aññāsī." Because of the statement, "in the same manner as stated in the training rule on gross misconduct (duṭṭhullā)," it is established that whatever bhikkhunī conceals a fault is indeed a concealer of faults (vajjapaṭicchādikā). Although the concealment of a fault occurs through the power of affection, nevertheless, because the mind that transgresses the training rule is associated with displeasure (domanassa), it is stated as "painful feeling" (dukkha-vedanā).

## The explanation of the commentary on the second Pārājika training rule is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Third Pārājika Training Rule
The phrase "having accused and reminded" (codetvā sāretvā) means only this much. In this regard, there is this investigation: A monk who has the same view as an expelled monk and is one who belongs to a different communion by his views (laddhi-nānāsaṃvāsaka) is not to be paid homage to, just like the expelled monk in formal acts (kamma)...
356:
A monk who follows the views of an expelled monk (ukkhittaka) cannot be a quorum filler (gaṇapūraka) in formal acts, nor does he obtain the right to share a bed, just like the expelled monk himself. However, it is not the same for a bhikkhunī. As long as she has not been admonished by a formal act (ñatti-kammavācā), she can still be a quorum filler and obtain communion (saṃvāsa). A bhikkhunī who follows one of separate communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) is also like one who follows an expelled monk. Even if the expelled person passes away, the monk who follows him remains one of separate communion. Likewise, some teachers say that even if that person disrobes, goes over to another sect, or gives up the training and remains in the status of a novice (sāmaṇera), it is the same. According to the view of those teachers, it implies that even if the expelled person is in such a state, the bhikkhunī who follows him must still be admonished by a formal act. The act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma) pertains only to the Saṅgha; it seems inappropriate for the Saṅgha to intentionally remove a previously incurred offense. An act of expulsion (ukkhepanīyakamma) is performed merely for not seeing an offense, for not making amends, or for not relinquishing a wrong view; if it is said that it is inappropriate to admonish and cause one to fall away from the Dispensation (Sāsana) merely for following such a person, that should not be said. This is because this matter is also connected to the Pārājika offenses in the Pārājika accounts, and because the Vinaya is not the domain of disciples other than the Buddha.

## The Commentary on the Third Pārājika Training Rule is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika Training Rule

It is written that the phrase "kāyasaṃsaggarāgena" (with lust for physical contact) is stated to show that state of being "flooded" (avassuta) by the power of forming friendships, which is called worldly enjoyment (lokayassāda). "Tissitthiyo" refers to either "in three women" or "three women." "Taṃ na seveti" means not associating with those women. "Anariyā" refers to a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka). "Byañjanasmiṃ" means in one's own genitals. "Na seveti" means not associating; "na cācareti" means not practicing. "Vaṇṇāvaṇṇo" refers to the emission of semen by both terms. "Gamanuppādanaṃ" refers to the act of matchmaking (sañcaritta).

In the phrase "nivatthaṃ vā pārutaṃ vā," it means that one takes pleasure in touching either the clothes being worn or the clothes being draped.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika Training Rule is finished.

## The Commentary on the Pārājika Section is finished.
357:
## 2. Commentary on the Saṅghādisesa Section

## 1. Commentary on the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

"Āhataka" means a slave who has been brought; "niyataka" means a permanent slave. What is called "unallowable legal speech" (akappiya-aḍḍa) refers to going to a place of judgment (court) and speaking on behalf of the Saṅgha or a monastery attendant (ārāmika) regarding property, either as a representative of the Saṅgha or by the monk himself, saying: "This man is our slave, this woman is our female slave, this well, field, monastery, monastery site, bull, cow, female buffalo, female goat, or hen is our property," and so on. This is unallowable. However, whether asked or unasked, it is allowable to say: "This person is our monastery attendant, this woman is our monastery attendant, this well was donated to the Saṅgha by such-and-such a donor for the purpose of medicine, the four requisites arising from this field or this monastery are donated to the Saṅgha, the milk and other flavors arising from this cow, female buffalo, or female goat are donated to the Saṅgha by such-and-such a donor."

By saying "they do" instead of "it is done," it is said to be an explanation based on the work done by this person. In the word "gīvā" (neck), it refers only to the cutting of the neck, and a Pārājika offense is not incurred. In the phrase "kārāpetvā dātabbā" (having it made, it should be given), if it is a weapon, one should not have the blade of that weapon made; one should only inform by other means. Because it is said "three minds, three feelings," it should be understood that it is stated by the method of predominance (tabbahulanaya) as "by the power of human nature, by the power of the arising of anger."

## The Commentary on the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

"Bhaṭiputtaka" refers to a group of people who serve the deity Mahāpinne (Bhaṭiputtagaṇa). "Kappa" means allowable; "kappagatika" means having an allowable nature. "Pakkantāsu" refers to the time when other bhikkhunīs have left, leaving behind their own group. It should be understood that "three minds" is stated either because it is considered that even Noble Ones (Ariyas) who do not know the regulation might perform an ordination, or because of being endowed with the resultant indeterminate (vipāka-abyākata) at the moment the offense is incurred at the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā). It is stated in the ancient Ganthipada (glossary) that "there is no dukkaṭa offense for giving the novice ordination (pabbājanā)."

## The Commentary on the Second Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is finished.
358:
## 3. Commentary on the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

Bhikkhunī Bhaddā Kāpilānī was reportedly the former wife of Venerable Mahākassapa. The village where her relatives' family resided is called the "village of the relatives' family" (ñātikula); the meaning is that she went to that village where the family was situated. Just as in phrases like "he leads the goat to the village," it is also appropriate to use a double accusative construction: "she went to the village, she went to the relatives' family."

Regarding the statement "for a bhikkhunī who passes beyond the precincts of an unfenced village," it should be understood thus: In the training rule on entering a village at the wrong time (vikālagāmapavesana), the precinct (upacāra) is defined only by the distance of two stone-throws. Otherwise, just as in this gāmantara-gamana (traveling between villages) training rule, a place worthy of being fenced is treated as if it were fenced and described as "passing beyond," so too in that vikālagāmapavesana rule, it should say "for a monk who passes beyond the precincts of an unfenced village." Since in that training rule, the precinct is intended to be one stone-throw beyond the area worthy of being fenced, the phrase "for a monk who enters the precincts of an unfenced village" is used to clarify that meaning. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated: "Taking only the area worthy of being fenced as the 'precinct,' the phrase 'entering the precinct' is used to show the lack of distinction between a fenced area and an area worthy of being fenced." Without considering the specific Pali wording, it says: "For a monk who passes beyond the precinct of an unfenced village, where the fence is the precinct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the first step beyond that precinct, and an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for the second step." This statement should not be accepted because of the specific wording in the Pali. In some versions, it is found as "for a bhikkhunī who enters (okkammantiyā) the precincts of an unfenced village"; other teachers say this reading should not be accepted.

In the words of those teachers, the phrase "without considering the specific Pali wording" is poorly said. Why? Because even in the vikālagāmapavesana training rule, the reading "passing beyond the precinct" (upacāraṃ atikkamantassa) is found in some places. The teachers say that reading was taken from the text of the Andhaka Commentary. The reading "entering the precinct" (upacārokkamana) of an unfenced village is more appropriate than "passing beyond" (atikkamana). Why? Because in many places, the Pali contradicts the Commentaries, or it contradicts this very training rule. How does it contradict? By falling behind the group, an offense occurs in the forest, not in the village. Indeed, it is also shown by the verse "Sikkhāpadaṃ buddhavarena" (Parivāra 479); therefore, it should be understood that an offense is incurred by crossing a river that is included within the entrance to the precinct.

Furthermore—the meaning of the Parivāra verses such as "Four offenses for one who goes, and the same for one who stands" (Parivāra 475) is consistent with the Commentaries, and thus it is finally decided that only the reading "entering the precinct" is appropriate. This is said, and it is well-noted. In this commentary passage—"In this training rule, only traveling by foot is intended; therefore, it is said 'for a bhikkhunī who passes beyond with the first step,' etc."—since such traveling by foot does not exist in rules like vikālagāmapavesana, it shows that an offense is incurred by a monk who enters by vehicle or by psychic power, or by one who travels a long distance. Some teachers say there is no escape from the offense because traveling by vehicle or psychic power is inappropriate; this should be considered carefully. The monastery grounds of bhikkhunīs should not be called "between villages" (gāmantara). Why? Because although it is included in the area between villages, it is allowable ground (kappiyabhūmi). Later, because it is said, "If bhikkhunīs enter the courtyard of the Mahābodhi and one bhikkhunī stands outside at a distance of one stone-throw, that bhikkhunī incurs an offense," the meaning that a bhikkhunī monastery is not kappiyabhūmi is established. Therefore, like the Khandhamāra monastery in Kañcipura, or the Sarīradhamma monastery in the city of Kāverapaṭṭana, other...
359: It is stated that a final decision should be reached that only the reading 'entering the vicinity' (upacārokkamana) in accordance with the Commentaries is appropriate for the meaning of the Parivāra verses; this point should be well noted and spoken. In this Commentary statement, 'Walking on foot alone is intended here, which is why it is said "for one who surpasses the first step" and so forth,' it is shown that in the training rules such as entering a village at the wrong time (vikālagāmappavesana), even those who enter by vehicle or by psychic power (iddhi), or those who travel a long distance, incur an offense despite not walking on foot. Some teachers say that because traveling by vehicle or psychic power is improper, there is no escape from the offense; this point should be considered and accepted. The ground of a nunnery (bhikkhunī-vihāra) should not be called 'between villages' (gāmantara), because even if it is situated within the village outskirts, it is allowable ground (kappiya-bhūmi). Other teachers say: 'Later, according to the statement "If, while the nuns are entering the Great Bodhi courtyard (Mahābodhiyaṅgaṇa), one nun remains outside, she incurs an offense," it is evident that a nunnery is not allowable ground. Therefore, like the Khandhadhamma Vihāra in the city of Kañcinagara or the Sārīdhamma Vihāra in Kāvīrapaṭṭana, for any other such monastery, a nun who enters or leaves for the purpose of a formal resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) without interruption in the state of being between villages for the sake of ease in marking a boundary (sīmā), incurs a gāmantara offense.' In the phrase 'because it is connected with four villages,' it should be understood that monks marking a boundary in such a monastery must clear all those four villages. For a nun who, after consultation, enters that monastery together with another nun, or a woman, or a caravan of thieves, four offenses occur simultaneously. Some teachers say, 'In every interval between villages, there is a Pācittiya offense.' In the statement 'A Saṅghādisesa offense occurs when taking the second step,' if the second step is on allowable ground, a Saṅghādisesa does not occur; it occurs only if it is on unallowable ground. The written statement 'Wandering on both banks is allowable because the possibility of visual range (dassanūpacāra) exists here' is correct and appropriate. It should be known that here, auditory range (savanūpacāra) on the other side of a river or in the village outskirts is not the measure. However, in the Andhaka Commentary, it is said: 'If one descends into the river from the opposite bank and searches for and brings wood or leaves from within visual range, there is no offense. If one dries the three robes on the opposite bank, there is no offense.' The statement 'If she returns only to this bank, she incurs an offense' is meant because she entered with the intention to cross over. It is said, 'For those who enter for purposes such as bathing, it is allowable because the place of bathing itself can be the residence (ālaya).' According to the Commentary statement 'The measure is in the village outskirts,' it means that it is not allowable to leave and enter by swimming even a little from one's own village to wood and leaves within visual range after descending into the river from the opposite bank.
360:
“Agāmake araññe” means in a forest characterized as not being a village. This term indicates the area where an offense is committed. Since this forest excluded from a village is the area of offense, if a bhikkhunī crosses the threshold (indakhīla) of the village from the bhikkhunī quarters, she commits an ohīyana offense, which is staying behind from the group of bhikkhunīs when there is no village. Even if there is no range of sight (dassanūpacāra) or range of hearing (savanūpacāra), she commits the offense at the very moment of crossing the threshold in the village. If there is another bhikkhunī present when crossing that threshold, she commits the offense only when she crosses beyond the range of sight and hearing of that bhikkhunī. This procedure should not be understood as occurring only when traveling on a forest path. To show that a bhikkhunī leaving a village commits an offense from the moment she crosses this threshold, it is said, “agāmakaṃ araññaṃ.”

Indeed, it is stated: “There are bhikkhunīs who are comforting, supportive, and conscientious (lajjī); one should not go elsewhere having upset those bhikkhunīs. If she goes, she is not free from the gāmantara offense, the nadīpāra offense, the rattivippavāsa offense, and the gaṇamhā ohīyana offense,” and so forth. Among those offenses, it should be understood that the gaṇamhā ohīyana offense is committed only once. The other three offenses are committed at every village, every riverbank, and every dawn. In saying so, the words such as “vuttañhetaṃ” are not conclusive evidence and should be taken only as they are applicable; thus, words like “Mahābodhiyaṅgaṇa” are written to show that this gaṇamhā ohīyana offense can also be committed in the vicinity of a village.

## Completion of the Commentary on the Third Saṅghādisesa Training Rule.

## 4. Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

“Paṭivattā” means they give a retort or reply. “Kammadosa” (fault of the act) is written to be “the consent of the group without knowledge,” and so forth. Ancient teachers, however, said it is a “fault in the place where it is performed.” “Kārakagaṇassa” means of the Saṅgha that performs the formal act. If it is said that because it is stated “having assembled the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha,” the performing Saṅgha is this very Bhikkhunī Saṅgha—the ancient Gaṇṭhipada states that without first informing the performing Saṅgha, this Thullanandā reinstated that bhikkhunī by force. Therefore, it is established that even in the presence of the performing monks, that act should not be settled without first obtaining their consent; the meaning is that the settlement of the act must not be done by force. It is also stated there that a bhikkhunī also gets the chance to perform the diṭṭhavikamma.

In the sentence “If she reinstates her when the performing Saṅgha is absent (asante), there is no offense,” to what extent does it constitute being “absent”? This point has not been investigated in all places.
361:
Some teachers say that [the Saṅgha is absent] because the monks who perform the formal act have passed away. Some teachers say it is because even a single monk is missing. Some teachers say it is because they are not within the jurisdiction of a single king. Some teachers say it is because they are not in a single country. Some teachers say it is because they are not in a single village. Some teachers say it is because they are not in a single monastery (āvāsa). Some teachers say it is because they are not in a place where it is possible to ask for permission (apaloketuṃ). Some teachers say it is because they are not within half a league (yojana). Regarding these views, the teachers praise the decision that there is no offense for reinstating [a bhikkhunī] when the performing Saṅgha is not present in that monastery. The statement "where it is possible to ask for permission" is the proper (sāmīci) statement.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

"Etaṃ na vuttaṃ" means it does not intend this restriction: that the state of the bhikkhunī being lustful (avassuta) should be considered. Not saying so is consistent with the Pāli. With which Pāli is it consistent? It is consistent with this Pāli: "Knowing him to be not lustful (anavassuto), she accepts." If the person's state of being lustful were not the standard, what would be the purpose of this Pāli? It should only have been said: "Both are not lustful; the one who is not lustful accepts; there is no offense." This is because only one's own state of being not lustful is the standard.

The meaning of this "no offense" section (anāpattivāra) is: If both are not lustful, there is no offense in any way. Alternatively, if the bhikkhunī is not lustful but, perceiving a lustful person as "not lustful," she accepts from his hand, even then there is no offense. Alternatively, if she is not lustful but knows another person, whether not lustful or lustful, as "lustful," then only an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs. Thus it was said in the preceding training rule: "Lady, why do you not accept? Sir, you are lustful... I am not lustful."

## The Commentary on the Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Sixth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

"Tena" means therefore. Because the inciting bhikkhunī does not give and does not accept, therefore it means there is no acceptance. For the other [incited] bhikkhunī, [the offense is analyzed] based on the reason of consumption. The phrase "unwholesome mind" (akusala-citta) is mostly used. Some say that even if she speaks thinking "it is allowable," an offense is committed.

## 7. Commentary on the Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

712-4. Offenses committed before the formal act (kammavācā) are not settled. Ancient teachers say that when reaching the Saṅghādisesa offense, if the motion (ñatti) is made, the dukkaṭa and thullaccaya offenses are settled. That view is consistent with the Pāli "ajjhāpajjantiyā." In the sentence "having heard, they do not speak," if they do not speak because of fear of danger to life or danger to the holy life (the Dispensation), there is no offense. Because it is said "perceiving an un-Dhamma act as an un-Dhamma act, there is an offense of dukkaṭa," the statement "there is no offense for one who does not formally follow up (asamanubhāsantiyā)" is said with reference to the Saṅghādisesa offense.

## 8. Commentary on the Eighth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

"Paccākatā" means those who are defeated (those who have reached Pārājika). The Kuladūsaka training rule and this training rule differ only in their origin (nidāna). For in that Kuladūsaka training rule, it is said: "He should be admonished only for the sake of relinquishing that speech, not for the purpose of preventing the corruption of families (kuladūsana)." If so, both these offenses have the same (sabhāga) meaning; therefore, this training rule would become similar to the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) of that Kuladūsaka training rule. If that were the case, would this training rule not become useless? It should not be regarded so. There is a difference between the two training rules due to the specific object (vatthu) and the specific formal act (kammavācā).

It should be understood by supplementing the remaining text "by association through body and speech."

## 2. Commentary on the Second Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule

They give the out-of-season robe (akāla-cīvara) either because the material requirements are met, or because they do not want that bhikkhunī to commit an offense, or because she did not command it. Since it is personal property (puggalika), it should be taken exactly as it was given; it means it should not be distributed. In fact, other robes should also be taken exactly as they were given. In the Ganthipada, however, regarding the robe obtained by relinquishing—obtained in the way "I give to the lady"—"exactly as given" means according to the arrangement relinquished by the donors, and "should be taken" means it should be distributed as an out-of-season robe. In this training rule, only the robe obtained by having it distributed becomes Nissaggiya; it is written that even after performing the Vinaya procedure, one does not get it for oneself. If this was said with reference to the robe obtained by relinquishing, because it is said "it should be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual; he should give, they should give; I give to the lady," all these three words should be mentioned. Therefore, not only the robe obtained by relinquishing should be taken as given, but also the portion obtained by other bhikkhunīs should be taken exactly as given.

The statement "there is no offense in perceiving an out-of-season robe as an in-season robe and distributing it" shows only that one does not reach the offense that should be reached due to the act of distribution. It does not show the meaning that the obtained robe should not be given as it was donated. If she takes it by a pretext (lesa), she must be made to pay the value of the goods.

## 6. Commentary on the Sixth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
758-762. Pāvārikassa means "of the cloth merchant." Whichever bhikkhunī causes [the cloth] to be bought, for that bhikkhunī there is a nissaggiya offense, and there is the regaining of the relinquished object. "As for the other bhikkhunīs, even if they knowingly enjoy the portion that comes to them through the distribution process, it does not entail a nissaggiya; specifically, those bhikkhunīs should also bring it only to the place where it was originally intended to be given," so they say. Because it is stated, "Having regained the relinquished object, it should be brought to the place where it was originally intended to be given," they say that the object taken by the remaining bhikkhunīs is well-taken. In this case, even if it is a sick bhikkhunī, she is not exempt from the offense.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Seventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
In the seventh training rule, although it is stated generally as "sayaṃ yācitakena" without specification, it should be understood to mean "with the object requested by oneself, referring to oneself for another purpose." This meaning [is understood by correlating with]: "The bhikkhunīs, with that requisite and also themselves..."
365:
"...having requested and caused medicine to be bought, they use it." This should be understood by correlating it with the meaning of this Pali text. The meaning of that Pali is as follows: wishing to show the meaning "having caused medicine to be bought with that requisite, and (indicated by the word 'ca') having caused medicine to be bought with the object requested by oneself," it is said, "having themselves also requested and caused medicine to be bought." Otherwise, the Pali should have been stated in this order: "Having caused medicine to be bought with that requisite, having themselves also requested, they use it."

In the word-analysis (padabhājana), however, it is stated only as the meaning of that word: "Saṃyācikena means having requested by oneself." Showing only the meaning in such a way is the nature of the padabhājana. This nature of explanation is clear in the analysis of words such as "the communal gain (saṅghika-lābha) diverted to the Saṅgha." Otherwise, what other special benefit would be included by the word saṃyācika? Since that special benefit is not apparent, that word would be useless, and this training rule would be no different from the previous one. One's own property may be used as one wishes. In this Pali as well, the object obtained by requesting together by virtue of requesting for the Saṅgha should be understood as "saṃyācika." Otherwise, this word saṃyācika would become indistinguishable from the word saṃyācika that follows. Therefore, this training rule "with a personal saṃyācika" should not be taught separately, because the offense reached by that saṃyācika (or saññācika) training rule would be included here. They are not included because there are two offenses. If it is argued that there is only one offense because they were bought in a mixed manner? No, it is not so. Not only would the word saṃyācika become useless, but it would also lead to the fault that there would be only one offense when buying by mixing communal (saṅghika), group (mahājanika), and personal (puggalika) items.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Eighth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
Gaṇassa means for a group such as the Abhidhammikas, or for a group of fewer than four (ūnacatuvagga).

## The Commentary on the Eighth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule
Saññācikena means only with the requisite obtained by requesting from a group, not with any other requisite.

## The Commentary on the Ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Dasamanissaggiyapācittiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
In the tenth training rule, there should be a Pali text arranged in this manner: "Whatever bhikkhunī should cause another thing to be bought with personal requisites intended for another person and donated by another person, there is an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya." This eleventh training rule, "Puggalikena saṃyācikena" (with personal requested items), should exist according to the sequence of occurrence. Indeed, although this training rule is not taught because there is no specific origin story (atthuppatti), it should be accepted according to its meaning.

In this training rule, a shadow of non-offense (anāpatti) is seen in places where the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual has been invited, as well as in places where there are relatives of the individual. All this is stated only according to our reasoning and should not be taken as the essential truth. Having reflected and seen the stable reason, whatever decision the masters who are experts in the Vinaya sequence allow, that decision alone should be taken. In the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada (Old Glossary), however, it is stated: "Even in times of danger, only other heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa) should be caused to be bought; other items are not allowable. For a bhikkhu, however, it is allowable."

## Dasamanissaggiyapācittiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 11. Ekādasamanissaggiyapācittiyasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā
The reason why it is called the "eleventh training rule" here instead of the "first training rule of the second vagga" is that when reaching the Tiṃsaka section in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, the sequence of vaggas is not mentioned. Since requesting (viññatti) is not prohibited in an invited place, it should be understood that the Blessed One shows the limit, saying, "A maximum of four kaṃsas should be requested," when a bhikkhunī is told, "Speak of what you need," by way of a Dhamma-invitation (dhammanimantana) in a place of non-relatives and those who have not invited her.

Otherwise, it would lead to undesirable meanings such as "the origin story (nidāna) and the training rule do not agree, and the training rule and the non-offense section do not agree," and "four kaṃsas should be requested by requesting without being invited." Therefore, in the Mātikāဋ္ဌကထာ (Mātikāṭṭhakathā), regarding the statement "should cause to be bought," excluding co-religionists (sahadhammikas), relatives, and those who have invited, if another person says, "Speak of what you need," either due to some virtue or out of pleasure, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated for "should be requested."

In the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "This statement is made with reference to a limited invitation. The Pali regarding non-offense for relatives and those who have invited is made with reference to permanent invitation (niccapavāraṇā) which occurs in every way. Permanent invitation means a type of request that arises thus: 'Whenever you need anything, please speak of it at that time.' Saying, 'Take the garment for wearing in the cold season,' and..."
367:
it is stated: "It is allowable to take even more than four kaṃsas from those who are giving their property." It should be understood that this same method applies to the tenth training rule as well.

## 7. Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule

820-822. "Nagaraṃ atiharanti" (carrying past the city) is the original text. In some versions, it is "Nagaradvāre atiharanti", which means "by the city gate". Or, this very text is the original. When it is said that this statement is contradictory to what precedes or follows, it refers to the view stated as "it is said again", and not to the view stated there previously. Here, the writing "it contradicts the statement 'even having asked the mother'" is poorly written, because this was not said with the intention of contradicting that Pali. If a Pācittiya offence is incurred for doing it oneself, then a Pācittiya should also be incurred for causing it to be done. If a Dukkaṭa offence is incurred for causing it to be done, then a Dukkaṭa should also be incurred for doing it oneself. The meaning is that there is no difference between doing it oneself or causing it to be done in terms of incurring an offence.

"Sampaticchituṃ vaṭṭati" (it is allowable to accept) means it is allowable to say "Sādhu" (it is good) without rejecting it. In truth, it is not allowable to physically receive it. Because it is anāmāsa (unallowable to touch), it is said that "raw grain is not allowable even in the case of relatives or those who have given an invitation." In the Anuganthipada, however, it is stated: "A Dukkaṭa offence is incurred by a bhikkhunī who eats grain obtained in an allowable way after roasting it. The same method applies to aparanna (various beans and pulses)." And it is said: "From the statement 'anāpatti ābādhapaccayā' (no offence due to the cause of illness), it is evident that the seven types of grain are also anāmāsa; therefore, in the commentary below, the seven types of grain are also taken as anāmāsa in the section on Dukkaṭa objects." If they were allowable objects (kappiya-vatthu) that could be touched, then just as it is said without distinction "she asks for aparanna" regarding relatives and those who have invited, it should have been said: "There is no offence for asking from relatives or those who have invited for the sake of another, or for one who is insane or the first-offender." Because it is a Dukkaṭa object and because it is anāmāsa, it is not allowable to ask even a mother for the seven types of grain; therefore, to clarify that meaning, it is said regarding the seven types of grain: "There is no offence due to the cause of illness." Just as it is allowable for a bhikkhunī due to the cause of illness, so too...
370:
...it should be understood that it is allowable for a bhikkhu as well. Alternatively, just as it is not allowable for a bhikkhunī to cause roasting and so on to be done, so it is for a bhikkhu. This is also stated in the Andhaka Commentary: "A certain foolish bhikkhu, not knowing what is allowable, said this: 'It is not allowable for bhikkhus to accept raw grain. Roast, pound, and cook this grain, and give it as gruel, snacks, and meals.' An offence is incurred only by the bhikkhu who gives the order, and there is no offence for all the others." Therefore, it is also not allowable to say to monastery attendants (ārāmikas), "Pound the grain for the bhikkhus on duty." However, it should be understood that it is allowable to say things such as, "Take the provisions for the day," "Prepare the rice," "You take this much, you take that much."

Regarding the statement, "It is allowable to accept grain obtained without asking for the sake of new construction (navakamma)," this is well-said because it refers to the method stated below: "If it is said, 'We donate this tank, field, or land for the monastery,' it is allowable to accept." If it is said, "We donate grain for the sake of new construction," one should say "Sādhu." Regarding the statement below, "Among those objects, it is not allowable to accept a Nissaggiya object for oneself, or for the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a shrine... a Dukkaṭa offence is incurred by a bhikkhu who accepts a Dukkaṭa object for the sake of anyone," that too is well-said. Why? Because if it is said, "I wish to give grain for the sake of a shrine; Bhante, please accept it for that purpose," it is unallowable to receive it. And it is said, "But this object is not of that nature." All these arrangements are said to be the view of Elder Upatissa. Elder Dhammasiri, however, says: "Even in the past, accepting for the sake of new construction was not forbidden; grain accepted for the sake of the Saṅgha is unallowable only for the one who receives it."

## The Commentary on the Seventh Training Rule is Finished.

In this training rule, throwing is the action (kiriyā), and not looking is the non-action (akiriyā).

371: ## 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule. The phrase "discarding after informing the owner" is absent in some books and present in others. Due to the nature of the training rule regarding action and non-action, its presence is better. In this context, field guards and garden guards are considered "owners." If there is no agreement stating "rubbish must not be discarded in the Sangha's field or garden," it is permissible for a monk to discard it there because it belongs to the Sangha, but it is not permissible for bhikkhunīs. For them, it is permissible in a field belonging to the Bhikkhunī-Saṅgha according to the method mentioned, but not for a monk there. Even so, it is said that it should be done only in a proper manner. ## The Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule is finished. ## 10. Commentary on the Tenth Training Rule. Regarding the phrase "sādhukīḷita-gītaṃ vā," it is not permissible to listen even to songs that are of a noble practice (related to the virtues of the Buddha). However, it is stated in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary that "it is permissible to listen to the Dhamma associated with song." In the ancient Ganṭhipada, it is said that "even Dhamma-related songs are not permissible," and if someone says, "Let us sing and play music for the Buddha," it is not permissible to accept; doing so results in an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If someone says, "Let us perform an offering, or let us preach a Jātaka or a story," it is permissible to accept by saying "Very well." "Eka-payoga" means watching at a single place for one day. "Tesaṃyeva" refers to those whose dancing one watches. The phrase "A bhikkhunī must not herself dance, sing, or play music," etc., is not present in this training rule. Why? Because it has the eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna (origin like the sheep's wool rule). If so, why is it mentioned? It is mentioned because of the Great Authorities in accordance with the Suttas (suttānuloma-mahāpadesa). If it is not permissible to watch or listen to dancing, etc., then how could it be permissible to do it oneself? It is mentioned because it can be understood through this method. Otherwise, the Great Authorities would be useless. The same method should be applied in other cases as well. It is written that "the origin (samuṭṭhāna) should not be taken only as mentioned in this training rule, but should be taken by way of the six origins (cha-samuṭṭhāna)." If that writing refers to vocal action (vacī-kamma) such as "You should not tell others to dance, sing, or play music," then it is well-written, because there is no speech in the eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna. If it refers to bodily action (kāya-kamma) such as "dancing oneself," then it is poorly written. For the eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna is strictly...
372: ...bodily action. Therefore, it should be understood that one should not take the extracted reason but only what is included by the word "ādi" (etc.) here. In the statement "eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhānattā" (because of the sheep's wool origin), when stating the reason, it should be taken as extracted in the phrase "suttānuloma-mahāpadesato" (from the Great Authorities in accordance with the Suttas); thus, it should be understood that the statement was written according to what was available. Thera Upatissa said, "It is of the eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna by way of the training rule taught specifically by the Buddha himself." Commentary on the Darkness Chapter (Andhakāra-vagga) ## 1. Commentary on the First Training Rule. Ancient teachers say, "Darkness can also exist during the day; the word rattandhakāre (in the darkness of the night) is used to exclude such daytime darkness." In the word "santiṭṭheyya" (should stand), all four postures are included by the indication of standing; therefore, a bhikkhunī who walks up and down (caṅkamana), etc., with a man within arm's reach (hatthapāsa) incurs only an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The phrase "sallapeyya vā" (or should converse) is mentioned only by way of the introduction because there is no distinction. Some teachers say that the statement "If she stands within arm's reach of a man and converses, she incurs an offense of expiation" is incorrect. Why? Because by merely standing within arm's reach of that man, one offense of expiation is already incurred. Another offense is not incurred by conversing. How is this known? It is known by way of the factors (aṅga). For the four factors of this training rule are stated as: it being the darkness of the night, standing or conversing within arm's reach of a man, the absence of a companion, and the desire for privacy. Among those factors, if an offense were to occur separately due to the reason of standing,
373:
In this training rule, there should be four factors. If another offense arises due to the cause of talking, there would be five factors in that offense as well. Therefore, although it should have been stated in the Mātikā Commentary as "four or five factors," it was not stated; thus, it should be understood that there is no separate offense due to the cause of talking. Some teachers, however, say that there is indeed [a separate offense] and that the statement in the Mātikā Commentary is intended for that purpose. How so? Because of the simultaneous arising of two offenses. What does this mean? It means that when there is talking, a four-factored pācittiya offense to be incurred due to the cause of standing, and a four-factored pācittiya offense to be incurred due to the cause of talking—these two pācittiya offenses are incurred simultaneously together. This [view of some teachers] is inappropriate because it contradicts the Pāḷi text. For in the Pāḷi text, it is stated: "'Or should talk' means she talks while standing within the arm's length (hatthapāsa) of a man; there is an offense of pācittiya." If there were two offenses, it should have been stated as "there is an offense of two pācittiyas" [but it was not so stated]. This method should be understood accordingly in the second training rule and so forth. In this training rule, if there is a desire for privacy with a male companion for a bhikkhunī, and if that man is not a companion [but the primary subject], offenses are incurred according to the number of men. If the companion is a bhikkhunī, and if that bhikkhunī also desires privacy with that man and is not [merely] a companion, some teachers say both incur an offense; however, this should be accepted only after investigation. In the Ancient Gaṇṭhipada, it is said: "There is a dukkhaṭa offense for standing within the arm's length," but that contradicts the Pāḷi text. For the Pāḷi text says: "She stands within the arm's length of a man; there is an offense of pācittiya." What more needs to be said? In the Mātikā Commentary on the fourth training rule, according to the statement "there are three pācittiya offenses in standing and so forth," the offense should be understood according to the number of bases (vatthu). It is concluded that it should be stated as "there are four or five factors here."

## The Explanation of the First Training Rule is Finished.

## 2-3-4. Explanations of the Second, Third, and Fourth Training Rules.

842-6. The second, third, and fourth training rules are clear in meaning. In all these training rules, it is stated in the Ancient Gaṇṭhipada: "Talking means speaking any kind of common talk (tiracchānakathā)."

In the fourth training rule, however, there is this distinction: Since it was first stated as "one [bhikkhunī] with one [man]," if she sends away the companion bhikkhunī, would it be said that a pācittiya offense cannot occur? It can occur. Why? Because it regards only the three acts such as standing and so forth, or because when the enjoyment of privacy is impossible for that bhikkhunī or for another bhikkhunī, it is possible for both bhikkhunīs to be in the same place; thus this statement is established.
374:
It is stated only this much: "Leaving the arm's length (hatthapāsa), she stands or talks." Why is "whispering in the ear" (nikaṇṇikaṃ jappeti) not mentioned? Because it is impossible [to whisper in the ear] when exceeding the arm's length. Because that third term is excluded, although it is possible, "sending away the companion bhikkhunī" was not mentioned. Therefore, according to the sense, it means that if she leaves the arm's length and stands, talks, or sends away the companion bhikkhunī, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa). This method applies also to [cases involving] a yakkha and so forth. In that context, it is not stated as "within the arm's length" or "leaving the arm's length" because in both cases there is an offense of wrongdoing. If it is asked whether "whispering in the ear" is not mentioned because it is impossible even in the section on non-offense (anāpatti-vāra)? It is possible; for when there is a duty to be done, whispering in the ear is possible. If so, why is it not stated thus? Because there is no purpose in whispering in the ear during blameless talk (anavajja-kathā), and because even in Dhamma talk, it was prohibited concerning Udāyī.

## The Explanations of the Second, Third, and Fourth Training Rules are Finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Fifth Training Rule

Because it is stated "A family (kula) means the four families," some [teachers] say it is allowable [to stay] in the monastery of sectarians (titthiya), as that monastery does not fall under the term "family." Some say it is not allowable because sectarians are included among the khattiyas and so forth. If it is said that it is inappropriate because that monastery is an allowable ground (kappiya-bhūmi)? No, because the aforementioned khattiyas and so forth are possible. Nevertheless, here, the family for alms-resort (gocara-kula) is intended. It is written: "The precinct (upacāra) is twelve cubits."

## The Explanation of the Fifth Training Rule is Finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Sixth Training Rule

Without saying "one [offense] for the sitting bhikkhunī, one for the lying bhikkhunī," it should not be said "for the bhikkhunī who goes after sitting" and so forth. For this offense is not due to the cause of going; it is stated by way of the intended conclusion [sitting or lying]. By the statement "two [offenses] for the bhikkhunī who sits and lies down," it is shown that going is not intended here. Likewise, it should also be stated "two for the bhikkhunī who lies down and sits." If so, why is it not stated "She lies down there; there is an offense of two pācittiyas for both bhikkhunīs"? Because lying down is possible even without sitting.
375:
Some teachers say that for a bhikkhunī who sits down and then lies down for the purpose of sleeping, only a single offense is incurred due to the effort of lying down.

## The Explanation of the Sixth Training Rule is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Seventh Training Rule

In the section on non-offense, the phrase "on a place permanently spread out" is not mentioned because it is stated as "having spread it out oneself or having had it spread out by another." In this training rule, as mentioned in the sixth training rule, if one sits or lies down on a place spread out in the usual manner, a pācittiya offense is indeed incurred. In other training rules, however, it refers to a place permanently spread out. In this training rule, as mentioned, if one sits or lies down having spread it out oneself or having had it spread out by another, a pācittiya offense is indeed incurred.

In both types of training rules, as mentioned in the fifth training rule, if one departs without asking permission, a pācittiya offense is indeed incurred. The teacher says that this interpretation is not mere speculation because no other time is considered apart from the time mentioned in the matrix (mātikā) of the section on non-offense. Alternatively, since the offenses included in these fifth, sixth, and seventh training rules are not mentioned in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) in the triads (tikas) such as "an offense is incurred in the morning, not in the afternoon" or "an offense is incurred at night, not during the day," it is appropriate to show these three training rules in conjunction with the three types of time as far as possible. Showing it this way is in accordance with the method of the Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa).

## The Explanation of the Seventh Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Eighth Training Rule

In the eighth training rule, a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred by a bhikkhu.

## The Explanation of the Eighth Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Ninth Training Rule

875-7. It should be understood that an offense is incurred when making an oath as mentioned, whether by way of a wrong view or a right view. Since it is stated in the matrix (mātikā), "oneself or another," if a bhikkhunī makes an oath concerning only herself, for her...
376:
...if she curses concerning only herself, a single offense is incurred. If she curses concerning only another, a single offense is also incurred. However, if she curses concerning both herself and another, two offenses are incurred. In this training rule, the triad division (tika) is intended for cursing concerning another only.

## The Explanation of the Ninth Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Tenth Training Rule

In the tenth training rule, the section on non-offense applies only to weeping, not to striking oneself. Therefore, even if one is afflicted by the loss of relatives and so on, if one only strikes oneself and does not weep, a dukkhaṭa offense is indeed incurred.

## The Explanation of the Tenth Training Rule is finished.

## The Explanation of the Andhakāra Vagga is finished.

## 3. Nagga Vagga

## 1-2. Explanation of the First and Second Training Rules

The first and second training rules of the Nagga Vagga have clear meanings. In the first training rule, there is this distinction: except for a bathroom and being covered by water, etc., a bhikkhu who bathes in such a way (without clothes) incurs a dukkhaṭa offense. Ancient teachers say that the Blessed One did not rebuke the wearing of a water-straining cloth because he himself had not yet allowed it. It is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: "It is not proper to bathe wearing or wrapping only a single piece of cloth."

## The Explanation of the First and Second Training Rules is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Third Training Rule

In the third training rule, an offense is indeed incurred even by a bhikkhunī who lays down her burden within four or five days. For a bhikkhunī who lays down her burden when her gender changes, a dukkhaṭa offense is incurred because it is a triad of dukkhaṭas (tika-dukkhaṭa). It is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: "In this context, 'together with many bhikkhunīs' means even four bhikkhunīs are considered many bhikkhunīs."

## The Explanation of the Third Training Rule is finished.
377:
## 4. Explanation of the Fourth Training Rule

In the fourth training rule, regarding the term "saṅghāṭicāra," it is said that this procedure applies only to robes that have been determined (adhiṭṭhita) as the saṅghāṭi and so on, and not to other robes. Among those robes, a nissaggiya offense is incurred due to being separated from the triple robes (ticīvara) only. Even during the robe-season, an offense is indeed incurred by a bhikkhunī who exceeds the five-day saṅghāṭicāra (exchanging five robes). It is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: "It is not proper to perform the higher ordination (upasampadā) without these robes."

## The Explanation of the Fourth Training Rule is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Fifth Training Rule

In the section on non-offense of the fifth training rule, the meaning "due to not being separated from that bhikkhunī" is obtained.

## The Explanation of the Fifth Training Rule is finished.

907-911. The sixth and seventh training rules have clear meanings.

## 8. Explanation of the Eighth Training Rule

It is said that the one called "sokajjhāyikā" is a female magician. Ancient teachers also say she is a destroyer or a contentious person.

## The Explanation of the Eighth Training Rule is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Ninth Training Rule

Because it is stated, "Why did she exceed it?", it is clear that Thullanandā caused it to be exceeded by saying, "Wait for the robe-season."

## The Explanation of the Ninth Training Rule is finished.

In the tenth training rule, regarding the phrase "eka-kulaṃ etadavocuṃ", the word "kula" refers to the people in that house; therefore, it is used in the plural form.

## 4. Commentary on the Chapter on Lying Down (Tuvaṭṭavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the First Training Rule
934-5. Regarding the statement, "If one nun lies down while another is already lying down, she commits an offense of Pacittiya," some say that the cause of the offense is not making the nun who lay down first get up, and that both action (kiriya) and non-action (akiriya) are involved here. However, this statement contradicts the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). This is because the Commentary states only "action" (kiriya). If so, who commits the offense? Both commit the offense based on the action of lying down. In the "non-offense" section of this training rule, the phrase "having shown a boundary" is not included; therefore, some say that it is not allowable to lie down even after making a boundary mark. Others say it is allowable in a very spacious bed. It is written in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada that "it is allowable to lie down after making a boundary between them."

## End of Commentary on the First Training Rule.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule
Regarding the phrase "having shown a boundary," some say it is allowable if one makes a coil of the upper robe in the middle and places it between the two. It should be understood that if the boundary object does not remain in its place and a nun lies down crossing that boundary, she indeed commits an offense. In the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada, it is stated as "action and non-action."

## End of Commentary on the Second Training Rule.
379:
## 3. Commentary on the Third Training Rule
If a senior (vuḍḍhatara) comes to the place where one is reciting, or if they come at the time of paying homage, there is no need to ask permission. However, in a single room, one must ask permission. It is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: "If a Mahātherī lives in the room and another is present before her, one must ask permission because it is her vicinity (upacāra)."

## End of Commentary on the Third Training Rule.

946-950. The meanings of the fourth and fifth training rules are clear.

## 6. Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule
The term "gahapati" (householder) should be understood as excluding fellow practitioners (sahadhammika). Therefore, the meaning that a nun who associates with a monk or a novice in an improper manner should not be admonished is indeed possible.

## End of Commentary on the Sixth Training Rule.

961-5. The meanings of the seventh and eighth training rules are clear.

## 9. Commentary on the Ninth Training Rule
"Ekindriya" (one-sensed) means having only the body-sense (kāyindriya), which is the view of the Nigaṇṭhas and Acelakas. The Kāpilas, however, considering that "there are five senses," say this: "Because they have eyes, vines such as gourds and māluva go towards an object. Because they have ears, banana trees conceive (take a 'pregnancy') upon hearing the sound of thunder. Because they have noses, trees such as jackfruit fruit due to the smell of rot. Because they have tongues, they drink water with their roots, which serve as tongues; therefore, all are called 'pādapa' (those who drink with their feet). Because they have the physical sensitivity of the body (kāyapasāda), Asoka trees bloom at the touch of a woman." "Saṅghāta" refers to destruction.
380:
In this training rule as well, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to the breaking of the rains-retreat (vassaccheda). It should be understood that a pācittiya offense is incurred due to wandering (cārikā) after having first entered the rains-retreat. If one wanders without having entered the rains-retreat, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred due to the failure to enter the retreat. In the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, however, it is said: "A nun who wanders within the rains-retreat during the seven-day period incurs a pācittiya. But it is allowable for a seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya); for a monk, it is a dukkaṭa."

"Kena ci ubbāḷhā" means due to a cause for breaking the rains-retreat, according to the teacher. To what extent does it constitute wandering? This question has not been analyzed in all gaṇṭhipadas. Since it is stated in the subsequent training rule, "even at least five or six leagues (yojana)," it should be understood that those five or six leagues are the lower limit (minimum distance).

## Navama-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

In the tenth training rule, they recite "āhundarikā," it is said.

## 6. Āရာမဝဂ္ဂဝဏ္ဏနာ
The first training rule has a clear meaning.

## 2. Dutiya-sikkhāpada-vaṇဏနာ
If a nun abuses a monk, she incurs a pācittiya by this training rule. If she abuses a nun, she incurs an offense by the omasavāda (insulting speech) rule. In omasavāda, the offense is reached only in the presence; here, however, it is incurred even in the absence.

In this matter, there is this analysis: In the omasavāda training rule of the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga, a nun stands in the position of an unordained person (anupasampanna); thus, the meaning is established that in the omasavāda training rule of the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga as well, a monk stands in the position of an unordained person to the nun. In this training rule, a dukkaṭa is stated for abusing an unordained person, and a pācittiya is stated for abusing an ordained person (upasampanna). Therefore, these two training rules, when compared regarding a monk, do not agree with each other.

They should be understood in such a way that they do agree. In that sequence of words, according to the method stated in the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, one should not take [the monk] as unordained in the omasavāda training rule of the nuns; this alone is appropriate in this decision. In the word "paribhāseyya" (should revile), it should be stated excluding the grounds for abuse (akkosa-vatthu). Some teachers say that if any one of those grounds for abuse is present, it is only an omasavāda pācittiya; that statement is not...
383:
That statement is appropriate. In the Omasavāda training rule, an insult not explicitly mentioned in the Pali text results in a dukkaṭa offense. In the context of dukkaṭa, the teachers have pointed out this pācittiya offense; therefore, the insult should be understood only by the power of the words appearing in the Pali text, such as 'these are fools.'

## The Explanation of the Second Training Rule is finished.

The third training rule has a clear meaning.

## 4. Explanation of the Fourth Training Rule

Regarding the phrase 'either invited or refused (pavārita)', it was first stated in the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada as follows: 'Even if one has refused (pavārita), one is allowed to drink rice gruel (yāgu), but one is not allowed to eat rice gruel mixed with curry. Here, rice gruel does not fall under the category of hard food (khādanīya) or soft food (bhojanīya). If an invited nun wishes to eat after going for alms, she may eat only after asking permission from the donors. There is no offense for nuns regarding consecutive meals (paramparabhojana). If an invited nun, whether she has eaten that meal or not, should refuse (pavārita), she is not allowed to eat even after having it made allowable (kappiya); a nun invited with an unallowable invitation is also not allowed to accept invitations.'

In that context of invitation, it is stated, 'Even if one has refused, one is allowed to drink rice gruel,' because it is permitted in both the Pali text and the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For it is said in the Pali text, 'An invited nun who has not refused drinks rice gruel.' In that Pali text, the following statement is the decision preceded by the explanation of the training rule: In the phrase 'either invited or refused,' by the word 'or' (vā), if a nun who is invited with an unallowable invitation and has not refused, eats or consumes any other hard food or soft food, excluding rice gruel and without asking permission from the owners, she commits a pācittiya offense.

If it is asked, 'What benefit do nuns gain by not having the paramparabhojana rule?' It is not that they gain a benefit; rather, it simply becomes more evident. Monks also are allowed to eat only after performing the vikappanā (assignment) and mixing. They receive it as they wish during the proper time. If it is asked, 'What is the benefit of this asking for permission?' It should be understood that nuns who have refused or those who were not invited do not receive even the remains of a sick person's food after having it made allowable (kappiya); and nuns who are both invited and have refused do not receive even rice gruel, even if they ask for permission.

## The Explanation of the Fourth Training Rule is finished.

## The Explanation of the Ārāma-vagga is finished.
