## 7. Explanation of the Gabbhini-vagga
## 1. Explanation of the First and Subsequent Training Rules

The word 'pregnant' (gabbhinī) is used because the state of pregnancy is known through seeing and other signs. In the word-by-word analysis (padabhājana), the state of having refused (pavārita) is not evident.

In the phrase 'or a wet-nurse' (dhāti vā), she takes the child from the owners and raises it to maturity; some teachers say that a mother also raises a child in the same way.

The teachers residing in Sri Lanka prefer the reading 'sikkhamānaṃ' because of its verbal or non-verbal nature, while the teachers residing in Jambudīpa (India) prefer the reading 'sikkhamānā'. The meaning of that reading is: she is called 'sikkhamānā' because she cherishes the training rules (sikkha-dhamma). Here, the action is not intended; only the name (saññā) is intended. Those sikkhamānās who have not yet trained in the six rules should not be ordained; if they are ordained, the preceptor nun and others commit an offense. Some teachers say, 'Her ordination is indeed valid.'

In the term 'dhamma-kamma', the act of ordination (upasampadā-kamma) is intended.

'The one who has ordained' (vuṭṭhāpitā) refers to the elder nun by whom the candidate for ordination is raised from the status of a novice (sāmaṇerī). That elder nun is called 'vuṭṭhāpitā'. For that very reason, she is further qualified by the term 'pavattinī' (preceptor).

## The Explanation of the First and Subsequent Training Rules is finished.
## The Explanation of the Gabbhini-vagga is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Kumāribhūta-vagga
## 2. Explanation of the Second and Subsequent Training Rules

Just as it is stated in this training rule, 'I allow you, monks, to give the agreement of training (sikkha-sammuti) to a maiden of eighteen years... and so on,' it is not directly stated, 'I allow you, monks, to give the agreement of training to a married girl (gihigatā) of ten years... and so on.' Therefore, it is said, 'The agreement of training should be given only to a married girl who has completed twelve years.' Some teachers, however, say that because it is stated that the agreement of training should be given to a married girl, even if she is ten years old...
385:
(Granting the training agreement to a gihigata probationer who is ten years old) is allowable. Why? Because it is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: "It is stated (in the Pācittaya Pāḷi) that 'There is no offense in ordaining one who has completed twelve years and who perceives that twelve years are completed' (Pāc. 1093-1095) and 'There is no offense in ordaining a gihigata who has completed twelve years... who has trained in the training' (Pāc. 1097-1101)." What is the benefit of this answer? It has already been stated that "The training agreement (sikkhāsammuti) should be given to a gihigata who is ten years old." If it is said that "It is not even allowable to say 'gihigata'," it is written that the legal act (kamma) is invalidated.

In the phrase "Aham eva nūna... alajjinī, yā saṅgho," the word "yā" means "Am I indeed the only foolish one?" There is also a reading "yaṃ saṅgho." In that case, "yaṃ" means because (the Saṅgha) gives, therefore am I indeed the only foolish one?

Why is one who associates with men, associates with boys, is harsh, or is given to sorrow called a sikkhamānā (probationer)? Why is this sikkhamānā described in the Padabhājana as "one who has trained in the training in the six dhammas"? It should be understood that she is so called because she has taken the training previously and because she has completed the training previously.

1166-7. Regarding the phrase "seeing much food to be eaten and enjoyed," it is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada: "It is said that the relatives of the sikkhamānā prepared (the food); seeing that preparation, she dismissed the elder monks. Having dismissed them, she took the consent (chanda) of those elders, and having formed a group with the monks who had previously given consent, she treated the consent of the remaining monks as mere consent and had the legal act performed." Regarding the phrase "relinquishing consent," it is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: "This act should not be done today; let it be as you wish," and thus it is relinquished. Therefore, even if a harsh-spoken or foolish person says "let it be as you wish," because it depends on the elder, it is relinquished only if there is the elder's approval; if there is no approval, it is not. Even so, they perform the act only after taking consent again; this is the preliminary effort (payoga). There is no special benefit in taking (consent), but if the Elder of the Saṅgha relinquishes it, it should be performed only after taking consent. Regarding the phrase "for one who has relinquished consent and risen with the body," the space here is narrow. If they leave the arm's length (hatthapāsa) saying "we will do it in such and such a place," there is no fault. Even if there is no fault, if those persons go without leaving the arm's length, this is the preliminary effort (payoga). "Performing Uposatha and Pavāraṇā during the stale night (rattipārivāsiya) is not allowable; however, other legal acts are allowable. Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are also not allowable on days that are not Uposatha or Pavāraṇā days; other legal acts are allowable at all times."
386:
In a stale assembly (parisapārivāsiya), if four monks go without leaving the arm's length (hatthapāsa), or in another act to be done by a group of four (catuvagga), if five, ten, or twenty monks go, it is allowable for the remaining monks to go separately to various places and then return to the meeting place to perform the act. In a stale intention (ajjhāsayapārivāsiya), if they remain sitting as they were without leaving the arm's length, it is allowable to perform the act again because the arm's length was not left; so it is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada. According to the opinion of those ancient teachers, only stale consent (chandapārivāsiya) is not allowable, and the reaching of the factor is shown; some teachers say that in this training rule, that stale consent is not shown separately because it is impossible. The teacher says: "Our thought is that if a monk who has given consent reaches the assembly and then leaves, that monk's previous giving of consent is called stale consent (chandapārivāsiya)."

In this matter, this is the final conclusion—in the Commentary regarding stale assembly, the statement "they rise without relinquishing consent, saying 'we shall go elsewhere' ... it is allowable to perform the act" does not clearly mention the leaving of the arm's length. However, in this case, it should be desired only that the monks eligible for the act do not leave the arm's length; thus it is stated in the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada. If one asks, "Even if it is not clear, is it allowable because it is not prohibited?" No, it is not, because it is prohibited. How? What is called consent (chanda) comes only when monks eligible for the act are assembled within one boundary (sīmā), not when they are not assembled. For here it is said "without relinquishing consent" and "because consent is not relinquished." It is not said "without relinquishing intention (ajjhāsaya)" or "because intention is not relinquished." Therefore, the non-relinquishing of consent occurs only by the non-leaving of the arm's length by monks eligible for the act, not by leaving it; this is the established meaning.

And here it is said:
"From whatever cause the arrival of consent occurs, its absence is the suppression;
Therefore, when monks are assembled, it occurs through the distinction of that (consent)."

Just like stale night consent (rattipārivāsiya-chanda), stale night purity (rattipārivāsiya-pārisuddhi) is also valid; therefore, in accordance with that stale night consent, consent, purity, or Pavāraṇā for the sake of the next day is allowable. It is allowable to perform the act with that consent etc., performed for the sake of the next day. Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, however, are not allowable on a day that is not an Uposatha day; other acts are allowable. Performing the fifteenth-day Uposatha on the fourteenth day is allowable because it is the proper time (khetta). Some teachers say that performing the fourteenth-day Uposatha on the fifteenth day is not allowable because it is not the proper time, because it is not the Uposatha day, and because it is the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada); therefore,
387:
According to the view of those teachers, it is not proper to perform the third or seventh Cātuddasī Uposatha on a Pannarasī day. Regarding what is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "If they are seated intending to perform the Cātuddasī Uposatha, it is proper to perform it as a Pannarasī day," they explain it as follows: "Only on a Pannarasī Uposatha day, if they are seated intending to perform the Cātuddasī Uposatha, it is proper to perform their Pannarasī Uposatha as a Pannarasī day on the following day." This view of theirs does not agree with the statement in the Mātikāṭṭhakathā: "When there is such a reason, it is proper to perform the Uposatha on another Cātuddasī day as well." This is because it is not stated in that Mātikāṭṭhakathā that "it is proper to perform the Cātuddasī Uposatha on another Pannarasī day as well." Even so, since it is included in the permitted days as "once a fortnight, on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth," it is established that the Pannarasī day following the six Cātuddasī Uposathas is not a non-Uposatha day. Even if this is established, it should be understood that the statement "Pannarasī for resident monks, Cātuddasī for visiting monks; visiting monks must follow the resident monks whether they are equal in number or fewer" is useless in this context.

## Nigamanavaṇṇanā (Conclusion)

Festivals like Giraggasamajja are stated to be "acittaka lokavajja" (worldly faults that incur an offense even without intention); therefore, if a bhikkhunī watches or applies perfumes without knowing it is a performance or a scent, she incurs an offense through a mind that does not know the object; thus they are acittaka. For a bhikkhunī who watches or applies perfumes while knowing it is a performance or a scent, they are lokavajja (worldly faults) because they are unwholesome. Acts such as ordaining a thief are sacittaka (with intention) because an offense is incurred only when done while knowing the object, such as knowing "this is a thief." Acts such as giving higher ordination (upasampadā) are paṇṇattivajja (prescribed faults) because they should not be done only with an unwholesome mind. It is written: "In this context, being sacittaka or acittaka should be taken not by the knowledge or ignorance of the regulation (paṇṇatti), but only by the knowledge or ignorance of the object (vatthu)."

In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated: "Because festivals like Giraggasamajja are said to be acittaka lokavajja, for a bhikkhunī who watches a magician's tricks such as the skull trick while reflecting on them without knowing the object by its name as 'dance,' 'saṅghāṇi' (waist-string), or 'perfume'; or for a bhikkhunī who ties a saṅghāṇi around her waist for the sake of ornaments like a collarbone-garland; or for a bhikkhunī who bathes after applying perfume with the thought 'I will worship the Buddha after removing the smell of sweat,' these are called acittaka because an offense exists even with a mind that does not know the object by name or along with the name. They should not be called acittaka because an offense is incurred when one takes a saṅghāṇi in the dark thinking 'this is a waist-string (kaṭisutta)' and wears it, or when one takes perfume thinking it is clay and applies it. In such a time of misperception, there is no offense. For this reason, the Pali text did not state 'there is a pācittiya offense' in the case of misperceiving a saṅghāṇi as a non-saṅghāṇi. Just as it is established that one can wear a saṅghāṇi etc. without an unwholesome mind because of the statement 'one may wear a waist-string (kaṭisutta) due to a disease of the field (khetta-ābādha),' likewise, it is clear that one cannot drink alcohol even without an unwholesome mind due to a disease. This is because there is no Pali text stating 'there is no offense if one drinks an intoxicant due to a disease.' It is also clear that a surāpāna (drinking intoxicants) offense is incurred when one swallows alcohol placed in a handful of honey without an unwholesome mind. This is because it is taught: 'Even if one perceives it as not being alcohol, if one drinks it, there is a pācittiya offense.' Not much more needs to be said; for a bhikkhunī who wears or applies these while knowing them as 'saṅghāṇi' or 'perfume' with the perception of desiring sensual pleasures, without a reason for exemption, they are called lokavajja because they are truly unwholesome. In this manner, the method should be applied to the remaining training rules. Among these statements, regarding surāpāna, it is said to be the view of Elder Upatissa. In the Asaṅkaccika training rule, the reading 'for a bhikkhunī who enters the precinct of an unenclosed village,' and also in the training rules of requesting superior food, the Acelaka training rule, going to the house of one who has invited, concealing a grave offense (duṭṭhullā āpatti), ordaining one less than twenty years old, traveling with a woman by appointment, entering the king's palace, entering a village at the wrong time without informing a present bhikkhu, sitting, and so forth..."

## Mahāvagga-vaṇṇanā
## Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Mahākhandhaka-vaṇṇanā
## Bodhikathā-vaṇṇanā
Now is the opportune time to reveal the distinctions of words and such that are hidden within the Khandhaka. Therefore, I shall speak only of the new meanings of the Vinaya in brief for easy comprehension.

In that context (the passage 'Khandhakovidā'), for what reason is this called 'Khandhaka'? It is called Khandhaka because it is a collection of 'Khandhas' (sections), similar to the Vibhaṅga. What are those Khandhas? They are called Khandhaka because they reveal and clarify the Khandhas. Here, 'Khandha' refers to the regulations known as Vinaya acts such as Pabbajjā (Going Forth), as well as the training rules of conduct (cāritta) and avoidance (vāritta). Indeed, because these Vinaya acts like Pabbajjā were prescribed by the Blessed One, they are called 'Paññatti' (regulations). The word 'Khandha' is also found in the sense of 'Paññatti' (a mass/group), as in 'dārukkhandha' (a log of wood), 'aggikkhandha' (a mass of fire), and 'udakakkhandha' (a mass of water). Because they reveal and explain these 'Khandhas' known as regulations, the twenty specific regulations such as the Pabbajjā-khandhaka are called 'Khandhakas.' The two Khandhakas at the end are also called 'Khandhaka' because they are similar to the Buddha's teachings. It is like calling virtue 'Sīlavelā' (the boundary of virtue) due to its similarity to a boundary. Alternatively, the meanings of 'portion' (bhāga) and 'mass' (rāsi) are also appropriate for this term 'Khandhaka,' because those regulations are analyzed by portion and by mass.

What is the sequential reason for these Khandhakas? This question is not appropriate. This is because even if they were taught in another way, one cannot avoid the necessity of such a sequence. Alternatively, since entering the Dispensation (Sāsana) is preceded by Pabbajjā and Upasampadā (Higher Ordination), the Mahākhandhaka, which encompasses the meanings of Pabbajjā and Upasampadā, is spoken of first. Who spoke it? It was spoken by the Elders who compiled the scriptures (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka). The Blessed One, however, taught according to the various events (vatthu) that arose in various places, not in this specific order. But the Elders, for specific purposes, grouped similar teachings together and recited them in sequence. The purpose of the remaining teachings will be made clear in their respective places.

'Khandhakovidā' means those Elders who are skilled in the meaning of Khandha in the sense of regulations, portions, and masses, and who have reached the far shore of Nirutti-paṭisambhidā (analytical insight into language). The explanation (saṃvaṇṇanā) of those words with obscure meanings will follow. Why is it distinguished in this way? Because the remaining portions from that Khandhaka are appropriate.
392:
In this context, the inclusion of the origin of the Mātikā (Matrix) should be understood through the inclusion of the Padabhājanīya (Word Analysis). If the meanings of specific words have already been revealed in the Aṭṭhakathā (Commentary), and if those specific words were to be spoken here again, when would the explanation of those various meanings reach an end? This statement is consistent with the Niddesa (Exposition) of that Khandhaka. What benefit is there in explaining the Pali that is already clear? Is it not that the meanings are already clear? If it is argued that the statement is possible through phrases like 'Adhippāyānusandhīhi' (by way of intention and sequence), it is not so. This is because specific words are grasped here by the term 'Attha' (meaning). Indeed, those meanings should be understood as 'Attha' either in the sense of meaning that is not separate from the essence, or in the sense of what is expressed by the word, or by way of metaphorical usage (upacāra) where the word is applied to the meaning. 'Saṃvaṇṇanānayo' means: Commentary (saṃvaṇṇanā) is called 'Naya' (method) because it demonstrates the process of adding or removing (uha-apoha) what is not explicitly stated.

'Uruvelā' is a village that received its name based on the aforementioned heap of sand. Therefore, the locative case 'Uruvelāyaṃ' is used in the sense of 'near.' To show that it is in the sense of 'near,' the phrase 'najjā Nerañjarāya tīre' (on the bank of the river Nerañjarā) and so on is spoken. Otherwise, it would imply that he was dwelling in that heap of sand, and it would also contradict statements such as 'He entered Uruvelā for alms' and 'Where the army town of Uruvelā is.' In the Aṭṭhakathā, however, only the root cause is shown. In that Aṭṭhakathā, the concluding statement 'Referring to that, it was said... [pe] ... should be seen' is made. If it is asked, 'What is the purpose of showing this?', the purpose is to show that the aforementioned word-meaning is possible with reference to the village. The statement 'That village receives this name by metaphorical usage (upacāra) of that nearby sand heap' is not spoken because it is understood even without being said. Alternatively, the name 'Uruvelā' is the name of the aforementioned sand heap, and it is also the name of the village near that sand heap. In this context, the Venerable Upāli Thera did not say 'He was dwelling in Uruvelā' with reference to the village, because there was no purpose for a resort village (gocara-gāma). Indeed, the Blessed One did not make that village his resort and dwell there at that time. Therefore, it should be understood that the Teacher of the Commentary said this because he wished to show that the Elder [Upāli] spoke this with reference to the dwelling at the foot of the Bodhi tree near the sand heap. Thus, it should be understood that by showing the Enlightenment of the Blessed One in the forest far from the village, the Elder [Upāli] established the second place of occurrence with three words. Otherwise, the speaking of the three words would be without purpose. In the Pali 'najjā Nerañjarāya,' when analyzed (viggaha): it is called 'Nadī' (river) because it goes along sounding. In the word 'Nelañjalā,' the letter 'la' is changed to 'ra' to become 'Nerañjarā.' It means a river with faultless water because it is free from mud and moss. Alternatively, 'Nīlajalā' (blue water) is the name of that river itself.
393:
In the phrase "Bodhirukkhamūle," "Bodhi" refers to the penetrative realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisambodha). In terms of essence, this Bodhi is the Blessed One's fourth path knowledge (catuttha-magga-ñāṇa). This is because it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "This is called the end of liberation" (vimokkhantikametaṃ nāma). Although the fourth fruition knowledge (catuttha-phala-ñāṇa), which is the basis for the name, could also be mentioned, here only the fourth path knowledge should be understood as "Bodhi" because it performs the necessary tasks. For this reason, the Pali text itself shows this very path knowledge by saying, "For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints by the third knowledge." However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is presented as "factors of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅgā) and "requisites of enlightenment" (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā). Since the knowledge in the four paths is called "Bodhi" in that Pali, it was stated in the Cūḷaniddesa with the intention of speaking generally: "The knowledge in the four paths is called Bodhi," because the knowledge of the path of Arahatship intended here is also included within those four paths.

Alternatively, since there is no place in the Pali where the Blessed One's first three paths are mentioned, the "four paths" are mentioned to prevent the sectarian view that only the fourth path knowledge directly arose in the Blessed One, or that the Blessed One did not become a Buddha after reaching the states of Stream-entry and so on. The first three paths are established by the designation of Bodhi because they serve as the decisive support (upanissaya) for the fourth path. Just as a tree that is the cause of fruit or produces fruit is called a "fruit tree" (phala-rukkha), the tree that is the cause of Bodhi knowledge should be understood as the "Bodhi tree" (bodhi-rukkha). Regarding this, it is stated later: "Because Bodhi is also the name of the tree, it is called Bodhi." The specific mention to distinguish it from trees like the Nigrodha is to prevent confusion with other Bodhi-tree sites. Since path knowledge is the root of wholesome states (kusala-mūla), it can be designated as both Bodhi and a root (mūla). The connection is: "Having first attained supreme enlightenment, he sits." By this, it shows that he sat in a single cross-legged posture for eight days, including the day of enlightenment. Here, the word "eka" (single) indicates that this posture, which is a form of sitting consistent with the practice of a recluse, was not interrupted by any other posture or was not disturbed.

In the term "vimuttisukhaṃ," it cannot be interpreted as bliss in liberation. Since the Blessed One is associated with the fifth jhāna, liberation, which is called the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), is itself the bliss of Nibbāna in the sense of the calming of defilements; thus it is "the bliss of liberation." He sat experiencing that bliss by entering that attainment. He sat with regard for the time of those to be tamed (veneyya) so as not to let it pass, not out of attachment to the bliss of liberation.

"Atha kho" are two particles used at the start of a new section. By these words, it is shown that he did not contemplate dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) while experiencing the bliss of liberation, but only after emerging from that attainment. The repeated contemplation of the already-penetrated dependent origination is because it is profound and because it produces joy and rapture (pīti-pāmojja). It is not because he wished to see a new method. Since the Blessed One has directly realized all phenomena, the contemplation by taking as an object the dependent origination which has been unconfusedly penetrated...
394:
The repeated reflection on the Dhamma of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), which has been well-attended to through penetration, is because it generates delight due to its profundity. It is not with the intention of showing a new method. Since the Blessed One has realized all phenomena and is free from delusion, reflecting on the penetrated Dependent Origination as an object generates a fresh rapture, similar to a king reviewing the territory he has conquered. It is said in the Dhammapada: "For one who rightly practices insight into the Dhamma, there is a delight that transcends human delight" (Dhp 373). The phrase "throughout the first watch of the night" is in the accusative case indicating continuous duration. By this, the various distinctions of that Dependent Origination are shown. Although it is said collectively as "reflected in forward and reverse order," it is stated as "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," etc., to show the reflection in this specific sequence. How is it known that only the process (pavatti) is intended for reflection there? It is known because it occurs first. Reflection in forward order is for the purpose of establishing the occurrence of causes and effects in that manner within forward Dependent Origination. Because only through the cessation of ignorance do volitional formations cease, and not otherwise. Therefore, it is shown that ignorance is the cause of volitional formations, and volitional formations are the result of ignorance. Similarly, in reflecting on Nibbāna, reflection in forward order is for the purpose of establishing the cessation of the effect due to the cessation of the cause. Here, Nibbāna is shown by way of its power (ānubhāva). That Nibbāna is not merely the cessation of ignorance and so forth. In that sequence of the Pali text on Dependent Origination, it is clear that forward order is not intended by the words "when he understood the destruction of causes." Regarding the reflection on the Path (magga), there is nothing more to say; the Path is shown there in both forward and reverse orders by way of function, object, and the scope of that Path.

There, an objector says: the statement "he reflected on Dependent Origination in reverse order" is inappropriate. Because Nibbāna, which is indicated by the reverse order (cessation), cannot be Dependent Origination (arising due to conditions). Let us reply that this is not so. It will become clear if one understands the meaning of that statement. The phrase "forward and reverse" (anuloma-paṭiloma) is an adverbial compound. The meaning should be taken as "he reflected on that Dependent Origination in forward order and in reverse order." Otherwise, cessation (nirodha) would merely be equated with the reverse order itself. It should be understood that the fixed sequence in the reverse order is established by the fixed sequence in the forward order. In this case, it is clear that the "reverse" of Dependent Origination means the non-occurrence (cessation) of Dependent Origination. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "Cessation is non-arising," and so forth. If so, could there be a contradiction between the preceding and following statements? How so? Because the term "paṭicca" (dependent) shows the orientation toward the arising of the effect by grasping the cause of the effect and by the dependence of causes on their own causes; thus, non-arising (appaṭiccasamuppāda) would not be possible. Therefore, it would be "non-dependent-origination." Some teachers say that the reverse nature of that cessation is shown by negating both cause and effect in this way. That statement is inappropriate. Because the forward nature of that cessation is established, and because there is no excessive meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that "appaṭiccasamuppāda" (non-dependent-origination) is the meaning of the reverse order. For that very reason, the Blessed One spoke of the cessation of conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena in the Pali text. To elaborate, by saying "with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance," the cessation of the cause is shown by the total cutting off of the condition's cause, and the cessation of the conditionally arisen phenomenon is shown by the absence of grasping the cause of the effect. In the Pali text, these two types of cessation are called "non-arising" (anuppāda) in terms of meaning. With this reflection, it is stated in the Commentary: "Cessation is non-arising."
395:
Some teachers say that because it shows the tendency towards arising, *asamuppāda* (non-arising) is not possible; therefore, by rejecting both cause and effect in this way as *appaṭiccasamuppāda*, the reverse order (*paṭiloma*) of that cessation should be understood. That statement is not appropriate. It is not suitable because the forward order (*anuloma*) of that cessation is determined, and because there is no special distinction in meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that *appaṭiccasamuppāda* is the reverse order of that cessation. For this very reason, the Blessed One spoke of the cessation of conditions (*paccaya*) and conditionally arisen phenomena (*paccayuppanna*) in the Pali text. In that Pali text, by saying "*avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā*" (through the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance), He shows the cessation of the cause by way of the absolute cutting off of the causal state of the condition, and the cessation of the conditionally arisen by way of the non-acceptance of the cause for the effect. Considering that the two kinds of cessation in the Pali text are, in meaning, called non-arising (*anuppāda*), it is said in the Commentary: "Cessation occurs means non-arising occurs."

If it be asked: "In that case, does it follow that Nibbāna is merely the cessation of conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena?" No, because the intention is to show the power (*ānubhāva*) of that Nibbāna. *Viditavelāyaṃ* means at the time of reflecting; otherwise, it could lead to a meaning of not yet knowing prior to that time.

In the word *jhāyato*, indeed, for the Buddha who contemplates with "meditation on characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) become manifest, or the four Noble Truths (*ariyasacca*) become clear. Nevertheless, in the preceding part, for the purpose of showing the distinction of the three vehicles such as serenity (*samatha*), "meditation on objects" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) is taken. Taking the four Noble Truths indeed contradicts the context of showing the forward dependent origination (*anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda*). However, it should be understood that it is done by the power of the view: "He who fully understands suffering (*dukkha*) abandons the origin (*samudaya*)."

"*Paccayakkhayassa*" (of the destruction of conditions) is said by way of a figurative expression for the function. By that term, the two kinds of Nibbāna—Nibbāna as the condition and Nibbāna as the conditionally arisen dependent on that condition—are shown. Indeed, that Nibbāna does not only effect the destruction of conditions; it also effects the destruction of the conditionally arisen. Because the cessation of both is shown, yet considering that "through the cessation of the cause, the effect ceases," it is said "*paccayakkhayassa*." In the phrase "phenomena of the described nature" (*vuttappakārā dhammā*), it should be understood that the taking of the four Truths is done by reversing the method stated in the first verse.

In the phrase "the meaning known as the cessation of the origin" (*samudayanirodhasaṅkhāto attho*), "origin" (*samudaya*) is by way of function, and "cessation" (*nirodha*) is by way of the act of taking as an object. By this, it means that two kinds of cessation are shown by the power of that influence. Because the place where one sits cross-legged is also called "*pallaṅka*," the place where the fruition (*phala*) is attained is called "*pallaṅka*."
