## Commentary on the Ajapāla Story
In the word *sammodi*, the Blessed One, desiring the welfare [of the Brahmin], exchanged friendly greetings with that Brahmin. In the phrase *vedānaṃ antaṃ*, Nibbāna is called the "end" (*anta*). Alternatively, because of having reached the end of the Vedas (or knowledge), the fruition of Arahatship is called the "end." Between these two methods, according to the first method, because one is a *vedantagū* (one who has reached the end of knowledge), for that very reason, one is a *vusitabrahmacariya* (one who has lived the holy life). According to the second method, because one is a *vedantagū*, therefore one is a *vusitabrahmacariya*; thus the connection should be understood. Although the discourse connected with the four Truths was spoken in meaning to the Brahmin, it is said to be "*dhammacakkappavattana*" (the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma) in reference to the absence of the penetration (*paṭivedha*) mentioned in the Udāna verse; this is the explanation.

## The Commentary on the Ajapāla Story Ends.

## Commentary on the Mucalinda Story
In the Mucalinda story, the phrase "this meaning" is said in reference to the meaning that is about to be spoken. That *viveka* (seclusion) means *upadhiviveka* (seclusion from the defilements). By the words "In the world, non-harming is happiness," the first path (the Path of Stream-entry) is shown. This is because, by that path, the accomplishment of abandoning ill-will (*byāpāda*) that arises with the intent to kill living beings is achieved. By the words "restraint towards living beings," the second path (the Path of Once-returning) is shown. Indeed, a person possessing the path (a Once-returner) is restrained towards living beings by way of the thinning out of the remaining ill-will, because there is no intention to harm. In this way, the four paths are also taken in succession.

## The Commentary on the Mucalinda Story Ends.

## Commentary on the Rājāyatana Story
*Rājāyatana* is the *pātali* tree. "Having come from the four directions" is the remainder of the text to be understood. It is said that there were marks of distinction on the rims of the four bowls offered by the [Four] Great Kings. Those merchants, because of showing respect to the deity and because of their devotion upon seeing the physical body of the Blessed One, took refuge (*saraṇa*). It should be understood that upon hearing the words of the deity, "The Blessed One has first attained Enlightenment at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree," they knew the absence of the community of disciples (*sāvaka-saṅgha*) and the presence of the Dhamma realized by the Buddha. In the phrase "they know," it should be connected with the word "*buddhā*."

## The Commentary on the Rājāyatana Story Ends.
397:
## Commentary on the Request of Brahma

In the passage beginning with "Adhigato kho me" (I have indeed attained), the term 'Dhamma' refers to the Four Noble Truths, which are difficult to see because they are deep. Because they are difficult to see, they are difficult to understand. 'Santo' means having a peaceful nature. 'Paṇīto' means having a sublime nature that one can never have enough of. Both these terms are spoken with reference only to the supramundane (lokuttara) Dhamma. 'Atakkāvacaro' means that it cannot be accessed through 'takka'—the process of logical reasoning—but is the domain of wisdom (ñāṇa) alone. 'Paṇḍitavedanīyo' means a Dhamma to be experienced only by the wise who have practiced rightly.

All terms beginning with 'Sabbasaṅkhārasamatho' (the stilling of all formations) refer only to Nibbāna. Although Nibbāna is one, it is described in various ways through the metonymy of the fruit (phalūpacāra). 'Rāmā' refers to the assembly of beings. The repeatedly wonderful verses are called 'anacchariyā'. These verses are for those who have previously heard of the Buddha's prior practice, or for those who have previously attained the depth of the Dhamma. Although all four paths of the Blessed One are 'sukha-paṭipadā' (pleasant practice), He said, "I have attained with difficulty," with reference to His practice as a Bodhisatta. There are two readings: 'pakāsitaṃ' and 'pakāsituṃ'. 'Paretehi' refers to those associated with lust, hatred, and so on. 'Rāgarattā' refers to those infatuated with sensual lust (kāmarāga) and the lust for views (diṭṭhirāga). Those who cling to notions of self (atta) and permanence (nicca) do not see that Dhamma, nor will they see it.

It is said that Sahampati Brahma uttered the cry, "Alas, the world is perishing!" so loudly that the Brahmas of the ten thousand world systems heard it and assembled. Those who have little dust of lust and so on in their eye of wisdom, due to their underlying tendencies, are called 'apparajakkhajātika' (those with little dust in their eyes). 'Assavanatā' means due to not hearing.

Associated with teachers who have unwholesome defilements. 'Apāpuretaṃ' means "Open this door of Nibbāna." 'Amatassa dvāraṃ' (the door to the Deathless) refers to the Noble Path or the Four Noble Truths. It is the Dhamma repeatedly penetrated by the three true knowledges (vijjā) and the four path-knowledges. 'Sele' means on a mountain peak made of rock. Just as a man with sight standing on a clear vantage point, free from dust, could see the people all around, so too, O Sumedha of excellent wisdom, You are the 'Samantacakkhu' (All-seeing One) due to the attainment of omniscience. You are 'Vijitasaṅgāma' (Victor in battle) because you have conquered all battles of defilements. You are 'Satthavāha' (Caravan leader) because you are capable of leading the assembly of veneyya beings to cross the wilderness of birth (jāti-kantāra) and so on. You are 'Aṇaṇa' (Debtless) because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire (kāmacchanda).

'Buddhacakkhu' (the Buddha-eye) consists of the knowledge of the degrees of faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of their underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). These two knowledges are called the 'Buddha-eye'. 'Uppaliniyaṃ' means in a pond of lotuses. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood in the remaining terms.
398:
The same should be understood for the remaining terms. In the phrase "anto nimuggaposīnī," it refers to those lotuses that grow while remaining submerged within the water. Among those lotuses, some stand having emerged above the water; they stand awaiting the touch of the sun's rays and will bloom today. Some stand level with the water; they will bloom tomorrow. Some have not yet emerged from the water; they will bloom on the third day. There are other lotuses that do not emerge from the water, such as the 'saroga-uppala'. Those lotuses that will not bloom and will only become food for fish and turtles are mentioned in the Pali text and are brought forth to be shown. These lotuses are to be compared with the four types of persons: the one of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through elaboration (vipaṭicitaññū), the one who is guidable (neyya), and the one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama). "Paccabhāsī" means He replied.

"Apārutā" means opened. The meaning of the last two words is as follows: I, the Buddha, having the notion that it would be a weariness to body and speech, did not speak this sublime and supreme Dhamma, even though it was well-mastered and well-retained by Me.

## The Commentary on the Request of Brahma is finished.

## Commentary on the Discussion with the Group of Five

Now, the Buddha said, "Let the entire assembly of people bring the vessel of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations." "Apparajakkhajātiko" refers to one who is pure, having suppressed defilements through meditative attainments. Regarding the word "ājānissati" (he will understand), if the editors of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka) who knew the sequence of the Vinaya had not made a definitive conclusion, the meaning would be: "I shall preach, and he will penetrate and understand." This is a hypothetical assumption (abhūtapari-kappa), similar to the expression "his head would split." In this context, this statement serves several purposes: to show that person's noble inclination in the world, to show that he did not know even though the Buddha pointed it out to him, and to show that he was not a disciple.

"Knowledge arose in the Blessed One" means that omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) arose in Him, taking that person's death as its object. By that Pali, it is shown that if there had been a Dhamma teaching prior to that time, he would have had the nature to understand quickly. It also shows the realization of death through direct experience, not through being told by others. This is well-stated because even for Buddhas, many knowledges do not arise simultaneously. Indeed, the occurrence of consciousness is preceded by a prior thought; otherwise, there would be the fault of a new being appearing. In taking all phenomena together, those phenomena that belong to conflicting times...
399:
In apprehending all phenomena simultaneously, the notion might arise that phenomena belonging to different times must be known at once. If that were the case, a single knowledge would be subject to the flaw of being erroneous. Therefore, without taking a multitude of knowledges (not referring to the totality of knowledge), the Blessed One should be understood as 'Omniscient' (Sabbaññū) only because He possesses knowledge that is unobstructed regarding all things that should be known, and not because of knowing all times simultaneously. If it is argued, 'The Buddha had a thought because He did not know that the ascetic Āḷāra and others had died,' that is not so. This is because merely by knowing such a death, even an ordinary person (puthujjana) would be liable to the state of omniscience. The principle that 'when this exists, that does not exist; when this does not exist, that exists' is well-known in the world.

According to the statement, 'Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One,' the fact of knowing the death of the ascetic Āḷāra is established. Therefore, if it is argued that the Blessed One is established as omniscient only by Your Honor's view, and not because He was unaware before the deities came to inform Him, that too is not so. This is because He knows in the interval by grasping the specific distinction, and also because it would lead to the flaw of the deity becoming omniscient. In truth, the Blessed One did not come to know through the words of another.

Furthermore, if it is asked, 'What is the meaning of knowing in that context? Is it the arising of knowledge by making that an object?' it is said that it is not so. This is because it would lead to the conclusion that there is absolutely no Omniscient Buddha in the world. In fact, I have established that at the moment of the arising of one knowledge, there is the arising of all knowledge, and that there is no ignorance regarding the various meanings of other knowledges at other times. Furthermore, for the Omniscient Buddha, the manifestation of knowledge in the sphere of all phenomena is established; if it is argued that such knowledge is not His own sphere, it is not so, because of the lack of supporting reasons and examples. Furthermore, in the phrase 'Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One,' there is a specific expression. For that reason, it appears as if knowledge arose in the Blessed One only after the deities came to inform Him. In truth, the mere sequence of words does not imply that the meaning of those words follows the same sequence. Therefore, this argument is improper.

'Abhidosakālaṅkato' means passing away in the first watch of the night. Some also say 'He passed away in the middle watch.' In both cases, it is a 'great loss' (mahājāni). One who suffers a great loss because of being deprived of the Paths and Fruits that could have been attained within seven days or within one day is called 'Mahājāni.' Among those two, the ascetic Āḷāra was reborn in the realm of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana), and the ascetic Uddaka was reborn in the Peak of Existence (Bhavagga, the realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception). Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One reflected in this way referring to their rebirth in a place where there is no opportunity to hear the preaching of the Dhamma, and not referring to their passing away from this human world. Our teachers say that He reflected referring to their being 'beyond the reach of a Buddha's guidance' (abuddhavaneyya); otherwise, it would lead to an undesirable conclusion.

At the time of the Bodhisatta's birth, there were eight Brahmins who interpreted dreams and marks. Among them, three Brahmins gave a dual prediction: 'One endowed with these marks will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) if he lives the householder life, but if he renounces, he will become a Buddha.' Five Brahmins gave a definitive prediction, saying, 'He will not remain in the householder life; he will surely become a Buddha.' Among them, the first three Brahmins...
400:
(The first three Brahmins) reached the end of the Vedas (they predicted according to what was in the Vedas). These five Brahmins (the Pañcavaggiya), however, went beyond the end of the Vedas, gave up the greatness of the merit they had acquired, and renounced first, dedicating themselves to the Bodhisatta. It is in reference to them that the term 'Pañcavaggiya' is used. Some also say, 'They were the sons of those Brahmins,' but that statement is rejected in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). Why, then, did the Blessed One reflect here, 'These people were of great help to me'? Does this Teacher preach the Dhamma only to those who have helped Him and not to others? It is not that He does not preach (He does preach). According to the method of the Commentary, it should be understood that He spoke this way merely out of mindfulness of their help. It was spoken to manifest His own quality of gratitude (kataññū-katavedī), to praise gratitude and similar virtues, to encourage others in gratitude, and to prevent the assumption that the Dhamma can be understood [by anyone] instantly.

'Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhiṃ' means in a place about three gāvutas away between Gaya and the Bodhi tree. In fact, Gaya is three gāvutas away from the Bodhimaṇḍa. The city of Vārāṇasī is eighteen yojanas away. Upaka saw the Blessed One between the Bodhimaṇḍa and Gaya. Because it is associated with the word 'antarā,' the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) is used. In such places, grammarians usually use the word 'antarā' only once, but that word should also be connected to the second term. If it is not connected, it does not reach the accusative case. In this Pali, however, it is spoken by connecting it [twice].

'Sabbābhibhū' means standing having overcome all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence. 'Taṇhakkhaye' refers to Nibbāna. 'Vimutto' means liberated from objects. 'Natthi me paṭipuggalo' means there is no person who is my rival; the meaning is that there is no one equal to me. Or, it means there is no person who is my enemy because no one is able to remain in the world after pointing out a flaw in my omniscience. 'Āhañchaṃ amatadundubhiṃ' means 'I go [thinking] I will strike the drum named the Deathless (Amata) so that the Eye of Dhamma (Dhamma-cakkhu) may be obtained.'

'You are worthy of being an Anantajina,' Upaka said; the meaning is 'You are fit to be an Anantajina.' This 'Anantajina' is also a name of the Teacher. 'Hupeyyāsi' means 'Friend, it may be so.' 'Pakkāmi' means he went to the Vaṅkahāra country. The Blessed One also spoke with that Upaka because He saw the perfection of his supporting conditions (upanissaya), seeing that 'In that Vaṅkahāra country, this Upaka will become dissatisfied because of Cāpā, the daughter of a deer-hunter, and after returning and renouncing again, he will become an Anāgāmī.' And that Upaka, just as the Blessed One had predicted, returned, renounced, became an Anāgāmī, and in due course, after passing away, was reborn in the Aviha realm and attained Arahantship.
401:
“Saṇṭhapesuṃ” means making an agreement. “Padhānavibbhanto” means falling away or declining from the exertion of meditation. It means He spoke a specific utterance such as, “Do you remember this having been said?” or “Do you remember such a word having been spoken?” “Bhagavantaṃ sussūsiṃsu” means they desired to listen to the words of the Blessed One. “Aññā” means for the sake of knowing (aññāya).

Then, for what purpose did He address them? It was to make them acknowledge the teaching even more firmly than their current state of mind, to demonstrate the profound and rare nature of the Dhamma, and to prevent the scattering of the syllables. In that Pali text, the word “dveme” refers to the two extremes. This is because other base qualities are also included within these two extremes. Alternatively, it is said as “dveme” by way of connection. Indeed, the two defilements of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā) are the primary causes for the continuation of saṃsāra. These two qualities are called extremes (anta) because they are the opposites of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Among these two, a fool who indulges in the devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) through the power of craving causes tranquility to decline. Similarly, a fool who indulges in the devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) through the power of ignorance causes insight to decline. Therefore, it is said that without abandoning these two extremes, one is unable to reach the Deathless Nibbāna.

Alternatively, this statement demonstrates the abandoning of sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca). One who is sluggish, having abandoned the exertion of energy, indulges in sensual pleasure. The other, who is restless due to excessive exertion of energy, indulges in self-mortification. Both of these are called extremes (anta) because they are the opposites of the balance of energy (vīriya). Alternatively, three practices are mentioned in the Dispensation: the āgāḷha practice, the nijjhāma practice, and the majjhima (middle) practice. Among these three, the practice such as “He is one who takes life; there is no fault in sensual pleasures,” is the āgāḷha practice. The practice such as “He is a naked ascetic (acelaka); he is one devoid of proper conduct,” is the nijjhāma practice. The practice such as “Only this Noble Eightfold Path is the excellent practice,” is the majjhima practice.

Among these three, devotion to sensual pleasure is the practice named āgāḷha because it is the root of all unwholesome states. Devotion to self-mortification is the practice named nijjhāma because it causes oneself to burn (suffer). Both of these are called extremes (anta) because they are the opposites of the Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā). Therefore, referring only to these two things, He said, “dveme.”

Why did the Blessed One say, “Should not be followed by one who has gone forth,” referring only to those who have gone forth (pabbajita), and not to householders? It is because those who have gone forth have a tendency toward these two things, because they are capable of avoiding sensual pleasure, and because by such avoidance they can attain the benefits of being a monk; therefore, in this context, only those who have gone forth are intended, not householders. If that is so, why did He mention the devotion to sensual pleasure? Have these monks not naturally renounced sensual pleasures and gone forth to escape from them? It is not so; it is because they are still dependent on the two extremes. In truth, they desire purification through sensual pleasure in this world. While practicing devotion to self-mortification, they long for celestial sensual pleasures in the next life as a result of that austere practice; thus, they are practicing devotion to sensual pleasure even more firmly.
402:
It should be understood in this way. In this context, the meaning of 'anta' (extreme) should be understood in the sense of being loathsome, as in the passage: "Monks, this life of gathering alms is the lowest (anta) among livelihoods" (Itivuttaka 91, Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.80).

In the phrase "devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure in sensual objects" (kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogo), the first 'kāma' refers to objective sensuality (vatthukāma), and the second 'kāma' refers to the sensuality of defilements (kilesakāma). The happiness associated with those defilements is called 'kāmasukha' (sensual pleasure). By calling it such, the Buddha shows the blameless nature of the happiness associated with resultant consciousness (vipāka). 'Allīyana' (attachment) means delighting in that sensual pleasure. 'Anuyoga' (devotion) means the longing for association with that sensual pleasure in a future existence. It is called 'hīna' (low/base) in the sense of being vile, because it causes the decline of the side of merit, because it is cultivated by low persons, and because it originates from low elements. It is called 'gamma' (vulgar) because it is the habit of beings living in villages. It is called 'pothujjanika' (of the worldlings) because it is common to ordinary worldlings. It should be understood as 'anariya' (ignoble) because it is not desired by the Noble Ones (Ariyas), because it is the opposite of the Noble Dhamma, because it makes one ignoble, because it is not the nature of the Noble Ones, and because it is the practice of those who are not Noble. It is called 'anatthasaṃhita' (unprofitable) because it brings the danger of Saṃsāra, which is called 'unprofitable,' and because it produces unprofitable results.

Making oneself purely weary is called 'attakilamatha' (self-mortification). That self-mortification exists based on a specific action of practice in the sequence of conduct preceded by wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). The repeated devotion to that self-mortification by the power of wrong view is called 'attakilamathānuyoga'. Because it is devoid of the wealth of wisdom that leads to benefit and proceeds by a wrong method, when it comes to fruition, it causes one to fall into the wombs of deer, cattle, dogs, or pigs. When it ripens, it leads to hell; thus it is called 'anatthasaṃhita' (unprofitable).

The phrase 'ete tve' means 'ete tu' (but these two extremes). By the word 'Tathāgatena', the Buddha reveals his own unerring arrival at the truth. With this word, he shows: "This Dhamma was not thought out by me through mere reasoning; rather, I, being the Tathāgata, have fully awakened to it through the knowledge of supreme enlightenment (abhisambodhi-ñāṇa)." With the words 'cakkhukaraṇī' and so on, he praises that very same path. Just as medicine purifies a sick person, the word 'cakkhukaraṇī' (giving vision) refers to the purification of the eye of wisdom (ñāṇa-cakkhu). By 'ñāṇakaraṇī' (giving knowledge), the destruction of the mass of darkness is meant. By 'upasamāya' (for peace), the subsiding of the fever of defilements is meant. By 'abhiññāya' (for direct knowledge), the penetration of the truths is meant. By 'sambodhāya' (for enlightenment), the penetration of the truths is meant. By 'nibbānāya' (for Nibbāna), it should be explained by connecting it as appropriate to the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna) and the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna).

Why did the Blessed One, unlike in other discourses, not teach in the usual sequence but first spoke of the two extremes that should not be followed and then taught the Middle Way? He taught the avoidance of the two extremes to prevent arrogance based on wrong views such as 'self' (atta) and to prevent the practice of the wrong path.

By showing his own attainment of the special Dhamma, he intended to show his state of being 'anavāhullika' (not living in abundance) and so on. Furthermore, by showing the Middle Way to those five monks, he intended to make them constantly devoted to that Middle Way. Then, wishing to teach the Four Noble Truths in brief and in detail to show the domain of that Noble Path called the Middle Way, the Blessed One said: "Now this, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering (dukkha)," and so on. This is the connection (anusandhi) in this context. To show the connection of the discourse starting with "This, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering, thus to me (vision arose)," this following sequence should be understood. It is said that upon hearing the aforementioned practice, Kondañña said: "How could the arising of the practice spoken of by the Blessed One be? Indeed, this practice..."
403:
By the method of showing his own attainment of the special Dhamma, the Blessed One taught the Right Practice (sammā-paṭipadā) afterwards to show the absence of living in abundance (bāhullika) and so on, and to cause those five monks to be constantly devoted to that Middle Way by explaining it to them. Thereafter, wishing to teach the Four Noble Truths in brief and in detail to show the domain of that Noble Path known as the Middle Way, he said: "Now this, monks, is suffering (dukkha)," and so on. This is the connection (anusandhi) in this context. To show the connection of the discourse starting with "Monks, this is the Noble Truth of Suffering, thus to me (the eye of wisdom arose)," this following sequence should be understood.

It is heard that upon hearing the aforementioned practice, Kondañña said this: "How can the practice taught by the Blessed One arise? Indeed, this practice can only occur when defilements do not arise; it cannot be otherwise. If defilements arise due to greed, like hunger and thirst, then by indulging in that greed, the non-arising (of defilements) should occur. Or, if those defilements arise because of the body which is not the basis of that practice, then by indulging in self-mortification (attakilamatha) which is the opposite of that basis, the non-arising (of defilements) should occur. Both of these have been called 'extremes' by the Blessed One. If so, how then can the arising of this Right Practice be possible?" The Blessed One spoke regarding the non-arising through the pursuit of wrong means. How? —

"From the root of Saṃsāra, ignorance (aññāṇa) arises;
That ignorance is abandoned by wisdom (ñāṇa).
That wisdom exists only when there is life,
And that life depends on the means of livelihood.

"Therefore, for the sake of wisdom, the wise man
Should protect his own life,
And he should thoroughly guard virtue (sīla),
Which is the support for wisdom.

"Just as in the world, when the body is broken,
Life does not exist,
Even so, for one whose virtue is broken,
There is no possibility for wisdom to arise.

"Therefore, the mindful one, guarding life and virtue
For the sake of wisdom,
Should not indulge in sensual pleasures,
Nor in the practice that destroys the body.

"One who approaches greed for sensual pleasures becomes low and vulgar;
The deluded one who approaches self-mortification becomes extremely distressed.
One who approaches the supreme Middle Way,
He quickly attains the supreme liberation (Nibbāna)."
404:
Having heard those words of the Exalted One, that monk, having attained wisdom born of hearing (sutamaya-paññā), and entering into the knowledge born of reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa), asked this question desiring to cut off [doubt].

"Having abandoned the basis for penetration (nibbedhapadaṭṭhāna), how should one practice severe austerity?" he asked. May the Blessed One speak on this matter. Let the monk practice only that Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā); such practice leads to Nibbāna, the state free from passion (virāga). Only by seeing the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) does [attainment of Nibbāna] occur. The experiencing of suffering within that Truth of Suffering is the cause for the arising of aversion (dosa).

As soon as the monk Koṇḍañña heard the words of the Buddha, he rose joyfully and quickly, and addressed him: "Exalted One, please explain this meaning to me: How does a monk see the Truth of Suffering?"

It is said that the Blessed One taught this sutta so that the accomplishment of wisdom born of mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā-sampatti), which is perfected by the wisdom of one possessing knowledge born of reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa), may be known through these points. Why did the Blessed One, without first expanding the teaching on the Truths to Koṇḍañña, teach the sequence of his own attainment? It was to show: "I do not teach a Dhamma received from anyone else; rather, I have realized it myself in this way." In that Pali text, by the words "in things unheard of before," he shows these two benefits. By saying, "I did not hear this Dhamma from Āḷāra or Udaka; rather, in things never heard or listened to before, my knowledge clearly arose," he demonstrates the power of the Middle Way. Alternatively, he shows this meaning: "One who practices in this way can see the Noble Truths even without the guidance of another. This being so, why is it that you cannot see them even with my guidance?"

The five terms beginning with 'eye' (cakkhu) are merely synonyms for knowledge (ñāṇa). It is called 'eye' because it observes and reflects upon the Truths, and because it knows the clear meaning within the eye. It is called 'wisdom' (paññā) because it knows in various ways. It is called 'true knowledge' (vijjā) because it breaks through the defilements and penetrates the Truths. It is called 'light' (āloka) because it destroys the darkness that veils the Truths and reveals the limit of the occurrence of those Truths. Among those terms, by the first rotation (parivaṭṭa), he shows the wisdom that keeps the Truths distinct without confusion. By the second rotation, he shows the knowledge that discerns the tasks to be performed regarding those Truths. By the third rotation, he shows the completion of the function of knowledge regarding the Truths.
405: By the first term, he shows the wisdom that keeps the Truths distinct without confusion. By the second term, he shows the wisdom that discerns the tasks to be performed regarding those Truths. By the third term, he shows the determination of the function of knowledge regarding the Truths. By the two words 'yāvakīvañca', the intended meaning is simply 'yāva', similar to 'iti cittamanā' and so forth. It is called 'unshakeable liberation' (akuppā vimutti) because it cannot be destroyed by passion and so forth. 'Veyyākaraṇa' refers to the teaching of the Dhamma (the Pali of the discourse). That teaching is called 'veyyākaraṇa' because it explains and clarifies the dhammas. In the phrase 'virajaṃ vītamalaṃ', it is called 'viraja' (stainless) because it is free from the view of an uneven cause (visama-hetu-vāda). It is called 'vītamala' (dustless) because it is free from the view of no cause (ahetuka-vāda). It is 'viraja' because it abandons the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). It is 'vītamala' because it abandons the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). It is 'viraja' because it abandons the obsessive defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna). It is 'vītamala' because it abandons the underlying tendencies (anusaya). The 'Dhamma-eye' (dhamma-cakkhu) is the knowledge that sees only dhammas; it is the seeing that therein there is no being, no soul, no doer (kāraka), and no feeler (vedaka). Therefore, he said: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." This statement is made to show the manner in which that Dhamma-eye arises. That Dhamma-eye arises by taking cessation (Nibbāna) as its object and penetrating the conditioned things (saṅkhata) by way of its function. In this context, 'Dhamma-wheel' (dhamma-cakka) refers to the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) is also obtained. Why did the devas sound the cry here? Reasons are given such as: because they obtained light by destroying the darkness of various wrong views; because they attained relief by transcending the fear of the lower realms; and because they experienced joy and rapture upon seeing the mansions of the host of devas. Some say that the earthquake and the great sound occurred merely by the power of nature (dhammatā). Others say the earthquake occurred because the devas wished to play, or because of the assembly of a great host of devas, and that the radiance appeared because the Blessed One emitted a net of rays from his body. It means a special going forth (pabbajjā) and a special ordination (upasampadā). In the words "Ehi bhikkhu," the word "iti" indicates the end of the speech which was the cause for that monk's attainment of the "Ehi Bhikkhu" ordination. His monkhood was established at the conclusion of that speech. The words beginning with "svākkhāto" (well-expounded) show the purpose of the invitation "Ehi" (Come). The connection of words should be: The Blessed One said, "Come, monk," and he also said, "The Dhamma is well-expounded; practice... to make an end [of suffering]." Therein, "practice the holy life" means to attain the holy life consisting of the remaining three paths. For what purpose? For the sake of making a complete end of suffering. Because it was accomplished by the Blessed One's words "Ehi bhikkhu," it is called "Ehi Bhikkhu ordination" by way of naming it after its cause. That Ehi Bhikkhu monkhood itself was that venerable one's lifelong ordination. Therefore, the Commentary shows two meanings: that venerable one's ordination was never interrupted, neither by disrobing nor by any other means, and there was no need for any other form of ordination to become a monk. Among the eight types of ordination, for one who becomes a monk through any of these four—Ehi Bhikkhu ordination, ordination by accepting advice (ovāda-paṭiggahaṇa), ordination by answering five questions (pañha-byākaraṇa), or ordination by accepting the eight heavy rules (garudhamma-paṭiggahaṇa)—there is no interruption in between, nor is there any need for another ordination.
406:
In the Commentary, two meanings are presented: the cessation [of monkhood] through the renunciation of the training and so forth, or the absence of any further task to be performed by another ordination (upasampadā). Among the eight types of ordination, for one who has become a monk through any of the four—namely, ehibhikkhu-upasampadā, ovādapaṭiggahana-upasampadā, pañhabyākaraṇa-upasampadā, and garudhammapaṭiggahana-upasampadā—there is no cessation in the interval, nor is there any task to be performed by another ordination; however, for the remaining [four types], such tasks exist. Other sects, however, say: "By dividing the ordination known as the entry into the fixed course (niyāmokkanti) of Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, and the ñatticatutthakamma-upasampadā into two based on the performance by a group of ten or a group of five, there are ten types of ordination."

What, in terms of meaning, is called 'ordination' (upasampadā) here? It is the internal continuity of the five aggregates, produced by the power of the action of attaining that monkhood, endowed with the qualities of one beyond training (asekha), and developed by the volition of dwelling in that monkhood. What is called 'development' (paribhāvanā) here? It is the state of being opposed to the transgression of those things that are contrary to the qualities of a monk. Because of reaching that state, by the power of that development, it is said in some places to be "samannāgato" (endowed with). It is as He taught: "Monks, one who is endowed with greed is unfit to develop the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth.

Here, other sects say: "There is a phenomenon (dhamma) associated with the attainment of the aforementioned ordination, which is dissociated from the mind and included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). As long as that phenomenon arises in succession and is not yet interrupted, one is called 'upasampanna' (ordained). Otherwise, at the moment another phenomenon arises apart from that, that monk would potentially fall into the state of being unordained." They should be told: "Bring forth a Sutta passage [to prove this]." If they should say: "The Suttas that teach that the acquisition and endowment based on those ten qualities of one beyond training are 'noble' or 'abandoned,' etc., are our Suttas." If that were so, the fault of being endowed with non-existent phenomena or with other beings would fall upon their view. Why? Because such a possibility exists in the Sutta passages. As He taught: "Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with seven treasures," and so forth, which should be understood in detail. In that passage, the word "samannāgata" refers to mastery (vasībhāva). This is because that king has mastery and acts according to his will regarding those treasures. If it is argued: "Although the word 'samannāgata' refers to mastery here, in other places it refers to a specific phenomenon called attainment," what is the special reason for this? There is no special reason. Therefore, ordination has only the characteristics already mentioned. This same method should be applied to renunciation (pabbajjā) and so forth.

Although the Eye of Dhamma arose individually on different days, such as for the Elder Vappa on the first day of the waning moon... and for the Elder Assaji on the fourth day...
407:
It should be understood that because the instruction was the same for Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, and Assaji, they are spoken of together in this Pāḷi text.

Why is the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) shown from the very beginning, as in "Monks, form is non-self"? It is because even during their time as worldlings (puthujjana), the other two characteristics—impermanence (anicca) and suffering (dukkha)—were already evident to them. For those monks, having seen the impermanence of pleasant sensual pleasures, became spiritually stirred and went forth; thus, the characteristic of impermanence was partially evident to them. After going forth, due to the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga), physical suffering arose, and since that physical suffering is a cause for mental suffering, the characteristic of suffering (dukkha) was also evident. Therefore, setting aside those two characteristics, the Buddha began to show only the characteristic of non-self. Even in showing that characteristic of non-self, He taught, "Monks, if this form were self," and so forth, in order to show it by way of the characteristic of suffering. Why? Because the characteristic of suffering was more clearly evident to them than the characteristic of impermanence. Since those monks were constantly devoted to self-mortification and were intent upon it, the characteristic of suffering was very clear. Therefore, after showing the characteristic of non-self through that very clear characteristic of suffering, He will later say, "Monks, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?" to show that same characteristic of non-self through both impermanence and suffering. "Kallaṃ nu" means "would it be appropriate?" "This is mine" is the grasping through craving (taṇhāggāha). "This I am" is the grasping through conceit (mānaggāha). "This is my self" is the grasping through view (diṭṭhiggāha). Here, grasping through craving should be understood by way of the 108 modes of craving's movement, grasping through conceit by way of the nine types of conceit, and grasping through view by way of the sixty-two types of views.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Group of Five is Finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Going Forth

The connection is made with the words "Yaso nāma" (named Yasa) at the time when the Blessed One, having established the Group of Five monks in Arahantship on the fifth day, and having taught the Nālaka practice to the Elder Nālaka on the seventh day, was staying in Vārāṇasī, awaiting the young man Yasa, knowing that his spiritual faculties (indriya) had matured on the full moon day of Poṭṭhapāda (Tawtalin). It is said that from the time of his birth, the fame (kitti-sadda) or the retinue (parijana) of that family increased significantly; therefore, his parents gave him the name "Yasa." Why did the Venerable Upāli Thera say "sukhumālo" (delicate), and so forth? It was to inspire future generations toward renunciation (nekkhamma). The Venerable Upāli's intention was that if even sons of wealthy merchants, endowed with such supreme wealth, could become stirred upon seeing even a slight sign of impurity (asubha-nimitta) in those supreme pleasures and leave home, abandoning a great mass of wealth like grass without regard for the time, then what need is there to speak of others? "Samappitānaṃ" means being one with those five cords of sensual pleasure, living a life that is not secluded. "Nivāretvā" means preventing the arising of interest in pleasant objects, overwhelming and subduing the mind of the young man Yasa, and leading it according to one's will. In the phrase "sabbavārassa"...
408: He departed from his home, having abandoned a great mass of wealth like grass, delighting in seclusion, and disregarding the time, being terrified even by a slight sign of loathsomeness (asubhanimitta). This means: 'How could this happen to anyone else?' It refers to one who is not secluded, being at one with the five strands of sensual pleasure. It means that sleep overcame and subdued the mind of the noble youth Yasa, bringing it under its own power, preventing the occurrence of pleasant objects. 'Throughout the three watches of the night' means all three watches. By saying this, the cause for seeing the disarray of his attendants is shown. Here, the word 'ratti' (night) should be understood to mean the time, the absence of the sun, and a watch (yāma). This should also be understood in the training rule regarding being separated from the three robes (ticīvaravippavāsa). 'At the side' means at the side of the armpit. 'Below the neck' means under the neck. It means he saw a drum at the neck of a woman who was sleeping with her neck placed on top of the drum (mudiṅga). 'Āḷambara' refers to a small drum called a paṇava. It is thin and long with two faces. It is a name for a drum that is played and has a flat, wide surface. 'Muttering' refers to those women who were muttering incoherent words due to dreaming and so on. 'He thought it was a cemetery' should be connected as: he saw his own attendants as if they were in a cemetery. It refers to the state of impurity (asubha). 'The mind is established in revulsion' means the mind inclined toward the weariness known as the desire for liberation. He uttered an inspired utterance (udāna): 'From this day forward, I shall not live with these women,' expressing words of joy. It is said that two aspects became clear upon seeing the attendants sleeping in negligence: the strength of the defilements and the extreme grossness of the state of impurity. While such an extremely gross state of impurity exists, the entire world is oppressed and infatuated by the power of defilements. Seeing 'Oh, how powerful are the defilements!', those two aspects became clear to the noble youth Yasa, which is why he spoke thus. By the words 'having put on his golden slippers,' his departure without attachment is shown. Because his heart was urged by strong spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he went freely, thinking that even if his attendants were to wake up, they would not be able to prevent his departure. 'Non-humans' (amanussa) refers to deities (devatā). They are called 'non-humans' because they share common qualities with humans, such as reaching a happy destination (sugati), attaining penetrative knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa), and having a similar form. Animals and others of a different species are not called 'non-Brahmins' or 'outcastes' (vasala). Rather, only those of the same species are called 'outcastes' and so on. Thus, deities are called 'non-humans' because they are similar to humans in some aspects.
409:
Deities are called 'non-humans' (amanussa) because they are similar to humans in some aspects. Otherwise, animals, who are not human, would also have to be called 'non-humans.'

Upon seeing the forest thicket, Yasa the noble youth was filled with joy, thinking, 'I am well-freed from the city,' and uttered an inspired utterance near the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, 'This is Yasa,' referring to Nibbāna. This is because Nibbāna is not oppressed or afflicted by defilements such as craving (taṇhā), and it produces delight even by merely seeing it with knowledge. 'I shall teach the Dhamma' means: 'I shall teach that Dhamma by which you, merely by sitting here, will attain Nibbāna.' The word 'kira' is a particle used in cases of lack of faith, lack of clarity, or jest; here it is used in the sense of lack of clarity (avyatti). 'Having descended from his golden slippers' (suvaṇṇapādukāyo orohitvā) means having stepped down from the golden slippers. Here, the nominative case 'pādukāyo' expresses the sense of the ablative case (from).

Why did the Blessed One, without speaking other pleasant words or greeting him, give the progressive instruction (anupubbīkathā) to the noble youth Yasa who had just sat down? It was because the noble youth Yasa had well-matured faculties (indriya), to ensure he did not miss the moment of penetration (paṭivedha), because his mind was inclined toward the teaching given to those not oppressed by defilements, and because He saw that the merchant householder would soon arrive.

Why did the Blessed One first speak about the causes and benefits of existence in various realms to the noble youth Yasa, whose heart was greatly terrified and who wished to be liberated from existence? It was to make him see the danger in all forms of existence. For that noble youth saw only the oppression and affliction of the human world, but not that of the heavenly realms, and might sometimes think of the heavenly realms as pleasant. If he held the perception of pleasure in the heavenly realms, he might not be able to direct his mind toward Nibbāna. Therefore, wishing to show the danger of the heavenly realms as well, He began the progressive instruction.

Here, preaching about giving and its benefits, and virtue and its benefits, is called 'talk on giving' (dānakathā) and 'talk on virtue' (sīlakathā). Preaching about the merits of the heavenly realms is called 'talk on heaven' (saggakathā). By preaching about the impermanence, the lack of appeal, and the great danger of the objects of sensual pleasure and the defilements of sensual pleasure in those heavenly realms, He revealed the danger (ādīnava), the vileness (okāra), and the corruption (saṃkilesa) of sensual pleasures. By preaching about the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma), which is the opposite of those dangers, because those dangers do not exist in renunciation and because it is the escape from those sensual pleasures, He revealed the 'benefit of renunciation.'

In that Pali, 'okāra' means the state of being vile (lāmaka). 'Saṃkilesa' means corruption, oppression, or torment. The 'ready mind' (kallacitta) occurs through the power of the wisdom faculty (paññindriya), because association with wrong view and doubt has been destroyed by the wisdom faculty. The 'soft mind' (muducitta) occurs through association with the mindfulness faculty (satindriya); by preventing the entry of defilements such as cruelty and anger, and allowing the entry of wholesome states such as malleability of mind, it makes the co-nascent mind soft. The 'mind free from hindrances' (vinīvaraṇacitta) occurs through the power of the concentration faculty (samādhindriya). This is because it is specifically the opposite of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The 'uplifted mind' (udaggacitta) occurs through the power of the energy faculty (vīriyindriya). This is because it is the opposite of the sunken state known as sloth and torpor (thīna-middha). Through the power of the faith faculty (saddhindriya)...
410:
Due to the power of the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), he had a clear mind; for that mind has the characteristic of clarity. The Elder Upāli explained this teaching, "Sāmukkaṃsikā" (exalted), by way of its scope. The Four Noble Truths are the scope of the exalted teaching. Alternatively, it means that suffering and so forth are the exalted Dhamma teaching, because the Truths are pointed out in the clarification of that teaching.

"Catu-ddisā" means in the four directions. "Abhisaṅkhāresi" means he performed a psychic construction (created by supernormal power). For what purpose did he perform this? It was to prevent obstacles to the special attainment to be reached by both father and son. If the merchant-banker had seen his son, the son's attainment of the Eye of Dhamma and his reaching of Arahantship might not have occurred, and the merchant-banker's attainment of the Eye of Dhamma might not have occurred. Even for one who has seen the Truth (a Sotāpanna), if he were told, "Give life to your mother," how could he not act accordingly? And Yasa, even though an Arahant, hearing those words and not rejecting them himself, looking up at the Blessed One, how would he remain in another state of knowledge?

Since both had reached the peak of the special attainment to be reached, the Blessed One then subsided that psychic construction. "Formerly a householder" refers to the time when the Venerable Yasa was a Sotāpanna. A Sotāpanna is fit to live in a house and, not yet having gone forth, is called a householder. Now, having gone forth, he is unfit to live in a house and is no longer called a "householder"; thus it was said. "Yassa diṭṭho" (by whom he was seen) is the connection of the meaning. Because the method was established by the words "formerly a householder," the merchant-banker father later referred to Yasa, even while he was wearing lay clothes, as "the clansman Yasa as the attendant monk."

In that text, "Lead the holy life" means to fully practice the holy life of the training in higher conduct (ābhisamācārika-sīla) until the making of an end of suffering, until the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). Ancient teachers say it refers to the holy life in the form of the monastic appearance, and that is also appropriate. For it was in reference to the monastic appearance alone that the Venerable Yasa said, "Venerable Sir, may I receive the going forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā)."

Why did the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to Yasa's mother and wife even before the meal? Because the arrow of grief was embedded in them due to Yasa's going forth, they would not be able to give the gift with a joyful mind, and having developed resentment toward the Teacher, they would not attain the penetration of the Path. Therefore, the Blessed One first made them those whose hearts were free from the arrow of grief, and then performed the meal-duty.

"Seṭṭhānu-seṭṭhīnaṃ" means of the successive merchant-bankers, according to the ancient teachers. Those families in which there are merchant-bankers and successive merchant-bankers are called "seṭṭhānu-seṭṭhāni" families.
411:
It is written, "of those successive merchant-banker families." Dhamma-Vinaya refers to the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya) and the Word of the Buddha (pāvacana); here, they are one in meaning. Alternatively, it is called Dhamma-Vinaya because it is discipline through Dhamma, not through sticks or weapons. It is discipline for the sake of Dhamma, not for the sake of harm; discipline by way of Dhamma, not by way of non-Dhamma; Dhamma itself is the discipline; discipline of Dhammas, not of others; or because the Blessed One is Dhamma by way of the Dhamma-body or being the Lord of Dhamma, it is the discipline of that Dhamma (the Buddha), not of speculators. Or it is Dhamma-Vinaya by way of apposition (samānādhikaraṇa), like "blue lotus" (nīluppala). Like "fruit great and small" (phalāphala), it is both Dhamma and Vinaya; its gender is established as masculine, not neuter, as it is designated in the masculine. Alternatively, like "a man with a white cloth," he who has the discipline of Dhamma is Dhamma-Vinaya. Or, like "a horse-drawn chariot," the discipline associated with Dhamma is Dhamma-Vinaya; thus the construction should be understood in various ways.

"Taking to a partial boundary" (khaṇḍasīmaṃ netvā) was said to exclude the announcement of the hair-cutting. Therefore, in a monastery with monks, it is not proper to say, "Have someone else cut this person's hair." To clarify the meaning of the word "having ordained" (pabbājetvā), it was said, "Come, having put on the saffron-dyed robes." If the preceptor (upajjhāya) gives the refuges for going forth without performing the shaving of hair and beard, etc., the going forth (pabbajjā) is not valid. If he confers the full ordination (upasampadā) by reciting the formal act (kammavācā), the full ordination is valid. Some teachers say this is appropriate because full ordination is seen to be successful for those without bowls and robes, and because there is no failure of the formal act (kamma-vipatti). On this matter, there is a summary verse:

"Going forth is valid only for one with the mark (of a novice),
For the other, full ordination is valid even without the mark;
For one who has discarded the former lay appearance, both are valid—
So say other teachers."

For a monk, only a robe given by his own hand or by command is proper; one not given is not proper. This applies only when robes are available; it is the intention of those teachers that it does not apply when they are unavailable. "Monks, in this way one should be ordained, one should be given full ordination. First... Monks, I allow the going forth and full ordination by these three refuges." Here, because it means I allow the going forth and full ordination by the three refuges given in this sequence alone, it is said:

"For one who has not previously taken the mark and is naked, both can occur,
But for another, it cannot—this is our view,
Because it is in accordance with all the Pali texts."
412:
The Venerable Teacher said: Regarding the statement "Taking an appearance not given by the teacher is not allowable," it is written that "the going forth (pabbajjā) does not take effect." It is written similarly in the ancient Gaṇṭhipada. Places such as the chest are called "locations" (ṭhāna). Actions such as closing (saṃvutta) are called "articulations" (karaṇa). It is written: "Words ending in a nasal sound (niggahita) should be made continuous and recited without stopping in between when giving [the refuges]. When giving by breaking [the words], one must break only at the aforementioned places; breaking elsewhere is not allowable." Upatissa Thera said that if one slips while giving a word ending in a nasal sound and it becomes mixed with a 'ma' sound as in "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi", it is allowable because it has reached the place of articulation. Dhammasiri Thera said that it is allowable to recite them mixed, but when reciting, one should do so without breaking at the end of the nasal articulation. It is said, "This is also the case in the Kammavācā." Regarding the statement "It is allowable only when there is purity on both sides," if a Mahāthera, due to reasons such as missing teeth, recites without making the sound perfectly clear (four-square), and a skilled novice standing nearby makes the skilled candidate recite, it should be understood as not allowable because he is making him recite what was not uttered by the Mahāthera. In the recitation of the Kammavācā, if another monk recites, it is allowable. The reason is that the Saṅgha performs the formal act (kamma), not an individual. It is allowable because it is not to be rejected by the general rule of Kammavācā occurring in different boundaries (sīmā). Alternatively, if the candidate cannot recite the words clearly uttered by the Thera, and the novice recites them himself and makes the candidate recite, there is indeed purity on both sides because he recites exactly what was uttered by the Thera. One who goes for refuge to the Buddha should be joined with the taking of what has not yet been taken, such as the unique qualities of the Buddha; one who goes for refuge to the Dhamma, Nibbāna; and one who goes for refuge to the Saṅgha, the Sekhadhamma and Asakhadhamma. Otherwise, there may be the fault of confusing the Three Refuges. "All that is allowable and unallowable for him" refers to matters outside the ten training rules, such as touching (parāmāsa) and non-touching. Because of the statement "He should be disciplined in the Ābhisamācārika," this novice must fulfill the Ābhisamācārika-sīla, such as the Sekhiya rules and duties toward the preceptor (upajjhāya). It is shown that in that regard, he becomes liable to punishment (daṇḍakamma) for not performing positive duties (cāritta) or for performing prohibited acts (vāritta).

## End of the Explanation on the Talk on Going Forth (Pabbajjākathā).

## Second Explanation on the Talk on Māra
Because of the phrase "tena hetunā" (for that reason), it should be understood that in the Pali text, the words "yonisomanasikārā, sammappadhānā" are in the ablative case (pañcamī vibhatti) in the sense of cause.

## End of the Second Explanation on the Talk on Māra.
413:
## Explanation of the talk on the miracles at Uruvelā (Uruvelāpāṭihāriyakathā)

37-8. "Vaseyyāma" means "Let you and I stay together"; it is said that this was spoken to favor Uruvelā Kassapa with pleasant words. "Tejasā tejaṃ" means (subduing) power by power, or (subduing) the fire-element by the fire-element. In the phrase "Ubhinnaṃ sajotibhūtānaṃ," the genitive case (sāmivibhatti) is used either in the sense of disregard (anādara) or in the sense of the locative absolute (bhāvasattamī). Only the fire-shed (agyāgāra) burned brightly; the group of beings living in that fire-shed did not burn. Indeed, the range of psychic power (iddhi) is inconceivable (acinteyya).

Why did the Blessed One not resolve that the fire-shed also should not burn? He did not resolve so because of the absence of suffering for himself and the avoidance of being overly unsurprising. For what purpose did He destroy that fire-shed, which was the property of another and consisted of many materials? It was destroyed because of the intention to rebuild it as it was before through the influence of psychic power. "Pariyādinno" means brought to an end (exhausted). "Tejasā tejaṃ" means (subduing) power by power. Since the fire-shed was small, the other meaning is not possible. This meaning is very consistent with the Pāḷi "makkhaṃ asahamāno" (not enduring the disparaging of power). In that context, "makkha" means the disparaging of psychic power. "Pattena" means with a lotus leaf, according to the ancient teachers. It was their opinion that the Blessed One was there, standing in a lotus thicket.

39. "Dinnaṃ" means permission (anumati). "Abhīto" means fearless. Why? Because the Blessed One has transcended fear through the Path. "Sumanamanaso" means a mind characterized by a good heart. It is also written as "sumano eva vā."

"Tejovā" means like fire. "Dhātukusalo" means one (the Naga king in human form) who is skilled in the fire-element. According to the grammatical rule "byavahitā ca," it is a prefix (upasagga). It means being skilled in the attainments (samāpatti) of the fire-element.

"Udicchare" means they looked up. It is also written as "sampavāresuṃ" (they surrounded). It means they spoke thus. "Hatā" means (the flames) were extinguished. The intention here is said to be that they became black. Without making even a slight effort, they remained in accordance with tranquility. To show the colors of the many-colored flames that arose, He said "nīlā atha lohitikā" (blue, then red), etc.

40. "Catuddisā" means in the four directions.

44. "Paṃsukūlaṃ uppannaṃ" means it arose by way of being obtained by the Blessed One who was searching for it. That search was for the purpose of showing a marvelous miracle. That "sā ayaṃ" means...
414:
"Sāyaṃ" means "so ayaṃ". "Tayimā" means "tā imā". These two terms are taken as one. "Āyamahaṃ" means "āyāmi ahaṃ". "Etaṃ" refers to "etassa". "Yathā mayaṃ" means "yasmā mayaṃ" (because we...).

50-51. "Udakavāhako" means a water current (flood). Ancient teachers say it is a water current. The phrase "Yāya tvaṃ" is spoken with reference to the preliminary stage of insight practice (vipassanā-paṭipadā). "Cirapaṭikā" means occurring from a long time ago; it is called "cirapaṭikā" because it has been a long time since the taming of the Naga. Some also say "cirapaṭisaṅkhā". In the passage beginning with "kesamissaṃ", ancient teachers say that hair and so on are called "kesamissa" because they are tied separately and put in without being mixed. In the context of "khārikājamissaṃ", "khārī" refers to the requisites of ascetics. "Jaṭile pāhesi" means sending two or three ascetics. It is said, "There were four thousand miracles exceeding sixteen."

Because they were practiced in fire sacrifice, the Blessed One taught them the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. In that Sutta, some things burn by way of the object; the eye and so on burn with the fire of lust. Some burn by way of association, such as feeling born of eye-contact. Some burn by way of oppression, the eye and so on burning with birth and so on. Some burn by way of cause, the eye and so on burning with sorrow and so on. Thus, the state of burning (ādittatā) should be understood here as applicable. In this Sutta, although only the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) is evident, it should be understood that by following that characteristic of suffering, they also saw the other two characteristics (impermanence and non-self), because the aspect of suffering illustrates the other aspects. It should be understood that because they were attached by craving for permanent happiness, the teaching was given with the characteristic of suffering as the precursor.

## The Explanation of the Account of the Uruvela Miracles is finished.

## The Explanation of the Account of the Meeting with Bimbisāra

55-57. Women who are objects of sensual desire are called "kāmitthiyo". The second and others are called "assāsaka". Through the verses beginning with "Tamaddasa Bimbisāro, pāsādasmiṃ patiṭṭhito," it is evident that King Bimbisāra had already been consecrated even when the Buddha was a Bodhisatta.

"Friends, in this Dispensation, a monk who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) is (1) one who has abandoned five factors, (2) one who is endowed with six factors, (3) one who has a single guard, (4) one who has four supports, (5) one who has abandoned individual truths, (6) one who has completely relinquished all searches (esanā), (7) one who has unclouded thoughts, (8) one who has tranquil bodily formations, (9) one who has a well-liberated mind, and (10) one who has well-liberated wisdom." These ten are called the "Noble Dwellings" (ariyavāsa). Ancient teachers also say that the eight attainments of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), and the attainment of great compassion are (Noble Dwellings). Among those Noble Dwellings, the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are the five factors to be abandoned (pañcaṅga). The six-fold equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) are the six factors to be endowed with (chaḷaṅga). Through the guard of mindfulness, there is the single guard (ekārakkha). Reflecting with wisdom, one uses one thing, endures another, avoids another, and removes another—these four are the four supports (caturāpassena). Because the various individual truths of many recluses and Brahmins are abandoned, he is called "one who has abandoned individual truths" (paṇunnapaccekasacca). Because the search for sensual pleasures and the search for existence are abandoned, and the search for the holy life has subsided, he is called "one who has completely relinquished all searches" (samavayasaṭṭhesana). Because thoughts of sensuality, ill-will, and cruelty are abandoned, he is called "one who has unclouded thoughts" (anāvilasaṅkappa). Because of the abandoning of pleasure... and dwelling in the fourth jhana, he is called "one who has a well-liberated mind" (suvimuttacitta). Because he knows that lust, hatred, and delusion are abandoned, uprooted... and are of a nature not to arise again, he is called "one who has well-liberated wisdom" (suvimuttapañña).

"The knowledge of what is possible and impossible, the knowledge of the results of actions (kamma), the knowledge of the way leading to all destinations, the knowledge of the many elements, the knowledge of the dispositions of beings, the knowledge of the maturity of the faculties, the knowledge of the defilement etc. of the jhanas, and the three-fold higher knowledge (vijjā)." These are the Ten Powers (dasa-bala-ñāṇa). The factors of one beyond training (asekkhā) are Asekha Right View and so on, up to Asekha Liberation and Asekha Knowledge and Vision of Liberation. Among those ten, the tenth is Asekha Knowledge and Vision of Liberation. Ancient teachers say that one who is endowed with these ten factors of one beyond training has reached the further shore (pāramī).

## The Explanation of the Duties towards a Preceptor (Upajjhāya-vatta)

Because the manner of dressing and robing of the other Ehibhikkhu monks, who had the Buddha as their preceptor, was individually similar, it is said: “They were poorly dressed, poorly robed, and not possessed of proper deportment.” Not only did they go for alms in such a state, but they also [behaved improperly] above people who were eating, and so forth. People criticized them because they [the people] could endure hunger, and because they had faith in the perfect deportment of the other Ehibhikkhu monks.

As to who should take which preceptor: “At that time, he [the candidate] receives the status of a novice in the presence of a certain teacher; now, he desires the status of a bhikkhu in the presence of that same teacher.”
417:
Some teachers wrote that [one becomes a monk] intending the acceptance by the preceptor saying “Sādhu.” Those teachers who are skilled in the Vinaya know this point thus: “When the preceptor accepts with words such as ‘Sāhū,’ the Saddhivihārika’s (resident pupil's) statement ‘Sādhu, suṭṭhu sampaṭicchāmi’ (It is well, I well accept) is merely a customary practice of monks; it is not found anywhere [as a rule]. Therefore, even without those words, the preceptor is indeed taken.” In that Pali, ‘Sāhū’ means ‘Sādhu’ (It is well). ‘Lahū’ means ‘It is light; you are not a burden to me.’ ‘Opāyikaṃ’ means connected to the means; it means ‘By this means, you have become a responsibility to me from this day forth.’ ‘Patirūpaṃ’ means ‘Your taking of the preceptor is suitable.’ One gives the same kind of water for washing the face in a season of similar nature.

“From this point onwards” means starting from the negative particle ‘na’ mentioned in this context: “Na upajjhāyassa bhaṇamānassa” (Not while the preceptor is speaking). Some teachers say that by the negative particle ‘na’ mentioned in the phrase “One should go not too far, not too near,” it indicates that there is no offense. Is this offense of violating a duty an intentional (sacittaka) offense or an unintentional (acittaka) offense? It is an intentional offense because it is caused by disrespect (anādariya). If it is asked, “How is it known to be caused by disrespect?” it is known because it is included among the causes of disrespect. In the recitation of the Pātimokkha, not making a numerical limit for the Sekhiyas serves the purpose of including offenses that belong to the Khandhakas. However, this characteristic of inclusion should be understood only in the case of Cāritta (prescribed duties), not in Vāritta (prohibitions). This is because offenses caused by reasons such as eating unallowable meat (akappiya-maṃsa) are unintentional (acittaka). The Vāritta rules appearing in the Khandhakas are counted (included) with those such as eating unallowable meat. The Teacher (Ācariya Ānanda) says that only in the Sekhiya Vāritta is there inclusion by reasons such as requesting curry or rice, which are unintentional.

Wherever a prohibition is made with the particle ‘na,’ is there a dukkaṭa (wrong-doing) offense in all such cases? Yes. In every case where the method is not shown in the Commentary, a dukkaṭa offense occurs. For later in the Commentary, the method is shown thus: “If the ground is black-colored, or plastered with lime, or free of dust, it is proper to place [the items] on such ground.”

Here, an objector says: “Since the method stated in the Commentary is appropriate by the power of the Buddha’s words in the Pali itself, such as ‘If dissatisfaction arises in the preceptor, or if a wrong view arises,’ what is the hint (reason) from the Buddha’s words in this phrase ‘not too far, not too near’?” The answer is stated: They say [the rule] “Having arrived earlier, the seat should be prepared,” etc., because of the restriction of the location. If it is said that the first going is only to the place permitted by the preceptor, that cannot be said. This is because it is not established, and even if it were established, it would be established by the aforementioned method.
418:
In truth, giving consent in a matter that is prohibited does not mean an offense is not committed; nevertheless, one should accept it only after careful investigation. Koṭṭhaka refers to a gatehouse. It should not be discarded, nor should it be kept.

## The Explanation of the Duties towards a Preceptor is finished.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Improper Conduct and So Forth

In the phrase "it is not excessive household-based affection (gehassitapema)", one should not regard household-based affection as being solely unwholesome, for this characteristic is also common to Arahants. If it is asked, "Is it not the case that Arahants do not have household-based affection because they lack improper conduct?" No, it is not that they should not be dismissed; rather, they should indeed be dismissed. This is because they have attained the fulfillment of being a preceptor (or the fulfillment of such affection). Therefore, the manifestation of cherishing, such as "This person is my responsibility," should be understood as "affection" (pema) in the context of household-based affection.

Just as in the passage, "A monk who is fulfilled in his duties... p... there is no offense for them," if a monk fulfilled in his duties says, "Venerable sirs, please remain unconcerned; I will attend to your co-resident (saddhivihārika), your pupil (antevāsika), or the sick; I will give the necessary admonitions; I will exert effort in these duties," and if those co-residents and others say, "Venerable sirs, please you alone remain unconcerned," or if they do not accept the performance of the duties, then from that time onwards, it is said that there is no offense for the teachers and preceptors.
