## Ornamentation of the Explanation of the Cessation of Dependence

"Gone to another region" means having abandoned the residence where one’s burden was laid down and gone to another village. In the statement, "Wherever dependence can be obtained, one should go there," just as in the method mentioned for the preceptor, if there is an effort to go, such as "I will go within two or three days," the dependence remains without being severed. "Do not return here" means "Do not come here." Those known as "similar" (sabhāga) are the pupils of the preceptor. One should live having taken dependence from them. If it is asked, "If so, what is the distinction?" for that reason, this is said: "If he should forgive." "It is proper to dwell" means that because the preceptor has relinquished him, dwelling together with the preceptor is of no use.

If the preceptor wishes to favor him only after a long time, from that time on, the preceptor himself is the teacher of dependence. If the preceptor is shameless (alajjī), even if the co-resident student has forbidden him many times and he does not desist, the student should leave that preceptor and live having taken dependence from another teacher, even if the formal dismissal of dependence (nissayapaṇāmana) has not yet been performed. If the preceptor’s gender (liṅga) changes, the dependence does not last even for a single day. If he becomes a half-month eunuch (pakkhapaṇḍaka), since he is of a nature fit for taking dependence, if it is said, "Wait for the preceptor’s bright side (sukkapakkha)" or if he waits of his own accord, it is proper. If the preceptor has undergone an act of suspension (ukkhepaniyakamma), the dependence ceases because he has entered the state of one of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka). However, if one sees the teacher practicing properly again, one has the right to wait for the cessation of the legal act. If he is one undergoing penance (mānatta), one should wait until he is rehabilitated (abbhāna). If he is undergoing a long probation (parivāsa), dependence should be taken from another teacher; dwelling together with the preceptor is not valid. This is because one undergoing probation or penance should not give dependence. The statement in the Parivāsika Khandhaka Commentary, "For a teacher who accepts the services of co-resident pupils, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," and so forth, confirms the meaning already stated.
420:
If sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith say, 'Venerable sirs, please perform only the Vinaya acts,' and continue to perform their duties and ask permission to enter the village, it is said that from the time of that prohibition, there is no offense. This statement should be understood as intended to show the mere absence of a dukkaṭa offense due to taking delight in duties, or it refers to the consideration shown by the saddhivihārikas. Therefore, if those saddhivihārika pupils practice only what is appropriate according to the preceptor's prohibition, the conclusion is that their nissaya (dependence) ceases.

By the measure of exceeding two clod-throws and returning, it is called 'departing to another direction.' Therefore, even if the antevāsika (pupil) has not laid down his burden, the nissaya ceases. It is written that the ācariya (teacher) and upajjhāya (preceptor), without exceeding two clod-throws, may stay in another dwelling within the distance of two clod-throws, whether it is enclosed or unenclosed. The teacher says that one should stay only in an unenclosed dwelling. In this teacher's view, the meaning is that they stay in another dwelling that is free from the area where an enclosure should be for a dwelling that is not yet enclosed. In this context, Upatissa Thera says that 'vihāra' (dwelling) refers to a small hut situated at the edge of such a dwelling.

In this regard, the view of Dhamma-siri Thera agrees with the general statement of the Commentary: 'If both the teacher and the pupil, for some reason... the nissaya does not cease.' Regarding the phrase 'whether unenclosed,' it may be enclosed or unenclosed within two clod-throws. Since it is also said to be 'outside the sīmā,' and the meaning is established that one may stay even exceeding two clod-throws within the monastery sīmā, the view of Upatissa Thera does not agree. In fact, whether enclosed or unenclosed, for one staying within a single residence, even at a distance of at least three yojanas, the nissaya does not cease. That residence is demarcated by the upacāra-sīmā (precinct boundary). That upacāra-sīmā is a single residence demarcated either by the enclosure of an enclosed dwelling or by the area where an enclosure should be for an unenclosed dwelling.

If it is asked whether this is because the sīmā is permitted in the case of doubt regarding a single residence in the Uposathakkhandhaka? It is not so, because it has been examined in the Cīvarakkhandhaka Commentary. As it is said: 'Let the Saṅgha standing within the sīmā divide and take [the gains].' By which sīmā should it be divided? It is said that Maha Siva Thera said, 'By the avippavāsa-sīmā (boundary of non-separation).' Regarding that, they said to him: 'The avippavāsa-sīmā can be as large as three yojanas. If so, monks standing within three yojanas will receive the gains. Standing at three yojanas, they will have to enter the monastery after fulfilling the duties of a guest. A traveling monk will have to go to those three yojanas and ask for lodgings. For a monk practicing under nissaya, the nissaya will cease upon exceeding three yojanas. For a monk undergoing parivāsa (probation), dawn will rise upon exceeding the three-yojana sīmā. A bhikkhunī will have to ask for permission to enter the monastery while standing at three yojanas. Such faults should be avoided by demarcating the upacāra-sīmā.' Therefore, it is said that for a monk staying beyond two clod-throws within the monastery sīmā, the nissaya does not cease because he has not exceeded three yojanas.

In this matter, it should be understood that whether the extent is three yojanas or more, the aforementioned faults would occur in the upacāra-sīmā. This is because it is said that the upacāra-sīmā expands when residents in the dwelling increase and contracts when they decrease. In this context, 'vihāra' refers to a single small hut situated at the edge of such a dwelling. That small hut is also called a vihāra.
421:
A traveling monk, having gone three yojanas, will have to ask for a lodging. For a monk practicing under nissaya, the nissaya will cease upon exceeding three yojanas. For a monk undergoing parivāsa, dawn will rise upon exceeding three yojanas. A bhikkhunī, standing at a distance of three yojanas, will have to ask for permission to enter the monastery. All this should be done by means of demarcating the upacāra-sīmā. Therefore, the decision is concluded that for one staying even beyond two clod-throws within the monastery precinct, the nissaya does not cease because he has not exceeded three yojanas. Indeed, in this matter, whether the upacāra-sīmā is three yojanas in measure or more, the aforementioned faults would apply. Because it is said that the upacāra-sīmā expands when residents in the dwelling increase and contracts when they decrease, here 'dwelling' (vihāra) refers to a single small hut situated at the edge of such a dwelling. Since that small hut is merely a hut of that same dwelling, that dwelling is called an āvāsa (residence). If a distinct residence were intended, one would not say 'a small hut situated at the edge.' The decision stating 'it is not my thought' regarding the non-cessation of nissaya in a distinct unenclosed residence even within two clod-throws, is stated by the method of the non-cessation of the acceptance of lodgings in such a distinct residence. For the acceptance of lodgings ceases in another place because it has the characteristic: 'By acceptance, the attachment to [previous] acceptance ceases.'

In that regard, this is the Pāḷi: 'At that time, the venerable Upananda Sakyaputta, being alone, spent the rains in two residences... Monks, give this foolish man one choice.' And in the Commentary, it is said: 'This was said regarding dwellings within a single sīmā with different gains and different precincts; however, in dwellings with different sīmās, the acceptance of lodgings ceases.' Distinct unenclosed residences come to be designated as a single precinct. A single precinct that is enclosed also comes to be designated as an unenclosed dwelling. By this much decision, the meaning is established that for a monk staying in another unenclosed dwelling within two clod-throws, the nissaya does not cease, but in an enclosed dwelling, it does cease.

In this matter, an objector says, 'The nissaya does not cease even for one staying beyond two clod-throws.' Is it not said in the Nissaggiya Commentary: 'If dawn rises in places not yet reached while they are still traveling, the robe becomes nissaggiya (to be forfeited), but the nissaya does not cease'? To answer that objection, that statement in the Commentary was made with reference to the effort to reunite with the preceptor. Here, however, it is stated with reference to permanent residence, therefore, each other not...
422:
They do not contradict each other. However, some teachers say that the phrase "beyond the distance of two stone-throws" is spoken in terms of living while reporting daily. In my opinion, that is merely their own view. For the statement that one should live while reporting daily is seen neither in the Pali nor in the Commentaries. Such a practice should be understood as a custom practiced by monks who are not well-versed in the Vinaya.

## Explanation of the Story of Former Members of Other Sects (Aññatitthiyapubbavatthukathāvaṇṇanā)

In the phrase "one who was formerly a member of another sect (aññatitthiyapubba)," there are two interpretations of the meaning. One meaning is: referring to the monkhood of that Pasūra, he is "formerly a member of another sect," and that monk went back to that very same sectarian monastery. Another meaning is: a monk who has thus gone over to a sectarian side and returns again in the guise of a layman is "formerly a member of another sect"; if such a person comes, he should not be ordained.

Excluding the one who has gone over to the sectarian side, in the phrase "Monks, he who was formerly a member of another sect," the word "formerly" (pubba) does not only refer to one wearing the guise of a layman, but indeed also refers to one who remains in the guise of a sectarian as undertaken by himself. Because of being a non-sectarian (atitthiya) by way of [right] view, he is called "formerly a non-sectarian" (atitthiyapubba). Such a person, having formerly been a non-sectarian, comes after having disrobed; for him, there is no task of giving probation (parivāsa).

For such a person who was formerly a member of another sect, does the novice ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) occur by taking the guise of a monk and establishing the refuges, or does it not? In this inquiry, if the novice ordination occurs, then the statement: "Monks, if any other person who was formerly a member of another sect desires the going forth in this Dhamma-Vinaya, desires the higher ordination, to him a four-month probation should be given" (Mahāvagga 86) would be contradicted.
423:
If the going forth (pabbajjā) had already occurred, the statement: "Monks... if another person who was formerly a member of another sect desires the going forth in this Dhamma-Vinaya, desires the higher ordination, to him a four-month probation (parivāsa) is given" would be contradicted. If the going forth has not yet occurred, then the non-performance of the going forth through the probation-legal-act-formula (parivāsa-kammavācā) would be contradicted. In this matter, the elders residing in the Mahāvihāra say: "Probation should be given only to one who is already manifest as a novice (sāmaṇera)." Other teachers, however, do not say so. Those teachers say that the sutta passage: "Monks, a person formerly of another sect who has thus satisfied [the community] should be ordained" (Mahāvagga 87) should be set aside. If it is said that because of the general meaning of the term "formerly a member of another sect" used before and after, he has not become a novice, then if that were so, it would follow that he should be given higher ordination without even having gone forth as a novice. If that were the case, it would contradict the sutta spoken at the very beginning. The reading "titthāyatanaṃ saṅkanto" (gone over to a sectarian monastery) is also not good. If he breaks any of the precepts such as killing living beings, it seems that even if the four months are complete, he must fulfill them again. They say that since his restraint (saṃvara) is permitted for the sake of making him a monk, there is nothing to be said regarding his virtue; this point should be accepted after investigation. If the refuges are broken, they are broken only in the state of being a novice.

## End of the Explanation of the Story of Former Members of Other Sects.

"Look at just my bowl and robes; I will give this bowl and robe," saying this is appropriate behavior because there is no offense. "Upadḍhupadḍhaṃ" means a little at a time (bit by bit).

"Desacārittaṃ" refers to the customs and practices of various regions, such as making announcements to everyone or recording inscriptions. It is written that "it is permissible (to ordain) the son of a female temple slave." Because they are offered with the words "We give these temple attendants to the Saṅgha of monks," they are not the slaves of those monks. One is permitted to make a masterless slave a free person oneself. It is also written, "They say there is no offense for a monk who, having been a slave and ordained, runs away upon seeing his former master." This means he was formerly the slave of that monk. The king is the master of a masterless slave; therefore, some teachers say he should be ordained after asking permission from the king or the people in that village. It is written, "having made him a free person (bhujissa)." Regarding him, the resolution is stated: "One should act in such a way that he becomes a free person." Having spoken with this intention, some have written, "it is of no use." In the context that it is only proper to make him a free person, it is said, "If they see him, they will pursue him." There is no offense. They say the statement "I hear I am not yet pure" is said in reference to that monk who was a free person.

Chattamangala refers to the parasol-crowning ceremony of the sub-king (crown prince). Vaṭṭānugata means following the round of defilements. It is called savighātaka (accompanied by distress) because it is a cause of exhaustion.

Why did the Venerable Sāriputta ask, "Venerable Sir, how shall I ordain Rāhula?" even though he had previously ordained the Brahmin Rādhā? It is because he intended to address the rejection of the [previous] method of higher ordination (upasampadā). Therefore, the Blessed One had indeed rejected that [old] method of higher ordination. Knowing that the Blessed One now intended to remove future doubts, the Elder made this request. It is said that the phrase "to the marrow of the bones" is stated by way of the power of mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa). The difference between Buddhas and Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) should be understood by their distinctiveness (vyatta) and other qualities. Otherwise, if the literal meaning were taken, Prince Nanda and others would also have become Buddhas upon ordaining, based on the statement, "If he ordains, he will become a Buddha."

Regarding the statement, "It is proper to show him by sending him back; it is proper to ordain him after asking permission"—this is because a person who has reached a foreign land (videsa) is, by worldly convention, considered free from the dwelling of his parents and lives according to his own will. Therefore, his parents are as if in a state of non-existence. For this reason, the statement "They do not show lack of faith in the teacher who ordained him" is not in vain. There is a worldly expression that those who have ordained have a similar destiny (samagatika). Therefore, in this context, going to another region due to suffering and such is also treated as having a similar destiny. Here, "foreign land" (videsa) means a place other than where the parents reside; it does not mean a place other than one's place of birth. If the literal meaning of the syllables were the only standard and not logic (yutti), it would follow that even one whose parents are deceased could not be ordained. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: a son should not be ordained without the permission of parents who are residing in a reachable place. Otherwise, it would contradict the Pali Canon, and it is not proper for a Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) to loosen the grounds for an offense. Let this matter be so for now. If it is asked, "Why does the method starting with 'I will burn the monastery' not contradict?"—it is because the ordination was given involuntarily out of fear of harm to oneself or others, or because it was given for the sake of protecting the son. In such a case, he is considered to have ordained by his own will, not because he was enticed by someone. It does not contradict because it is in accordance with the origin (nidāna) that "there is love for the son, or love for the one who protects the son."

## The Explanation of the Story of Rāhula is finished.
428:
## Explanation of the Story of the Punishment regarding Training Rules

"Attano pariveṇañca" refers to a private dwelling located within one's own compound. "Mukhadvārikaṃ" refers to nutriment to be consumed by way of the mouth. In prohibiting that novice, those who are urged to do so perform the act of barring or preventing him from receiving food. Alternatively, the meaning is that they apply the prohibition to the food consumed by mouth, which is the prohibition allowed by the Blessed One in the statement, "I allow you, monks, to impose a prohibition."

## The Explanation of the Story of the Punishment regarding Training Rules is finished.

## Explanation of the Story of the Prohibition without Asking and Others

This means "also to other immoral monks." Some teachers write "dussīlabhikkhūpi"; that writing is not good. Ancient teachers, however, say: "If he does not desist even after being spoken to up to three times, he should be expelled (nāsetabba) after informing the Saṅgha. Even if he begs for ordination again, he should be ordained only after informing the Saṅgha."

In the phrase "similar to the motion for higher ordination (upasampada-kammavācā) of monks," it is meant: "Just as a monk who has given up the training and, while still wearing the robes as before, later receives higher ordination again, must again perform acts of respect such as bowing to those who were previously junior to him or of the same seniority; likewise, a novice who has retaken the refuges must again perform acts of respect such as bowing to a novice who was previously junior to him or of the same seniority. The outward mark (liṅga) in this novicehood does not establish seniority."

Some say, "Eating at the wrong time is indeed a transgression for novices." He should be made to confess the fault (accaya) in the manner starting with, "Venerable Sir, a fault has overcome me." It is said, "By not relinquishing a wrong view, as soon as it is said, 'Hey novice, go away,' he becomes one who is defeated (pārājika)." Others say, "Because it is said 'up to three times,' the refuges are not broken merely by speaking dispraise of the Buddha and others, or merely by holding a wrong view." If this is so, I think that such [re-ordination] is also possible for a novice who commits killing and so on. Some say, "The expulsion (nāsanā) is stated again for one who is immoral," and that seems appropriate. Indeed, it should be considered that the Blessed One does not allow the destruction of the outward mark (liṅga-nāsanā) of a virtuous person. Ancient teachers say, "By the designation of a defiler of bhikkhunīs, both those who are capable and those who are incapable [of ordination] are included." Just as the meaning is shown here as "he does not even receive ordination," likewise: "Monks, a paṇḍaka (eunuch), if not ordained, should not be ordained; if ordained, he should be expelled" (Mahāvagga, 109) ...
429:
It is shown that for those persons mentioned by the method beginning with "A paṇḍaka should not be ordained, and if already ordained, should be expelled," there is no state of being a novice (pabbajjā). Indeed, apart from this matter of ordination, there is no other place where the pabbajjā of those such as paṇḍakas is prohibited. Other teachers say that the term "bhikkhunīdūsaka" (defiler of a nun) is taken again to show that, just as pabbajjā is prohibited for a bhikkhunīdūsaka, it is also prohibited for those such as paṇḍakas, because it is similar to what was stated: "Monks, an unordained bhikkhunīdūsaka should not be ordained, and if already ordained, should be expelled" (Mahāvagga 114). What is the benefit of this statement? Is it not stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā): "With reference to the person for whom pabbajjā is prohibited in this Dispensation, this statement was made: 'An unordained person should not be ordained, and if already ordained, should be expelled'"?

## The explanation of the case of Anāpucchāvaraṇa and others is finished.

## Explanation of the Case of the Paṇḍaka

Because an opakkamika-paṇḍaka (one made a neuter by surgical means) has deficient organs, pabbajjā is prohibited for one who is not yet ordained, and upasampadā (higher ordination) should not be given to one who is already a novice. The teacher says, "It is our opinion that if there is an examination of one who was previously ordained, he should not be expelled." A person with severed genitals is not a paṇḍaka. Among the five types of paṇḍakas, only the napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka (congenital neuter) is one who lacks the sexual characteristic (bhāva). It should be understood that the remaining four types of paṇḍakas possess the sexual characteristic. However, their sexual characteristic is deficient. Some teachers say that these four types are indeed men. Some teachers say that a woman can also be a pakkha-paṇḍakī (a female neuter by the half-month). When an effort such as castration is made, the state of being a paṇḍaka inevitably occurs; therefore, such a person does not obtain pabbajjā. It is stated that "If, however, the state of being a paṇḍaka does not occur in someone, the decision is that pabbajjā is not prohibited."

It is written: "The prohibition of pabbajjā means that if one is ordained during the non-paṇḍaka phase, he should be expelled during the paṇḍaka phase." In the ancient glossary (Gaṇṭhipada), however, seven types of paṇḍakas are mentioned, including the māsa-paṇḍaka and lekha-paṇḍaka. Among those paṇḍakas, the lekha-paṇḍaka is said to be one whose seed (fertility) is destroyed by the power of a mantra. In that regard, it is also stated: "If an opakkamika-paṇḍaka and a lekha-paṇḍaka have been ordained, they should not be expelled. Whichever teacher ordains them, that teacher incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

## The explanation of the Case of the Paṇḍaka is finished.
430:
## Explanation of the Case of the Theyyasaṃvāsaka

In this matter of the theyyasaṃvāsaka (one who lives in communion by theft), although by the literal meaning of the words it is known that only one who steals communion is a theyyasaṃvāsaka, in reality, there are three types of theyyasaṃvāsakas. Here, "communion" (saṃvāsa) does not mean performing major or minor ecclesiastical acts together, but rather, in this context, saṃvāsa refers to the distinction of actions such as counting the years of seniority (vassa) as a monk. The meaning of the Commentary is that this counting of vassa can be done by theft, but not the other (performing ecclesiastical acts). There is an offense for one who, having gone to a foreign country and been ordained, says "I have ten years of seniority" and so on when questioned. Some teachers say there is no offense in saying this to laypeople. For those who have taken the appearance of a monk due to fear of the king and so on, even if there is a deceptive mind thinking "Let the layperson know me as a monk," no offense arises because there is no desire to deceive monks or to live in communion with them. It is written that "it is difficult for one who comes to the monastery and takes communal property (saṅghika) thinking 'this is the food of all sects' to avoid communion; therefore, this was stated." Because it is said "one who is well-ordained," if a layperson is given higher ordination, he reaches the state of being well-ordained (one who incurs the offense). By the phrase "even during the time when not yet ordained," it is shown that if one hears of it at the time of higher ordination, even if he does not report it, he is indeed a well-ordained one (one who incurs the offense). It should be understood that in the Andhaka Commentary and the ancient glossaries, an immoral monk is called a "theyyasaṃvāsaka" by this figurative method: "Monks, you eat the country's alms-food by theft" (Pārājika 195). For that very reason, it was said, "He should not be accepted." By the phrase "in the Mahāpeḷā and so on," the property of laypeople is shown.

If a novice (sāmaṇera) himself counts false years of seniority and takes (benefits), it is a pārājika (defeat), but he is not a theyyasaṃvāsaka. The same applies to a monk. With the intention that such a person should be punished according to the value of the goods, the phrase "if a novice himself" and so on was stated. Since this theyyasaṃvāsaka can only be one who is ordained and cannot be one who is not ordained, it is not possible to say, "Monks, an unordained theyyasaṃvāsaka should not be ordained, and if already ordained, should be expelled." Therefore, by the power of this theyyasaṃvāsaka, the Pāḷi text is established starting from the paṇḍaka with "An unordained person should not be ordained" and so on. This is not because they are merely unfit for higher ordination, but because the view that they are worthy of pabbajjā for all eleven types might become prevalent (thus the prohibition includes pabbajjā). Furthermore, the Pāḷi text is established in that way because undesirable offenses might arise. This is because going over to other sects (titthiya) and causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda) can only happen to one who is ordained (upasampanna) and not to one who is not ordained...
431:
Both of these types of persons are indeed those who have gone forth (ordained); they are not those who have not gone forth. Therefore, it should be understood that if there is a Pali text such as, "Monks, one who has gone over to heretics is one who has not gone forth and should not be given the going-forth," then the undesirable consequence would arise that both of them should not be given the going-forth. Among those three types of theyyasaṃvāsaka (those who live in communion by theft), one who assumes the guise of a novice (sāmaṇera) is called a liṅgatthenaka (thief of appearance). One who assumes the guise of a fully ordained monk is called a saṃvāsatthenaka (thief of communion). One who does both is an ubhayatthenaka (thief of both). In truth, in this matter of communion, the communion of a novice is not called "communion" (saṃvāsa). For that reason, some say in the Commentary, "All the various monastic acts, such as the counting of a monk's years of seniority, are called communion in this sense." The Teacher says that it is not so, because paying homage according to seniority, enjoying a seat, or being denied a seat are common to the communion of a novice.

## End of the Explanation of the Story of the Theyyasaṃvāsaka.

## Explanation of the Story of the Titthiyapakkantaka

Although the words "Monks, one who has gone over to heretics" and so forth are spoken only in the story of the monk Pasūra, which is its origin, because there is no prohibited matter in that story, they do not become excluded persons (abhabba). It is mentioned here because it can occur independently of a theyyasaṃvāsaka in this matter of the titthiyapakkantaka. In that regard, the words "furthermore, he should not be given the going-forth" should be understood as being spoken here because of seeing the desire to request only the full ordination (upasampadā) for the monk Pasūra, and because the Blessed One prohibited only the full ordination by saying, "If he comes, he should not be given the full ordination," fearing the fault of appearing to permit the going-forth (pabbajjā). By merely taking the appearance of those heretics, whether one adopts their view or not, one becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. If one reaches the state where the naked appearance, which should not be paid homage to, is considered noble, one is not released. In this matter, some say, "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred at every step; it does not happen by going naked because of going with an unstable mind thinking 'I will become an Ājīvaka.'" My opinion is that it is appropriate in both ways. As long as the view is not yet accepted, that view still protects him. How is it known that this was spoken by a fully ordained monk? Some say it is known only by taking the words of the Commentary as the authority. Some say it is known by way of the origin (nidāna). Some say it is known because Pasūra was a fully ordained monk, and thus the state of titthiyapakkantaka is spoken of only for monks. As it is said: "The preceptor has either gone away, or disrobed, or passed away, or gone over to another side (sect)," says the Teacher. Some say it is because "going over to another side" is not present in the stories of the expulsion of novices. Some say it is known by the prescription of the probation (parivāsa) for the sake of full ordination for one who was formerly a heretic and is now a monk, for fear of him going over to another side.
432:
Some teachers might say, "The probation is prescribed for the sake of the going-forth (pabbajjā) as well"; that should not be said. This is because it has been investigated previously, and because one who has not gone forth does not possess higher virtue (adhisīla). Indeed, Pātimokkha virtue is called higher virtue, and that does not exist for one who has not gone forth. And for this person who was formerly a heretic (aññatitthiyapubba), higher virtue is mentioned in the duties of probation. As it is said: "Furthermore, monks, a former heretic has a strong desire for the recitation, for questioning, and for higher virtue" (Mahāvagga). Alternatively, it is known because in the passage, "Monks, if a Sakyan by birth who was formerly a heretic comes, he should be given the full ordination when he arrives," only the full ordination (upasampadā) is shown. Here, showing only the full ordination is because it is accomplished by the granting of probation to him. Indeed, this Pali text is for the purpose of showing the fact of granting probation.

## End of the Explanation of the Story of the Titthiyapakkantaka.

## Explanation of the Story of the Animal (Tiracchānagata)

"Nāgayoniyā" means because of being of the Naga species, due to the cause of one's own Naga birth. Why (is he weary)? Because for all Nagas, when they frequently indulge in sexual intercourse with their own kind, and when they fall into a deep sleep, (their Naga form becomes manifest, and thus they are weary).

## End of the Explanation of the Story of the Animal.

## Explanation of the Story of the Matricide, etc. (Mātughātaka)

112-5. "Apavāhanaṃ" means giving away (the robes), meaning desiring to wear the saffron-colored cloth. With a corrupt mind. What kind of mind? The meaning is with a murderous mind. Some teachers say it is a corrupt mind by way of causing blood to flow; that explanation is not good.

## End of the Explanation of the Story of the Matricide, etc.

## Explanation of the Story of the Hermaphrodite (Ubhatobyañjanaka)

It is written: "If they receive this name by the sex organ that arises at the moment of rebirth, that is the meaning."

## End of the Explanation of the Story of the Hermaphrodite.
433:
## Explanation of the Story of the One Without a Preceptor and Others

Some say, "It is invalid (kuppati)." Regarding the statement that this view "should not be accepted," it is well-stated by considering that the act (kamma) is invalid only in the capacity of a paṇḍaka and others completing the quorum (gaṇapūraṇa), but not that the entire act is invalid. This is because it was spoken in the manner of: "Monks, if a group of five monks performs a kamma where a bhikkhunī is the fifth, that kamma is not a kamma and should not be performed," and so forth. Otherwise, if another meaning were taken, there would have to be a Pali text such as: "If one performs a kamma with a paṇḍaka preceptor, that kamma is not a kamma and should not be performed."

Just as during the time of the higher ordination (upasampadā) of one who has an incomplete bowl and robes, if the ritual act (kammavācā) is performed by reciting the non-existent fact that "the bowl and robes are complete," the ordination is successful despite the absence of those items. Similarly, even if one performs the act by reciting a non-existent fact—such as a paṇḍaka preceptor who is not a valid basis, or an absent basis—saying, "This Buddharakkhita is the candidate for ordination of the Venerable Dhammarakkhita," the ordination is indeed successful because of the presence of the monks who complete the quorum. This meaning is already evident because there is no such statement as: "Monks, one should not be ordained by a paṇḍaka preceptor; if one should ordain him, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), and that person is also not ordained."

Indeed, the Buddhas do not remain without teaching what ought to be taught; they certainly teach it. Therefore, He taught: "Whatever monk, knowing a person to be under twenty years of age... that person is also not ordained," and so forth.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "The assembly should be informed by a competent and capable monk," the statement that "if the proclamation (anussāvana) is performed by teachers such as those living in communion by stealth (theyyasaṃvāsaka), the ordination is not successful because they are not monks," should also not be accepted. To say it another way, when the success or failure of legal acts is described in the manner of "These four acts fail in five ways," and so forth, this view should not be accepted because it is not taught that "Acts fail in seven ways: due to the basis (vatthu), the motion (ñatti), the proclamation (anussāvana), the boundary (sīmā), the assembly (parisa), the preceptor (upajjhāya), or the teacher (ācariya)."

If it is argued that the teacher and preceptor are included in the term "due to the assembly (parisa)," it is not so. This is because in the detailed analysis of the Pali, "Acts fail in twelve ways due to the assembly," those teachers and preceptors are not mentioned or touched upon. This meaning is stated as: "Since this can be known only by the power of the Pali taught specifically in various places, the beginning of the method is shown and summarized; this is the search for the suitability of the statement that 'the act is not invalid'."

In this matter, this point should be examined: Did those monks who were ordaining one without a preceptor recite that false basis according to the aforementioned method, or did they omit those words without reciting them out of fear of false speech (musāvāda)? In this inquiry, your objection as an objector is but a little. If...
434:
If they did not recite the preceptor's name because of the absence of a preceptor, there would be the consequence of the failure stated as "not referring to the person (puggalaṃ parāmasati)." If they did recite it, would it be a lie (musāvāda) for them? It is said: They certainly recite it, both out of fear of the aforementioned failure and because it is stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) that "the act, however, is not invalid," and because a lie is not possible [in that context], and because an act can be successful even with a lie. Indeed, it is not possible to cause the failure or success of a legal act merely by a lie. Therefore, one should seek the meaning that is free from both faults regarding the statement "they ordain one without a preceptor."

In this matter, this is the logical reasoning: "Just as in the past, even when preceptors for the going-forth (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā) existed, it was said 'at that time, monks [ordained] one without a preceptor' because they were not taken according to the sequence of taking a preceptor; similarly here, it is said 'they ordain one without a preceptor' because he was not taken even though a preceptor existed. The teacher of the ritual act (kammavācācariya), however, should recite the ritual act by identifying that person as the preceptor and mentioning the preceptor. Or, for some reason, he recites the ritual act after taking the consent (chanda) of a preceptor who cannot come in person (cannot provide physical presence). Or, the preceptor gives the status of preceptor to the candidate, and later, in such a case where the one who has become a monk is questioned or not questioned, he confesses to being a novice even before the preceptor was given, or confesses to being one who has rejected the training or committed an extreme offence (antimavatthu); or like those who convey consent, the preceptor has gone to another boundary (sīmā). It is stated in the Ancient Glossary (Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada): 'Having said that the ritual act is successful, because it is stated: "Monks, I allow ordination in the border regions with a group of five including a Vinaya expert," some say that the preceptor who is the fifth as a Vinaya expert must indeed be present nearby.'"

That text is also authoritative because that statement does not exist regarding the middle regions. If it is asked, "Does it not follow that the ritual act is successful even if the preceptor is not present nearby?"—it does not. Why? Because only the text stated in the success of an act as "referring to the person" is our authority. Indeed, in that case, the person known as the preceptor who is not present does not deserve to be referred to; therefore, in that case, referring to the person should be understood like referring to the Saṅgha. They ordain by making the Saṅgha or the group the preceptor, because in essence, they are persons. The ancient teachers (Porāṇā) say that they ordain by making a paṇḍaka and others the preceptor because it was unknown at the time of ordination.
435:
## Explanation of the Story of Those Without Bowls and Robes

In ordaining a person who does not possess a bowl and robes, the Kammavācā teacher, either with the perception that "the bowl and robes are complete" or by simply reciting the existing words without particularly regarding the fulfillment of the literal meaning, makes the Kammavācā heard as "the bowl and robes are complete." This is like the present day when a person whose parents are deceased or separated is asked, "Have you been permitted by your parents?" and they answer, "Yes, Bhante."

What is the use of many words? The essential decision in this matter is as follows: Since the characteristic that "at that time, the four formal acts fail in five ways" had not yet been laid down, they ordained those without preceptors and so forth. Since the excluded persons had not yet been mentioned, they ordained by making eunuchs (paṇḍaka) preceptors and so forth. Since the thirteen obstructive questions had not yet been shown, they ordained those without bowls and robes. It should be understood that the absence of the phrase "the bowl and robes are complete" in the very first Kammavācā allowed by the words, "I allow you, monks, to ordain by a motion-and-fourth-proclamation act (ñatticatuttha-kamma)," is the evidence in this matter. This is because that phrase was allowed later in due sequence.

## Explanation of the Story of Those with Severed Hands and So Forth

Let this matter be as it is in every respect. A question is raised: "How is it possible for this to occur—that they give the going forth (pabbajjā) to a mute or a deaf person? For it was allowed from the beginning with the words, 'I allow you, monks, the going forth by these three refuges.'" The answer is stated: In the Pali passage, "Monks, thus should one be given the going forth. He should be told: 'Say this... for the third time I go to the Sangha for refuge,'" they ordained mutes by misinterpreting the meaning of the words "He should be told: 'Say this.'"

Having commanded the candidate for going forth, "Say this," the preceptor himself says, "For the third time I go to the Sangha for refuge." Whether that candidate, having been so commanded, can repeat the preceptor's words or not, the Blessed One says in various Pali passages: "He makes it known by body, he makes it known by speech, he makes it known by both body and speech; the preceptor is taken; the consent is given; the purity is given; the invitation (pavāraṇā) is given." Either by considering that meaning, or because the candidate makes the refuges known by the body, and since in the world one who makes something known by the body is also said to be "saying this," it should be understood that they ordained mutes by adopting that figurative sense. In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada (glossary), a question is raised: "How do they give the going forth to a mute?" and it is stated that because his physical sensitivity (kāyappasāda) is possible...
436:
"...by making physical contact and making it known through hand gestures, they gave the going forth." What is the use of many words? This is the essence here: Just as previously, when the topic of going forth (pabbajjā) was being discussed, the term for going forth was set aside and the expression was made through the power of ordination (upasampadā) in such ways as, "Monks, a eunuch (paṇḍaka) is one not ordained; he should not be ordained." Although in the case of one who lives clandestinely (theyyasaṃvāsaka), going forth is not possible and thus not mentioned, in all cases, the term for ordination is intended because of its influence. This is done because when going forth is forbidden by way of ordination, ordination itself is forbidden.

Similarly, in this case, while the topic of ordination is being discussed, it should be understood that the term for ordination is set aside and the term for going forth is used, referring specifically to ordination. Although it seems that the term for ordination should have been used from the start because going forth is not possible for a mute, the term for going forth is used from the start for the purpose of preventing a wrong view. How? From the words, "Monks, a mute has not yet reached the inclusion (osāraṇa); if the Sangha includes him, he is included (ordained)," the fact that a mute is ordained is established. A wrong view might arise that "He is merely ordained, but not one who has gone forth, because going forth is impossible for him." To cause that wrong view to be abandoned, the Blessed One establishes the right view that whoever is ordained is indeed one who has gone forth. Among those who have gone forth, however, there are some who are ordained and some who are not ordained.

Furthermore, the term for going forth is used here to show that those with severed hands and so forth who have been given the going forth are "well-gone-forth" (supabbajita), and to prevent the suspicion that they have not gone forth. How? Because of the prohibition, "Monks, one with a severed hand should not be given the going forth," and because there is no place where it is stated, "those who have gone forth are well-gone-forth," a suspicion might arise that those with severed hands and so forth have not gone forth. In whatever way suspicion arises, that suspicion should be set aside. In the Khandhaka, referring to ordination, the Blessed One prevents it by saying, "Monks, one with a severed hand has not yet reached the inclusion; if the Sangha includes him, he is included." By that same method, He shows that all of them are indeed well-gone-forth. Otherwise, if the meaning is taken differently, one would arrive at the undesirable conclusion that those with severed hands and so forth are only ordained but have not gone forth. How would this be reached? By such rules as, "Monks, one with a severed hand should not be given the going forth; if he has gone forth, he should be expelled," or "Monks, one with a severed hand should not be given the going forth; whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa), and he is not one who has gone forth..."
437:
Because it is stated in the Pāḷi text, "He is not a novice (pabbajita)," and in the Campeyyakkhandhaka, "He should be rehabilitated (osārita) by the Saṅgha," it implies that one might arrive at an undesirable conclusion: "These individuals, such as those with severed hands, are only fully ordained monks (upasampanna), not novices," or "Even if they are monks, if they were novices, they should be expelled."

In this matter, it should be considered: Since the statement "He is not a novice" is absent, does it not lead to the undesirable conclusion that a mute person (mūga) can achieve novicehood, and that novicehood can be attained through a one-sided purity (ekatovisuddhi)? This conclusion is not reached because it is correctly understood that in this context, higher ordination (upasampadā) is intended by the desire for novicehood (pabbajjā). Otherwise, if the meaning is taken literally according to the words, another undesirable conclusion would be reached—namely, the absence of the prescribed dukkaṭa offense.

How so? The dukkaṭa offense stated as, "Monks, a mute person should not be given the novice ordination; for the one who gives it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa," occurs at the completion of the ordination, not while it is still unfinished. Indeed, the preliminary dukkaṭa (pubbapayoga) is incurred first. Therefore, since the completion of novice ordination for a mute person is impossible, the opportunity for this dukkaṭa offense would never arise. However, if the meaning is taken in terms of higher ordination (upasampadā), it is possible because the formal act (kamma) is completed. For this reason, in the Pāḷi text, regarding the paṇḍaka, it was not prescribed as: "Monks, a paṇḍaka should not be given higher ordination; for the one who gives it, there is an offense of dukkaṭa." Because it was not so prescribed, only the preliminary dukkaṭa is possible here, not the other. By this much, it is clearly established: "In that context, higher ordination is intended by the desire for novicehood, not novicehood itself."

Here, one might ask: "How is it known that the novice ordination (sāmaṇerapabbajjā) does not occur through physical action (kāyapayoga)?" It is answered: It is known because the triad (tika) beginning with "communicating by body" is not found. In this regard, there is the following:

"A small hare might perhaps find a footing in the great ocean; but in the ocean of the Vinaya, which has four depths and is difficult to penetrate with wisdom, [the ignorant] will certainly not find a footing."

In the term "Brahmūjugatto," taking the word "Brahma" in the sense of being faultless and noble, one who has a straight body without defects is called "Brahmūjugatto." Alternatively, without using examples like Sakka (the king of gods) who enjoys sensual pleasures, one who has a straight body like a Great Brahmā is called "Brahmūjugatto." A pot with a large belly is called "Mahākucchighaṭa." One who resembles such a pot is called "Mahākucchighaṭasadisa" (pot-bellied). How is it known that "Galagaṇḍī" (one with a goiter) is merely a teaching? Because of the statement: "Monks, one afflicted by the five diseases should not be given novice ordination," kilāsa (skin disease) is also intended by this term...
438:
Because of the statement "should not be given novice ordination," kilāsa (skin disease) is also intended here. It is not only that one (galagaṇḍī), but also the ten types of persons are intended here: those afflicted by the five diseases, those from royal servants (rājabhaṭa) to slaves (dāsa) mentioned in the Pāḷi, and those without parental consent mentioned in the Rāhulavatthu. To clarify that meaning, the Elder Upāli spoke again in this Hatthacchinnapāḷi, bringing forward the previously mentioned likhitaka (wanted/marked), kasāhata (flogged), and lakkhaṇāhata (branded).

For this reason, in the Campeyyakkhandhaka, in the analysis (vibhaṅga) of the statement: "Monks, there is a person who has not reached rehabilitation (osāraṇa); if the Saṅgha rehabilitates him, some are well-rehabilitated (sosasārita), and some are wrongly rehabilitated (dosārita)," the seven types of persons—those afflicted by the five diseases, royal servants, thieves, jailbreakers (kārabhedaka), debtors (iṇāyika), slaves, and those without parental consent—are not included and are not obtained. Otherwise, they should also have been mentioned in that analysis. If it is argued, "They are not mentioned because they are unsuitable for that act," then they should have been mentioned like the paṇḍaka and others in the analysis of the statement: "The Saṅgha rehabilitates, and some are wrongly rehabilitated," but they were not mentioned. Since they are not mentioned in either case, these people cannot be "neither" (anubhaya). Therefore, to include the ten types of persons mentioned above who were not yet stated, the likhitaka and others were mentioned again.

Why are they mentioned here out of sequence (uppaṭipāṭi)? It is to show the state of dependency of debtors and slaves—that even if they are well-rehabilitated (sosasārita), they must be returned to their owners. Therefore, it is stated in that commentary: "Even if he has fled, he should be brought back and given [to the owner]," etc. Here, if a thief who has committed a crime ordains, or a royal servant who has committed an offense ordains, it should be understood that they are included under the category of "debtor." Otherwise, since all those with the aforementioned characteristics are not worthy of being called "sosasārita" like debtors and slaves, the out-of-sequence teaching is given to exclude them, showing that it "ascends but does not descend." Because the likhitaka is called "sosasārita," he should be taken to another region. The same should be understood for jailbreakers and others.

By this sequence of words, it should be understood that the Blessed One, being skilled in His teaching, showed the completion of the acts of pabbajjā and upasampadā for the ten aforementioned persons by repeating what was previously taken, and showed the distinction between individuals for those skilled in the teaching by speaking out of sequence. In this regard, there is this verse:

"By speaking what is fit to be spoken in the Pāḷi sequence, and by showing what is necessary though unfit to be spoken through the method of teaching (desanā), the word of the Sugata makes the mind truly wondrous."
439:
In this context, the objector asks: Since a person under twenty years of age is not mentioned in either category (the sussārita or dosārita) in the Campeyyakkhandhaka, could such a person be a 'neither' (anubhaya)? He cannot be an anubhaya simply because he is not mentioned. If there were a third category (anubhaya), the Blessed One would certainly have taught it; but He did not. Therefore, he is not an anubhaya. To which side then does he belong? He belongs to the dosārita (unfit) side. Why then was he not mentioned? Because he is already prohibited by the training rule.

"Upanāhaṃ bandhitvā" means binding again. It is written: "It is the name of a procedure performed by binding the foot with various medicines and placing it in a pit." "Kappasīso" refers to one with a flat head like an elephant's forehead. "Gobattanaḷikā" is a tube made for cattle feed and water. "Upakkamukho" refers to one with an acrid mouth. "Vātaṇḍiko" refers to one with a swelling disease (vuddhi-roga) in the testicles. "Vikaṭo" refers to one with deformed feet that move sideways. It is said there are two readings: "guṇi" and "kuṇī." For those whom novice ordination is prohibited, higher ordination is also prohibited. Since those with severed hands and so on were taught only in the context of higher ordination, he spoke with reference to those with severed hands and so on.

## End of the Commentary on the Story of Those with Severed Hands, etc.

## Commentary on the Story of Dependence on the Shameless

By the words, "Monks, dependence (nissaya) should not be given to the shameless," both types of usage—usage of the Dhamma and usage of material requisites—with shameless monks or novices are prohibited, because giving them dependence leads to shamelessness. As the Blessed One taught: "Monks, a teacher should support and help a pupil through instruction, questioning, exhortation, and advice" (Mahāva. 79), and since a preceptor (upajjhāya) can also dismiss dependence (nissayappāṇamana), it should be understood that he too is the dependence for the co-resident (saddhivihārika). Therefore, it is established that if a preceptor is shameless, one should not live in dependence on him.

A monk who has a share similar to the good practice of monks is called a bhikkhusabhāga. The state of being such a monk is bhikkhusabhāgatā. One may live with that bhikkhusabhāgatā with the intention "until I know." This means knowing the teacher's shamelessness. It is written that one does not get to live by laying down the burden of knowing, thinking, "I will stay for about seven days; what is the use of knowing the shamelessness of the monks?" Knowing the bhikkhusabhāgatā, one cannot let the dawn rise while saying, "I will go only tomorrow; what is the use of announcing my dependence?" If one falls asleep while intending to "get up and go before dawn," and the dawn rises, it is allowable.

## End of the Commentary on the Story of Dependence on the Shameless.

## Commentary on the Story of Dependence for Travelers, etc.

"The story of a monk traveling on a journey... living without dependence when not obtaining it" is said only for the non-rainy season. This is because traveling during the rainy season is prohibited even in the Pali. That statement is not a standard (to be taken as absolute). Because traveling is possible during the rainy season by the power of the seven-day limit for breaking the retreat (vassacchēda), etc...
440:
...by knowing the similar nature of monks (bhikkhusabhāgatā-jānana), it is written that one does not get to live by laying down the burden of knowing. Knowing the similar nature of monks, one cannot let the dawn rise while thinking, "I will go only tomorrow; what is the use of announcing my dependence?" If one falls asleep while intending to "get up and go before dawn," and the dawn rises, it is allowable.

## Commentary on the Story of Dependence for Travelers, etc.

"The story of a monk traveling on a journey who, not obtaining a giver of dependence, lives without dependence, refers only to the non-rainy season, because traveling during the rainy season is prohibited even in the Pali"—this statement is not a standard. This is because traveling during the rainy season is possible, such as for a seven-day period to break the retreat, or because the rainy season might begin while one is already traveling. "On the way... no offense" applies only when there is no giver of dependence. In accordance with the text "tassa nissāya," it means "depending on him." By the words "when a suitable giver of dependence arrives," it is clear that this procedure is only for the time before the rains. It is said that this is because no one arrives during the rainy season. If that monk, while living at a sea-port or a land-port, hears that "such and such a Great Elder (Mahāthera) will arrive" when the time for entering the rainy season is near, it is allowable if he waits for that elder. If the day for entering the rainy season arrives while he is waiting, so be it; he must go to a place where he can find a giver of dependence. If it is allowable to go because there is no one to recite the Pātimokkha, how much more so when there is no giver of dependence? Some teachers say that if one sees a danger to life or a danger to the holy life (brahmacariya) while traveling, one should stay right there.

In saying "I am not able to utter the elder's name," it is said by way of designation: "this named venerable to this named venerable." According to the words "gottenāpi" (even by clan name), it is clear that it is allowable to use the common way of address. Therefore, it is established that even when asked, "What is your preceptor's name?" one should speak using the clan name (gotta) as the name. Thus, they say that the proclamation (anussāvana) should be made using any one of the four types of names. A person may have many names; among them, it is not allowable to use one name in the motion (ñatti) and another name in the proclamation (kammavācā). The proclamations must be identical in meaning and in phrasing. In some cases, saying "to the Venerable Buddharakkhita Thera," and in some cases, only...
441:
Some teachers say that when reciting "Buddharakkhitassa," it should not be said that "the recitation of the Kammavācā is diminished," because the name itself is not diminished. Some teachers also say that if one says "Āyasmato Buddharakkhitassa" in one place and "Buddharakkhitassa Āyasmato" in another, it merely falls into the category of a momentary variation (khitta) because it conforms to the Pali text. Other teachers say that such a practice is not allowable in the recitation of the Kammavācā because it may lead to the corruption of the syllables (byañjanabheda). However, if one recites it in the same way in all places, it is allowable because it conforms to the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) granted by the Blessed One. If it is asked, "Is it not allowable if done otherwise because it contradicts the characteristics?" The answer is: No, it is allowable because it conforms to the application (payoga). If it is asked, "Is the application in that Pali text one way, and in this Pali text another?" The answer is: No, because it would contradict the characteristics of failure (vipatti). It is not so in every respect. Since only the diminution of the recitation is mentioned in the Pali to clarify that meaning, the diminution in reciting other words is not possible as it would contradict the customary practice (āciṇṇakappa). If asked, "What is the measure of that customary practice?" it should be said that the measure is the learning from the teacher, for the learning from the teacher is the standard.

Regarding the phrase "Dve ekānussāvane," it is first written in the Gaṇṭhipada as "for the purpose of performing the Kammavācā together." This statement is a prohibition intended for the act of proclamation (anussāvana) where there are different preceptors but only one teacher. It means that such an act of proclamation is permitted with one preceptor and different teachers. It also means it is not permitted with different preceptors and only one teacher. In the Porāṇa-gaṇṭhipada, it is stated in the same way, saying, "It is not allowable in any manner to perform it together for more than three persons." This statement is appropriate. The teacher says this is because the Saṅgha does not perform a legal act (kamma) for the Saṅgha. In this matter, this point should be considered: How so? Four or more candidates for ordination (upasampadā-pekkha) do not obtain the designation of 'Saṅgha' because they have not yet attained the status of bhikkhus. The teacher says it is not our own speculation, but it is because the Blessed One specifically defined the limit as "three," and therefore it is said that it is not allowable for more than three. In the Anu-gaṇṭhipada, this meaning is also stated after much investigation. Likewise, it is stated in the Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā. There is no disagreement in any of the texts regarding this variation of meaning. There is a Parivāra-kathā which states: "Two candidates for ordination who have completed twenty years of age, both having the same preceptor, the same teacher, and with a single Kammavācā (being recited), one becomes ordained and the other does not." Pointing to that Parivāra-kathā, some teachers say that if one teacher recites a single Kammavācā for two or three candidates with a single preceptor, it is allowable. That statement is not appropriate. This is because it is impossible at that moment to demonstrate a Kammavācā endowed with the phonetic characteristics such as lax (sithila) and tense (dhanita) sounds. This is because it could fall into faults such as the fault of being released (vimuttadosa). For the purpose of showing that this was said with reference to performing it separately, it is said "Three..."
442:
"...persons of full twenty years, one preceptor for the three, one teacher, one Kammavācā; two become ordained, and one does not"—this is not stated (in the Parivāra). If it were stated thus, it would be possible to exclude the one standing in the air among the three and present a Kammavācā suitable for the two standing within the boundary (sīmā); to prevent that undesirable consequence, it says "both."

In that passage, the accomplishment of the object (vatthu-sampatti) is shown by the phrase "full twenty years." Since the assembly is primary, the accomplishment of the assembly (parisā-sampatti) is shown by the mention of the teacher and preceptor. The accomplishment of the announcement (anussāvana-sampatti) is shown by the Kammavācā. Only the accomplishment of the boundary (sīmā-sampatti) is not shown. Because of that [omission], failure (vipatti) arises because the Kammavācās occur at different moments. If there were a single moment, there would be either accomplishment or failure for both; it is not possible for there to be accomplishment for only one and failure for the other, as it would lead to defects in phrasing such as "released" (vimutta). That statement proves that if both are within the boundary, since it shows the accomplishment of the act for both together, the simultaneous recitation for two with one preceptor and one teacher is allowable. The simultaneous following of the formal act (sasammanubhāsanā) for two or three is shown in the Pali itself, and this accords with that Pali. Although the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariya) did not explicitly permit it, they did not reject it either. The teacher says, "It should be accepted after consideration," but that statement contradicts the natural custom (dhammatā).

This is the natural custom of the Buddhas: wherever there is a variation in phrasing, they teach what is appropriate to be said in important matters. Ordination by a messenger (dūtena upasampadā) and so on are examples here. Since there is no variation in the previously permitted Kammavācā here, although He said, "Bhikkhus, I allow the performance of two or three in one announcement," He did not say, "And thus, bhikkhus, should it be performed." If it is argued that even though there is variation, it was not stated because it should be adopted according to the Kammavācā taught by the power of two or many in various Pali passages, the teacher says that it is not the natural custom to speak on minor matters and remain silent on important matters.

In another Gaṇṭhipada text, it is explained in detail: "Two in one announcement" means reciting for two together. There is a reading "ekena" (by one), meaning by one teacher. It is in the same manner as the previous method, "by one or two teachers"; therefore, two or three should be announced by one teacher. There is also a reading "dvīhi vā tīhi vā" (by two or three). Regarding the phrase "different teachers, different preceptors," if it is argued that it is not allowable because it was said, "And that [should be done] with one preceptor, but not with different preceptors," the answer is: It is allowable. How? Since the analysis (vigga-ha) of "one announcement" as "recitation by one" is well-known, the analysis "recitation together" was stated to show the hidden meaning. Therefore, only the direct meaning...
443:
Regarding that ordination, it is permitted only for a single preceptor (upajjhāya) through the recitation of the kammavācā by a single teacher (ācariya); it is not permitted for various preceptors. With this meaning in mind, a two-fold analysis is stated. Therefore, it is also said in another way: "The meaning that it is not allowable with various teachers and various preceptors is thus established." That ordination is also permitted only by the kammavācā recited by a single teacher for a single preceptor; it is not permitted for various preceptors. What does this mean? It means: "A single teacher does not permit the candidates for ordination (upasampadāpekkha) of two or three preceptors (simultaneously)." In another Ganthipada, however, it is written: "Since the analysis 'by the recitation of a single teacher' is clear, the word 'ekena' (by one) is used to clarify that meaning. If stated thus, the wise will certainly understand. If it is clear and they understand, what is the use of the word 'ekena'? Even if they understand, if the reason is not firm, there could be a dispute, and it is not easy to understand. If 'ekena' is said, all such disputes will no longer exist." Thus, in this matter, many teachers and thinkers elaborate in various ways. Having thoroughly investigated all of them and having attended upon the lineage of teachers (garukula), one should only accept the meaning that is consistent with the lineage. It is indeed stated: "In all these variations of meaning, there is a difference of opinion."

## Upasampadāvidhikathāvaṇṇanā

In the phrase "leprosy, boils," the ancient teachers say that by taking leprosy and so on, those with severed hands and so forth are also included. Therefore, with these questions "Are you a human being? Are you a man?", one performs the exclusion of those who are capable and those who are incapable. With "Are you a freeman? Are you free from debt?" and so on, among the variations of meaning stated previously in the section on those with severed hands, the second variation is supported. In that Pali, by saying it in reverse order instead of the regular order "Are you free from debt? Are you a freeman?", it means that he is a freeman. He must also not be a servant who eats the king's rations. Because he is connected to the king, he might belong to the group of royal officers (rājabhaṭa); therefore, to ask if he is not such a royal officer, it is said: "Are you not a royal officer?" Otherwise, if the inclusion of all is accomplished by taking those afflicted with the five diseases, the others should not be mentioned. If they are to be mentioned, then all should be mentioned.

## Cattāronissayādikathāvaṇṇanā

128-9. "At that very moment, the shadow should be measured" and so on, is stated to know the status of senior and junior monks, because of the words "having made them pay homage to the feet of the monks." There is an ancient reading: "Have you come after a long time?"; there is also a reading: "He has done it for a long time."
444:
Because of the reason of associating (sambhoga) or living in communion (saṃvāsa) with a suspended monk (ukkhittaka), a pācittiya offense has been laid down; it means that there is no offense from that prescribed pācittiya. How is this known? It is known by taking the word "saṃvāsa" (communion). However, one certainly falls into a dukkaṭa offense which should be reached because of associating with a shameless monk (alajjī), but not because of living in communion. This is because living with a shameless monk is not prohibited. In this context, "saṃvāsa" means living together in a dwelling sufficient for sleeping together; it is not the kind of "saṃvāsa" mentioned in "he becomes a parajika and is not in communion (asaṃvāsa)." Such living together is not allowable with a suspended monk. With a shameless monk, however, it is allowable for someone to live together. The other suspended monk is indeed excluded from the communion of the Dhamma (dhammasambhoga).

"The suspended monk disrobes (vibbhami)" and so on—this sutta is stated here because it is common to showing who should be ordained and who should not be ordained. To say it in another way: purification from an offense occurs only through the sequence of practice (paṭipatti); it is not purified merely by disrobing. Therefore, even if a person who has become a monk falls into even a dubbhāsita offense at the least, and later disrobes and returns to be ordained, he is purified only after confessing that offense; he is not purified in any other way. This is stated to show the sequence of purification for one who has been ordained.

If a suspended monk, who was expelled because of not seeing an unshared offense (asādhāraṇāpatti), undergoes a change of sex (liṅgaparivattana) and thereby rises from the offense, and later the original sex (the original male sex) appears again, he remains as one of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka). Even when he returns after disrobing, if he is ordained according to the aforementioned method, he remains as one of a different communion because he has not yet risen from the offense. If it is asked why? It is not because of the appearance of a different sex. It is also not because he is not purified from the act (kamma) by disrobing. Even if he is not purified from the act, it cannot lead to the failure of the act of ordination (upasampadākamma). It is neither the failure of the act nor the cessation of the act. By disrobing, he becomes a non-monk, and as one of a different communion, he causes the act to be disturbed, because it was directly spoken by the Lord of the Dhamma (the Buddha). For that very reason, the future tense was used: "You will see." Such a person, like a monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) who has laid down his duties, remains either in the state of a regular monk (pakaṭatta) or in the nature of a non-monk through disrobing and so on. It should be understood that this was stated to show all these variations of meaning.

A suspended monk of the type mentioned before, who, after a change of sex, stands again in the original sex, should be asked again: "Do you see (the offense)?" One who says, "Yes, I see it," should be rehabilitated (osāretabba). It should not be said, "Confess (the offense)," because he has already risen from the offense through the change of sex. A suspended monk whose offense has been remedied should be asked: "Has the act of remedy been done by you?" One who says, "Yes, it has been done," should be rehabilitated. Some teachers say that one who says, "I have no act of remedy to be done," should not be rehabilitated. This procedure applies only to an unshared offense (asādhāraṇāpatti), not to a shared one (sādhāraṇā). In that shared offense...
445:
Some teachers say that for a suspended monk (ukkhittaka), the legal act of suspension is settled simply by the change of status (disrobing). The Teacher, however, says that one should investigate and accept what is appropriate. In the Anugaṇṭhipada, the use of things belonging to a shameless person (alajji) is distinguished by acts such as giving with one's own hand. The view of teachers who say that it is allowable to give with one's own hand to a shameless monk, by pointing to monks who fulfill the sāraṇīyadhamma (virtues of fraternal living), should be rejected. Why? Because according to the decision that it is not allowable to give with one's own hand to a suspended monk, it is only allowable to cause others to give.

Even though a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by using things belonging to a shameless person, this newly ordained monk is not shameless. Therefore, referring to the absence of offense in every way, it is said: "There is no offense in communal eating (sambhoga) and communal living (saṃvāsa)." How can this be known? In terms of meaning, because sugarcane juice and sugarcane pulp are sattāhakālika (seven-day medicine) and yāvajīvika (life-long medicine), one might perceive that "it is allowable to chew and eat sugarcane at the wrong time," and by eating that sugarcane, one does not see the pācittiya offense because of such a perception. Or, a monk who, while admitting he has committed an offense, firmly resolves, "I will not remedy it." These two types of persons—

"He intentionally commits an offense, he conceals the offense,
and he follows a wrong course (agati); such a person is called shameless (alajji)."

—do not fall under the aforementioned characteristics and thus are not shameless. Therefore, because of the statement specifically made: "There is no offense in communal eating, etc., with one who does not perform the confession or remedy of an offense," and also because the method is given that although there is no transaction with money (rūpiyasaṃvohāra) with another, an offense is indeed incurred through buying and selling (kayavikkaye). The method is also given that there is no offense in any way with the five classes of co-religionists.

Because it is specifically stated in cases where there is an offense, and it is not so stated here in this case of "no offense," there is no "use of things belonging to a shameless person" (alajji-paribhogha) with him. Some other teachers say: "If one associates with him, he joins the faction of the shameless"; by this method also, the meaning should be sought by comparing various Pali passages in all places. But the teachers do not say so. Because it is said, "If he says, 'I will not see the offense,' he should not be ordained," it is clear that offenses committed previously in the former life as a monk are not settled even if he disrobes. For this very reason, the teachers have the training renounced only after making the monk confess the offense. This statement, "There is no offense in communal eating and communal living," should be considered as referring to not seeing even an offense that was previously committed and has already been settled. It is said for the purpose of making it known that the offense is settled.
446:
Some teachers say this: The statement "You will see the offense" is spoken in the future tense because, being a layman, it is not appropriate for him to confess the offense. In saying "You will see after being ordained," it is spoken in the future tense because there are still duties to be performed, such as parivāsa (probation), and thus it is not said "You see." The phrase "after being rehabilitated" (osāretvā) is spoken by way of abbhāna (rehabilitation). In that case of disrobing, because there is no further act to be performed, it is said "You see." All these statements are made with reference to the admission in all cases. If he does not admit it again in any single case, one should not engage in communal living with him in a manner appropriate to that offense, because he is shameless. In the passages beginning with "By view" (diṭṭhiyā), "rehabilitation" (osāraṇa) means performing the same legal acts, etc. "No offense in communal eating" means no offense in communal eating with a suspended monk (ukkhittaka). Why? Because the act of suspension is settled by the fact of his becoming a layman. For this very reason, it is said: "By a harmony that is not obtained." Some teachers say that there is no offense because it is now something to be done in the state of a monk. Only those teachers know the procedure for the settlement of the act in both cases. Therefore, one should speak after carefully considering what is appropriate and inappropriate in all cases.

He who knows the Mahākhandhaka named Pabbajjā,
which has various methods and is the foundation of the Dispensation,
and explains it well to others,
attains pre-eminence in the Dispensation of the Sage.

## The Commentary on the Mahākhandhaka is finished.
447:
## 2. Uposathakkhandhakavaṇṇanā

## Sannipātānujānanādikathāvaṇṇanā

132-3. "Tena samayena" (At that time) refers to the time when the Blessed One, having laid down the burden of reciting the Ovāda Pātimokkha himself, remained after allowing the bhikkhus to perform the Uposatha separately. What time was that? It was the middle period of Enlightenment (Majjhima-bodhi) when the collection of training rules (sikkhāpada) sufficient for the Pātimokkha recitation was completed. For that very reason, he said, "I allow those bhikkhus to recite the Pātimokkha." The phrase "Bhikkhus, it should be recited thus" was spoken because he wished to prescribe the Nidānuddesa (Introduction) and to show the divisions of the training rules. Alternatively, since the sequence for reciting all training rules had already been shown by the phrase "Bhikkhus, this training rule should be recited thus," the current Pāli "Bhikkhus, it should be recited thus" would now become meaningless [if it referred to individual rules]. This Pāli is spoken with reference to the entire Saṅgha Uposatha.

"If the venerable ones... should assemble" is a statement following the wish of many bhikkhus. In that context, the bhikkhu who is proficient in the Vinaya is the authority, not merely the Saṅgha Elder (Saṅghatthera); to show this, and to show that it should be spoken with words of respect for the Saṅgha, he said, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sir." In this regard, if the speaker himself is a senior Elder, it is appropriate to say "Friend" (Āvuso) with reference to a [junior] bhikkhu. How is this known? Because in the Buddha's time, an incompetent Saṅgha Elder was rare. If it is argued that the Buddha showed the pattern in all formal acts (kammavācā) as "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sir," then that is indeed so, because he showed it in that manner. With reference to the Saṅgha, even the Saṅgha Elder should say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sir." However, saying "Friend" (Āvuso) with reference to a bhikkhu is known from seeing the pattern in the kammavācā of the Venerable Mahākassapa, and from the pattern shown by an Elder bhikkhu in the Pārisuddhi Uposatha saying, "Friend, I am pure." The phrase "If it is the right time for the Saṅgha" was spoken with reference to obstacles to performing the Uposatha that would be prescribed later. Since there are many types of Uposatha, he said, "He should recite the Pātimokkha" to specify the form. With this much Pāli sequence, he concluded the motion (ñatti). Indeed, the Uposatha act is completed by a motion and one announcement (ñattidutiya-kamma). If it is asked, "Should it not be through a third announcement (i.e., ñatticatuttha)?" No, because it is unlike other acts consisting of a motion and four announcements. For here, one does not begin "Let [the Saṅgha] hear me" four times. If it is argued, "Since it is unlike other acts of a motion and one announcement, let it not even be a motion and one announcement," no...
448:
...because a motion and one announcement (ñattidutiya-kamma) can be performed in other ways as well. Indeed, some motion and one announcement acts may be performed by way of announcement (apalokana), while others may not be performed differently. How is this known? This Uposatha act itself is the indicator (ñāpaka).
