The phrase "What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha?" should not be said after concluding the motion, because that statement is performed before the motion. Therefore, one might ask: Should it be said, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sir, what is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha, if it is suitable for the Saṅgha"? Even so, it should not be said, because that [preliminary duty] is not performed within the motion. If it is then argued that it should not be said at all because it is useless in all places, no, because it is said only in its traditional place; it means it is said in expectation of subsequent words. A Saṅgha or an individual who performs the Uposatha without doing these preliminary duties exceeds the prescribed scope. If that scope is exceeded, there is no release from the offense [incurred] by [not] sweeping, preparing seats, water, and lamps. That offense occurs because of the failure to perform the duties that should be done before the Uposatha act. That offense does not depend on the completion of the act, unlike the offense of deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda) mentioned in this Uposatha section. Therefore, the bhikkhu reciting the Pātimokkha, wishing to say "Venerable ones, report your purity," first reminds them of the preliminary duties which are the cause of purity or impurity. Performing them is the cause of purity; not performing them is the cause of impurity. With that intention of considering both, he does not say "It is done" or "It is not done," but simply says "What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha?" Among those two, to show the sequence of reporting purity in the case of non-performance, he will say later, "If anyone has an offense, let him reveal it." In the case of performance, he will say, "If there is no offense, one should remain silent."

"Venerable ones, report your purity." Why? "Because I shall recite the Pātimokkha." Here, some say that by using the future tense "I shall recite" (uddisissāmi) instead of the present tense "I am reciting" (uddisāmi), it refers to the Pātimokkha recitation mentioned in the Pāli: "I now allow them to recite the Pātimokkha" (Mahāvagga 150). Others say that because it is said, "Bhikkhus, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha," and because the questioning of purity from "Are you pure in this?" up to the third announcement occurs at the end of the Pātimokkha known as the Nidānuddesa (Introduction) which is currently being recited, and since a part can be referred to by the name of the whole, it is said "I shall recite the Pātimokkha" with reference only to the field of offense (āpattikhetta)...
449:
It is said, "I shall recite the Pātimokkha." When this is said, since the section on offenses (āpattikkhetta) will follow, this meaning is possible: "All of you who are fearful of offenses, declare your purity (pārisuddhi) from the very beginning." If it were said in the present tense (vattamānakāla), the statement "Venerable ones, declare your purity" would not even be possible. This is because such a declaration is desired beforehand; without that being done first, what need is there to say, "I shall recite the Pātimokkha"? This method is appropriate in the declaration of an evident offense, but not in silence (tuṇhībhāva), because silence is attained only until the completion of the legal act. Nevertheless, even if that is the case, it is still appropriate in that silence. Indeed, the monk reciting the Pātimokkha, seeing the monks remaining silent without revealing offenses to one another, becomes one whose purity is declared by that very silence, and begins the recitation of the Pātimokkha, saying, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me."

In this matter, the objector says: Since it was first said, "Let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha, let it recite the Pātimokkha," here also it should be said, "The Saṅgha will perform the Uposatha, it will recite the Pātimokkha." Even if it is so said, because it has the characteristic of "recitation by an individual," it should be said exactly as it is heard. However, he asks, "Should it be said, 'I shall perform the Uposatha, I shall recite the Pātimokkha'?" It should not be said so, because it would contradict the characteristic and lead to an undesirable meaning. In fact, the Uposatha of the Saṅgha is completed only by the recitation by an individual, not by the individual's performance of the Uposatha. If it were said so, it would lead to the undesirable meaning that only that individual will perform it, and not the Saṅgha. When it is said, "Listen," for fear that there might be unity without conscious intent (acittasāmaggī), it is said, "We are listening." If it is asked, "Since it was said 'I shall recite,' should it be said 'We shall listen'?" It should not be said so. Because there is no regard for the desire to see the section on offenses, it should only be said, "We are listening." Indeed, that monk's desire is fulfilled by that single word. If it is so, for what purpose do all the monks undertake that recitation of the Pātimokkha? It is for the purpose of preventing the monk who has committed an offense from falling into unity without conscious intent through this specific statement, "I shall recite." By the word "remembering," it shows the state of having conscious intent in the deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda) of that monk. By the words "The Blessed One has stated it is an obstructive factor," it shows the great fault of this deliberate lie, which arises from non-action (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna) and is even so slight. In the phrase "one who desires purity," why should one who desires purity—whether it be the purity called 'the state of being without offense' with reference to a remaining offense, or the purity called 'the state of being a layman' with reference to an offense without remainder—reveal it? It is because by not entering the state of having an obstruction, it becomes a cause for living in comfort.
450:
In this context, it was not said, "Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha." This is because there was a desire to specify the day later. Because it was not said, those monks recited the Pātimokkha every day.

In the phrase "Ādim-etaṃ," although the Pātimokkha as a text (ganthapātimokkha) is intended, it primarily refers to the Pātimokkha of virtue (sīlapātimokkha). "Pañcannaṃ vā" refers to the five classes of offenses mentioned in the Mātikā. "Anajjhāpanno vā" is a teaching in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). In the ancient Gaṇṭhipada, however, it is stated that the motion (ñatti) consists of the words up to "Uposathaṃ kareyya." The proclamation up to the third time (yāvatatiyānussāvanā) consists of two parts: the three statements beginning with "Yassa siyā āpatti" and the final words "Dutiyampi tatiyampi pucchāmi." Among these, the first is for a monk who remains seated while remembering an offense, and the second is to remind a monk who has forgotten. The phrase "vacīdvāre" (through the door of speech) is stated directly in its evident sense. Although it can be done through bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), because it is not a bodily action, it must be made manifest only through vocal intimation (vacīviññatti).

"Saṅghamajjhe vā" and so on is said to be a defining statement (lakkhaṇavacana). If one sits in the midst of the Saṅgha to perform the Saṅgha-Uposatha, it is in the midst of the Saṅgha; if one sits in the midst of a group to perform a Gaṇa-Uposatha, it is in the midst of that group; if one wishes to perform a Pārisuddhi-Uposatha in the presence of a single monk, it must be made manifest to that individual. By this statement, it is not only in the midst of the Saṅgha that this deliberate lying occurs; even in a Gaṇa-Uposatha, if one wishes to perform the Uposatha while having an offense and remains silent without declaring it, one incurs an offense of deliberate lying (sampajānamusāvāda). The logicians (takkika) say this is a defining statement because it makes this meaning clear. Otherwise, they intend that "Gaṇamajjhe vā" would not have been said. The teacher says, "Our view is that it is stated according to the intention to declare." If one makes it manifest with the intention "I declare to the Saṅgha," it is called making it manifest in the midst of the Saṅgha. If one declares to the monks sitting on both sides of oneself, it is in the midst of a group. If one declares with the intention "I will declare to a single fellow monk (sabhāga)," it is called declaring to a single person. It should be understood that the re-analysis of a term already analyzed previously is for the purpose of showing that there is no special difference in meaning.

136-7. Having said, "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited daily... there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," the statement "Monks, I allow the Pātimokkha to be recited on the Uposatha day" shows the meaning that the offense of wrong-doing occurs only on a non-Uposatha day, whereas on the Uposatha day, it is allowable even daily. Therefore, those monks, having recited on the 14th day, also recited on the 15th day. Thus, it is said "Sakapakkhassa." By the earlier Pali, it shows the meaning that the day the Saṅgha is in concord is indeed the Uposatha day. By both Pali passages, the eighth-day Uposatha is rejected. In rejecting the daily performance of Uposatha, excess is prohibited. What is the intention? It means that on whatever day the divided Saṅgha becomes united, if they perform the Uposatha on that day, the Saṅgha has prohibited the monk who would incur two offenses of wrong-doing by means of both Pali passages. In another way, the Uposatha of concord (sāmaggī-uposatha) should not be performed daily. If it were to be performed, and if the regular Uposatha has not yet been recited in that period day and night, then the Uposatha of concord should be performed. This is the meaning arrived at. Taken by the method of exception...
451:
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa); however, it is shown that on the Uposatha day, performing it daily is also permissible. Therefore, those monks, even after reciting the Pātimokkha on the fourteenth day, recited it again on the fifteenth day; because of such actions, it was taught: "It should be recited only once a fortnight." In that text, the earlier Pali passage shows that the day of harmony (sāmaggī) of the Saṅgha is indeed the Uposatha day. By both the earlier and later Pali passages, the eighth-day Uposatha is rejected, and in rejecting the daily performance of Uposatha, an excess is prevented.

What does this mean? It means that if a divided Saṅgha becomes harmonious on the first day of the lunar month (pāṭipada), the monk who would otherwise incur both types of dukkhaṭa offenses by performing the Harmony Uposatha (sāmaggī-uposatha) on that day is prevented from doing so by both passages combined. In another way, the Harmony Uposatha should not be performed daily. If it were to be performed, it would have to be done continuously day and night. If the regular Uposatha (pakati-uposatha) has not yet been recited in that fortnight (pakkha), it would lead to the meaning that the Harmony Uposatha must be performed. If it is argued that this does not apply because it should be taken as an exception (apavāda), that cannot be said because it would lead to an undesirable meaning. What is meant is this: after performing the Harmony Uposatha on the day of harmony, when the regular Uposatha day arrives within that same fortnight, the regular Uposatha should not be performed again. An exception (apavāda) means the prohibition of the general rule (ussagga-vidhāna) in places other than where the exception is specifically made.

Regarding the phrase "By how much extent does harmony (sāmaggī) exist?", this is the intended meaning: Harmony is the assembly of those who are similar. Does "those who are similar" mean all fellow practitioners (sahadhammika) who exist, or does it mean those who are similar by virtue of residing in the same monastery (āvāsa-sabhāgatā)? Between these two, if the harmony of fellow practitioners is called sāmaggī, then the harmony of all monks who are separately divided would be required. Or, if it is by way of residence, it means the harmony of monks who share the same monastery. In another way, it implies harmony within a single monastery. "May it not come to us" means may the arrival not occur.

## Explanation of the Consecration of Boundaries (Sīmā)

Wishing to reject harmony based on those residing in the same monastery and to allow it based on those within the same boundary (sīmā), the Blessed One said: "Monks, I allow you to consecrate a boundary." If He had intended to speak of the limit of a residence (āvāsa), He would have said: "As far as there is one boundary, so far is there one residence (ekāvāsa). Monks, I allow you to consecrate a boundary." Therefore, it should be understood that in this Pali text, the definition of a single residence is not by way of the consecrated boundary (baddha-sīmā) that was allowed, but only by way of the vicinity boundary (upacāra-sīmā). How can this be known? It can be known from the Pali itself, as it is said: "At that time..."
452:
The venerable Upananda Sakyaputta, being alone, spent the rains retreat in two residences... it is said (in Mahāvagga 364) that 'he has a single intention.' Otherwise, it would lead to the undesirable meaning of breaking the rains retreat (vassaccheda). How so? If harmony (sāmaggī) were only by way of a single residence, it would not be possible in many residences or in non-residence areas. Therefore, if that monk goes to that residence and performs the Uposatha outside, it would contradict the Pali passage: "Monks, on the Uposatha day, one should not go to a non-residence where monks are present," etc. This is because even if the Saṅgha is present, the Uposatha should not be performed in a non-residence. If harmony is obtained even in a non-residence, then one should not say, "As far as there is one residence, so far is there harmony." Therefore, considering that the former method is rejected by the latter in every way, it should be understood that harmony exists even by way of multiple residences. As in the phrase, "Having said 'we will perform that act,' they did not do so," it also regards the future. Therefore, some say that if one says "we will perform it," it is not proper. It is written: "Even without clearing the boundary, it is proper to proclaim the markers (nimitta)." At the minimum limit, it is seven and a half cubits (not quite eight cubits) in height, the size of an elephant. In the case where it is said "if it is a single solid rock, it should not be used," it is stated in the Anugaṇṭhipada: "Because it stands on a rock similar to a flat rock-slab beneath four mountain peaks in the four directions, even if it is a single connected piece, if there is no connection between those peaks above the ground, one may treat the mere connection underground as negligible and proclaim them. For that reason, it is said that even if a flat rock-slab is very large, it is counted only as a rock. If the greatness of that rock beneath the ground is taken into account, it becomes a mountain." Elder Dhammasiri said: "If grass and trees grow on a mound of earth made by piling it up, it becomes a mountain." Elder Upatissa said: "It does not."

Regarding 'rock' (pāsāṇa): some say, "A rock made of plaster is also suitable." This should be investigated because bricks are rejected. The size of a lump of sugar weighing thirty-two pala should be taken by comparison of size, not by the count of weight. That rock also is a standing stone pillar like a tree stump.

In the phrase "even with the markers of four or five trees," the word 'nimitta' (marker) is absent in some versions. Here, if three trees are heartwood trees (sāra-rukkha) and two are non-heartwood trees, the majority of heartwood trees is desired. It is said: "A cemetery is also counted here as a 'forest' because it grows spontaneously." However, some teachers say: "Among four trees, if two have internal heartwood, it is suitable. If those with internal heartwood are more or equal, it is suitable. Therefore, even among many trees, if two have internal heartwood, it is suitable."
453:
In this word "Parabhāge," it is said: "It is allowable because it arises from the place separated by those journeys (or) the place connected. Likewise, in a long journey, it is allowable because the place of departure is different from the place of arrival."

In this word "Anvaddhamāsaṃ," it is written: "The consecutive fortnight (or) the frequency of the fortnight." Because it is said "the inner robe (antaravāsaka) becomes wet," some teachers say it is allowable to perform [the act] only in water of such depth. By the word "becomes wet," the characteristic of a river is stated by the minimum (lowest) limit. Some teachers say that in a river of such nature, where water overflows and flows for four months, whether it be little or much, it is allowable to perform [the act] even while standing in a place with little water. Because it is said "the river-sign is in the place where it flows," they say that if such an amount of water flows outside the bridge, it is indeed a river.

Regarding lakes (jātassara), etc., even if there is no gap between the standing water and the area of the lake, etc., it is allowable to make it a sign (nimitta), like a sign in a river-bank boundary (nadīpārasīmā). If that area becomes village land (gāmakhetta) after a long time, it is allowable to designate another boundary (sīmā) there. "Ukkhepimaṃ" means water that is to be drawn up or taken out.

In the phrase "Leaving aside the precinct (upacāra) of the boundaries of unestablished monasteries (abaddhasīmavihāra)," it is written: "Leaving aside the space for a boundary to be designated in the future." In the phrase "Antonimittagatehi," it is said: "Because of the desire to include half of a village within, considering that there is no benefit for all monks to come, it is said 'Antonimittagatehi'; and that word is spoken by way of respect." In the phrase "It is allowable even if they do not come," it is written: "Because the boundary is not yet established, it is not called a group (vagga)." It is said: "There is no benefit in coming when announcing the signs while standing on other village land, or when designating a boundary of common communion (samānasaṃvāsakasīmā)." In the phrase "Or the drum signal (bherisaññaṃ)," it is written: "Saying 'We shall perform the conclusion of the designation'"; therefore, it is established that at such a time, that drum signal is allowable.

What is the benefit of this? In the phrase "For the sake of performing it easily (sukhakaraṇatthaṃ)," it means a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) is established for the sake of performing it easily with fewer monks, without the hardship of gathering a great multitude of monks. Some teachers say that "firstly" is said to show that if there is an obstacle when establishing a great boundary (mahāsīmā), one can live happily even with that much [a small boundary]. If asked, "How is it known that it is not allowable with a number less than that?" it is known because a formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) is at most an act to be performed by a group of twenty. If one includes twenty-one monks along with the person eligible for the formal act (kammāraha), it is allowable. That much area should be known by way of comfortable sitting. Some teachers say that if other monks also announce that same sign and establish it, it is allowable.
454:
This phrase, "When established thus, the boundary interval (sīmantarikā) belongs to the village land," is said to show that the definition of harmony (sāmaggī) is not by way of the residence (āvāsa), but indeed by way of the boundary (sīmā). The phrase "Leaving aside the stone near the sign" is said because of that sign, in terms of a movable sign.

From this word onwards is the sequence of the Gaṇṭhipada (glossary). In the place "They will not be able," those monks, without noting the boundary for non-separation [from robes] (avippavāsa), though they strive saying "We shall abolish only the boundary of common communion," they will not be able to abolish it. "Having the measure of one cubit and one span" is said with the intention of making it easy to understand. Even a single inch is allowable for establishment. Establishing (designating) starting from a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) is the practice of the teachers. It should be known that by following the practice of the teachers, one is free from confusion.

Kuṭigehe means in a hut-house or an underground house. Udukkhalaṃ vā means a small pit like a small mortar in the ground. Some teachers say that "Pamukhe" (in the front/porch) refers to an underground hut. In saying "It does not descend below," it means that because the signs are placed and designated inside the wall, it does not descend to the space below, but applies only to the palace (pāsāda) built above. Bhittilagge means in palaces attached to the wall. It is said that these, even if attached to the wall, are not called "connected as one." Since the entire palace stands within the boundary, whether it is connected as one or not, it is simply a boundary.

The mountain named Tālamūlaka is gradually small. Ākāsapabbhāra means a mountain slope (overhang) without an enclosure. Susirapāsāṇa is a hollow stone cave. Antoleṇa is a cave inside the mountain. Referring to the door, it is later said "inside." The meaning is that in every way, it enters through the cave outside the boundary.

In the place "Having cleared the great boundary (mahāsīmā)," it means that even if a tree, etc., standing in the boundary goes far, it stands in the boundary and is connected to the boundary. Therefore, the meaning is that one should remain without touching or handling that tree, etc. If it is so, it should be said: "It is allowable to perform the formal act after removing the tree that depends on that boundary." In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā also, only this much is said: "It should be performed after clearing the boundary." Some teachers say that the Great Elders also say only "It should be cleared." There is also a reading: "The formal act should be performed even after clearing the great boundary." It will be said later: "Only by the method already mentioned." Therefore, some teachers say that the common reading is better.

"In the previous method also" means even when rising from a small boundary and inclining towards a great boundary. It is not allowable to perform [the act] by causing [the tree] to be lifted. Why? Because it stands inside the boundary. Other teachers say that the root standing in the earth beneath the tree is just the small boundary. Or it is negligible (abbhohārika). It is also said: "If it is cut in the middle, the root standing in the great boundary belongs only to the great boundary. The root standing in the small boundary belongs only to the small boundary. This is because they are supported by the earth-nutrients, etc., connected to them." "Sitting on a tree that grew after the boundary was designated, to perform the formal act..."
455:
Performing a legal act (kamma) while staying on a tree that grew after the boundary (sīmā) was established is valid, just as it is valid in a monastery built after the boundary was established. However, they say: "It is not valid to perform a legal act while staying on a tree that existed at the time of the boundary establishment, because it does not reach above the boundary." If that were the case, there would be no such thing as growing again at the time of establishment; it would mean it only grows after the establishment. A tree that grows later is considered part of the boundary because it is connected to it; likewise, a tree that existed previously should also be considered part of the boundary. Because of the phrase "whatever it may be" (yaṃ kiñcipi), grass and such are also included. The Great Elders also perform legal acts only after clearing the grass.

140. Because it is from the middle to the corner, it is said "from corner to corner." They say, "An offense is incurred because it is acittaka (committed without intention)." "Pārayati" means it overwhelms or covers. What is it that covers? It is the boundary itself. Some say that because it is stated as "a boat capable of carrying at least three people," a boat smaller than that does not count as a boat. That statement is not appropriate, because even such a small boat is intended in the context of the second Pārājika regarding goods on a boat (nāvaṭṭhabhaṇḍa). Some say it is stated according to the weight of a medium-sized man. There is a reasoning of the teacher that for bhikkhunīs, since a boundary can exist on the other side of a river, this is to avoid the fault mentioned in the teaching, "If she should go alone to the other side of a river." In both cases, the word "dhuva" (regular/permanent) is used. Therefore, to avoid obstacles to the Uposatha, the Uposatha day is stated as a rule. In this context, the teacher says that "boat" refers to a log boat (dugout canoe) of sufficient size and common use, not a raft. It means a boat made by cutting a tree. If it is a single village territory, the monks within all the marks (nimitta) should be brought within the hatthapāsa (arm's reach) to establish the boundary. If they are different village territories, it is also valid not to come. An island is not included merely by proclaiming the marks on both banks; therefore, the marks must be proclaimed on the island itself. They say, "A monk sitting below the river level spoils the legal act, because the river exists only above."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Authorization of Boundaries is finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Uposatha Hall, etc.

Because of the words "Whatever monastery the Saṅgha desires... or a cave," it is established that the boundary is authorized not only on the ground but also above monasteries and such, because the Uposatha act is primary. If it is asked, "How is it known that the Uposatha act is primary in the boundary?" it is because it is authorized in the context of the Uposatha, and in the establishment of the boundary, the phrase "samānasaṃvāsa" (communion)...
456:
...is completed by this much of the Pali sequence, yet it is also known because of the separate teaching of "eku-uposatha" (single Uposatha) and so on. It is written: "Excluding the Uposatha act, the remaining acts are called communion (samānasaṃvāsa)." "Having removed one" (ekaṃ samūhanitvā) is the original Pali text.

"Katovassa" (having completed the rains) is said with reference to monks who are united in a single boundary. Otherwise, if another meaning is taken, it would lead to the undesirable conclusion that the hearing (of the kammavācā) by monks staying in different boundaries is the standard, or that even within a single boundary, the hearing by those staying outside the hatthapāsa is the standard. In that context, "sammutāyā vā asammutāyā vā" (whether authorized or unauthorized) refers to the authorization of the Uposatha hall, not the authorization of the boundary. How is this known? It is known by the context, and by the later prescriptions for giving consent (chanda) and giving purity (pārisuddhi). Among those reasons, the former reason prevents the former undesirable consequence, and the latter reason prevents the latter. "Uposathamukha" means the place for performing the Uposatha. It is written: "'Of the uposathamukha' means of the place for the Uposatha hall."

If it is asked, "How is it known that it is valid to proclaim whatever marks (nimitta) there may be?" it is known because it is only stated: "First the marks should be proclaimed; having proclaimed the marks."

If it is argued, "Because they were mentioned first, they should not be mentioned (again)," that reason is not valid. The reason is that there is no laziness in the teaching of the Buddhas. Some teachers say that when removing a boundary, the removal of the boundary is successful only after removing the Uposatha hall. That statement is not appropriate. The teacher named Notakko says this is because the authorization of an Uposatha hall can be achieved even in an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā). Teachers say that "uposathamukha" is the front (entrance) of the Uposatha hall. The proclamation of marks for the entrance of the Uposatha hall should be done in the same manner as stated for the boundary. Some teachers say it is valid to proclaim even once. They say, "Whether it be a multi-storied building or one of the pavilions (maṇḍapa) and so on, in the kammavācā, one should only say 'uposathamukha'." It is written: "'Porāṇaka āvāsa' (ancient residence) means the original home monastery." The phrase "Vadati ghaṭamattā" is a notable characteristic.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Authorization of the Boundary of Non-separation

143-144. There is also a reading "manamhi vūḷho." In that phrase, "manamhi vūḷho" means "I am slightly many (increased)." "Excluding the village and the village precinct" means excluding the village known as the inner houses (antaraghara) and the vicinity of the village (gāmūpacāra). Some teachers say, "'Gāma' refers to a fenced village, and 'gāmūpacāra' refers to an unfenced village." However, that contradicts the Commentaries. Therefore, "gāma" is said with reference to houses, crossroads, etc., and "gāmūpacāra" is said with reference to places suitable for fencing. In this matter, it is read in many ways. What benefit is there in such talk?
457:
One should carefully investigate the Pali and the Commentaries and accept them in such a way that they are consistent. The statement, "The previous formal act (kammavācā) of the monks is not valid," is appropriate when designating a samānasaṃvāsaka boundary (boundary of common communion) by including a village and its precinct (gāmūpacāra), and then designating an avippavāsa boundary (boundary of non-separation from robes) over that boundary. If, however, only the forest is designated, why would it not be valid? If it is argued that in that kammavācā, the phrase "excluding the village and the village precinct" would be purposeless, the answer is: This is true; however, that phrase must be spoken because there is a possibility of the failure of the proclamation (anussāvana-hāni). It is with this intention that it is said, "The previous formal act is not valid." Alternatively, it is said because there cannot be two kammavācās for a single purpose. 

If it is argued that this same rule should apply to two different groups of monks of separate communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) because it is said, "They do not serve as completers of the quorum (gaṇapūraka) for each other's acts," it does not apply. This is because the storing of what has been received (paṭiggaha-sannidhi) is permitted, because there is no distinction regarding insulting speech (omasana) and so forth, and because it only regards the suspension of the act. "Tassā" refers to the Bhikkhunī Sangha. "They do not make the kammavācā a group (vagga)" means they do not ruin the act. "In this matter" refers to the phrase "excluding the village."

If it is asked, "If the monks' avippavāsa boundary does not extend to the village and its precinct, why then do they designate an avippavāsa boundary when binding a boundary in a village?" it is written, "They designate it by traditional practice (āciṇṇakappa), not out of regard for any other purpose." It is also said, "In meaning, that boundary is indeed not bound even on the outside." Some teachers say that the samānasaṃvāsaka boundary bound within a village is not called a 'village' because it has been so bound. "That boundary also attains only the name of a boundary" means it attains the name of an avippavāsa boundary. 

In this matter, this should be considered: When designating an avippavāsa boundary again within a boundary bound by including a village, should the avippavāsa kammavācā be performed while standing in a forest area or while standing in the village? Even if performed while standing in the village, it pervades the suitable ground. The teacher says, "It is our opinion that it should not be performed while standing on unsuitable ground, as that would be consistent with the fault of designating while standing outside the boundary; this same method applies to the removal (samūhanana) of a boundary." When designating an avippavāsa boundary while standing in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the great boundary (mahāsīmā) is reportedly called the "avippavāsa-sīmā."

In the Andhaka manuscript and in some Sinhalese manuscripts, there is the reading: "If the removal of this samānasaṃvāsaka-ekūposatha boundary is pleasing to the venerable one, let him be silent." In some manuscripts, they first write "samugghāto etissā sīmāya," and in some, "etissā sīmāya samugghāto."
458:
## Explanation of the Discussion on Village Boundaries and So Forth

In the phrase "Sā cāti," it includes both the village boundary given by demarcation and the other (natural) village. If one asks what that village is, he says, "Pakatigāma" (natural village) and so forth. "They are just like bound boundaries (baddhasīmā)" means it refers to both the demarcated village and the other. For that very reason, the singular form is used: "He receives the privilege of non-separation from the three robes (ticīvara-vippavāsa-parihāra)." Some say this usage is inappropriate because both are villages. Others write in the plural: "honti, na labhanti." It is also said that the village boundary given by dividing the middle and the natural village, etc., mentioned as "Sā ca itarā ca," are not different. Just as there is the reading "bhikkhu vasati" (a monk dwells), it is also written as "vasanti" (they dwell). Because it is said, "athassa ṭhitokāsato," the singular form alone is appropriate.

By the Pali statement, "Monks, every river is not a bound boundary (asīmā)," which boundary is rejected? It is the bound boundary (baddhasīmā) that is rejected. Teachers say this is because of the possibility of it being one of the eleven types of defective boundaries (vippattisīmā). If a boundary is bound first and then a river or such appears later, it would lead to its rejection; therefore, it is only the unbound boundary that is rejected. Just as every village is a village boundary (gāmasīmā), so every river is not a bound boundary. However, the teacher says, "It is not our thought that it shows the diversity of boundaries as the water-splash boundary (udakukkhepasīmā) of various monks." The statement "the water-splash all around of a middle-sized man" is spoken to show the demarcation of the boundary when groups of four (catuvagga) and so forth perform separate formal acts in a single river. Teachers say it is also spoken to show the demarcation of separation or non-separation from the three robes, similar to showing the demarcation of a boundary of seven abbhantaras. Therefore, it is established that even in the absence of a water-splash demarcation, it is allowable to perform a formal act within a river.

This is the distinction: If one has gone there by boat, it is according to the method stated for boats. If one has gone by caravan (sattha), it is according to the method stated for caravans. If that caravan has settled for more than the four months of the rainy season, the non-separation from the three robes should be understood according to the method stated for a village. There is also this distinction: Some say if the caravan is within the water-splash area, the measure is the water-splash boundary. Teachers say the caravan itself is the measure.

If, in the phrase "bahu bhikkhū" (many monks) and so forth, the word "bhikkhū" is used instead of "bahu saṅghā" (many Sanghas), it is because of the desire to refer to Uposatha by determination (adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha) for some, Uposatha by a group (gaṇuposatha) for some, and Uposatha by the Sangha (saṅghuposatha) for others. Elder Upatissa says that in the context where a deficient boundary is not valid, it is because of the possibility of overlapping boundaries (sīmāsambheda). Monks who are establishing a boundary should not establish a deficient one. It is said, "It is also allowable not to establish one at all." In the context of "gacchantiyā pana" (but of a moving one), it is written, "It is allowable to perform the act in a boat that is moving without exceeding the water-splash distance." Is the proclamation (ñatti) in another boundary mentioned for fear of the failure of the act due to the boundary...
459:
Is it said to be due to the boundary (sīmā), or is it said to be due to the assembly (parisā)? Since a single legal act (kamma) cannot occur in different boundaries, it must be said to be due to the boundary. Some say it is also due to the assembly because a single act cannot be performed by a Saṅgha residing in different boundaries. The reasoning that it is due to the fault mentioned as "causing the hearing to fail" is not correct. In fact, the Teacher says that leaving a single act incomplete within a single boundary is what constitutes "causing to fail."

Whether it be on a branch of a tree growing on the outer bank that has entered into the river, or by erecting a post on the riverbank, if a bridge or the pillars of a bridge are established on the outer bank, "clearing the boundary" (sīmā-sodhana) means bringing the monks residing in the village boundary (gāma-sīmā) into the hand-reach (hattha-pāsa). It is proper to perform the act by separating it from a tree growing in a small boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā). Why? Because for a boat tied to a tree on the bank, the village is the support (ādhāra). It is also written: "A bridge that stands touching the village boundary on both sides should be compared to a tree that stands touching both the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the great boundary (mahā-sīmā)."

In such a case, according to the former method, this point should first be investigated: Does an act performed in such a place count as being performed in the river, or is it counted in the village boundary, or is it counted in both? If that act is counted in the river, only the water-boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) should be cleared, not the other. If it is counted in the village boundary, the water-boundary need not be cleared. If it is counted in both, it would lead to the undesirable fault that a single act is being performed in two boundaries. In that case, would it not lead to these undesirable points: "The motion (ñatti) occurs in one boundary and the proclamation (anussāvana) in another," and "The act should be performed by the physical unity (kāyasamaggi) of monks residing in both the khaṇḍa-sīmā and mahā-sīmā"?

Regarding this, it is said: The aforementioned act is counted in both, yet it does not lead to the aforementioned undesirable fault. Why? Some say, "Because the motion and proclamation occur in each boundary, and because the monks performing the act reside in each boundary." However, because it is possible to stand on both sides, that reason is not the primary cause. The firm reason is that the act is performed in a boundary area that has attained unity. Indeed, it is proper to perform the act in a river-boundary and a village-boundary that have become unified.

If there is a river, an ocean, or a natural lake (zātassara) within a boundary of seven usabhas, a monk standing in that river etc. is not counted as standing within the seven-usabha boundary. If there is a small island, a rock, or a tree in that river etc. which does not possess the characteristics of a river, it is counted as standing within the seven-usabha boundary. If that place is a place used by people, it is counted as village land. Which village land? The place from which people travel; and the Teachers say that if everyone travels there, it is counted as a separate village land.
460:
In the latter method, if a bridge stands without touching the water-area which is the characteristic of a river, it is counted as the village boundary (gāma-sīmā). If there is only one village there, that village must be cleared; if there are two villages on both banks, both villages must be cleared before performing the Saṅgha act. Only when done this way is it considered performed in both places. By this method, the accomplishment of a single act in two rivers or natural lakes should be understood. This method is also applicable to the khaṇḍa-sīmā and mahā-sīmā. If the bridge touches the water that has the characteristic of a river, the water-boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) must also be cleared.

When there is unity of boundaries, excluding those situated in the air,
Knowing the nature of a single act, one should point this out due to the boundary.
Whether it be in one boundary, two, three, or four boundaries,
His act may be one, but there may be a failure of the act due to the assembly.

The distinction here is: for those performing a Saṅgha act in the river, connections to trees etc. outside the water-boundary (udakukkhepa) are not a measure (not taken into account). For those performing a Saṅgha act in the village, a monk standing on a connected tree in the river outside the water-boundary is also not a measure; only if he is closer than that is he a measure. In a fixed boundary (baddha-sīmā), it should be understood that a monk standing within the baddha-sīmā on a connected tree is a measure. Therefore, it was said, "The act should be performed after clearing the boundary." The statement, "If a bridge or bridge-pillars are established on the outer bank, it is not proper to perform the act," also establishes the meaning that the entire boundary must be cleared, just as in the case of aerial roots (pāroha) etc.; this point should be investigated.

In the phrase "Ativuṭṭhikāla pana," excessive rain (ativuṭṭhi) means a condition as if water remains for the entire four months of the rainy season. Therefore, if there is indeed excessive rain for four months, the entire area covered by the flood is the river itself. If the flood from a single instance of excessive rain remains or flows for four months, the entire area covered by the flood established on the outer bank is also the river itself.

"Starting from the place where it flows, overwhelming the river" means that starting from the place where it flows and overwhelms—whether it be that river, another river, or a new area—attaining the characteristics of a river by the power of its own flow, it is suitable. The phrase "overwhelming the boundary of a village or town" is said in reference to a flow lasting four months. "Agamanapathe" is written to mean a place where it is impossible to go and return within that same day. The statement made in the Andhaka Commentary should not be accepted. Why? Because that fault would also apply to the river. In the word "tipusakādi," the word "ādi" includes red lotuses, white lotuses, and so on.
461:
In this context, in the phrase beginning with "tipusa", the word "ādi" (etc.) includes red and white lotuses and so on. Every lake is also considered not to be a jātassara lake. It is called a gāmasīmā (village boundary) by those who establish it; for them, it is designated as a gāmasīmā. If it is established by villagers living on the surrounding banks, it is designated as the entire village. If it is established in a place not connected to other village fields, it is designated as a visuṃgāmasīmā (separate village boundary).

The phrase "saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapa" indicates proximity. By that phrase, the partial connection in this context is shown as "sambheda" (overlapping). In the case where that boundary expands and causes an overlap of boundaries, it is called a "bound boundary established in one part" (ekadesabaddhasīmā) according to the procedure of establishing a baddhasīmā, and thus the fault of overlapping (saṅkara-dosa) occurs. Regarding the statement, "Monks, a boundary should not overlap another boundary," some teachers explain the meaning as: "A previously established boundary should not be overlapped by a boundary one intends to establish later." Since there is no overlapping by encroachment in a boundary first authorized, one's own intention is appropriate. Therefore, a previously established boundary should not be overlapped by a boundary to be established later. Indeed, it is called "overlapping" because one authorizes it without making known the inter-boundary space (sīmantarika) of the previously established boundary, by including the marks (nimitta) either entirely or partially within. It is called "encroaching" upon the baddhasīmā of others by including the marks entirely or partially within. For that very reason, it was said: "One who authorizes a boundary, having set aside the inter-boundary space," and so on. The meaning of that statement is: one should authorize a boundary later, having set the inter-boundary space of the previously established baddhasīmā as the mark for the boundary to be established later. Both of these failures do not occur between the boundaries of monks and nuns. In the case where it is said that the boundary expands and causes an overlap, it only causes an overlap of boundaries. Some say that the legal acts (kamma) performed in that overlapping boundary do not fail, but that is not appropriate. This is because the cutting of branches and hanging roots and the clearing of the boundary have been mentioned. Having carefully investigated all this and having attended upon teachers, one should accept what is worthy of being accepted and discard the rest.

## Description of the Discussion on the Breach of Uposatha, etc.

The statement, "Monks, there are these two Uposathas," was made because at that time the sāmaggi-uposatha (Uposatha of harmony) had not yet been allowed. In the preliminary duties of the sāmaggi-uposatha, it should be said, "Today is the sāmaggi-uposatha." Although the Blessed One did not show the application in the kammavācā (formal ritual text), the teachers of the commentaries have shown the order to be recited according to the Pali method. Likewise, it should be understood that the order of recitation for the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is completed. In the case where it is said that three or two monks recite the Pātimokkha, it is called "harmony through grouping" (vaggakathā) by unrighteous means because harmony is truly defined according to the act through the vaggakathā of the Saṅgha.
462:
Indeed, it is truly the harmony (sāmaggi) of the Saṅgha because harmony is defined according to the act in the talk of groups (vaggakathā). Nevertheless, it is called samagga (harmonious) because it is the opposite of vagga (group/schism), and it is called vagga because it is the opposite of samagga. Or else, it is so stated because it is separate, because of the possibility of group acts (gaṇakamma) etc., and because of the possibility of that act being either harmonious or grouped.

In the phrase "a group according to the Dhamma," the performance of purification (pārisuddhi) is lawful. It is called a group (vagga) because it is only the arrival of the consent (chanda) of the Saṅgha, and not of the group (gaṇa). Some say, "What is done once is well-done, but one commits an offense, and they do not get to do it again." Others say, "Among five monks, it is allowable to recite the Pātimokkha with four monks by bringing the consent of one monk." That statement is appropriate. When the monk who brings the consent reaches the presence of the monks, the Saṅgha is sufficient (to perform the act) with him; therefore, it is said with the understanding that the consent has reached the Saṅgha.

## Description of the Discussion on the Recitation of the Patimokkha

In the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī), it is said: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs... the disclosure of an offense is for his comfort; therein I ask the venerable ones... therefore they are silent. Thus I record this," and after saying this, it is said that the recitation is completed when the rest is announced through hearing in the manner beginning with "Venerable sirs, the Introduction (Nidāna) has been recited." Therefore, in the phrase "Thus I record this; have the venerable ones heard?", it should be understood that the words "Venerable sirs, the Introduction has been recited" are abbreviated after saying "I record this." For that reason, it is written by way of the minor abbreviation (khuddakapeyyāla).

In the same way, in the Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā, some say that in the phrase "the disclosure of an offense is for his comfort; therein to the venerable ones...", the words "Venerable sirs, the Introduction has been recited" should be understood as being abbreviated. Some teachers say that when it is said "one should train without dispute," the recitation of the Introduction (Nidānuddesa) is finished; therefore, a monk who does not disclose an offense commits an offense. That statement is not appropriate. Why? Because the completion of the Introduction is stated by the concluding words "having recited the Introduction," and the offense is stated at the end of the Introduction.

"Sarabhañña is chanting with a melody," so it is written. "Having determined upon recitation (sajjhāya)" means having produced the thought, "I will perform the recitation." Some say, "It is allowable to speak just by saying 'I ask permission.'" That is appropriate in the case of remaining silent. They also say, "However, if one is overcome by gain etc. and forbids it, that prohibition is not valid." According to this same method, if one interrupts while speaking, one should ask permission again.
463:
## Adhammakammapaṭikkosanādikathāvaṇṇanā
In the phrase "tesaṃ anupaddavatthāya" (for their non-oppression), it is stated so because the Saṅgha does not perform the formal act of the Saṅgha, and other dangers also arise for many people.

## Pātimokkhuddesaka-ajjhesanādikathāvaṇṇanā
Although it is said "therādhikaṃ pātimokkhaṃ" (the Pātimokkha is the responsibility of the elder), later it is stated without distinction: "In that Saṅgha, whichever monk is competent and capable, it should be entrusted to him." Therefore, the address "Bhante" (Venerable Sir) is understood to apply to the elder as well. According to the words, "Friend, go [recite] either in brief or in detail," it is established that even if there is no danger, one's own ability is the measure.

## Disaṃgamikādivatthukathāvaṇṇanā
There is the text: "sacassa saddhiṃcarā bhikkhūpaṭṭhākā atthi." Regarding the word "utuvasse," it is written as "in the seasonal year, in the winter and summer seasons."

## Pārisuddhidānakathāvaṇṇanā
Regarding the giving of purity (pārisuddhi), the teacher wrote: "A monk with an offense gives purity to the elders; an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) should occur due to intentional lying." Why is that? Because the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭāpatti) caused by intentional lying, according to the Buddha's teaching, is merely an offense originating from non-action (akiriyasamuṭṭhāna). However, in this context of "pārisuddhiṃ dammi" (I give purity), the action (kiriyā) is evident; therefore, it appears like an offense of expiation (pācittiya) in intentional lying. This point should be carefully considered. Those teachers are indeed great. In that term, the word "dammi" (I give) is spoken as the cause for the completion of one's own Uposatha act. The terms "hara" (take) and "ārocehi" (inform) are spoken to free one from the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in case the monk who conveys it fails to inform.

The same method applies to the giving of consent (chanda). There, the word "dammi" is a statement showing one's mental concord; the rest is just as previously mentioned—thus Elder Upatissa explains. Alternatively, the first term is spoken with reference to the state of concord, the second with reference to what is to be arranged later, and the third with the intention of freeing the monk who conveys the consent from a dukkaṭa offense. In both cases of consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi), because of the words "having reached the Saṅgha, he departs," etc., it is established that the giving of consent and purity is valid only when the Saṅgha is in concord; if not in concord, it is not valid. Because of the words "the suspended monk (ukkhittaka) who has reached the Saṅgha acknowledges, and purity is conveyed," etc., it is established that the giving of consent and purity is valid for suspended monks and others as well. Such validity...
464:
...is also only through the perception of being a regular monk (pakatatta), not otherwise—this is the reasoning. Some teachers say that if one gives it to a novice (sāmaṇera) while knowing [he is not a monk], it does not reach, and an offense is incurred. If given without knowing, it reaches and no offense is incurred. In the phrase "biḷālasaṅkhalikā pārisuddhi," the word "saṅkhalikā" refers to being connected with an immediate link or with another iron chain link. Therefore, Elder Upatissa says it is called purity that is merely like an iron chain link. If this were the case, the qualifier "biḷāla" (cat) would be useless. A "biḷālasaṅkhalikā" (cat-chain) is indeed tied up, as it is used only inside a house. Just as that chain link does not go anywhere, so too that purity does not reach any monk—this is said to be the meaning.

## Explanation on the giving of consent, etc.
165-7. A monk who, after giving consent (chanda), goes to a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), an intermediate boundary (sīmantarika), or outside the boundary (bahisīmā) and returns, does not invalidate the formal act. Therefore, it is said that they do not take the consent of monks who are about to travel for the purpose of establishing a monastery boundary (vihārasīmā) again after having established a partial boundary by taking their consent. According to the words "Stay in one place for a moment," etc., it is established that if laypeople or others enter within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa), any formal act of the monks is not allowable. "Nissīma" means outside the boundary. Since there is no business of granting authorization (sammuti) to that monk, it means the act is allowable even if he is present. "Water together with a seat" means placing drinking and utility water along with the spreading of a seat. In the word "pannarasopi," the particle "api" includes the fourteenth-day Uposatha. Therefore, it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: "If it should be so for us." Some teachers say that the determination "Today my Uposatha is the fifteenth-day Uposatha" always occurs, and not otherwise or in any other way.

## Explanation on the procedure for the remedy of offenses, etc.
169-170. Regarding the word "paṭidesemi" (I confess), some teachers say that even if spoken in any language, the confession and the acceptance of the offense indeed take place, because purification is said to be through the declaration of what is seen (diṭṭhāvikamma). A monk who is in doubt (vematika) should say: "Venerable Sir, I have a doubt regarding a thullaccaya (grave) offense; when I am free from doubt, I will then remedy that offense." When this is done, as long as he is not free from doubt, he is not allowed to accept a common offense (sabhāgāpatti), but he is considered pure regarding other formal acts. He should confess again only when he is free from doubt. The phrase "na ca" is found neither in the Pali nor in the Commentary; however, it should be known that there is no fault even if one confesses. Similarly, in the phrase "Having risen from here, I will remedy that offense," the same method applies when the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense or for one who is in doubt. When the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense, one should say, "When I see a pure monk, I will then remedy that offense with him," and...
465:
When all the Saṅgha are guilty of a shared offense (sabhāgāpatti), and in the case of a monk who is in doubt (vematika), it is similarly written: "When all the Saṅgha are guilty of a shared offense, at whatever time they shall see a pure monk, at that time they shall remedy that offense in his presence," and saying thus, "they are allowed to perform the Uposatha."

## Commentary on the Section Beginning with the Fifteen Cases of Non-offense

172-3. In the previous section (vāra), there is the reading "atthanye," and in the subsequent section, the reading is "athanye." They see someone who has entered or is entering the boundary (sīmā). Monks who perceive it as the Dhamma, however, do so out of ignorance. There is the reading: "The fifteen cases of doubt are indeed clear."

## Commentary on the Elaboration of Entering the Boundary

According to the statement, "It should not be given without desire," it is established that it should be given only when there is desire.

## Commentary on the Explanation of Gender and Other Signs

Regarding the statement "nābhiwitarantī," those persons are said to be of a different communion by view (laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka). For a person who is of a different communion by a legal act (kammanānāsaṃvāsaka), however, he should be made to renounce his view, and the act of rehabilitation (osāraṇakamma) to readmit him into the Saṅgha should be performed. Only after this is done is it proper to perform the Uposatha with him. For others who are of a different communion by view, it is meant that they can perform the Uposatha merely by renouncing their view. If a monk, knowing that a monk is suspended (ukkhittaka) for not seeing an offense or for not remedying it, or suspended for not renouncing a wrong view, performs the Uposatha with him, he incurs an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Therefore, some teachers say these monks should be known as followers of the suspended (ukkhittānuvattaka).

## Commentary on the Section on Where One Should and Should Not Go

What does the statement "one should not go" refer to? According to the words "except for the Saṅgha," in a monastery where a hundred monks reside, all those monks, for some business, may divide into groups of ten and, staying in various water-splash boundaries (udakukkhepasīmā) and so on, are allowed to perform the Uposatha. One should not go to the boundary or the river for the purpose of determining the Uposatha at various boundary limits, such as halls for new constructions (navakamma). Because one should not abandon the heavy recitation of the Pātimokkha to perform a light act, the statement "except for the Saṅgha" is established. In that (statement about not going), "Which...
466:
According to the words, "Those performing the Uposatha in a monastery ... should not go without having performed it," it is clear that it is also proper to go from monasteries where the Uposatha has been waived. It is stated, "Furthermore, for the purpose of performing the Uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha), monks for whom the Uposatha has been waived should go, or they should enter a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), so say other teachers." By this statement, it is meant that there is no danger to the Uposatha, and thus it is written as "one's own danger to the Uposatha."

## Commentary on the Explanation of Persons to be Excluded

A monk who has committed an offense of expulsion (pārājika/antimavatthu) should sit in the seated assembly with the thought, "I will not perform the Uposatha," due to the fear of quarrels and so on. Some teachers say that in other legal acts, there is no offense for the assembly in which that monk is sitting. According to the words, "Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day except for the unity of the Saṅgha," it appears as if it is said by way of meaning that the day of unity is a non-Uposatha day. This is said by virtue of the statement, "Monks, these two are the Uposathas." Otherwise, teachers say it would contradict the Parivāra Pali. If the Saṅgha is united on the 14th or 15th day, it should be understood that the teaching was given to show that it should be performed according to the normal procedure without saying, "Today is the Uposatha of unity (sāmaggi-uposatha)." Otherwise, if there is unity on the two aforementioned Uposatha days, the fault would arise that the Uposatha should not be performed on those days but only the Uposatha of unity on a non-Uposatha day. Otherwise, since it was prohibited before, there is no need to prohibit it now. For it was said before, "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited daily." Or, because it was said before, "Monks, I allow the recitation of the Pātimokkha on the Uposatha day," and later it was said, "Once a fortnight, on the 14th or 15th day," and "Monks, these two are the Uposathas," the undesirable meaning that the Uposatha should not be performed on any other day arises by implication. To prevent this, it should be understood that this teaching was given to show that if there is unity of the Saṅgha, even a day that is normally a non-Uposatha day is called an Uposatha day.

## The Commentary on the Uposathakkhandhaka is Finished.
467:
## 3. Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā

## Vassūpanāyikānujānana-kathā-vaṇṇanā
In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, there is also the reading "saṅkāsayissanti"; however, it is said that the monks residing in the island of Ceylon (Dīpavāsino) read it as "saṅkāpayissanti". When considering "How many ways are there to enter the rains-retreat?", if one asks "For what reason?", it is said: "Monks, I allow you to enter the rains-retreat." Regarding that entry into the rains-retreat, one should enter by saying, "I enter the rains-retreat for these three months." The rainy months are four. Among those four months, there are two types of three-month periods: the first three months and the later three months. Therefore, such a thought occurred to those monks.

## Vassāne-cārikā-paṭikkhepādi-kathā-vaṇṇanā
In this statement, it should be understood that an offense is incurred either by going away without care or by letting the dawn rise in another place. First, if that monk departs because of some business within seven days before the Pavāraṇā day of the full moon of Assayuja. Because it was said, "Monks, whether that monk returns to that monastery or not, monks, his Purimikā (first rains-retreat) is evident, and there is no offense regarding the promise," it should be understood that this was said in reference to a period of less than seven days. For this very reason, it was said: "If that monk departs on that very day without business, or departs with business, monks, his Purimikā is not evident, and he incurs a dukkaṭa offense regarding the promise."

## Sattāha-karaṇīyānujānana-kathā-vaṇဏနာ
187-8. Secondly, because of the statement, "If that monk spends those seven days outside, monks, his Purimikā is not evident, and he incurs a dukkaṭa offense regarding the promise," it should be understood as referring to more than seven days. For this very reason, it was said: "If that monk returns within those seven days, monks, his Purimikā is evident, and there is no offense regarding the promise." Even if there are two reasons, it should be understood that an offense is incurred because there is no cause for breaking the rains-retreat. Therefore, all three of these statements are definitions (viggaha) applied as they may occur. "Three are diminished" is because of the absence of those bhikkhunīs.
468:
## Pahiteyeva-anujānana-kathā-vaṇဏနာ
Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to go for Sangha business; a return must be made within seven days," it is proper to go during the rains-retreat with the intention of returning within seven days. In going thus, even if one comes merely out of a desire for Dhamma (Dhamma-chanda), the source of the Sangha's gains may be destroyed. Therefore, it is also said, "having prepared the lodgings." "Āgata" means coming. Here, the suffix "-ta" is used in the sense of "bhāva" (state). In this phrase "to go for Sangha business," the Elder Dhammasiri reportedly says, "One should go only for Sangha business connected with lodgings, not for other matters." In the Commentary as well, that word is extracted and lodgings alone are shown by saying, "if there is any business in lodgings such as the Uposatha hall, etc."; therefore, it should be investigated and considered.

To go without being invited is not proper; for the monk who goes thus, there is a breaking of the night and a dukkaṭa offense is incurred; this is also called "breaking the rains-retreat" (vassaccheda). In this phrase "only one who is invited," it is proper to go even by a pact made by lay devotees saying, "On such a day, we will perform alms-giving, etc.; let all assemble." From the ninth day after Pavāraṇā, it is proper for all monks to go to search for Pāṃsukူla robes, as in the city of Kāvirapaṭṭana, because the lay devotees prepare and set them aside annually without fail. This matter is also stated in the Andhaka Commentary: "If a pact is made by the Saṅgha saying, 'Let the monks from all around come,' or if an announcement is made by lay devotees, there is no breaking of the night for the monk who goes there. Likewise, it is proper even if invited once, saying, 'Please come every year.'" Others say, "The manner of performing it by announcing in the city of Kāvirapaṭṭana is well-known because they prepare and give to those who come from all around, making it a rule starting from the robe-season." However, the Teachers (Ācariyas) do not say so.

## Antarāye-anāpatti-vassaccheda-kathā-vaṇဏနာ
Because of the statement, "If he has gone far, the dawn should be allowed to rise once every seven days," others say, "It is shown that when there is a danger for which it is proper to break the rains-retreat, it is proper to pass the time by the seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya) without breaking the rains-retreat during that very danger." However, the Vinaya experts (Vinayadharas) do not accept this. Therefore, it should be understood that this statement, "the dawn should be allowed to rise once every seven days," was said in reference to causes such as the requisites arising in that monastery. With reference to that reason, it was said, "However, the Teachers (Ācariyas) do not say so."
469:
It refers to either a cow or a bull. 'Those standing outside the boundary (sīmā)' includes those monks standing in the partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), according to the Elder Upatissa. There is no offense for a monk whose rains retreat is broken due to such reasons. Monks who leave the rains retreat in places other than a monastery should assemble only in that place and act only after making it known: 'For such and such a reason, we shall move this monastery to such and such a place and end the rains retreat there.'

## Explanation of Entering the Rains Retreat in Cattle Pens, etc.

The statement that there is no offense for a monk traveling with a cattle pen (vaja) even if the rains retreat is broken means that the intention is that the retreat is not considered broken. Since a caravan (sattha) is not a monastery (vihāra), one should not say 'in this monastery' but simply say 'I enter the rains retreat here.' Regarding the statement 'It is not proper to enter the rains retreat in a caravan,' it is written that the intention is that it is not proper to say 'in this monastery for these three months' or 'I enter the rains retreat here,' but it is proper only by making a shelter (ālaya). That statement contradicts the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). This is because the Commentary states, 'One should say "I enter the rains retreat here" three times.' If it is asked whether the words of the Commentary are also contradictory from beginning to end—no, they are not; it is because the meaning is not understood. There are two types of caravans: stationary and moving. Among them, if there is a hut (kuṭī) in a stationary caravan, one should stay there after saying 'I enter the rains retreat here.' It was with reference to this that it was said, 'Monks, I allow you to enter the rains retreat in a caravan.' In a moving caravan, however, it is not proper to enter the rains retreat because there is no hut. But if there is a palanquin (sivikā) or a wagon-hut (sakaṭakuṭī), it is proper. The same applies to a cattle pen. In these three places, there is no offense for a monk due to the breaking of the rains retreat.

Regarding the phrase 'He also receives the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā,' there is this investigation: Was the statement 'Monks, I allow you to go where there is a cattle pen' said for the sake of protecting the rains retreat, or for the sake of protecting against the offense of breaking the rains retreat? If it was for the sake of protecting the rains retreat, it contradicts the statement 'Monks, one should not enter the rains retreat without a lodging (asenāsanika).' If it is said that it was for the sake of protecting against the offense of breaking the rains retreat, then it is established that the monk does not receive the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā. What is the logic here? The reason is that only these three types of monks receive the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā, and no others. A monk who is oppressed by wild beasts and the like receives the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā because he does not abandon the place where he entered the rains retreat. If he abandons it, he does not receive it. This is the logic here. One teacher says that a monk who goes to a village also receives the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā. A monk who previously did not enter the rains retreat saying 'I enter the rains retreat here,' but entered saying 'in this monastery'...
470:
That monk is also one who has abandoned (the monastery for the rains retreat). Otherwise, is it permissible to enter the rains retreat by intending only the village, separate from a monastery, saying 'I enter the rains retreat in this village'? If it is said 'let it be so,' it should not be said. This is because there is no such statement as 'Monks, I allow you to enter the rains retreat in a village,' like the statement 'Monks, I allow you to enter the rains retreat in a cattle pen, a caravan, or a boat.' Because the statement 'In three places, there is no offense for a monk even if the rains retreat is broken' indicates that there is an entry into the rains retreat in those boats, caravans, and cattle pens. This is because if those boats, etc., are not present, there is no breaking of the retreat. Therefore, the statement 'It is not proper to enter the rains retreat in a caravan' should be understood as being said with reference to a time when there is no hut (kuṭī). In the context of 'In three places, there is no offense for a monk even if the rains retreat is broken,' it is written that there is no offense only for a monk traveling with those boats, caravans, or cattle pens; there is an offense if he travels after abandoning them, and he does not receive the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā. Therefore, the statement in the Commentary, 'If a caravan reaches the place desired by the monk during the rains retreat and passes beyond... or stays in a village in between, or disperses,' etc., should be understood as being said for the purpose of showing that for those monks who travel after abandoning, it does not constitute traveling after abandoning, and therefore Pavāraṇā should be performed.

In that context, because of the statement 'One should enter the rains retreat after making a hut with a wooden roof (padaracchadana),' it is established that climbing a tree for the sake of a lodging is proper. If it is said that it is not established because it contradicts the Pāḷi, it is not so. It is established by the very rejection of climbing that tree, and because this monk without a lodging (asenāsanika) is rejected again in this place. If it is asked whether the rejection 'Monks, a monk without a lodging should not enter the rains retreat' is like the rejection 'Monks, one should not enter the rains retreat in the open air,' it is not so. This is because it would lead to the open air being accepted as not being a lodging. In fact, the open air is established as a lodging because of the statement 'in the open air, in a straw heap.' Even one who lives in the open space of a four-pillared hall (catusālā) is said to 'live in a four-pillared hall.' Therefore, it would follow that it is proper in that straw heap. Thus, in this context, one 'without a lodging' (asenāsanika) should be understood as a monk who has not obtained a lodging for his permanent residence, whether provided by himself or by others. Otherwise, one of the two rejections would be redundant, and it would follow that it is proper to enter the rains retreat at the foot of a tree or under the eaves, and it would also follow that a monk without a lodging is allowed to stay in a room (gabbha). If it is asked how it is known that only a lodging with a door-fastening is intended here, it is known from the origin story (nidāna). This offense of entering the rains retreat without a lodging was prescribed because of this origin story: 'At that time, monks entered the rains retreat without lodgings; they suffered from both cold and heat.'
471:
Therefore, it is established that at this time of entering the rains retreat (vassūpanāyika), only a place capable of warding off cold and so forth is intended as a lodging (senāsana). If it is asked, "In this case, is the presentation of the preliminary position (pubbapakkh) established?" it should be said, "Not yet," because it indicates the occurrence of the subsequent meaning earlier. In the explanation of the second jhāna, the words "with the subsiding of thought and examination, without thought and without examination" serve as evidence. By the origin (nidāna) that rejects the open air (ajjhokāsa), only the outer open air is rejected; it follows that the open air in the middle of a four-pillared hall (catusālā) and so forth is not rejected. Therefore, shall we say that the origin is not the standard? No, it is because of the lack of restriction (aniyama). It has been established that certain training rules (sikkhāpada) depend on the origin. How can it be known that "this training rule is dependent" and "this training rule is independent"? For in this Khandhaka, is there not a word-by-word commentary (padabhājanī) or a section on non-offence (anāpatti-vāra) as in the Suttavibhaṅga (ubhatovibhaṅga)? In this Khandhaka too, it can be known by the method of teaching. By these two introductory statements—"When it rains, they run to the foot of a tree or to an exposed place"—every place where one gets wet by rain, whether outside or inside, is called "open air" (ajjhokāsa) here. It is also established that in a place where one does not get wet, only a place where rain does not leak is intended here. Therefore, by the words "one should not approach," it is not the making of an abode (ālaya) that is rejected, but rather the rejection of the statement "I enter the rains retreat here." The Andhaka Commentary states that a hut (kuṭī) is made for the ashes or for the bones after burning a corpse. It is written: "A ṭaṅkitamañca is a stone house with a plastered hut." It is said: "If a lodging without a door is assigned to one, if one stays in a similar lodging that has a door, it is allowable." There is also an application; it is stated in both the Pali and the Commentary that "one who has no lodging should not enter the rains retreat." Therefore, it should be investigated.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Unlawful Agreements and so forth

Regarding the statement "It has been said in the Mahāvibhaṅga," the words of the Andhaka Commentary are: A novice (sāmaṇera) under fifteen years of age must not stay in this monastery, must not wander for rag-robes (paṃsukūla), must not accept cloth for robes, must not eat in another monastery, must not use the property of another monk or nun, they should not address or converse with one another, they should not recite, they should practice with a clay bowl, and a novice whose requisites are incomplete must not stay.

By "false speech" (musāvāda), "deception" (visaṃvāda) is intended. Some teachers say, "It is said by way of accepting with the intent to deceive," and others say, "Laypeople take it as false speech because it accords with the king's words."
472: The former rains retreat (purimikā) is also not evident. Why? Because when the thought "I will stay in the second lodging" arises, the first acceptance of lodging is subsided. Again, when the thought "I will stay in the first lodging itself" arises, the second acceptance of lodging is subsided. It is written that there is no regulation in both lodgings. In the Ancient Glossary (Porāṇagaṇṭhipada), however, it is said: "Without staying in the place first accepted, one accepts a lodging in another monastery and stays for two or three days; because of such staying, the first acceptance of lodging is subsided, and therefore the former rains retreat is not evident. The subsequent acceptance of lodging does not subside. This is called subsiding by the power of days. Otherwise, if one stays in another monastery for the subsequent three months, the former rains retreat is not evident; this is called subsiding by the power of the acceptance of lodgings." Neither of these two alternative interpretations is intended here. Wherever this monk has made a promise, there the former rains retreat is not evident, and because of the promise, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). When is the former rains retreat evident? Among two lodgings on a journey, in whichever lodging there is a subsequent acceptance on that very day, for the monk who goes from that first accepted place for a seven-day business, there is no fault due to the breaking of the rains retreat. In the passage beginning "That monk departs on that very day without business," it is written that "business" (karaṇīya) means business to be done within seven days. In the decision on the breaking of the night not mentioned in the Pali (Pāḷimuttakaratticcheda), it is said: "listening to the Dhamma and so forth." In the first four sections (vāra), because departure without concern is intended, it is not said "for a seven-day business." This is because if there were such business, departure without concern would not be possible. Among those four sections, the first two sections are spoken by way of a monk who has not entered the rains retreat. Therefore, the meaning is established that for a monk who has entered the rains retreat, if he goes for a seven-day business on that very day and returns within seven days, there is no breaking of the rains retreat. The latter two sections are spoken by way of the departure without concern of a monk who has entered the rains retreat. The statement "He departs with business seven days before the Invitation (pavāraṇā)" is said to show that for a monk who lets seven days pass, excluding the day of departure, there is a breaking of the rains retreat. Since the words "He departs without business" are not in that Pali, the meaning is established that it is not proper to go without a reason for breaking the night. But after having performed the Invitation, it is proper to go, because the Invitation is dependent on that day. In that Pali, "if he should not come" means not coming due to an obstacle. But the teacher says that even if one has no concern, thinking "I will not come here again," one only gets permission to go if there is business; therefore, it is not said "without business" to show this. It is said: "In the island of Sihala (Sri Lanka), there is what is called the Minor Invitation (Cūḷapavāraṇā). Having performed that Invitation, they go wherever they wish as those having business, and they also show the application to be performed." In going thus, the six dawns within the rains retreat...
473:
