Some teachers say that six dawns occur within the Rains-residence and one dawn occurs outside; therefore, that monk has completed the three-month residence. It is also said, "The Teacher does not say so." In all cases, "entering the monastery" means entering the chamber reached according to one's seniority in the Rains, as stated by the ancient teachers. Regarding the failure to enter the Rains-residence due to lack of mindfulness, it is because of not saying, "In this monastery, for these three months." It is written that for a monk who goes away thinking, "I will stay in another monastery and then return," without a reason for breaking the night as mentioned in the Commentary, the Rains-residence is broken.

"He undertakes the later Rains-residence" means it is undertaken by one who was ordained in the interval or one whose Rains-residence was broken; one should not undertake the later Rains-residence without entering the earlier one for any other reason. They say, making a decision, that in all cases where there is a break of the night, the Rains-residence is broken. Some, however, do not desire this and elaborate extensively to establish that statement; what is the use of such elaboration?

## The Explanation of the Chapter on Entering the Rains-residence is finished.

## 4. Pavāraṇākkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Explanation of the Discussion on Living Uncomfortably
Because it is said, "Venerable sirs, I invite the Saṅgha," it appears as if it should also be said later, "Let the Saṅgha speak to me." The meaning here is: "Since I invite the Saṅgha, let all the venerable ones included in that Pavāraṇā—whether elders, those of middle standing, or newly ordained—admonish me without distinction."

## Explanation of the Classification of Pavāraṇā
In this Pali passage, "Monks, there are these two kinds of Pavāraṇā," when there is such a business, it is proper to invite in any place whatsoever. For this very reason, even now in the Mahāvihāra, the monks invite on the fourteenth day and give the physical harmony (kāyasamaggi) on the fifteenth day. They go on the eighth day to see the great festival at Cetiyagiri; such going is only for those monks who wish to perform Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth day. It is written that this practice has become customary because of the statement: "If one goes with a business to attend to seven days before the Pavāraṇā, there is no offense." The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) taught for a single monk, "If he does not resolve, there is an offense of wrong-doing," and the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) taught for him, should also be applied to the Saṅgha and the group (gaṇa).

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Allowance for Giving Pavāraṇā
"And by that monk" refers to the monk who gives the Pavāraṇā.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Fifteen Cases of No Offense, etc.
They say that because of the statement, "When that Pavāraṇā has been announced and the Saṅgha has invited, it is well-invited for all," the monk who gives Pavāraṇā on the Pavāraṇā day is also considered to have invited.

"While the assembly has not yet risen" refers to the assembly that is conversing with one another after performing Pavāraṇā. "While some of the assembly have departed" means while some remain seated as they were and some have gone to their respective places. "They should invite again" means that again all the monks...
475:
...having assembled in harmony, should perform Pavāraṇā. Regarding the statement that Pavāraṇā should be performed in the presence of those monks who have come in harmony: "It is written that Pavāraṇā should be performed only in the presence of those who are still seated, without calling back the monks who have left; this same method applies in the Uposathakkhandhaka as well." Regarding the statement that if the entire assembly has departed but they return in harmony, Pavāraṇā should be performed in their presence: "They say that if everyone has departed and it is not possible to assemble them all, it is proper to assemble some monks and perform Pavāraṇā." Why? It is said that because there is no formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) performed by setting aside the motion (ñatti), there is no schism (vagga). In this matter, however, whether some monks have left or all have left, everyone should be assembled and Pavāraṇā should be performed simply without setting aside the motion. It is not proper to assemble only some monks and perform Pavāraṇā, because of the statement, "Venerable sir, I invite the Saṅgha." Indeed, only when all are assembled can they be those who speak of what has been seen, heard, or suspected later on. It would be like speaking the words of Pavāraṇā in the presence of only some monks while knowing that there are monks who have not yet arrived. Unlike the relinquishing of robes and so on for which one has incurred a Nissaggiya offense by assembling four monks who are present, Pavāraṇā cannot be done like that because it depends on everyone. The statement, "The Pavāraṇā of monks in harmony is prescribed," is the evidence in this matter. Elder Upatissa says, "It is not proper in any other way, because it is not allowed in the Commentary." It is said, "Pavāraṇā should be performed in the presence of a few monks without setting aside the motion." Incoming monks (āgantuka) are those who arrive from the ninth day of the waxing moon onwards, or those who have spent the Rains-residence in cattle-pens, carts, or boats.

It is written, "There is wrong view with ten bases, such as 'The Tathāgata [exists after death],' etc." It is said, "[There is wrong view] such as 'There is nothing given,' etc."

It is written, "One should perform Pavāraṇā together with that monk, thinking, 'We shall know after investigating and examining.'"

## The Explanation of the Chapter on the Invitation is finished.
