## 5. Commentary on the Chapter on Leather
## Commentary on the Story of Soṇa Koḷivisa
The phrase "Asītiyā ...pe... kāreti" is an explanation of the reason for the statement "Asīti gāmika-sahassāni sannipātāpetvā" (having assembled eighty thousand village headmen). In that Pali text, although it should be said "gāmānaṃ asītiyā sahassesu," it is stated as "asītiya gāma-sahassesu." Those who act as leaders in a village are called "gāmika"; it refers to thousands of such village headmen. The phrase "kammacittīkatāni" is spoken metaphorically. In fact, the appearance of those hairs being like the color of dark collyrium occurs in a place produced by physical conditions (utu) which has kamma as its cause. Although it should be said "kenacid-eva karaṇīyena," it is stated as "kenacid-evā." In this term "kenacid-eva," the word "evaṃ" occurs in the sense of a simile or comparison. The word "evaṃ" occurs in the senses of comparison, reference, questioning, restriction, affirmation, and analogy. The phrase "purato pekkhamānānaṃ" is a term where the genitive case (sāmivibhatta) is used in the sense of disregard (anādara). At that time, seeing the door-leaf of the Buddha's Gandhakuṭi well-closed, he went by psychic power due to his skill in the desired manner, entered the hut, and made his report. In the phrase "vihārapacchāyāyaṃ," it means in the lengthening shadow of the monastery. In the phrase "aho nūna," it is written as "Oh, how wonderful!" because of the state of having great power. The Buddha's wandering together with many monks was intended to inspire those who had not yet initiated effort by pointing out the initiation of effort by the Venerable Soṇa, and also to show that sandals were allowed for the protection of the feet of such delicate monks.

## Commentary on the Story of Soṇa's Going Forth
In that Pali sequence, in the phrase "nimittaṃ gaṇhāhi," it means "observe the manner of those faculties (indriya)."

In the phrase "adhimutto hoti," it means he stands having penetrated and realized it. By the terms beginning with "nekkhamma-adhimutto," Nibbāna and Arahantship are spoken of. "That Nibbāna is called 'nekkhamma' (renunciation) because of its departure from all defilements; it is called 'paviveka' (seclusion) because of its being empty of the household-like round of defilements; and it is called 'abyāpajja' (non-ill will) because of the absence of ill will. Arahantship is called 'upādānakkhaya' (destruction of clinging) because it arises at the end of the destruction of clinging; it is called 'taṇhakkhaya' (destruction of craving) because it arises at the end of the destruction of craving; and it is called 'asammoha' (non-delusion) because of the absence of delusion." Some teachers say that Arahantship is spoken of by all these terms. In the phrase "siyā kho evam-assa," it means "it might be so at times," or "such a thought might occur to that venerable one." "Paccāgacchanto" means being aware. In the phrase "karaṇīyam-attānaṃ," it means one's own (duty to be done). That very word "atta" is the original reading.
477:
Or there is also the reading "vā." In this term "nekkhamma-adhimutto" alone, Arahantship is spoken of. Some teachers say that in the remaining terms, Nibbāna is spoken of. Some say that in this term "asammoha-adhimutto" alone, Nibbāna is spoken of, and in the remaining terms, Arahantship is spoken of. Others say that in all these terms, both Nibbāna and Arahantship are spoken of. In the terms "pavivekañca cetaso, adhimuttassa, upādānakkhayassa ca," the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. It means "having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases (āyatana)."

## Commentary on the Rejection of All-Blue Cloths etc.
There is the reading "wiping with a cloth dyed with dye-liquor." Because it is said "having removed the khallaka etc.," the view of those who say it is allowable to use them by making two or three holes should not be accepted.

## Commentary on the Rejection of Vehicles etc.
Because it is said "more than four finger-breadths," some say that what is less than four finger-breadths is allowable. In this place regarding "pillows red on both sides," it is written: "Robes dyed with bark-dye (kāsāva) are allowable; only robes dyed with safflower (kusumbha) etc. are not allowable."

## Commentary on the Rejection of All Hides etc.
"Kissa tyāyaṃ" should be resolved as "kissa te ayaṃ."

A seat made for the benefit of laypeople is called "gihi-vikataṃ." It is written that it means "He allows sitting in any place whatsoever." Although it is said in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary that "except for the cotton mattress (tūlikā), all rugs such as gonaka sewn with jewels are allowable," when it comes to the Vinaya teaching, one must abide by the weightier rule; therefore, the meaning should be taken only according to the method stated here in this Vinaya. Other teachers say that in that commentary, because it was spoken by way of the Suttanta teaching for the sake of householders etc., it appears as if it were said "except for the cotton mattress ... they are allowable" for the purpose of including them.

"Migamātuka" is the name of that creature. "Vātamiga" is also the name of that creature. It is written that "kāḷasīha is a black-faced monkey." In this place where it says hides are not allowable, the reason by which hides will be allowable will become clear later. One's own...
478:
It is said that carrying [hides] for personal use is forbidden. Although it is accomplished by this much Pali: "Monks, no hide whatsoever should be worn," this training rule "Monks, cowhide should not be worn" was spoken later in the context of "Monks, I allow leather mats in all border regions (paccantima janapada)" because of the fear of over-extending the permission beyond what was intended.

## The Commentary on the Chapter on Leather is Finished.
479:
## 6. Commentary on the Chapter on Medicines (Bhesajjakkhandhaka)
## Commentary on the Discussion of the Five Medicines, etc.
The statement "Whatever medicine there may be" should be understood as being said according to what is obtained, without regard to the origin (nidāna), because it is seen to be contradicted later by the statement "with both those medicines, they become excessively lean." Why was it not said in accordance with the origin? Because the intention was to regard a meaning other than that origin. Indeed, even in the time of all Buddhas, there is regard for the status of ghee and so on as seven-day medicines (sattāhakālika); such a statement is the Blessed One's intention. For that very reason, it was said: "It should spread for the sake of nutriment, but gross nutriment should not be apparent."

Similarly, here in the phrase "to be received at the proper time and consumed at the proper time," the delimitation of time was not made. Since there is an intention regarding something other than that origin, where could one obtain the delimitation of time as life-long (yāvajīvika) for those medicines such as the Blessed One's original medicines (mūlabhesajja) after they have been received? However, the statement "Monks, I allow those five medicines to be received at the proper time and consumed at the proper time" should be understood as being said with the intention: "I allow them to be consumed only at the proper time on subsequent days after having stored them (sannidhi)." Otherwise, because there would be no excellence in meaning, the arising of the thought "Whatever medicine there may be," etc., would not be possible.

If it is argued that these were spoken with regard to what is suitable (sappāya) according to the illness, because the allowance for choice food (paṇītabhojana) is well-known—that is not so, because it is shown that they reach a state of being excessively lean, and so on. If it is argued that fresh butter (navanīta) should not be mentioned separately because it is said "molasses (phāṇita) is derived from sugar-cane juice," and thus "ghee (sappi) is derived from fresh butter" should be said—that is not so, because of the intention to show a distinction. Just as sugar-cane juice (ucchurasa) was allowed separately later, even though it was established by the mention of molasses, because of the intention to place it in the position of molasses-water due to the common nature of sugar-cane; likewise, it should be understood that fresh butter was allowed separately because of the intention to show a special procedure for fresh butter.

That special procedure for it should be understood by way of the commentary on the training rule on medicines (Bhesajjasikkhāpada). For it is said there: "One who wishes to consume it by cooking it into ghee is allowed to cook even unwashed fresh butter" (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.622). In that text, ghee is only cooked, not uncooked. Molasses is the same. Fresh butter, however, is only uncooked.

Here, if an objector asks: "Should not sugar-cane juice, like fresh butter, be mentioned only in the text concerning seven-day medicines (sattāhakālika)?"—it should not be so mentioned. Why? In the text concerning seven-day medicines...
480:
If sugar-cane juice were mentioned by referring to molasses (guḷa), it would follow that just as molasses is forbidden for a monk who is not sick, so too would sugar-cane juice be forbidden. But if it is not mentioned, it does not come under the designation of molasses, like molasses itself. Not being mentioned here, it is placed only in the position of molasses-water by a later statement. If it is argued: "For that very purpose, it was mentioned in the section on drinks allowed in the afternoon; therefore, it is indeed a watch-period medicine (yāmakālika)"—no, because it contradicts the commentary.

If it is argued: "It is yāmakālika because the meaning of 'derived from' (upādāya) has the sense of 'dependence' (nissaya)"—what is meant by this? There is this statement in the Nissaggiya Commentary: "Molasses should be understood as a sugar-cane product derived from (upādāya) sugar-cane juice" (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 2.623). In that commentary, the meaning of this word 'upādāya' is "having made it a dependence-condition (nissayapaccaya)." This is not so, because a subsequent action (aparakiriyā) is not seen later. Just as in such passages as "dependent on the eye and forms" (cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca), a subsequent action "arises" (uppajjati) is seen for this gerund 'paṭicca'; here in "derived from sugar-cane juice," a subsequent action is not seen.

This is incorrect, because it is established even in the absence of that [subsequent action] there. Just as in the passage "the four great elements and the form derived from (upādāya) the four great elements" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 584), the gerund is established even in the absence of a subsequent action, could it not be the same here? No, because there it regards the remainder of the text (pāṭhasesa). Just as that Pali text regards the remainder "is said" or "proceeding" in "form [is said to be] derived from the four great elements," this commentary statement does not regard any such remainder. For the teachers of the commentary speak completely. Or, it is merely the making of a designation for that form. Just as in "there is form derived from," etc., it is merely the making of a designation, so too should it be understood here.

In this commentary, however, "derived from sugar-cane juice" means "starting from sugar-cane juice, from then onwards." Therefore, it is said: "A monk who is not sick, who asks for and eats rice mixed with sugar-cane juice, should be dealt with according to the Training Rule on Choice Food (Paṇītabhojana Sikkhāpada); a nun, by the Training Rule on [Offences] to be Confessed (Pāṭidesaniya)." Some teachers say that this statement is incorrect. Those teachers should be made to understand by showing the absence of a special reason.

By this much sequence of words, the meaning of the words "derived from sugar-cane juice means starting from sugar-cane juice," etc., having been wrongly grasped—if sugar-cane juice were molasses by the statement "derived from sugar-cane juice," then the statement "or uncooked" (apakka) would be useless, because sugar-cane juice would have been included by the word "uncooked." If it is established that sugar-cane juice is molasses by the statement "or cooked" (pakka), then the statement "derived from sugar-cane juice" would be useless. This answer has been given, and it is proved to be an unsurpassable answer. In that phrase "or uncooked," the monk himself...
481:
"Apakkā vā" or "avatthukapakkā vā" means cooked by the monk himself without the raw material (sugarcane). Therefore, it is shown that it should be stated as "savatthukapakkā vā" in another way; this explanation is poorly presented. Why? Because in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: "Molasses made from sugarcane heated by fire or molasses made from crushed sugarcane is allowable only before the meal (in the morning)"; and because the phrase "savatthukapakkā vā" should not be said as it contradicts the established doctrine. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, a question is raised: "Is this savatthukapakkā allowable or not?" and it is stated: "There is no such thing as sugarcane molasses being unallowable in the afternoon"; this statement is appropriate. Therefore, since the meaning of "savatthukapakkā vā" has already been stated, it is concluded that the previous explanation was poorly presented. "Āhāratthaṃ" means for the purpose of nutriment, for the sake of sustaining the function of nutriment.

"Telaparibhogena" means by the consumption of a seven-day medicinal (sattāhakālika). Regarding "sati paccaye" (if there is a cause), the existence of a cause should be understood in two ways: for the sick (gilāna) and for the healthy (agilāna). In the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra) of the training rule on eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana), the existence of a cause for the three types of temporals starting with yāmakālika is stated without distinction (generally). In this Khandhaka, however, it is stated: "Monks, I allow molasses for the sick, and molasses-water for the healthy. Monks, I allow loṇasovīraka medicine for the sick, and loṇasovīraka medicine mixed with water for the healthy." Therefore, it is concluded that the existence of a cause is of two kinds: for the sick and for the healthy. Otherwise, if one consumes molasses-water and so on without a cause, an offense is committed. If that were the case, it would contradict the Pāḷi text.

"Piṭṭhehi" means with ground sesame oils. "Koṭṭhaphalaṃ" is the fruit of the costus tree (saminsā tree). It is also written as "madanaphalaṃ". "Hiṅgujatu" is the asafoetida obtained by cooking the stems, leaves, and sprouts of the asafoetida tree. "Hiṅgusipāṭikā" is the asafoetida obtained by cooking the roots and branches of that tree. "Takaṃ" is the water from cooking the bark of that tree. "Takapattī" is the water from cooking the leaves of that tree. "Takapaṇṇī" is the water from cooking the fruit of that tree. Alternatively, it is written that "takaṃ" is lac (lākhā). "Takapattī" is artificial hair lac. "Takapaṇṇī" is cooked lac. "Ubbhidaṃ" is salt produced from saline soil.

"Chakaṇaṃ" is cow dung. "Pākatikacuṇṇaṃ" is raw (uncooked) astringent powder; therefore, it is said, "Excluding scented powder, all are allowable." "Cālitehi" means with sifted powders. "Nānāsambhārehi kataṃ" means made with various medicinal ingredients.
482:
## Guḷādianujānanakathāvaṇṇanā
It is shown as if there are two kinds of cooking: cooking by oneself and cooking thoroughly all around. Therefore, in the case of milk and so on, even just heating it is called cooking. Because of cooking by merely heating in this way, they are similar to rice and so on that contain partially cooked grains.

276-8. In the place where "Buddhappamukha" (headed by the Buddha) appears, it is said that instead of saying "bhikkhusaṅgho," the word "saṅgho" is used to include the Blessed One as well. "Nāga" means an elephant.

"Sambādha" (confined place) is stated to be conformable (allowable) in the anus, and also in the urinary tract of monks and nuns. Fomentation (heating with fire) is allowable because there is no prohibition. If it is asked whether surgical operation (satthakamma) is unallowable by conformity, the answer is no, it is allowable. It is allowable because only what should be prohibited is prohibited, and because the extent of what is to be prohibited is shown. What does this mean? Having combined the surgical operations previously prohibited, later the Blessed One prohibited surgical operations twice, saying, "Monks... there is a thullaccaya offense." Due to this prohibition, it is meant that the area within two finger-breadths around the confined place (sambādha) is prohibited. It is shown that there is no prohibition beyond that regarding surgical operations. To put it another way: previously, surgical operation was prohibited only in the confined place itself; later, the two finger-breadths around the confined place were also prohibited. Therefore, it should be understood that the prohibition applies only to the area within two finger-breadths of the confined place, and there is no prohibition beyond that. In this context, "sattha" (knife/weapon) means any object that cuts, as in "satthahāraka" and so on. Therefore, it is stated as "even with a thorn," etc. Here, "khāradāna" (application of caustic) should be understood as allowed in the Pasākha (groin area) for the purpose of "lepa" (anointing) in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga. Some teachers specially interpret the text "satthakamma" and change it to "vatthikamma" (binding with cloth). They say that "vatthi" refers to a coarse cloth. They define "vatthikamma" as cutting with that coarse cloth. Those teachers should be refuted by pointing out the word analysis (padabhājanīya) of "satthahārakaṃ vāssa pariyeseyyā." "Aṇḍavuḍḍhī" refers to one with swollen testicles (hydrocele). "Ādānavattī" refers to the insertion of a coarse cloth (ānahavatti).

## Manussamaṃsapaṭikkhepakathāvaṇṇanā
Because it was said, "Monks, human flesh should not be eaten... there is a thullaccaya offense," and because it was said, "Monks, it should not be eaten without reflecting (without checking)... there is a dukkaṭa offense," two offenses are committed: a dukkaṭa offense for not reflecting and a thullaccaya offense. Therefore, even in the case of allowable meat (kappiyamaṃsa), a dukkaṭa offense is committed due to the lack of reflection. Some teachers say, "An offense is committed only if one knows it is meat; for one who does not know in the case of cakes and so on, how could there be reflection?" Others say that because it was taught generally, an offense is committed even if one does not know.
483:
## Explanation of the Prohibition of Elephant Flesh and Others

The phrase "all these... are not allowable" is a statement merely showing the unsuitability of the ten types of flesh, such as human flesh, and is not a statement showing the classification of offenses. The statement that an offense is incurred by one who eats any [of these] flesh, whether knowingly or unknowingly, is an indefinite statement because it does not specify "such-and-such an offense." The meaning of both these [decisions] can be understood through the methods previously mentioned, that grave offenses (thullaccaya) and offenses of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) occur regarding the flesh and so on of humans and others; thus it is stated.

In this regard, this is the meaning: Since the flesh and so on of these humans and others are unallowable, therefore, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is incurred regarding the flesh and so on of humans. An offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is incurred regarding all the flesh, blood, and so on of the remaining nine types of beings. Indeed, in the Pali text itself, treating blood and so on as similar to flesh, it is said: "Monks, human flesh... a grave offense (thullaccaya) is incurred." In that same Pali text, an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is prescribed regarding the flesh and so on of elephants and others. Therefore, it is stated in the Sihala Commentary: "Regarding human flesh, or hair, or nails, or bone, or blood, it is only a grave offense (thullaccaya)." By this statement—

"The bone, blood, skin, and hair of these [elephants, etc.] are not allowable"—

the sense and meaning of the verse from the Khuddasikkha are easily understood. In the context of "receiving," it refers to an offense of wrongdoing through disrespect (anādariya-dukkaṭa). Some say: "The flesh of water-humans (Nāgas) and others is also not allowable." Although there are disadvantages mentioned by the Nāga King, taking only the grounds for criticism, it is said: "Because it is loathsome."

## Explanation of the Discussion on Rice Gruel, Honey-balls, and Others

"It should be dealt with according to the Dhamma"—this phrase is the word of the Council compilers (Saṅgītikāra). Indeed, the Blessed One did not prescribe the same training rule twice; some teachers say that in training rules of such nature, it should be understood thus. It is stated with reference only to the first prescription; however, those monks did not become offenders. Why? Because of the origin (uṭṭhappatti) of the training rule on out-of-turn meals (paramparabhojana). Alternatively, it is said: "We have already eaten after wandering for alms early." In the Mātikā-vibhaṅga, it is also stated: "What is called an out-of-turn meal (paramparabhojana) is when one is invited to one of the five types of meals, and setting aside that invited meal, eats another of the five types of meals; this is called an out-of-turn meal." Therefore, it is evident that "another meal" means any meal received through an invitation. Since substantial rice gruel (bhojjayāgu) is not a meal received by way of invitation...
484:
...therefore, those monks consumed it, thinking "There is no offense here." In this regard, because it was said "It should be dealt with according to the Dhamma," it is permitted that an offense is incurred only for a monk who eats a meal received through another invitation, and not for others (uninvited meals). From the time of that permission, in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra) of that paramparabhojana training rule, it is said: "[There is no offense] in a regular meal (niccabhatta), ticket-food (salākabhatta), fortnightly meal (pakkhikabhatta), Uposatha meal (uposathikabhatta), or a meal on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipadikabhatta)." These did not exist at the time of the first prescription in Vesālī; if they had, the origin (uṭṭhappatti) would contradict the Mātikā-vibhaṅga. Therefore, because it is stated in the origin: "Venerable Sir, we have already eaten after wandering for alms early," and because in the word-analysis (padabhājanī) it is stated without distinction: "He eats one of the five types of meals," the statement that an offense is incurred for a monk who, setting aside a meal invited first or later, eats only uninvited food, and no offense for eating other meals, indeed follows. However, because it was said: "Monks, substantial rice gruel (bhojjayāgu) other than that which is invited should not be consumed," it appears as if an offense is incurred for a monk who eats a meal received by a later invitation other than the first invited meal, or regular meals (niccabhatta) and so on. Preventing the implication that this would be a secondary prescription (anupaññatti), and preventing the implication of an offense regarding uninvited food, and directing the first prescribed training rule to this aforementioned meaning, the Blessed One said: "It should be dealt with according to the Dhamma." Therefore, from the time of that permission, an offense is incurred only for a monk who eats a meal from a later invitation. Among those invited meals, the meaning follows that no offense is incurred for a monk who eats regular meals (niccabhatta) and so on. For that very reason, the Venerable Upāli Thera included the five terms such as "regular meal" (niccabhatta) and recited them in the section on non-offense of that training rule. Indeed, those Great Arhats knew the intention of the Blessed One. Therefore, the teachers say that the Blessed One’s earlier statement, "Setting aside the five types of meals, there is no offense in all cases," was maintained later by mentioning only substantial rice gruel (bhojjayāgu) without touching upon honey-balls (madhugoḷaka), which is not a [standard] meal.

In this regard, the objector asks: Just as the Elder included regular meals (niccabhatta) and so on by way of the reason obtained later, why is it not said in the Kathina Chapter (Kathinakkhandhaka), by including out-of-turn meals (paramparabhojana): "Monks, for you who have spread the Kathina, six [allowances] will be allowable"? The answer is: It is not said in order to show the aforementioned reason. If understood otherwise, this training rule would have been prescribed half in Vesālī and half in Andhakavinda. If that were not the case, the monks would have been guilty of an offense; however, those monks were not offenders because their remorse (kukkucca) was seen even though the Blessed One had not prohibited it. Indeed, it is stated: "Brahmin, if so, give to the monks," yet the monks, being remorseful, did not accept. Indeed, although they consumed it by the command of the Blessed One saying "Consume it," to dispel the doubt of those monks who had reached a state of uncertainty, thinking "Was this allowed specifically for us?", He said: "Monks, I allow rice gruel (yāgu) and honey-balls (madhugoḷaka)."
485:
It is stated: 'Madhu-goḷakañcā' (and honey-balls). In this matter, it should be understood how they would eat a successive meal (paramparabhojana) by transgressing the paramparabhojana training rule (sikkhāpada) that was prescribed. Here, some teachers say that even though they knew 'another's meal is not allowable' by the paramparabhojana training rule itself, they ate with the perception that 'it is allowable like the Paṭaggidāna and Mahāvikaṭa training rules, etc.,' because the Buddha separately allowed it, saying, 'Monks, I allow rice gruel (yāgu).'

Therefore, the statement beginning with 'Api ca mayaṃ kālasseva bhojjayāguyā dhātā' is made. That statement is not appropriate. This is because it contradicts the origin story (aṭṭhuppatti), the matrix (mātikā), and the analysis (vibhaṅga) of that training rule; it would lead to the impossibility of regular meals (niccabhatta), etc., in the section on non-offense (anāpattivāra); it would not overcome the state of the monks having an offense; and it would imply that the Blessed One allowed it based on a wrong view.

Because the Blessed One, in some instances, rejects even what is allowable according to the Vinaya, saying, 'That which is sung over with verses is not to be eaten by me,' those monks, based on the Blessed One's intention, are said to 'not accept it, being scrupulous.' Regarding the training rule, the Blessed One also said, 'Monks, I allow rice gruel (yāgu),' specifically to make His intention clear. Indeed, the Blessed One's intention is difficult to grasp. For instance, He rejected Bhāradvāja's milk-rice (pāyāsa) because it involved an improper request (akata-viññatti). However, regarding the tekaṭula-yāgu (gruel with three ingredients) prepared at the request of the Venerable Ānanda, He did not say, 'Ānanda, that gruel obtained by request is also not allowable,' but said only, 'Ānanda, that gruel which has been stored indoors (antovuttha)...' and so forth. Therefore, by showing the meaning that 'if it is not stored indoors, it is allowable,' He strengthens the training rules on superior food (paṇītabhojana), bean curry and rice (sūpodana), and requests (viññatti). He strengthens it by the logic: 'If it is allowable even for the Blessed One, what need is there to say for us?'

The Blessed One allowed molasses (guḷa) only for a sick monk; this is stated by the power of the words, 'Those medicines which are to be enjoyed by sick monks...' (Pārājika 622). For that reason, they were scrupulous in accepting it here. But in this Khandhaka Pāḷi, because it is said, 'Monks, I allow molasses water (guḷodaka) for a sick monk,' and because it is the section on molasses, after mentioning the previously allowed training rule, He also allowed molasses water for a monk who is not sick. Therefore, He shows this distinction: a sick monk should consume molasses if there is a cause, but molasses water is allowable even if there is no cause.

Among those molasses waters, some say, 'Molasses water is a seven-day limit (sattāhakālika) among the kālikas; because the Blessed One allowed it specifically, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred if seven days are exceeded.' That statement is not appropriate. Because it is mixed with water, it relinquishes the state of being a seven-day limit. 'Just as mangoes and such become evening-limit (yāmakālika) when mixed with water, so too, relinquishing the state of being a seven-day limit...'
486:
Immediately after that (relinquishing the seven-day limit), they say it stands as a life-long limit (yāvajīvika); that statement is appropriate. And because the Blessed One specifically allowed that molasses water, there is no fault in the absence of reflection (paccavekkhaṇā). Because it is called 'molasses water,' they say it follows the nature of water. If being mixed with water makes it follow the nature of water, then honey (madhu) should also be so, as it is allowed in the same way. Even if that were not the case, because it follows the nature of water, it would have to be consumed without being formally accepted (akappiyakata); but that is not so. It is stated in another Gaṇṭhipada text: 'In all cases, it should be taken after investigation.'

'Empty place' (suññāgāra) refers to the fourth jhāna.

## Explanation of the Allowance of the Allowable Ground (Kappiyabhūmi)

'Oravasadda' refers to a loud sound. In the phrase 'surrounded by many people,' it is allowable even with one person. They say, 'Among many, it should be in accordance with the word of even one.' Because it is said 'having touched,' it is not allowable if not touched. By the words 'there is no fault,' the remaining commentaries are also allowed. They say, 'If they fill that hole after demarcating the wall, it is not allowable to do it there; it is only allowable to do it on the natural ground.' That statement seems to contradict what was said in the above commentary, such as 'constructed with bricks, etc.' In the phrase 'even a clod of earth,' it is stated: 'If one forgets and does not make a determination (adhiṭṭhāna), and then makes a determination above the place remembered, the goods below are not allowable, only the goods above are allowable; this is the distinction here.' Here, 'allowable to obtain a kappiyakuṭi' means it should be made again in such a place. In the phrase 'we give it to make a kappiyakuṭi,' the intention is to perform the task of a kappiyakuṭi. Other teachers say that a refectory (bhojanasālā) is indeed a dwelling (senāsana), therefore it should be made in that refectory. It is stated: 'It is allowable even if not made.'

It is written: 'Mukhasannidhi means storing (sannidhi) at the time of eating.' Mukhasannidhi is the name for that storage of food. It is stated: 'If it were storage (sannidhi), it would be a pācittiya offense; but mukhasannidhi is a dukkaṭa offense, therefore storage (sannidhi) is not intended here.' Because it is said 'having made it his property,' a relinquishment without regard is not intended. Some teachers say that just as in the formal assignment (vikappanā) of robes, one should know only what is allowable.

## Explanation of the Story of Keṇiya the Ascetic

They say, 'If one relinquishes what was accepted by oneself in the forenoon and a novice (sāmaṇera) or others make a drink (pānaka) and give it, it is allowable only in the forenoon; it is not allowable in the afternoon because it was accepted along with the physical substance.' In that matter, because there is no fault in accepting it again, and only in the forenoon...
487:
Because the accepted object has been relinquished and because one has not yet handled it oneself, it is seen as faultless; it should be accepted after consideration. Sālūka is a type of tuber; it is called "ito kiñcitaka". It is also written that "Phārusaka" is a type of tree found in the Goḷa region. Since "pakkāḍākarasa" (juice of cooked vegetables) is specifically mentioned, it means that raw juice that has not been cooked is allowable. According to the Kurundī, this is also established. Rice-washing water is also a grain-juice (dhanyarasa). It is written that strained sugarcane juice is a seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika). Sāvittī refers to the Gāyattī meter. Chandaso refers to the Vedas. Because it was said, "Monks, a monk should not encourage [another] in what is unallowable," it is said to mean that novices (anupasampanna) should not be encouraged not only in the ten training rules but also in whatever is unallowable for a monk.

"Dve paṭā" (two cloths) refers to Cīnapaṭṭa (made in China) and Somārapaṭṭa (made in the Somāra region), named after their regions. "Tīṇi" (three) refers to the three types including cloth from Pattuṇṇa. The Iddhimayika robe is the robe that appeared for the Ehi Bhikkhu monks. The Devadattiya robe is the robe obtained by the Elder Anuruddha. It is written, "When the watch [of the night] has passed, [an offense occurs] by way of storage (sannidhi); when seven days have passed, [an offense occurs] by way of the medicinal training rule."

## The Explanation of the Chapter on Medicines is Finished.
488:
## 7. Explanation of the Chapter on Kathina
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Allowance of Kathina
"Kathina" means "firmness" because it is capable of internalizing the five benefits. Saying "they will be allowable" (kappissanti) in the future tense, rather than "they are allowable" (kappanti), is appropriate when taking the word "vo" in the sense of possession (genitive case); the reason is that at that moment, those monks have not yet spread the Kathina.

Between these two variations of meaning, the latter is appropriate because all those Pāveyyaka monks were observers of all the dhutaṅga practices. Indeed, the training rule of wandering without informing (anāmantacāra) is prescribed only for a monk who consents to an invitation (nimantana); likewise, the training rule of group meals (gaṇabhozana). For a monk who has not determined the triple robe (aticīvara), there is no [offense of] wandering without taking [the robes] (asamādānacāra), because he can accept as many robes as he desires, such as a fourth robe. For other monks, it can be obtained by way of not determining [the robes]. The benefit of the arising of robes occurs only for a monk who does not observe the Pāṃsukūla dhutaṅga.

"In the boundary where the Kathina is spread" refers to the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā). It should be understood that only the upacārasīmā is intended here in spreading the Kathina, because a monk staying in the upacārasīmā is entitled to a share of the robes of the deceased (matakacīvara) and so on, and because those monastery-arisen items do not arise in the formal boundary (baddhasīmā).

"Who receives the spreading of the Kathina?" means who completes it. Five persons complete it. This is because there are at least four donors who offer the Kathina cloth, and one recipient. Since it is stated in the Campeyyakkhandhaka, "Monks, that four-fold community of monks (catuvagga bhikkhu-saṅgha), excluding three acts—ordination (upasampadā), invitation (pavāraṇā), and rehabilitation (abbhāna)—[can perform other acts]," it should be noted that this Kathina act is not an act to be performed by a five-fold group.

"The Saṅgha gives the Kathina cloth to a certain monk; it is allowable to give it even if he is standing outside the boundary without being within reach (hattha-pāsa)," but it should be given only by placing that monk within reach. Why? It is said, "Because he has reached the [legal] act (kammapattattā)." It is said, "When cloths are purchased with rice and so on that arise in that monastery, those cloths reach only the monks who have spread the Kathina. However, when rice and so on are purchased with cloths, those rice [items] reach all monks."

"Monks who have performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) at the first invitation receive it" is said as the highest limit. If one asks, "How is it known that for monks who have completed the rains-retreat but could not perform the invitation due to an obstacle, the Kathina can be spread by making other monks the group-completers (gaṇapūraka)?" It can be known because in the Parivāra, the singular form is used: "The Kathina is spread for two persons: the spreader and the one who appreciates (anumodaka)," and in that same text, it says, "The Kathina is spread for the Saṅgha; the Kathina is spread for the group (gaṇa) and for the individual (puggala)."
489:
Regarding the statement that monks who have spent the Vassa in another monastery do not receive (the Kathina benefits)—does this occur within a single boundary (sīmā) or in separate boundaries? If it were within a single boundary, it would contradict this statement from the Commentary: "If there are many monasteries within a single boundary, all monks should assemble and spread the Kathina in one place; it is not proper to spread it separately." This statement indicates that there is only one Kathina-spreading for all. If it were in separate boundaries, it would contradict the granting of the single wish to the Venerable Upananda. For it was said: "Monks, give the single wish to that foolish man (moghapurisa)." (Mahāvagga 364). This statement shows the accomplishment of his Kathina-spreading in both dwellings.

Since it is not prohibited, non-contradiction is to be desired. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: whether in the same boundary or in separate boundaries, monks who have spent the Vassa in another monastery with a different precinct (upacāra) do not receive (the benefits). It is said: "One who is ordained during the later Vassa is allowed to perform the Pavāraṇā on the first Pavāraṇā day, is one who has spent the Vassa, and receives the benefits." Thus, the entering of the Vassa is permitted for novices (sāmaṇeras), and they say that novices receive the Kathina benefits.

This statement, "incompleteness of any of the three robes," seems to contradict the Pali: "Kathina is not spread except with the saṅghāṭi, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antaravāsaka." Does this Pali indicate that Kathina is not spread even if one of the three robes is missing? No, because the meaning of that Pali is understood. The Blessed One spoke that Pali desiring to show that Kathina is not spread if any of the three robes is missing. If so, should it not be said "except with the saṅghāṭi, uttarāsaṅga, and antaravāsaka"? No, it is because the intention is understood. For a monk who wishes to spread it with the saṅghāṭi, it is not spread except with the saṅghāṭi. This method is the same for the other robes. This is the intention here.

For that very reason, in the bright side (sukkapakkha), only one robe is mentioned in the manner of "it is spread with the saṅghāṭi," etc. This being so, it should be understood that it is stated according to the highest limit as: "Kathina is not spread by 24 ways; Kathina is spread by 17 ways." Therefore, it should be understood that Kathina is not spread due to the total absence of the 24 possible ways in the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) such as ullikhita (marked), etc., or due to the presence of any of the impossible ways such as nimittakata (made with a sign), etc.
490:
The meaning should be understood in this way. Also in the bright side (sukkapakkha), it should be understood that Kathina is spread by the presence of any of the seventeen ways starting from ahata-ahatakappa, etc., up to sīmaṭṭhānumodanā (approval within the boundary), and by the total absence of the others such as animittakata, etc. Otherwise, there would be mutual contradiction; it should be understood by applying it as possible.

Here is a brief illustration: In the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), based on the authority of the statement "When Kathina is spread with the uttarāsaṅga, it is not spread except with the saṅghāṭi and except with the antaravāsaka," that Kathina would be unspread. And in the bright side (sukkapakkha), based on the authority of the statement "Kathina is spread with a robe that is not made with a sign (animittakata)," if that Kathina spread with an unmarked robe was made through indirect talk (parikathā), even then the Kathina is indeed spread. Thus, there is this twofold contradiction. It should be understood that if the intention is taken according to the aforementioned method, there is a resolution.

Although the statement "That Kathina which gives many benefits" seems to indicate a state of greed for requisites, it is for the sake of favoring the Saṅgha, considering that the Blessed One gave an opening by way of prescribing the seeking of robes as needed. It is written that "It is not to be left undone," and for a monk who does not do it out of disrespect, there is an offense of dukkaṭa. In the phrase "We approve (anumodāma)," it is said thus in a collective sense. Each individual should say "I approve (anumodāmi)"; otherwise, it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that it is not proper. By merely uttering the words "I spread the Kathina with this saṅghāṭi" after determining the Kathina robe, it is spread for the individual. It is written that in the statement "The kammavācā (formal act) is proper only for one," the kammavācā is only for the Kathina cloth; for the giving of the remaining robes, it means there is only an announcement (apalokana). "In one boundary" means it is appropriate to mean "in one precinct boundary (upacārasīmā)." However, some teachers say: "A tied boundary (baddhasīmā) is intended; when it is spread in one place within one boundary, it is spread everywhere because it is said 'all monks having assembled'; for those who approve, it is indeed spread; when the precinct (upacāra) is delimited, the robes obtained in various places are to be received by those respective monks. Even those who enter that assembly should receive it because it is spread by all; this is the distinction. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is also said in this very way." This should be examined.

It is called Mahābhūmika because it possesses twenty-four aspects. It is written: "Dīghasibbita (long-stitched) means stitched again or stitched by rolling." What is called Kaṇḍusa is the initial binding. "The cimilikā (cloth layer) is first joined and placed" means the Kathina cloth is weak...
491:
Seeing that weak Kathina cloth, because they wish to sew it by joining it with their own strong (thick) ordinary cloth to make it double-layered, and because the ordinary cloth is larger than the Kathina cloth, it means that it is made by first joining a reinforcement (*bandhakaṇḍusa*) corresponding to that size and binding it with strings. Because the Kathina robe is weak, the cloth first joined becomes a belly-lining (*kucchi-cimilika*). The statements mentioned in the *Mahāpaccari* and *Kurundī* commentaries serve as evidence. It should be understood that those statements are made to show that there is only a difference in phrasing (*byañjana*) and no difference in meaning (*attha*).

If it is asked, "What is shown by this Pali?" Although one might think that such a double-layered robe, because the ordinary cloth is large, should only be designated as an 'ordinary robe' and not as a 'Kathina robe,' it should not be viewed in that way. A Kathina robe that exists in the form of such a *kucchi-cimilika* is indeed a Kathina robe, and even though that ordinary cloth is large, it is also one's own Kathina robe. Because a robe of at least five sections is desired, it is written that a monk who wishes to sew the Kathina cloth by cutting it into many small pieces takes a strip from the Kathina robe and applies it to another non-Kathina robe.

Alternatively, many very small *paṃsukūla* (rag-cloth) Kathina cloths are given to make one robe, and large cloths are given to fulfill the requirement. Regarding the phrase "*kathinacīvarato*," it means a monk takes a strip from some Kathina robe and applies it to another Kathina robe. Here, a question arises: "Should Kathina cloths that are *paṃsukūla* be given in the minimum size suitable for assignment (*vikappanā*), or can even smaller pieces of cloth be given?" Some teachers say that because such small pieces of cloth are not counted as robes, they are not fit to be given, and the formal act (*kammavācā*) does not take effect on them. However, because the Pali gives the method "it is spread with a *paṃsukūla* robe," and because the commentary allows it by way of consenting to the status of a Kathina robe—even for a Kathina cloth that exists as a *kucchi-cimilika* which is insufficient for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) by its own nature but is fit for determination only as an old robe—even small cloths are fit to be given. This is because some teachers say it is allowable, considering that the monk who spreads the Kathina will join them to make a Kathina robe; the more appropriate view should be adopted.

Accumulation and storage (*nicayasannidhi*) belongs to the Saṅgha because it is performed by the Saṅgha. It is called "*nissaggiya*" (forfeiture) because it must be forfeited if a night has passed. It is called "*pañcaka*" (five-fold) because its measure is five sections or strips. The meaning is "by that robe of five sections or by one with more sections than that." Regarding "*tadaheva sañchinnena*" (cut on that very day), it must be a robe that is given only after the Saṅgha has recited the *kammavācā* for the monk who spreads the Kathina, and it must be cut and made with its circular patches (*samandalikata*) on that very day. Only a robe given in this manner is described in the *Parivāra* as "the preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*) are comprised of seven factors"; it does not refer to the robe as it is being donated by the donor. Therefore, only a robe with completed preliminary duties...
492:
If the donor gives (the Kathina cloth) to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha must receive it and give it (to a monk) by *kammavācā*. That monk must then determine (*adhiṭṭhāna*) it and spread it within that same *sīmā* (boundary), and then have the Saṅgha express their appreciation (*anumodanā*). This is because there is no need to perform the preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*) again for a robe whose preliminary duties have already been completed. The statement beginning with "*na ullikhitamattena*" (not merely by marking) is intended only for the robe that has already reached the hands of the monk who spreads it.

If it is argued that even if the preliminary duties are finished, one must still wash and unpick the seams based on the authority of the Pali text, this is not acceptable. This is because it is impossible to cut again what has already been cut. If it is argued that it must be cut in another place, this is also not acceptable. This is because, based on the authority of the Pali text in the context of ordination (*pabbajjā*) which says "having had the hair and beard shaved," it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭhappasaṅga*) that one would have to search for the already cut hair of a bald person, place it on his head, and have it shaved again before ordaining him. If it is argued that this is not possible here because it is prohibited by the word "*na*" (not), this is not acceptable. Because of the prohibition by the word "*na*" in "*na aññatra saṅghāṭiyā*" (not without the outer robe), it would lead to the undesirable consequence that spreading with the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) would not count as spreading. Therefore, such dogmatic adherence should not be made. Also, because it is said "*bahi-upacārasīmāya thito*" (standing outside the precinct boundary), only the decision mentioned previously should be adopted.

Regarding the phrase "*asannidhikatena atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ*" (the Kathina is spread with what is not stored), it should be examined: is the two-fold storage (*sannidhi*) intended only during the month of spreading Kathina, or even before that? When should the donor give it? Should it be given only during the month of spreading Kathina, or even before that? During the month of spreading Kathina, is it allowable to give it saying, "I give this for the purpose of spreading on such-and-such a day"? The two-fold storage is required only during the month of spreading Kathina. It is not allowable for a donor to donate a robe specifically as a Kathina robe in advance, like a rains-residence robe (*vassāvāsika*). Why? Because it is stated in the commentary by the method beginning with "*kathinadāyakassa vattaṃ atthi*" (there is a duty for the Kathina donor). If it is said that this is merely the highest standard (*ukkaṭṭha*), it is not so. This is because it is stated, "What is called Kathina is allowable only when it is of the highest standard." If it is said that this was not stated regarding the arrival (of the cloth), it is not so. This was indeed stated regarding the arrival; it should be understood that a robe given beforehand is not allowable.

"*Kathinassa*" means of the spreading of the Kathina. "*Ubbhārāya*" means for the cessation or non-continuation (of the privileges). If it is asked, "What is the use of showing the withdrawal (*ubbhāra*)?" it is for the purpose of producing restraint during the period when one is free from offenses by showing the time limit of the five privileges, such as *anāmanta* (not asking permission). Otherwise, because it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*, "The robe-season is the last month of the rainy season when Kathina is not spread, and five months when Kathina is spread," one might wrongly assume that there is no offense for the entire five months even if there is no withdrawal of Kathina through 'departure' (*antarāpakkamanantika*) and so on.
493:
Such a wrong view might occur. Therefore, at a time when an offense should be incurred, one might commit various offenses with the perception that no offense is incurred. It should be understood that this also constitutes an obstacle to the gains of other monks.

## Explanation of the Seven Cases of Taking Away (Ādāyasattaka-kathā-vaᅅᅅanā)

In the removal of the Kathina through decision (sanniᅡᅡhānantikā), both impediments are cut simultaneously; this statement made here and in the Parivāra Commentary (Aᅡᅡhakathā) is consistent with this Khandhaka Pali. This is because the relinquishing of the burden (dhura-nikkhepa) for both occurs at the same time. "This decision refers only to the sanniᅡᅡhānantikā occurring outside the boundary (sĩmġ). In the Parivāra Pali, it is stated: 'There are four removals of the Kathina: some are removed within the boundary, some outside the boundary; they are niᅡᅡhānantikā, sanniᅡᅡhānantikā, nāsanantikā, and āsāvacchedikā' (Pari. 416). Among these four, the sanniᅡᅡhānantikā outside the boundary is as shown in this commentary. How does sanniᅡᅡhānantikā occur within the boundary? A monk who takes an unfinished robe and leaves thinking, 'I shall not return,' but failing to find a comfortable dwelling wherever he goes, returns to that very monastery. For him, the robe-impediment (cĩvara-palibodha) remains. As soon as the thought 'I will not have this robe made' arises in his mind, the impediment is cut. Therefore, it is removed within the boundary. Thus, sanniᅡᅡhānantikā is of two kinds"—so it is written in the Porāᅅa-gaᅅᅡhipada (Ancient Glossary). This writing is appropriate. Otherwise, the removal of the Kathina occurring within the boundary with the thought "I will not have this robe made" would not be included among the other removals and would be redundant. Sĩmātikantikā means exceeding the time limit for the robe. In the removal of the Kathina, although the robe-impediment seems to be cut first, because there is still concern (expectation), there is still effort in making the robe; referring to this reason, it is stated in the Parivāra Pali that "the two impediments are cut neither before nor after, but simultaneously" (Mahāva. Aᅡᅡha. 311). Since it is stated as "a monk who has completed the robe," this (simultaneous cutting of both impediments) is not possible here.

A monk who departs taking all his requisites without exception is said to "depart taking them (samādāya)." In all Gaᅅᅡhipadas, it is written: "There is no distinction in the removal of the Kathina. The taking-away sections (samādāya-vāra) are mentioned only to show the sections according to the specific intention of the person." However, here, the benefit should be considered according to the person's intention. Because there is no pakkamanantikā (ending with departure), it is said "as far as possible" (yathāsambhavaᅃ). If it is argued that even if the robe is unfinished, pakkamanantikā can occur by way of relinquishing the burden (dhura-nikkhepa), and therefore the pakkamanantikā-vāra should also be mentioned—no, it should not be mentioned. This is because it would lead to confusion with the characteristics of sanniᅡᅡhānantikā. Also, for one with an unfinished robe, savanantikā (ending with hearing) is not possible.
494:
Here, the clarification of the sections (vāra-vibhāvanā) from the beginning is as follows: there are seven cases of taking away (ādāya-vāra) and likewise seven cases of taking with (samādāya-vāra), making two sets of seven. Then, excluding pakkamanantikā (ending with departure), there are two sets of six (chakka-vāra) for one with an unfinished robe: ādāya-vāra and samādāya-vāra. After that, three triads (tika) are shown by way of niᅡᅡhānantikā (ending with completion), sanniᅡᅡhānantikā (ending with decision), and nāsanantikā (ending with loss). Among them, the first triad occurs outside the boundary with the thought "I shall not return," without considering this procedure within the boundary. Therefore, pakkamanantikā, sĩmātikantikā, and sa-ubbhāra do not apply there.

"Āsāvacchedikā (ending with loss of hope) is possible, but it is not mentioned for the reason already stated. The second triad occurs within the boundary with the thought 'I shall not return.' Here, although pakkamanantikā is possible, it is not mentioned because only those cases where the robe-impediment is cut are intended"—so it is stated in the Porāᅅa-gaᅅᅡhipada. It is reasoned that in all the sets of fifteen (pannarasaka), only the unfinished robe is intended. The ancient teachers say: "If a robe suitable for determination (adhiᅡᅡhāna) is being made, niᅡᅡhānantikā is not possible. If there is a remainder to be completed, nāsanantikā is not possible."

The third triad is presented as distinct with the word "un-determined" (anadhiᅡᅡhita), but in meaning, it is the same as the first triad. The purpose of showing the meaning of that third triad is said to be this: since these three variations of meaning can be shown only by these three removals of the Kathina, they are joined by way of a single connection. Otherwise, the first triad would be a set of six, like the set of six at the end of this set of fifteen.

The fourth triad occurring immediately after the third triad arises with the specific words "I shall return" within the boundary. When so joined, it follows a sequence not inconsistent with other cases like savanantikā (ending with hearing). Therefore, it should be understood that instead of a fourth triad, it becomes a set of six (chakka). Thus, the first set of fifteen (pannarasaka) should be understood as consisting of three triads and one set of six.

Now, this same set of fifteen is named the second "Samādāya Pannarasaka" by way of a specific prefix (upasagga). Again, the third set of fifteen is shown as "taking an unfinished robe (ādāya)," and the fourth set of fifteen as "taking with (samādāya)." Thus, four sets of fifteen should be understood. Among them, in the first and second sets of fifteen, a completely unmade robe is intended; in the other two, an unfinished (in-progress) robe should be applied.

"It is stated in the Porāᅅa-gaᅅᅡhipada: 'A robe should be taken with the expectation of obtaining a robe (cĩvarāsā) in a place where one was previously settled; it is not allowable elsewhere. If a robe arises after the expectation of obtaining a robe has been cut off, that robe does not create a robe-impediment.' It is reasoned that 'cĩvarāsā' here refers to the 'expectation of an incoming robe' (āgata-cĩvara-paccāsā) mentioned in the third Kathina training rule of the Nissaggiya section. Since the place where there is an expectation of a robe is called 'cĩvarāsā' by way of metonymy (adhikaraᅅũpacāra), it is said 'he attends to that cĩvarāsā,' etc. Therefore, 'he obtains without expectation' (anāsāya labhati) means he obtains it in a place where there is no expectation, and so the meaning should be taken.
495:
The meaning should be taken as follows. In this context, one turn (vāra) occurs by way of completion (niṭṭhāna), decision (sanniṭṭhāna), loss (nāsana), and the severing of expectation (āsāvacchedika); this constitutes one fourfold set (catukka). Therefore, the three threefold sets (tika) mentioned previously, along with the three fourfold sets characterized by the severing of expectation, should be understood as one twelvefold set without expectation (anāsāyadvādasaka).

Immediately following that twelvefold set without expectation, in the twelvefold set with expectation (āsāyadvādasaka), although the sequence of the first twelvefold set is obtained, because there is no distinction, that twelvefold set is not explicitly mentioned but treated as established. To show the distinction, it is stated from the beginning: "I will return within the boundary (antosemā)." This twelvefold set should be understood as providing the opportunity for the words in the second fourfold set, such as "That monk goes outside the boundary and hears," and for the third fourfold set, such as those ending in hearing. It should be understood that although this twelvefold set could be obtained by way of being without expectation, it is not shown as established through this twelvefold set with expectation. Thus, two twelvefold sets are extracted here. In the twelvefold set of duties (karaṇီyadvādasaka) also, two twelvefold sets should be extracted: the twelvefold set without expectation already shown and the twelvefold set with expectation which is established without being explicitly stated.

Now, there is the ninefold set of one going to another direction (disaṅgamikanavaka). In that ninefold set, by the very words "The monk going to another direction departs," the phrase "I will not return" is already established without being stated; therefore, that ninefold set is not mentioned. By this sequence of words, the absence of the impediment of residence (āvāsapalibodha) is shown.

By the phrase "desiring a portion of robes," it shows that the monk is possessed of the impediment of robes (cīvarapalibodha). 'Paṭivīsa' means the portion of robes that one is to receive. 'Apavilāyamāna' means desiring. When that monk receives robes, one ninefold set should be understood by way of three threefold sets: one threefold set by way of completion, decision, and loss in the residence where he spent the Vassa; one threefold set in the midst of the journey; and one threefold set at the destination. After that ninefold set, the fivefold set of comfortable living (phāsuvihārapañcaka) is mentioned, ending with completion, decision, loss, crossing the boundary, and the removal of the Kathina. In both types of impediments, the impossibility of the remaining removal of the Kathina is clear. The distinction in this fivefold set is that the turn of taking (samādāyavāra) is not possible because of the intention to return, saying "I will return."

"Monks, these two are the impediments of the Kathina" means this should be noted as the reason for the continuation of the Kathina spreading.

## The Commentary on the Kathina Chapter is finished.
496:
## 8. Commentary on the Cīvarakkhandhaka
## Commentary on the Story of Jīvaka
'Rājagahako' means a resident of Rājagaha. Because he was of an undeluded nature, he attained wisdom and skill in no long time. "I am your father; for what reason? Because you were brought up by me," is the meaning. In the text "sake vissaṭṭhamatte," in the eighth training rule, it means just as it was released.

## Commentary on the Story of King Pajjota
Regarding the phrase "to one sitting to eat," it is said: "In the Dhammapada, it is stated 'having seen outside the city'; therefore, because it was given on two days, taking one for each of those days, the statement in the two commentaries is appropriate."

## Commentary on the Story of the Thirty Purgations
Regarding the phrase "at every mouthful," even if it was put into molasses and so on, because only the Blessed One consumed that molasses etc., there is no fault.

## Commentary on the Story of Requesting a Boon
'Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojava' is said to be a rug with a floral pattern exceeding four finger-breadths.

## Commentary on the Story of Allowing Blankets, etc.
'Upacāre' means in the vicinity of the cemetery. Some say it is also allowable outside. Showing the reason for making an agreement, they say: "If one says, 'Let my property be yours and mine,' and the other says the same, it is allowable," describing the method of shared requisites.

Because it is stated, "It is allowable to perform the 'sammannituṃ' (authorization) even in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā)," it is said that it is allowable to perform the remaining formal acts (kamma) while sitting in that small boundary. "If this is so, it is like performing it by theft...
497:
it becomes; therefore, it is not allowable," so say the monks residing in the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka). They say that the Sutta (text) appearing in the Senāsanakkhandhaka, which says "It cannot be obtained because it was taken by theft," is also evidence. Therefore, according to the view of those monks, this characteristic should be understood as a specific characteristic.

## Commentary on the Story of the Designation of a Storehouse, etc.
"This characteristic is a specific characteristic in the word 'bhaṇḍāgāra' (storehouse)," it is said.

## Commentary on the Story of Dyeing Robes
There is no offense in cow-dung water, but it is forbidden because the color is not beautiful (distorted). They say, "The saffron flower is not allowable." There is also a reading "allikāyā."

## Commentary on the Story of Allowing Sitting Cloths, etc.
Regarding the phrase "aṭṭhānametaṃ," in the Rūpakaṇဍe, because it is stated as "catusamuṭṭhānika" (arising from four causes), it should be taken by comparing with the Kathāvatthu whether the matter produced by kamma is not released because of the absence of lustful thoughts, or whether it is produced by kamma when there is the cause of lust.

'Aggaḷaguttiyeva pamāṇaṃ' means that a monk who keeps [robes] by these four reasons for keeping should keep them only in a monastery that is secured with a bolt.

## Commentary on the Story of the Arising of Sangha Robes
If the Kathina has not been spread, one should not say "the one-month robe season." Why? Because there is no Pali text saying, "Monks, I allow those robes to that monk for as long as the one-month robe season." Therefore, does it mean it is not allowed for a monk whose Kathina is not spread? No, because it was allowed below, and because it is stated here in that way to clarify the hidden meaning from that allowance.

In fact, in the Vibhaṅga below, it is stated: "Out-of-season robes (akālacīvara) mean robes arising within eleven months when the Kathina is not spread, robes arising within seven months when the Kathina is spread, and robes given specifically even during the season; these are called out-of-season robes." Thus, it is already established that for monks who have not spread the Kathina, robes arising within the one-month robe season belong to those monks only. Therefore, without stating that point here, the phrase "until the removal of the Kathina" is stated to reveal this hidden meaning: that even a single monk can spread the Kathina by obtaining three monks to complete a group (gaṇapūraka). Otherwise, this meaning would not be known.
498:
Other teachers say that it was taught in this manner: "It should be known by the Vinaya experts (vinayadhara)." When the kaṭhina has been spread, for five months, all robes belong only to that monk who received the kaṭhina; this is the connection of the meaning. The accusative case (upayogavacana) is used in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). Because it is specified as "to the Saṅgha that spent the Vassa here," and because in the phrase "We give to the monks who spent the Vassa," the word "here" (idha) follows by context, it is obtained when so stated. In another Gaṇṭhipada text, it is written: "It is said so because it arose in the later period, because it is close to the robe-season, and because it is a place permitted for both monks who have not spread the kaṭhina and those who have completed the Vassa."

Some teachers say: "From the words starting with 'to the Saṅgha that spent the Vassa here' up to the word 'in the future Vassa,' after questioning, the phrase 'Why? Because it arose in the later period' should be written at the end of the phrase 'it reaches all monks present there.' Why? Because it is no different from the later statement 'from the robe-month until the winter.' Therefore, some wise ones say so." In this Khandhaka, it is distinguished by the word 'idha' (here); it is not in that Vibhaṅga. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no mutual contradiction. The statement "These robes reach me" is the determination (adhiṭṭhāna); this is said here specifically. Even if one says "These robes are for me," it is still a determination. Some say: "When saying 'These are for me,' the name 'robes' is not there; therefore, one should only say 'The robes reach [me].'" In the word 'duggahitāni,' they are only communal (saṅghika) property. Regarding the phrase "It is called 'taken' indeed," the meaning is: although it is not known that "this robe reaches this person," those portions have effectively reached those various monks; this is the intention. It is said: "If it has not yet fallen to one monk, the monks who come again receive it."

## Description of the Story of Upananda Sakyaputta (Upanandasakyaputtavatthukathāvaṇṇanā)
In the words "Monks, it should not be received except by one who has spent the Vassa," the prohibition is made with reference to the robe-season. Even in a single monastery, it is given saying, "Whether in various dwellings as in the Rājavihāra, or here, let only the monks who spent the Vassa receive it." The statement "He causes the dawn to rise every seven days" is merely a figure of speech, because there is no seven-day duty (sattāhakicca) within a single monastery.

## Description of the Discussion on the Belongings of a Deceased Monk (Matasantakakathāvaṇṇanā)
"Bhikkhussa" means when a monk has passed away. In that Pali, the phrase "patta-cīvere" (bowl and robe) should be understood as representing all requisites by way of showing the principal requisites. Unrighteously...
499:
Some teachers say that even if that requisite arose unrighteously, because the owner has died, it is allowable (kappiya) for the Saṅgha. In the decision regarding the four bowls, it is considered unallowable because it contradicts the method for unallowable bowls in every way. There is no offense for a monk living in a dwelling obtained unrighteously.

If two monks live in a monastery and one dies, and the other takes his requisites with the intention to steal without letting them reach the Saṅgha, it is considered taking Saṅgha property; he should be penalized according to the value of the goods. If he takes it in a place that is not a monastery, no penalty is decided because it is taking ownerless property. If at the time of death, being unable to speak, he gives only with his mind, he gains merit; the Saṅgha is the owner of that property. If another person who is not an intimate friend takes it on his own, the taking is not valid; if taken with the intention to steal, he should be penalized according to the value of the goods.

Who is the owner of that property that has reached the monastery? Some say the Saṅgha should forcibly prevent [others] based on the statement "The Saṅgha is the owner." Some say the Saṅgha is not the owner because it was taken while [the monk] was still alive. Others say that just as the owner himself has the right to see and take it back, the Saṅgha also has the right to take it back because it stands in the place of the owner; it should be taken after investigation.

If the deceased has unallowable goods such as gold and silver, if they are handled, one should act according to the method stated in the Ugghita training rule. If it is property that arose righteously, it should be told to one who makes things allowable (kappiyakāraka). If a slave was accepted, the Saṅgha is not the owner; if it is a monastery attendant (ārāmika), the Saṅgha is the owner. If there are cows, buffaloes, etc., if they are in the monastery, the Saṅgha is the owner; if they are outside the monastery, the Saṅgha is not the owner. If the Saṅgha brings those animals to the monastery and makes them its own, and later keeps them nearby outside the boundary (sīmā), the Saṅgha that did so is the owner; the same applies to monastery attendants. If there is someone who has stored the requisites of the deceased, that person alone is the owner. If it is a valuable item, the Saṅgha owns the remaining requisites.

The sequence of what should be said is shown by this Pali: "To a certain attendant of the sick (gilānupaṭṭhāka)." Furthermore, when there are many attendants, the Blessed One said in the formal act (kammavācā), "to the attendants of the sick," showing the act of giving to all. In the section on novices (sāmaṇeravāra), there is the reading "robe" (cīvara). Because it is stated that the characteristic of giving (dāna-lakkhaṇa) is when one says "I give this to you, I donate, I bestow, I dedicate, I relinquish, I release, I hand over" or "I give to so-and-so... I hand over," whether said in the presence or absence [of the recipient], the gift is indeed made; and the characteristic of receiving (gahana-lakkhaṇa) is when one says "I take it for myself" when told "Take it for yourself," it is called "well-given and well-received"...
500:
It is written that teachers say it is permissible to make shared requisites (parikkhāra) with words such as, “Let my property be both yours and mine.”

In the Anugaṇṭhipada, however, after making a very extensive explanation, it is stated again: “This is the decision of the teachers in this matter—if many monks or two monks wish to make shared requisites, all those monks renounce their current property along with future property to a single beloved and virtuous monk. That monk then renounces it back to those very monks. By this act of renouncing and giving, those monks become holders of shared requisites. This characteristic of shared requisites, because it falls within the characteristics mentioned in the Pāli and other texts, reaches a state of being firm and unshakable. Nevertheless, because it exists by overriding ancient methods, it should be prohibited; however, another group of teachers says that a monk who wishes to act according to the teachers' views may do so.” It is also said: “A novice (sāmaṇera) who has emerged from the rains-residence (vassa), if he transgresses one of the five precepts and takes the precepts again, he does not receive the gains (robes); he is called a novice who has committed an offense of defeat (pārājika).”

## Commentary on the Explanation of Unarisen Robes for Those Who Spent the Rains

In the matter of “leaving when the robe has arisen but is not yet distributed,” even after it has been announced, “The Saṅgha is pleased to give this much rains-cloth (vassāvāsika) to each monk because it arose in this monastery,” if he disrobes, he does not receive it because of that disrobing. Even if he ordains again as a novice and then as a monk and reaches the time of robe distribution, he still does not receive it, because he has fallen and renounced his original status. However, it is also said that if he disrobes after having received it, he may keep it.

## Commentary on the Explanation of Robe Arising when the Saṅgha is Split

“Para-samudda” refers to Jambudīpa.

## Commentary on the Explanation of the Eightfold Robe Matrix

Because it is difficult to know the area fit for fencing in a monastery that is not fenced, “api ca” and so on is said. In that commentary, even the permanent assembly place should be taken only as what is situated at the boundary. In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is written: “Regarding the words ‘reaches even the monks...’, it is said only with reference to robes offered with the words, ‘We give to the vicinity boundary (upacāra-sīmā).’” When it is said, “to the boundary of common communion (samāna-saṃvāsaka-sīmā),” it does not reach monks staying in small boundaries (khaṇḍa-sīmā) and so on, because those khaṇḍa-sīmās are separate boundaries of common communion. This is the difference between the boundary of common communion and the boundary of non-separation (avippavāsa-sīmā)—an object offered with the words, “I give to the boundary of non-separation,” does not reach monks staying in the village. Why? Because it is said, “excluding the village and the village vicinity...”
501:
...because it is said, “the village and the village vicinity.” However, an object offered with the words, “to the boundary of common communion (samāna-saṃvāsaka-sīmā),” reaches monks staying in a place where there is a boundary of non-separation (avippavāsa-sīmā) and those staying in other places. It is said: “If one stands in a small boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā) and says, ‘I give to the Saṅgha staying in the boundary,’ it should be given by delimiting it only with the vicinity boundary (upacāra-sīmā).” Some teachers say that if one stands in a khaṇḍa-sīmā and offers with the words, “I give to the boundary of non-separation,” it reaches only that place. Regarding the words, “they dwell filling up to a hundred yojanas,” some teachers say that the vicinity (upacāra) is within a forearm’s length (hatthapāsa) in the monastery vicinity, and twelve cubits in places outside villages and so on. Some teachers say that if one says, “I give to the Saṅgha in this monastery,” it does not reach monks who stay beyond the area fit for fencing, even if it is connected. They say: “If one stands anywhere outside a nunnery (bhikkhunī-vihāra) and says, ‘to the Saṅgha,’ only the Bhikkhu-saṅgha is the owner.” Regarding the words, “even a single monk goes,” he must go after making it reach all monks, or he must bring it and make it reach them; otherwise, it does not reach the monk who went. An agreement on shared gains (samāna-lābha) exists only if there is an original residence (mūlāvāsa). With the destruction of the original residence, the agreement is also destroyed. The term “shared gains” is appropriate only when there are two or many monks. Therefore, our opinion is that it is appropriate even when only one remains.

“By temporary time, or by total severance,
Another’s act may belong to another; it is not a residence-union.”
—The Teacher.

Because it is given to all monks, they say, “it is only a shared portion.” They say that if one says, “each of us receives one,” it is permissible because the distribution has been made. They say: “If robes are given to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, it is not permissible for rag-robe wearers (paṃsukūlika).” When it is said, “to both Saṅghas (ubhato-saṅgha),” because “to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha” is not specifically said, and because it is mixed with the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, and because he is not included therein, an individual receives it separately. If this is so, if one asks, “Does saying ‘I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha’ contradict the statement ‘It is only an offering to both Saṅghas’?”, it does not contradict. That statement only shows the fact of giving to both Saṅghas, not the technical designation of Ubhato-saṅgha. For that very reason, the sequence (vāra) “to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, and to you” is not mentioned. Alternatively, some say that only the words of the Commentary are the authority, not investigation. Because a single person cannot be of two types like a traveler, by taking the term “both Saṅghas,” a single monk is not included. “To the whole residence and to the Cetiya...”
502:
Regarding the phrase "And to the Dhamma" (dhammassa ca), it is said that a portion for each individual monk should be given for the shrines (cetiya) and the Dhamma in all monasteries. If it is asked whether this contradicts the statement "To the Saṅgha of monks and to the shrine," the answer is that it does not. The explanation given is that because it was stated as "to the Saṅgha of monks" in those previous instances, and because it is stated here in connection with the monastery, a portion must indeed be obtained in each respective monastery.

In the phrase "having caused it to reach oneself," if it is argued that the entire object should be allowable because it cannot be used during the wrong time (afternoon), it is not allowable, both because it was stated as "Carry it to the Saṅgha of monks" and because that monk accepted it saying, "I shall carry it."

In the phrase "pacchimavassaṃvutthānampi," the word "api" has the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa). It means only for those monks who have emerged from the later rains-retreat (pacchimavā). Otherwise, if taken in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), the statement "Those who know the characteristics say" (lakkhaṇaññū vadanti) would be meaningless. They exert effort to elaborate on why this is so. What benefit is there in such elaboration? Since it is already established by the later statement, "Starting from the month for robes... it reaches only those monks who have emerged from the past rains-retreat," it need not be further examined. Therefore, it is stated as "lakkhaṇaññū" by way of being unshakeable (acala).

If it is said that it reaches all monks who have arrived... staying within the outer precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), it means for monks who have emerged from the rains-retreat in any place whatsoever. This is because it is stated in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary: "It reaches all those who have arrived, monks who have emerged from the rains-retreat in any place whatsoever." However, when speaking from the first day of the summer season, they are said to have emerged from the retreat only in the immediately preceding winter season, not in the rainy season. Therefore, it is said, "The schedule (mātikā) should be established." Or it means it also reaches those monks sent by the elders.
