## 9. Explanation of the Campeyya Chapter (Campeyyakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Two Expulsions, etc.
In the phrase "appatto nissāraṇaṃ," what is called "expulsion" (nissāraṇa) is an act (kamma) permitted only for monks who are "corrupters of families" (kuladūsaka). This monk is not a corrupter of families; therefore, it is said "appatto" (it does not apply). If it is asked, "If that is so, how is he properly expelled?" it is because it is stated in the Cūḷavagga: "If the Saṅgha wishes, it may perform the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma)." According to the statement, "They perform the act of 'further punishment' (tassapāpiyasikakamma) for a monk deserving of further punishment," it should be understood that they "bind the wheel" (cakkaṃ bandhanti).

## Explanation of the Discussion on Upāli’s Questions
"Parato" is written to mean "after Upāli’s questions." In the Dosārita Pali, it is stated: "A person under twenty years of age (ūnavīsativassa) does not come because the basis (vatthu) is defective." In this Campeyyakkhandhaka, it should be understood that the unrighteous acts (adhammakamma) themselves are divided into two types, resulting in five kinds. For this very reason, it is stated in the Parivāra regarding this chapter: "Five unrighteous acts." By the statement "One who is blind, mute, or deaf is admitted," it is established that higher ordination (upasampadā) can be attained even by one who has not yet been ordained as a novice (apabbajita).

## The Explanation of the Campeyya Chapter is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Kosambaka Chapter (Kosambakakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Discussion on the Kosambī Dispute
In the word "suttantiko," although it is said "expert in the Vinaya (vinayadhara), expert in the codes (mātikādhara)," it is said with reference to the recitation of the two-fold Vibhaṅga (ubhatovibhaṅga), and he is not a reciter of the Khandhakas (khandhakabhāṇaka). Based on the statement "Friend, there is an offense here," it is said, "He has the view of an offense regarding that offense." Later, the Vinaya expert regained mindfulness, thinking, "If the basis (vatthu) exists, it is the standard; the regulation (paññatti) is not the standard," and he held the view of an offense regarding that offense. Therefore, it is stated at the end: "Other monks have the view of an offense regarding that offense."

The reason they write "yathā mayā ñattī" is because of the singular word "paññattā."

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Story of Dīghāvu
They write: "Monks, formerly in the city of Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta..." In the ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, the reading "in the city of Bārāṇasī" does not exist; they say, "Its absence is indeed better."

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Journey to Pālileyyaka
"Rakkhitavanasaṇḍa" (the Protected Forest Thicket) is stated by the elders who conducted the Council (saṅgītikāraka) to make it easy to understand. They also say, "Pālileyya is a village, and it is named after that village"; this statement does not contradict the Dhammapada Commentary.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Eighteen Matters
In the phrase "I say it should not be prohibited," if a monk prohibits a monk who is worthy of a lodging from using that lodging, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs only for that monk. There is no fault for the Buddha who, having stated the Saṅgha's agreement such as "There is no place here for those who create quarrels and strife," does not lay down that rule; nor for the Buddha who prohibits a monk who, acting overbearingly and saying "I am the Buddha," informs his own disciples and takes [lodgings], by saying "Take them according to what is proper." Here, for the Kosambī monks who have come to settle the dispute, it is not said "according to seniority," but because it is stated "If there is no secluded lodging, it should be given after making it secluded," [it should be given] after making it secluded...
507:
## Cūḷavagga-vaṇṇanā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Kammakhandhaka-vaṇṇanā
## Adhammakamma-dvādasaka-kathā-vaṇṇanā
The triads (tikas) beginning with "It is done in the absence [of the person]" (asammukhā kataṃ hoti) are merely for the sake of teaching (desanā-matta). It is not that an unrighteous act (adhamma-kamma) occurs only when these three factors meet; it occurs even with a single factor. This meaning should be proven by the Pali passage (Cūḷavagga, 6) beginning with "Monks, three...". The phrase "It is done without acknowledgment" (appaṭiññāya kataṃ hoti) is stated with reference to a conscientious person (lajjī).

In the dark side (kaṇhapakkha), it is stated: "It is done with an offense not leading to confession" (adesanāgāminiyā āpattiyā kataṃ hoti). In the light side (sukkapakkha), it is stated: "It is done with an offense leading to confession" (desanāgāminiyā āpattiyā kataṃ hoti). These two Pali passages conflict with the later passage: "Monks, if the Saṅgha wishes, it may carry out a formal act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma) against a monk endowed with three factors: he is one whose virtue is impaired in regard to higher virtue (adhisīle sīlavipanno)." This is because one who has committed an offense not leading to confession is called "one whose virtue is impaired in regard to higher virtue."

This objection is appropriate; here the intention of the author should be considered. Regarding this, Upatissa Thera said: "The factor of the tajjaniya-kamma is specifically being a maker of quarrels (bhaṇḍanakāraka)," as stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). This statement agrees with the origin (nidāna) found in the Pali. Therefore, in all triads, quarrels should be presented, and this formal act should be carried out by virtue of the offense committed due to quarrels. Thus, even in the phrase "impaired in higher virtue," whether in the earlier or later part, during the time of accusation (codanā) or reminding (sāraṇā) etc., it should be carried out only by virtue of the offense committed due to quarrels, not merely because of a Saṅghādisesa offense.

It is written that "An offense not leading to confession means a Pārājika offense," and later in the Porāṇa-ganthipada it is stated: "Transgressing Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa in higher virtue." In the Ganthipada, it is written: "Impaired in higher virtue refers to Saṅghādisesa." This agrees with the earlier statement in the Porāṇa-ganthipada; therefore, the later Pārājika term in that Porāṇa-ganthipada was stated by way of extracting the meaning (atthuddhāra).
508:
In the Commentary as well, it is stated: "An offense not leading to confession (adesanāgāminī) is either a pārājika offense or a saṅghādisesa offense." In that context, the mention of the pārājika offense would be by way of extraction of meaning. Since it is written in the Gaṇṭhipada only that "'one whose virtue is fallen in regard to higher virtue' refers to saṅghādisesa," therefore, in all Gaṇṭhipada contexts, by every method, an act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) should not be carried out because of strife arising from a pārājika offense, as it would serve no purpose. The meaning is established that it should be carried out because of a saṅghādisesa offense. If it is argued, "But it is not so, because of the statement in the light side (sukkapakkha) that 'it is done with an offense leading to confession (desanāgāminī)' (Cullavagga 5)"? That should not be said, because by one figurative method (pariyāya), a saṅghādisesa offense can also be designated as an offense leading to confession.

The act by which a threat is made is called an act of censure (tajjanīyakamma). The act by which one is made to live in dependence (nissāya), being made to associate [with a teacher] because they have no refuge, is called an act of subordination (niyassakamma). The act by which they expel a corrupter of families from that monastery and from that village is called an act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma). The act by which a monk who reviles [laypeople] is sent back to the presence of the non-angry householder is called an act of reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīyakamma). The act by which an offending monk is expelled or cast out from the status of communal living (samānasaṃvāsakabhūmi) by the Saṅgha is to be known as an act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma).

The phrase "you must live in dependence" is spoken with reference to the heavy dependence (garunissaya), not the other. In the story of Assaji and Punabbhasuka, it is written: "Even if those monks disrobe, although permission is given to revoke the act, it is granted only to those who conduct themselves properly." Speaking in the presence [of the layperson] is called "connected with the laity" (gihipaṭisaṃyutta). Speaking behind their back reaches the ears (desanā).

A monk who asks for forgiveness only needs to say "Please forgive me"; there is no need for formal duties such as squatting. 'Anudūta' means a companion monk. An act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) should be carried out only for not seeing an offense, not otherwise. It is written: "When performing an act of censure etc., it should be carried out by charging the offense and [doing so] for not seeing that offense, or for not making amends, or by the factors such as being a maker of strife."

In the acts of censure etc., this following miscellaneous decision (pakiṇṇakavinicchaya) should be known: What is an act of censure? What is the root of an act of censure? What is the basis (vatthu)? What is the conclusion?
509:
Why is it called "Tajjaniyakamma"? What is Tajjaniyakamma? It is the completion of the act when the basis (vatthu) exists. What is the root of Tajjaniyakamma? The Saṅgha is the root. What is the basis of Tajjaniyakamma? It is the basis of an offence arising from quarreling. What is the conclusion? The conclusion is the completion of the formal recitation (kammavācā). Why is it called Tajjaniyakamma? Because the Saṅgha, by showing the danger in quarreling and schism to the person who causes quarrels, generates patience and peace; therefore, it is called "Tajjaniyakamma."

How is the Act of Censure performed, and how is it not performed? In what way is the Act of Censure said to be performed, and in what way is it not performed? By whom is the Act of Censure performed, and by whom is it not performed? Where is the Act of Censure performed, and where is it not performed? At what time is the Act of Censure performed, and at what time is it not performed?

How is the Act of Censure performed? It is performed by a complete Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma). How is it not performed? It is the performance by an incomplete Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations. In what way is it said to be performed? It is performed through the completion of the act (karaṇasampatti). In what way is it said to be not performed? It is said to be not performed through the failure of the act (karaṇavipatti). By whom is it performed? It is performed by the Saṅgha. By whom is it not performed? It is said to be not performed by a group (gaṇa) or an individual. Where is it performed? It is performed in the presence of the person against whom the Saṅgha performs the Act of Censure. Where is it not performed? It is said to be not performed in the absence of the person against whom the Saṅgha performs the Act of Censure. At what time is it performed? It is performed when an offence arising from quarreling exists. At what time is it not performed? It is said to be not performed when an offence arising from quarreling does not exist.

By how many factors is the Act of Censure valid (pattakalla), and by how many factors is it invalid (apattakalla)? The Act of Censure is valid through seven factors and invalid through seven factors. By what seven factors is it valid, and by what seven factors is it invalid? [The factors for invalidity are:] the absence of an offence arising from quarreling, the person not being present, the Saṅgha being incomplete, a person not in communion (asāṃvāsika) being present in that assembly, the person not having been accused, not having been reminded, and the offence not having been charged. Through these seven factors, the Act of Censure is invalid. Through the other seven factors, it is valid. The same should be understood for the remaining formal acts.

## The Commentary on Kamma-kkhandhaka is finished.
510:
## 2. Pārivāsikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Pārivāsikavattakathāvaṇṇanā
In the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka, it is said that if it is stated, "Do not ask me for permission to enter the village," it is allowable to enter the village even without asking. The Saṅgha should take it at the place where they arrive. Oṇojana means relinquishing. It is stated, "Regarding that oṇojana food, a monk undergoing probation (pārivāsika) should perform the relinquishing for the sake of the next day, etc., only of the object which has reached him and which he himself has accepted; if he relinquishes it without accepting it, it is not allowed."

Regarding the words "natural dependence" (pakatinissaya): "As long as there is attachment (ālaya) of the pupils, it is allowable until the day of entering the rains-retreat; if the attachment of that pupil is evident, the dependence does not cease." If one says this, it is not allowable. In that case, it is stated, "I will now ask for forgiveness," etc. In that case, because it is truly relinquished, it ceases. Regarding this matter of whether it ceases or not, some say that only the harmony of the two pupils is desired. Regarding the words "for a capable monk": it is written that a monk who has received authorization (sammuti) cannot admonish even the monk who gave the order, whether with the weighty principles (garudhamma) or with other teachings. Regarding the words "more depraved than that": it is stated, "The offense of emission of semen (sukkavissaṭṭhi) is more depraved than the offense of acting as a go-between (sañcaritta) committed unintentionally; this method should also be applied." Requisite (paccaya) means the monastery where one resides for the rains. He does not get the monastery because the sleeping places must be shared. It is said, "He is also not allowed to give instructions (uddesa), etc." It is stated, "If two monks undergoing probation see each other at the place they arrive, both must inform each other without distinction, because it is stated, 'The incoming monk should inform, and it should be informed to the incoming monk.'" A monk going to another monastery has no duty to inform again a monk he has already informed there before. It is said, "Just as a monk who has not laid down his duties and has informed outside has no duty to inform again in the monastery, so too the statement 'It should be informed on the Uposatha day for the sake of clearing incoming monks' is evidence in this case."

Some say that for a monk sitting under a single roof, there are dukkaṭa offenses for the interruption of the night (ratticcheda). "Without distinction" means without making this distinction between a monk undergoing probation and one who has been suspended (ukkhittaka). Because of the statement "even in a regular monk (pakatatta) ordained on that day," it is allowable to live with novices. It is written that by the word "equal years" (samavassa), it shows that both incur an offense of breach of duty (vattabheda) for lying down in a bed neither before nor after the other.

## Pārivāsikavattakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
511:
## Mūlāyapaṭikassanārahavattakathāvaṇṇanā
"One younger than oneself" means one who is younger among those undergoing probation, etc. A monk who first took probation in the midst of the Saṅgha and then laid down the duty is allowed to undertake it again or lay it down in the presence of even a single monk. In the case of mānatta (penance), it is allowable to lay it down. Some teachers say it should not be taken in an incomplete group because there is a fault in the practice. In the Porāṇagaṇṭhipada, it is stated that just as it is allowable to lay down the duty first taken in the presence of a single monk, so too it is allowable to undertake it.

## Pārivāsikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
512:
## 3. Samuccayakkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Sukkavissaṭṭhikathāvaṇṇanā
Regarding the word "vedayāmi," it is written that it means: "I know, I accept with the mind and experience happiness; I do not suffer because of the reason of undergoing this probation (parivāsa)." If a monk has not yet been informed outside the boundary (māḷaka), he should be informed and the duty (vatta) should be laid down. If he has already been informed, there is no need to inform him again; there is only the laying down of the duty. For a monk who lives having laid down the duty, there is no need to inform all monks who enter the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā). Those who are seen and those whose voices are heard should be informed. Even those who are not seen or heard, but are within twelve cubits, should also be informed. It is said, "This is the characteristic of a monk living with the duty laid down." Although the phrase "from the enclosure of the enclosed monastery" and so on is not in the Pali text, it is said that one should practice exactly according to the words of the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). "Noting the existence" means noting within the twelve-cubit precinct; noting the arrival of monks who have not laid down their duty into the precinct boundary, one should know the communal living and so forth. It is also said, "A monk who lays down the duty should inform and then lay it down; there is a benefit," but that benefit is not shown. In the statement "a monk who has practiced mānatta should be rehabilitated (abbhetabba)," since there is no difference between one who has practiced mānatta and one who is worthy of rehabilitation (abbhānāraha), it should alternatively be said, "one worthy of rehabilitation should be rehabilitated." Even for a monk subjected to the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma), if there is a monk of similar views (sabhāga), he is not allowed to remain without informing that monk by virtue of holding his own view.

## Parivāsakathāvaṇṇanā
There is a text: "Even if one conceals with the perception of danger for a monk who has no danger, it is indeed non-concealing." A similar portion by way of being without enmity is called "aviri-sabhāga." It is stated right here as a relevant point: "It is not proper to reveal (āvi-kamma) in the presence of a monk who has committed a similar Saṅghādisesa offense." There is no prohibition regarding light offenses (lahuka-āpatti). Since it is permitted to perform the Uposatha by revealing light offenses through a motion (ñatti), it is proper to reveal a similar light offense. However, it is said that it is not proper to inform of a similar Saṅghādisesa offense through a motion. Because it is said, "He will remedy that offense in the presence of that monk..."
513:
Such announcement (ārocanā) is permitted only for light offenses (lahuka-vatthu). It is written that one cannot remedy a Saṅghādisesa offense in the presence of a single pure monk. It should be understood that even in light offenses, it is not proper to reveal a common offense (sabhāga-āpatti). Therefore, revealing by way of a motion (ñatti) is permitted; otherwise, that announcement by motion would be useless. It is proper by way of mutual announcement; revealing by way of a motion is permitted only to show that it is not proper in any other way. Therefore, here it is said: "For a monk who has fallen into a common Saṅghādisesa offense..." This meaning is already explained in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī: "By this much, those two monks become free of offense; in their presence, the remaining monks should confess their common offenses."

However, it is proper to perform the Uposatha after announcing the Saṅghādisesa offense by way of a motion. The meaning of that motion is: "When I see a pure monk, I will remedy it by way of announcement in his presence." When remedied thus, one is released from the offense stated: "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be listened to by one with an offense; if one listens, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." Therefore, it is said: "Whether it is a grave offense (garuka-vatthu) or a light offense (lahuka-vatthu), it is proper to reveal it by way of a motion." Between these two methods, the more appropriate one should be taken.

In the phrase "Nāmañceva āpatti ca" (Both the name and the offense): "The offense fallen into by such and such transgression is the offense; 'name' is the name of that offense." In the phrase "It should be kept after announcing," announcement serves the purpose of removing the Dukkaṭa offense of breaking a duty (vattabheda). "This is not the reason" refers to the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from the statement "He fell into many Saṅghādisesa offenses."

"Dasa-sataṃ ratti-sataṃ" (Ten hundred, a hundred nights) should be construed as "concealing a thousand offenses for a hundred nights." Aggha-samodhāna (Combined according to value) is given by including many offenses of the same nature (sabhāga-vatthu) concealed for many nights. The other (Missaka-samodhāna) is given by way of offenses of various natures (nānā-vatthu). This is the difference between these two probations (parivāsa).

## Parivāsakathā-vaṇṇanā is finished.

Because "of the village" is not said, it is written that the meaning is that it is proper even in the vicinity (upacāra) of the village. And it is said: "But this is the distinction." It is written: "In this matter, only the teacher of the Commentary is the authority; what is appropriate is not seen." In the Anu-ganthipada: "But this is the distinction: if an incoming monk... enters and goes, there is indeed an interruption of the night (ratticcheda)." This is below: "Having gone out within the dawn from the vicinity of the village..."
514:
Because it was spoken with respect [to the rule] “beyond two stone-throws” and so forth, and because the training rules were prescribed in various places specifically out of respect for the Bhikkhunīs, the commentator, in accordance with those prescriptions and out of respect for the Bhikkhunīs, stated “Yattakā purebhattaṃ vā” and so forth to demonstrate the procedure for the Mānatta observance. To show that there is no fault even if one acts according to the words stated in the Kurundī and other [commentaries], only the mere characteristic (lakkhaṇa) is mentioned. The statements in both [commentaries] are appropriate according to their respective reasons. When a decision is reached, one should abide by the noteworthy characteristic; therefore, the words in the Kurundī and others are mentioned later. However, the practice (payoga) follows the former statement. Just as in this case, if a Bhikkhunī allows the dawn to rise without exceeding the distance of two stone-throws, there is no fault. Even though there is no fault, because it is stated in all commentaries, it is said: “It is only the former practice.” Regarding the Parivāsa observance and so forth, it is written: “Since the limits of staying on Parivāsa, the suspension of dependence (nissaya), etc., are defined by the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā), only the precinct boundary of the Bhikkhunīs’ monastery should be taken, not the village.” The statement “Alms-gathering is possible in that village” and so forth is spoken in terms of invitation (pavārita). It is also written that this is because there is no monastery within that village. It is further written that while that statement is appropriate for that reason, it is not appropriate in terms of the actual meaning.

## Paṭicchannaparivāsādikathāvaṇṇanā
Regarding the statement “Mānatta must be practiced separately,” it is also written that it should be practiced with a separate formal act (kammavācā) without performing the rehabilitation (mūlāyapaṭikassana). Since it is stated as a “saṅghādisesa offence,” a saṅghādisesa arising from a single basis is called an offence mixed with thullaccaya and dukkaṭa. Hypocrisy (makkha-dhamma) means the desire to conceal.

“Dhammatā” means by nature or by the true nature. It is the same as in the case of “alajjitā” (shamelessness).

In the matter of “one must stay on parivāsa for two months based on the former parivāsa,” it is written: “The days spent on parivāsa also enter into the count.”

“Tasmiṃ bhūmiyaṃ” means in that ground or in that plane. In the passage “one commits many saṅghādisesa offences, and the amount,” etc., the singular number is used by way of class (jāti).

## Samuccayakkhandhakavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
515:
## 4. Samathakkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Sammukhāvinayakathāvaṇṇanā
186-187. In whichever formal act (kammavācā) there is a rule for designation in the presence [of the person], such as “this person” or “these persons,” all such acts must be performed in the presence (sammukhā); it is not only the five types of acts such as the act of censure (tajjanīya-kamma). Indeed, the extraction and presentation of only the five types of acts is because only those five acts are recorded in the Pali of the Kammakkhandhaka. This should be understood as being similar to the extraction and presentation of only the four Pārājikas mentioned in the Pārājika section, even though there are twenty-four Pārājikas. In that Pali, it is said: “The presence of the person is only the approach to within reach (hatthapāsa).” The reason for this is that in an act to be performed in the presence, there is no rule that one must designate [the person] in the presence.

This meaning is indeed established in the Kammakkhandhaka itself by the words: “Monks, a tajjanīya-kamma endowed with three factors is an illegal act... it is not performed in the presence...” (Cūḷavagga 4). However, the offence was not shown in that Kammakkhandhaka. It should be understood that this [Samathakkhandhaka] was undertaken to show the offence that would occur in performing that tajjanīya-kamma, etc., [by saying]: “If anyone should perform it, there is an offence of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).” To show that “even if it is settled by an illegal act resembling the Sammukhā-vinaya, it still enters the count of being settled by the Sammukhā-vinaya,” the passage beginning with “a person who speaks what is not Dhamma” was undertaken, and so it is written. The teachers say that this statement was undertaken to show that such a settlement is called being settled by an act resembling the Sammukhā-vinaya, and not by the Sammukhā-vinaya itself or by any other act.

## Sativinayakathāvaṇṇanā
In the formal act for the Venerable Dabba, although there is no designation in the presence such as “The Sangha [gives] to this Venerable Dabba...”, the fact of it being performed in the presence of the Venerable Dabba is established by the words: “First, Dabba should be requested.” Similarly, in other places as well, the reason should be understood as it may occur. The disciplinary procedure (vinaya) given to one who has reached fullness of mindfulness is called Sativinaya.

## Amūḷhavinayakathāvaṇṇanā
196-197. It is written: “For whichever insane person there is no offence due to various transgressions, it is proper to give the Amūḷhavinaya only to such a person. Thus, the disciplinary procedure performed for one who is not deluded is called Amūḷhavinaya.” Such writing is appropriate. This is because it is said: “The Sangha gives the Amūḷhavinaya to the monk Gagga who is not deluded,” and because of the occurrence of the Vibhaṅga of the Pali: “Monks, these three are the illegal acts of giving Sativinaya,” which refers to the time of transgression with the words “I do not remember.” However, when giving the Amūḷhavinaya, the state of not being deluded is determined.
516:
Because of the statement, “The Saṅgha gives the Amūḷhavinaya (verdict of past insanity) to the monk Gagga,” and because in the Vibhaṅga of this Pāḷi text, “Monks, these three are the unrighteous givings of Amūḷhavinaya,” the word “I do not remember” was spoken with reference to the time the offense was committed, thus that Vibhaṅga arose (therefore Amūḷhavinaya should be given). However, at the time of giving the Amūḷhavinaya, the state of his not being insane must be determined.

## Commentary on Paṭiññātakaraṇa
The reason for the statement beginning with “They perform formal acts without the admission of the monks” has already been stated. Performing [a formal act] based on an admission is called Paṭiññātakaraṇa (acting on admission).

## Commentary on Tassapāpiyasikā
The Pāḷi text proceeds by showing five factors, starting with “Monks, a Tassapāpiyasikā-kamma (formal act of further misconduct) is endowed with three factors.” It is written that “it should be understood that the Pāḷi text proceeds by abbreviating with a peyyāla (ellipsis).” The same applies to the sukkapakkha (bright side).

## Commentary on Tiṇavatthāraka etc.
Because it is said, “All must assemble together,” the giving of consent (chanda) is prohibited. Also, in the Pavāraṇakkhandhaka Commentary, it is said: “In these three instances—when making a divided Saṅgha harmonious, in the Tiṇavatthāraka-samatha (settlement by covering with grass), and in this Pavāraṇasaṅgaha—it is not proper to give consent.” If one asks: “Does it not seem contradictory to say that they sit in the monastery precincts (pariveṇa) etc., having come here or having given consent?” To the teachers who know the intention, it does not seem so. The intention here is: All monks who wish to be purified must assemble; there is no purification for one who gives consent but does not assemble. That formal act is successful only for those who have assembled. In the Commentary, the intention is that it is not proper for those who wish to be purified to give consent. Otherwise, it would contradict the Pāḷi text. For this Pāḷi text, “excluding those who are not there,” indicates the presence of those who have come to the assembly and stand having given consent. If one asks: “Could it be said referring to those who have gone outside the boundary (sīmā)?” If those outside the boundary are excluded, what benefit would there be here? Therefore, if a monk stands having given consent in the Sāmaggī-uposatha, he stands only on the ground of those who belong to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka); for that monk who gives consent, there is no Pavāraṇasaṅgaha. It should be understood that if a monk does not come to the Tiṇavatthāraka-kamma, he is not purified from those offenses. If this [procedure] is not pleasing to a monk, because of the assembly mentioned in the Parivāra...
517: The Kamma-vipatti-kkhandhaka (section on failure of formal acts) would be contradicted. Why? Because in that Parivāra, if the consent of monks entitled to give consent is not brought, it is said that Pavāraṇā should not be performed, as it shows success (sampatti) in the opposite way. Likewise, the Pattakalla-lakkhaṇa (characteristic of fitness) of that monk would also be contradicted. If it is said: “In those three instances, all monks are suitable for the formal act, and there is no one there entitled to give consent.” That should not be said. In the classification of formal acts performed by a group of four etc., because the person entitled to give consent is mentioned without distinction, that statement is made in a general sense. If it is said: “This is a specific characteristic (āveṇika-lakkhaṇa); therefore, even if there is a declaration of views (diṭṭhāvikamma), this act is not one performed separately (paṭikuṭṭhakata).” No, it is indeed an act performed separately, because it has a different nature. In this Dispensation, because of the statement “they perform a declaration of views to one another, saying 'this does not please me,'” a declaration of views is not performed to the Saṅgha. When there is such a declaration of views, it is indeed performed separately. Otherwise, those motions (ñatti) would occur only in the preliminary part and would be useless. Also, in the Parivāra Commentary, in the section on those entitled to give consent, the method is not given. If it is said: “It contradicts because it is stated in the Pavāraṇakkhandhaka Commentary that 'it is not proper to give consent in the three instances.'” That should not be said. When the Commentary is taken as the authority, if one takes the statement “having given consent here, they sit in the pariveṇa etc.” only with the desire for purification, then some teachers say that the whole statement is not contradictory. The statement “having come or having given consent, they sit in the pariveṇa etc., those monks do not emerge from the offenses” should also not be said. Why? Because of the statement below prohibiting the giving of consent, “All monks must assemble together,” and because it is stated in the [Pavāraṇakkhandhaka] Commentary “it is not proper to give consent in the three instances,” and because it is stated likewise in the Andhaka Commentary. No, when the formal act is performed only in unison, if a monk in this Dispensation sets aside the general motion (sādhāraṇa-ñatti) “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me, our... connected with the laity,” and again sets aside specific motions (asādhāraṇa-ñatti) with “Venerable sirs, listen to me,” etc., and after making the concord of the monks on one side with “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me, our... thus I uphold this,” he goes away having given consent for some business immediately after that concord is made, for that monk there is no emergence from the offenses. Other teachers also say this very meaning mentioned above, because of being situated in the midst of the monks on the other side and because of the clarity of the performance. When the second motion is set forth in a general way, those monks who go away having given consent at that moment before the motion-and-second-proclamation (ñattidutiya-kammavācā) has begun or before it is finished, those monks also certainly do not emerge from the offenses. Regarding the word “ye na tattha honti” (those who are not there), the meaning should be taken as “those monks who are not in that assembly according to the method already mentioned.” And to show the variety of meanings already mentioned, the Commentary says “having given consent, they sit in the pariveṇa etc.”
518:
Without stating only this meaning, it is said: 'those who, though committing an offense along with those monks, did not come to that place, or having come, gave their consent and are sitting in the front of the monastery, etc.' In this way, the preceding and following statements are consistent. It is also stated: 'In the Pāḷi, in that commentary's explanation, it should be understood that the act is not invalidated by a clear formal procedure (vikamma).'

## Adhikaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The arising of thought (cittuppāda) is dispute (vivāda). The word 'dispute' also comes to be designated as wholesome, etc., by way of metonymy. With reference to that, it is said: 'It is called a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) because it must be settled by means of settlements (samatha).' Alternatively, by the settling of the arising of thought which is the cause of dispute, the sound (of dispute) that has arisen also settles. Therefore, the arising of thought can figuratively be called a legal issue that must be settled by means of settlements. In the case of dispute where it is said 'those with wholesome minds dispute,' it is also called 'speaking in opposition (vohāra).' It should be understood that this is not due to the power of the words already spoken.

If it is asked: 'Since it is said "one who commits an offense may even have a wholesome mind," could a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) also be wholesome?' No. That statement was not made with reference to āpattādhikaraṇa. To show that one who commits an offense does so while being endowed with one of the three types of minds, it is said 'one commits an offense with a wholesome mind,' etc. If someone says, 'A legal issue arising from an offense is merely a designation (paṇṇatti),' then in his view, it would not be appropriate for āpattādhikaraṇa to be unwholesome, etc., just like legal issues arising from disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa), etc. This is because it would conflict with the statement 'There is no wholesome legal issue arising from an offense.'

However, in the Anugaṇṭhipada, it is said: 'Āpattādhikaraṇa is a designation for the unwholesome arisings of thought and the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) occurring in that way. Among the remaining wholesome, indeterminate (abyākata), and designations, since it is said "an āpattādhikaraṇa may be unwholesome, may be indeterminate," its status as a designation is prohibited because it is not included (apariyāpanna) in the wholesome triad. By the very prohibition of the wholesome, since they follow the same course, the prohibition of functional indeterminates (kiriya-abyākata) should also be understood. Because they follow the functional indeterminates, the prohibition of resultant indeterminates (vipāka-abyākata) is also already made. Nevertheless, because they are generally indeterminate, it should be understood as a designation for resultant and functional indeterminates along with the aggregate of matter.' In that commentary, the statement 'a wholesome mind is a factor' is made with reference to a monk unskilled in the Vinaya, regarding the clearing of green grass, etc., where a wholesome mind is the factor (aṅga) of committing an offense. Therefore...
519:
Because it is impossible to say that a legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) is wholesome, it means that a wholesome mind is not a factor (aṅga) of the offense. If that is so, why is it said 'three minds, three feelings'? To answer that question, some teachers have exerted effort starting with 'Nayidaṃ', etc. The mind that causes an offense to arise is called a mind sufficient to be a factor. 'Absolutely' (ekantato) means 'for the most part' (yebhuyyena); otherwise, it would conflict with the statement that 'in the category of those with mind (sacittaka), the mind is only unwholesome' (in the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Commentary). What is the benefit of taking it thus? Since it is strictly unwholesome, there is no resultant (vipāka); therefore, there is no discussion there. To show where there is a result in an offense by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), he said 'Yaṃ pana paṇṇattivajjaṃ', etc.

Unintentionally or not knowing something... 'it is indeterminate' means: when a monk is lying down with a mind established in a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), or is drowsy, if a woman comes and lies down with him, even though he has a wholesome mind, it is not a factor of the offense. Therefore, at that moment, only the material form (rūpa) occurring in the manner of lying down is called āpattādhikaraṇa. Even when the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta) is present, the method is the same. In fact, because he does not get up when he should at that moment, only the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is called the offense, not together with the resultant. If one were to say it is together with the resultant, then in the view of such a speaker, in the training rules without mind (acittaka), a wholesome mind would reach the state of an offense. What does this mean? It means that for one who takes wool and crosses three leagues while reflecting on a meditation subject, and for one who teaches Dhamma word-by-word without knowing the regulation, a wholesome mind would reach the state of an offense in the offense that must be committed. If it is asked, 'Does it not indeed reach the state of an offense?'—No, it does not. Why? Because of the word of the Buddha: 'There is no wholesome legal issue arising from an offense.'

'The moving body or the occurring speech is one or another factor' means it is one or another offense. Specifically, because unwholesomeness, etc., cannot occur in a mere regulation (paṇṇatti), it is not appropriate for it to be an offense. To show that one who commits an offense does so while being endowed with one of the three types of minds, it is said 'one with a wholesome mind,' etc. The meaning is: in digging the earth, etc., because of the existence of material form occurring by way of transgression while a wholesome mind is arising, one with a wholesome mind also commits an indeterminate offense. Likewise, one with an indeterminate mind also commits an indeterminate offense known as indeterminate material form. In taking life, etc., one with an unwholesome mind commits an unwholesome offense. Here, the material form is negligible (abbohārika). When one commits taking life, etc., during a dream, or commits an offense that must be committed by way of sleeping together (sahaseyya), etc...
520:
It should be understood that one with an unwholesome mind falls into an indeterminate (abyākata) offense. The statement "The legal issue of an offense is unwholesome" refers to the arising of an unwholesome thought. However, in the ancient glossaries (Gaṇṭhipada), four types of persons are shown: the worldling (puthujjana), the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), the trainee (sekha), and the Arahat. Among them, the legal issue of an offense for an Arahat is only indeterminate. Similarly, for trainees, and for a virtuous worldling when committing an offense unintentionally, it is only indeterminate. For other worldlings, it can be both unwholesome and indeterminate. Since it is only unwholesome when that worldling commits an offense intentionally, it is said, "There is no legal issue of an offense that is wholesome." In all cases, the term "indeterminate" is used with reference to the mere absence of resultants (vipāka) from those wholesome or unwholesome states; this should be accepted after careful consideration.

"Is a dispute a legal issue of dispute?" is a single question asking whether any dispute whatsoever is entirely called a legal issue of dispute. In the ancient glossary, regarding the question "Is a dispute a legal issue?", it is said to be asking whether the legal issue of dispute is itself the dispute, or whether it is both the dispute and the legal issue, or whether both are simply the legal issue of dispute. In some palm-leaf manuscripts, this question does not exist. If it is absent, there should be five questions: "Is a dispute a legal issue of dispute?", "Is a legal issue of dispute a dispute?", "Is a legal issue of dispute both a dispute and a legal issue?", and so on. In some versions, there are three questions, in others four, but never five. Among those questions, two have already been analyzed. In the remaining questions, "Is a legal issue a dispute?" asks whether any legal issue at all comes to be called a dispute. "Is a dispute a legal issue?" asks whether any dispute at all comes to be classified as a legal issue. This method applies in all cases.

"In the settlement in the presence" (sammukhāvinayasmiṃ) means in the state of the settlement in the presence.

"By reason of" (antarena) is written as "because of a cause."

In the case of criticism regarding the referral to a committee (ubbāhikā), a Pācittiya offense is not mentioned because there is no giving of consent (chanda) there.

"This of his" (tassa kho etaṃ) means "this is," as in the phrase "this is the foremost" (etadaggaṃ).
521:
It is said that there is also a reading: "And what is his further misconduct?" (kā ca tassa pāpiyasikā).

According to the statement "The obligation itself is the legal issue of obligations," this is a designation for formal acts of announcement (apalokana-kamma) and so forth. That legal issue of obligations (kiccādhikaraṇa) is not to be settled by the [other] settlements like the legal issues of dispute, but rather it is accomplished through the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya).

## 5. Explanation of the Chapter on Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Discussion on Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukathā-vaṇṇanā)

An action done with the back of the hand is called "puthupāṇika."

It is written: "of earrings and so forth, such as ear-ornaments that hang loosely from the ear." "Kāyūraṃ" is the original Pali text. The teacher has extracted it as "keyūrādīni" (bracelets, etc.).

It is written: "What is called 'Sādhugīta' is a song sung at the place of Parinibbāna (or concerning the subject of Parinibbāna)." "Dantagīta" refers to the refinement of the pleasant voice of those who wish to sing. To clarify "Dantagīta," the phrase beginning with "yaṃ gāyissāma" (what we shall sing) was spoken.

"Caturassavatta" is the duty of reciting a verse consisting of four lines (pāda). It is written: "The methods of recitation such as the Tarangavatta have become obsolete practices." "Bāhiralomi" (outer-haired) is a neuter noun expressing a state (bhāvana-pumsaka). Just as the hairs are seen on the outside of that woolen coverlet, it means that a monk who wears it in such a way incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

The word beginning with "Virūpakkhehi" is an instrumental case used in association with the word "saha" (with). "Sarabhū" refers to a gecko living in a house. It is said that if that gecko is white, it is poisonous. In the phrase "sohaṃ," the connection is: "I who have loving-kindness for these tribes of snakes, I pay homage to the Blessed One." In the phrase "in another... (see the detailed explanation)... in the place to be cut," it refers to cutting something else when the latent tendency of lust (rāgānusaya) should have been cut.

"Uṭṭitvā" means having put in. "Otaratu" means "let them take it down by psychic power." "Anupariyāyī" means wandered around.

"Na acchupiyanti" means they do not stick or adhere. "Rūpakākiṇṇāni" means crowded or interspersed with figures of women and so forth.

"Ālindakamiḍḑhikādīnaṃ" refers to the porch-sockets or pivots (pamukha-miḍḑhikā) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "parivattetvā tattheva" (having turned, right there), it is written: "Having turned, on the third time, it stays right there in the socket." "Paribhaṇḍa" refers to that which is made to strengthen the base of the outer wall of a monastery...
523:
A small rim of a support is called a tanukamiḍḍhikā. In this commentary, it is written: "It is allowable to place [the bowl] in a location where there is no suspicion of it breaking due to rolling over." A bowl-stand (pattamaḷaka) is made by enclosing it with bricks, etc., in a circular or square shape and roofing the stand to prevent the bowls from rolling and falling. It is also written: "The bowl-base-circle (pattamaṇḍalikā) and the bowl-resting-basket (pattapacchikā) are made of palm leaves, etc." It is allowable to place the bowl-rest (ādhāraka) on the rim (miḍḍhanta), as it is mentioned for the purpose of supporting the bowl. It is not allowable to place it on a couch (mañca) even with a bowl-rest, because it is forbidden due to the reason of it being a sitting place. It is allowable to hang it because it is close to the ground.

Some say: "Because of the words 'hanging on the edge of the shoulder,' it is not allowable to hang it on the fingertips and place it in the lap." This is not good (incorrect). It was said with the thought: "If there is a perception of breaking regarding a bowl held by hand, not only for one's own bowl, etc., how much more so when held by other parts of the body?" In the Pali, however, it is spoken according to common usage. Ghaṭikaṭāha is a bowl-cover made of a potsherd. A skull-bowl is spoken of according to the usage such as "the body of a stone-child, the stream of milk." It means one has come to sit on a couch. Some also say: "Pisācillikā means demon children." Only an offered object is called a received object. Cabbetvā means having chewed or sucked. Bones and thorns are called aṭṭhikakaṇṭaka. It is written: "In all these, whether one knows the regulation or not, it is an offense."

Vipphāḷetvā means having split or dropped. "To fill with yeast" means to fill with liquor yeast or ground lime powder. Bidalaka is the name for a specific action called doubling. Doubling what? It is the doubling of the coarse mat, etc., with which the large Kathina frame is spread. That Kathina spreading should be doubled by folding at the edges according to the size of the stick-frame (daṇḍakathina). Otherwise, there would be no space for the hand when performing the arrangement of the border and binding of a small robe. If there is a pin (salākā), one can easily know which of the two robes is sewn or unsewn. When the daṇḍakathina is made, many companions are not necessary. It is written: "Without wrinkling, the robe is even; the corners are also even." Since it is said "making a mark with turmeric thread," it is established that it is allowable to sew the robe with turmeric thread. In that matter, some have the perception that it is unallowable. Paṭiggaha is a finger-stall (thimble).
524:
257-8. Pātī is a vessel made in the shape of a ring. Paṭiggahatthavika is a bag for holding the finger-stall (thimble-bag). Since the needle-bag was previously allowed for needles and small knives, it was said: "Monks, I allow a medicine bag." In this bag, needles, small knives, etc., should also be placed; this is indicated by the introduction. Even if Upananda Bhikkhu is a shameless person, it is appropriate to say that the property is allowable for a monk who does not cut off the root (of the training), even if he is a shameful monk. "Does not fit" (na sammati) means it is not enough (na pahoti).

260-1. A low structure built all around the outside of a wall is called a maṇḍalika. For a monk whose nakedness is not visible due to being covered by a sweat-house (jantāghara), etc., only for such a monk should the work of rubbing the body be done. This same method applies to covering with water, covering with cloth, etc.

262-3. Paṇiya refers to vegetable sellers. A drawing machine (like a lever) rotates over the well when pulled. Arahaṭaghaṭiyantra is a machine in the shape of a cartwheel (a water-wheel). It should be understood that water is drawn by binding pots to each spoke of that machine and rotating it once or twice. Āviddhapakkhapāsa is where the "duck-wings" (fencing/surroundings) are arranged in a circular manner like solid objects that are not pierced. Such arrangements are called āviddhapakkhapāsaka. Although previously allowed for the security of the bowl, now the bowl-rest (ādhāraka) is allowed for using the bowl that has been placed.

In the phrase "it goes into another's throat," it is allowable because there is no effort (payoga) by this monk. Kammasatena means with great effort.

277-8. Lohabhaṇḍa refers to metalware other than bronze (kaṃsa). Muddikakāyabandhana is a waistband made without being square. The pāmaṅgadasā (fringes) are square. "Mudingasaṇṭhānena" means in the manner of sewing the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭī) in the shape of a drum or a grain-head. Pavananta is the end of the loop (pāsanta). It is also written as "dasāmūla." Whether intentional or unintentional, entering a village without a waistband is an offense. It is written: "From the place where it was forgotten, one should enter after fastening the waistband, or one should return."

In the phrase "seven finger-breadths or eight finger-breadths," since it is not said "by the Sugata finger-breadth," there is no fault if they make it larger using the ordinary finger-breadth for the sake of suitability.

It is like the women of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) wearing [ornaments] in the shape of a palm-leaf fan.

## 6. Senāsanakkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Vihārānujānanakathāvaṇṇanā
Monks reside (or take shelter) in these dwellings such as vihāras; therefore, dwellings such as vihāras are called 'leṇa' (shelters). Regarding the phrase 'āgatānāgatassa cātuddisassa saṅghassa' (to the Saṅgha of the four quarters, present and future), some teachers say that according to the word 'āgata' (present/arrived), only the Saṅgha that has arrived owns the dwelling, while the Saṅgha that has not yet arrived does not. This statement is inappropriate because it is established by a covenant of equal gain (samānalābha-katikā).

296-7. In the phrase 'dīpinaṅguṭṭhena' (with a leopard's tail), it is written that the word 'dīpi' (leopard) indicates unallowable (akappiya) skin. A 'thambhakavātapāna' (pillar-window) is a window made only of upright timbers without placing timbers horizontally. In the phrase 'bhisīnaṃ anujñātaṃ' (the allowance of bolsters), it means that since bolsters (bhisi) are allowed, they are also allowable as pillows (bimbohana). It is not allowable to lean against a bolster filled with cotton (tūla), because only wool and such materials are allowed for that purpose. This is said with reference to sitting and lying down; therefore, if one asks whether it is allowable for leaning, some teachers say it is not allowable as it is an unallowable object. If it were not allowable in that way, it would also not be allowable to lean against an unallowable couch. Since that is allowable, there is no fault. Alternatively, a pillow is allowed for a sick monk even for lying down; therefore, a bolster is also allowable for leaning. Some teachers also allow and use them. A robe sewn with thread made from silk-cotton (simbali-tūla) is allowable. Why? Because it is similar to cotton. Those same teachers also say, 'A robe made from the thread of the Calotropis fruit (akkaphala) is also allowable; only a robe made from Calotropis bark (akkavāka) is to be rejected.'

297. 'Anibandhanīyo' means that which should not be attached or stuck. 'Paṭibāhetvā' means having made it smooth and polished. It is written, 'For white and other colors, substances such as resin (ikkāsa) are mentioned respectively for the purpose of making them firm (binding).'

300. 'Pakuṭṭaṃ' means a hole or an entrance-front pierced all around.

303. 'Sudhālepo' means plastering with lime and fine clay.

305. 'Āsatti' means clinging craving (taṇhā). 'Santiṃ' means the absence of anxiety (adara).

307. 'Ketunti' means to acquire by buying.

308. 'Citāti' means it is understood to be made by cutting bricks in pairs (or sets) through the process of extraction.
526:
In the phrase 'antevāsika (pupils) of the Chabbaggiya monks,' the Chabbaggiya monks appeared after twenty years had passed. Since it was said (in the Majjhima Nikāya), 'The monks have satisfied my mind,' it is appropriate to say that the story which occurred during a journey to Sāvatthī at another time is brought here for the purpose of showing the offense; this should be accepted after investigation. 'Vuddha' refers to a more senior elder (mahāthera).

'Santhara' refers to grass mats and the like.

## Senāsanaggāhakathāvaṇṇanā

It is written, 'Seyyaggena means by the division of bed-places; vihāraggena means by the sequence of rooms.' 'Thāvara' refers to permanent things. 'Paccayeneva hi taṃ' means that in that dwelling, the great elders, because of that requisite (support), will stay without going elsewhere and will look after that dwelling. To show the act of not disturbing, it is said, 'People are not there,' and so on. There is a text: 'Having cut off thoughts (vitakka), one should go only according to the duty of going with a pure mind.' 'Muddavedikā' is the top-railing (hammiyavedikā) of a cetiya. 'Paṭikkamma' means having withdrawn.

A covenant of equal gain (samānalābha-katikā) can only exist if the original dwelling exists; if the original dwelling is destroyed, the covenant is also destroyed. The term 'samānalābha' (equal gain) is appropriate only when there are two or many dwellings; therefore, it is our opinion that if only one dwelling remains, that term is not appropriate. A teacher says that 'tāvakālika' (temporary) means that either by time or by the cutting of the root, the work of others may belong to another, like a meeting on a boat.

'It should be done only by the power of the individual' means that when performing the act of notification (apalokana), the Saṅgha should give to the monks who have completed the rains retreat individually, referring only to the person: 'This much cloth for the rains is given; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha.' It should not be done by the power of the Saṅgha. It means the Saṅgha does not give this much to the Saṅgha. It is written, 'Because of the statement "one performs the act of the Saṅgha in a single dwelling," it should be done by the power of the Saṅgha.' Even if it is said so, no act is actually considered performed for the Saṅgha. It is written, 'If there is no appointed person to assign dwellings, even if it is assigned by another, the assignment is valid, just as the higher ordination (upasampadā) of one who has not yet taken a preceptor (upajjhāya) is valid.' It is also written, 'Authorization (sammuti) by means of a formal act (kammavācā) is also allowable.'

Regarding the question of whether it is allowable for eight or sixteen people individually or together, it is allowable even together. For they are not considered as having an act performed by the Saṅgha just by being so authorized...
527:
(They are called those for whom the act is performed). Therefore, in the Sattasatikakkhandhaka, it is stated: "Eight persons were appointed together." The appointment of these persons is valid through a kammavācā as well as through a ñattidutiyakammavācā. If that kammavācā is obtained through the objects of an apalokanakamma, it is indeed obtained. If the apalokanakamma is obtained through the objects of that kammavācā, it is indeed obtained. It should be understood that no other kammavācā is obtained. A person who wrongly grasps this method holds that "it is allowable to perform an apalokanakamma as a ñattidutiyakamma, and it is allowable to perform a ñattidutiyakamma as an apalokanakamma." If this were so, the fault of mixing formal acts (kammasaṅkaradosa) would occur.

In the phrase "maggo pokkharaṇī," magga refers to a long rest-house built on a road. Pokkharaṇī refers to a pond built for bathing. In the phrase "etāni hi asenāsanāni," the kitchen (bhattasālā) is not included. Therefore, if one asks whether that kitchen is called a lodging (senāsana), it is indeed included in the term senāsana. However, it is because it was not built for the purpose of residing. The dining hall (bhojanasālā), however, is not included in either senāsana or asenāsana. Although not included, it is called senāsana because it was stated above that "the dining hall is indeed a senāsana." Some teachers say, "A kappiyakuṭi (allowable storehouse) should also be built in this dining hall." Others say that this statement is not appropriate. Lodgings such as the foot of a tree or a bamboo thicket are called senāsana only if they are roofed and fitted with a door. Regarding "alābhakesu āvāsesu," it is written as "when lodgings are not obtained." This writing is appropriate because there is no separate senāsana. In the phrase "taṃ saññāpetvā," it is also allowable to use force to compel monks who do not go to the assigned places. In the word "ayampi," the abandoned requisites are also included.

"Upanibandhitvā" means residing at the foot of a tree or similar places near that monastery and performing duties in that monastery. There are three divisions by way of study (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha). There is the text: "dasakathāvatthukaṃ dasaasubhaṃ dasaanussati." In the phrase "paṭhamabhāgaṃ muñcitvā," it is written that if this object is more valuable than the object first received, it should be relinquished. The rains-residence cloth (vassāvāsika) of monks who have broken their rains-retreat refers to the rains-residence cloth of those who first received it but later broke their retreat. "Bhatiniviṭṭhaṃ" refers to requisites sought as if by paying wages. The phrase "saṅghikaṃ pana...pe... vibbhantopi labhateva" is said with reference to the arising of that object. Some teachers say that by this commentary, only the apalokanakamma is the standard, and making one receive it is not the standard. Vinaya experts, however, say that even if it was announced as "the Saṅgha will give a set of three robes to each of the monks who have entered the rains-retreat in our monastery," a person who disrobes before the robes are distributed does not receive them. They say he does not receive them because it was stated, "it should be made to be received by performing an apalokanakamma," and because it was previously stated, "he disrobes before distribution." Regarding "paccayavasena," it is written that one should receive either the robes offered by a householder or other rains-residence cloth by the power of the requisites. In the phrase "ekameva vatthaṃ dātabbaṃ," to the monks residing in that monastery...
528:
It is written that one piece of cloth reaches each of the monks residing in that monastery. The second portion is the portion suitable for the elder's seat (therāsana). It should be understood that the first portion was taken by the elder in another way.

## Explanation of the Story of Upananda

"Tivassantarena" means by a monk who has remained for three years. It is called "hatthinakha" because there are nails on the elephant (feature) of that palace. The "nakha" of a palace is the lower boundary. "Gihivikaṭanīhārena" means only by the markings made by laypeople. It is written that only when those laypeople have spread them and offered them is it allowable to sit; a monk should not relinquish (spread) them by spreading them himself or by having the Saṅgha spread them.

## Explanation of the Story of Non-disposable Items (Avissajjiya)

The statement "it should not be disposed of by the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual" fulfills the statement made in the commentary: "Whatever communal property (saṅghika) is not a heavy item (garubhaṇḍa) and is disposable and distributable, if a group or an individual residing in that monastery disposes of it, it is just the same as if the Saṅgha disposed of it." Otherwise, the inclusion of 'group' and 'individual' in this Pali text would be useless. "Arañjara" is a water jar; it means it holds much water. It is written that it is a pot made like a round jar, having a slightly long mouth and showing a partition in the middle. There are five eyes by way of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Dhamma eye, the Buddha eye, and the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu).

Regarding "garubhaṇḍena ca garubhaṇḍaṃ," this is said with reference to movable property. "To place the bowl and robes" refers to a couch made with a sloping roof on one side. "Vaṭṭaloha" is bronze that has a golden color. "Pārihāriya is not allowable" means it is not allowable to take an item from the hand of an attendant by having one's name written on it without giving it to a visiting monk, and then carrying it as one pleases. "Gihivikaṭanīhāreneva" is written as giving it after taking it only for as long as one's own business is completed. "Sikhara" is the name of the chisel with which they cut by turning it around. "Pattabandhaka" is one who performs the binding of the bowl, etc. Some also say "paṭimānaṃ" is one who makes bowls of gold, etc., with a smooth finish. "Aḍဎabāhu" is written as from the elbow to the point of the shoulder. "From this point onwards" means starting from this Pali text. "Daṇḍamuggara" is the mallet with which they beat the dyed robes. Because it is said to be "in the category of floor coverings (paccattharaṇagatika)," and because it is said that "that mallet is also indeed garubhaṇḍa," they say that by the word 'api', all floor coverings such as woolen blankets (pāvāra) are indeed garubhaṇḍa.
529:
By this Sutta (Pali), another meaning is stated: "Floor coverings such as pāvāra are not heavy property (garubhaṇḍa); they are only distributable items (bhājanīya). Only floor coverings given for the purpose of a dwelling are heavy property." This statement should be carefully examined. Gaṇṭhikā refers to a stick for beating robes (cīvaragaṇṭhikā). Bhañjaka refers to a ladle-cup (saraka).

## Navakammadānakathāvaṇṇanā

323-4. Even by merely making the door-bolt and the socket (a building becomes a monastery). It is written: "Kapotabhaṇḍikā is either a ring (valaya) to be placed above the door frame, or a ring to be placed under the ridge-pole of a grass-roofed house; it refers to the wood that reaches both these types." Kārantara refers to dwelling in a monastery that has fallen into various states of disrepair, being previously unjoined and now being re-entered. It should be understood as dwelling not by way of absolute renunciation. Dwelling in a place that is ruined in all respects should be understood as having no one to prohibit it. Because one is unable to give away doors, windows, etc., without removing them, it is said: "They must indeed be returned." Some say that because the monastery of a monk who gives away rafters, beams, and cross-beams is liable to collapse, it is said: "The original value should be given," and so forth. It is written: "If the resident monks place items on the ground that is naturally without a covering, there is no offense for those monks." It is also written: "Even if doors, windows, etc., are not yet finished/polished, they should not be leaned against without being covered."

## Saṅghabhattādi-anujānanakathāvaṇṇanā

## Uddesabhattakathāvaṇṇanā

There are standing orders (ṭhitikā) that exist naturally in the refectory which is the place for designating gruel and meals (bhattuddesatṭhāna). Regarding the phrase "dinnā pana," the Blessed One, wishing to show the manner in which that donor gives, said: "Venerable Sir, from the Saṅgha..." and so forth. Ekavaḷañja means to be used through a single door. Regarding the phrase ticīvaraparivāra, it is written: "Just as one might receive only water, if another monk does not receive the designated meal (uddesabhatta) but receives many items such as robe-material and cloths, those objects belong only to that monk." It is said: "Because it was brought after saying 'Give it for the designated meal-ticket (uddesapatta),' it is not yet relinquished to the Saṅgha, but has come into the hands of that monk; therefore, they should all divide and consume it according to the stated order." Paṭipāṭipatta means a bowl received in sequence or a bowl placed in sequence (ṭhitapatta). It is written: "It is called a 'deceptive sequence' (kūṭaṭṭhitikā) because even sequences that should not be taken are accepted." It is also written: "Monks who unknowingly take the exquisite meal sequence (paṇီtabhattaṭṭhitika) by mixing it should also practice in this same manner."
530:
It is also written: "It should be practiced." If bowl-carrying monks take away that exquisite meal with a mind to steal, the responsibility lies with the monk who gave the order. In the context of "setting aside the past standing order (ṭhitikā)," it is written: "If alms are received only on that day, they cannot be received from the next day onwards." Later, even if it is not said, "Let the whole Saṅgha enjoy it," it should be shared and consumed. It is written: "Giving by saying 'Take food for this many monks' without saying 'Designate and give this many monks from the Saṅgha' is called a Saṅghika invitation (saṅghika-nimantana)."

## Nimantanabhattakathāvaṇṇanā
"In order" (paṭipāṭiyā) means according to the order in which they were received. "Breaking off" (vicchinditvā) means summarizing and cutting short the measure of the morsel of food without saying the word "Take the meal." This method applies only to invitation meals (nimantanabhatta); however, in designated meals (uddesabhatta), the standing order remains only for the amount sufficient for one monk. "One time" means that as long as the monks reside in that monastery, all of them receive it, as it is written.

## Salākabhattakathāvaṇṇanā
Regarding the phrase "There is no Saṅgha gain outside the boundary (sīmā)," it is meant that in designated meals and so forth, if donors give to a monk who is outside the boundary, he is allowed to take it, and it is permitted to have it brought for oneself; however, here it is not allowable. "They do not reach" means they do not reach even if designated. "Village by turn" (vāragāma) refers to a village that must be visited by turn because of its distance. "Only an increase" (phātikamma) means there are surplus gains. "To one who is present" (sammukhībhūta) means that generally, if monks have gone outside the boundary, it should be brought for the monk who is present. Because they are of a common nature (sabhāga), what is received by one is sufficient for all; if no one is present, it should be brought and given for oneself. The phrase "whether received or not" is said for the sake of euphony. The ticket-food (salākabhatta) that has not yet reached the monastery is designated at the monastery. By that given ticket, that monk... "Of that person" means it seems to mean that the ticket of the monk who has taken it and gone should be taken. The name "Anupiya" is found in the singular; however, in the locative case, it is found as "in the region of Anupiya". There is a text: "the ten messengers beginning with Kāḷudāyī". It is written: "does not descend from the palace" or "does not descend to the lower palace".

To show that those who desire protection for more than one night have such a nature, he said: "these five", and so on. ## 8. Commentary on the Chapter on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka)

## Commentary on the Duties of Incoming Monks (Āgantukavatta)

Even within a single village, a monk coming from another monastery is also an āgantuka (incoming monk). Regarding this term āgantuka, some teachers say: "If an āvāsika (resident) monk goes to a certain monastery and returns, it is said that 'he too should eat the āgantuka-meal'; therefore, it refers to coming from a distance, not within the village. Thus, [to say one is an āgantuka just by coming from another monastery] is not appropriate."

Those teachers should be told: "The so-called āgantuka-meal is permanently established by laypeople. Where it is permanently established, it carries the meaning of coming from another village. Similarly, because of the jurisdiction of the monastery, a monk coming from another monastery is also an āgantuka." This is the conclusion of the teachers. Regarding the phrases "one should ask for drinking water, one should ask for utility water," the teacher says that the first refers to water in pots, cups, etc., and the second refers to water in wells, ponds, etc. In the second instance, because it is one's own dwelling place, it must be asked for separately; therefore, it is said, "or a village with designated almsfood." In many palm-leaf manuscripts, both versions are appropriate.

## Commentary on the Duties of Giving Thanks (Anumodanāvatta)

362-4. In the fifth [sentence], while sitting for the purpose of giving thanks (anumodanā). "The place where people serve" is written as the place where people live with their wives and children and give offerings. In this Khandhaka, there are 14 great duties (mahāvatta): the duty of incoming monks (āgantukavatta), the duty of resident monks (āvāsikavatta), the duty of departing monks (gamikavatta), the duty of giving thanks (anumodanāvatta), the duty of the refectory (bhattaggavatta), the duty of the alms-round (piṇḍacārikavatta), the duty of forest-dwellers (āraññakavatta), the duty of lodgings (senāsanavatta), the duty of the sauna (jantāgharavatta), the duty of the latrine (vaccakuṭivatta), the duty of the preceptor (upajjhāyavatta), the duty of the teacher (ācariyavatta), the duty of the co-resident (saddhivihārikavatta), and the duty of the pupil (antevāsikavatta). If counted without taking repetitions, there are 80 Khandhaka duties.

402-3. "Sūnehi" means "sutehi," which means having flowing blood. "Setaṭṭhikā nāma roga-jāti" is the Pali text. "Setaṭṭhikā" is the Commentary. "Yadaggena" means starting from which day. "Tadeva" means on that very day. There is the text "anuññattiyā." The text "anupaññattiyā" is not good.

If it is asked: "Having said 'I accept the [Garudhamma] which are not to be transgressed for life,' why does she now ask for a boon?" It is to avoid the blame of others. 410-3. "Kammapattāyo pi" means those who are worthy of legal acts. "Āpattigāminiyo pi" means those who have fallen into an offense. "Dve tisso bhikkhuniyo" means together with two or three nuns. There is the text "manosilikāya."

"That monk should be invited" is said by way of showing respect (sāmīci).

422-3. "I allow... temporarily": The teacher says this refers to personal property, not communal (saṅghika) property. In serving food, if donors wish to offer the four requisites to the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha who have finished their meal, it must be according to seniority (vassa-order) only.

*Vikāla* means they invite until the wrong time (afternoon). *Ajjattanā* means until today.

*Anuvāda* refers to the position of authority (giving commands). All these words should be understood as being spoken for the purpose of laying down an offense for transgressing the *Garudhamma* (Heavy Rule) which was laid down as: "From today, the path of speech for Bhikkhunīs towards Bhikkhus is closed." Otherwise, there might be doubt as to whether, since the ordination (*upasampadā*) of Bhikkhunīs was granted upon the acceptance of these *Garudhammas*, they would cease to be ordained upon transgressing them.

*Itthiyutta* refers to traveling by a vehicle yoked with female animals such as cows at the front. *Purisantara* refers to traveling by a vehicle driven by a man. The phrase "with a male companion" means a vehicle where a man acts as the charioteer. Since it is stated "extremely unwell," it is clear that it is allowable for a sick Bhikkhunī to ride in a vehicle. The intention is: "I will receive ordination in a place permitted by the Blessed One after asking for permission."

"That Bhikkhunī, due to some danger" is a phrase encompassing all dangers. Therefore, the teachers say that instead of mentioning all those dangers, it should be established by the stated danger, "danger from kings" (*rājantarāyena*).

431-2. It is written: "Having performed a new work (*navakamma*), requesting 'Let her stay for this many years,' and giving communal (*saṅghika*) land." Because it is said "with a house" (*sāgāra*), some teachers say that rules such as the *rahonisajja* training rule related to houses are excluded; this is appropriate. Why? Because it is stated in the Commentary: "Except for merely sleeping with a house." Because of the statement "Monks, I allow [one] to support [one's mother]," all work related to supporting is allowable for a Bhikkhunī towards her mother, but not for others. If she cannot live without a companion, we hold that she should be given one only after formal agreement (*sammannitvā*). For how long? If the companion wishes to leave after staying, it is appropriate until another is appointed. The teachers say that she may have the child she has given birth to.

It is written: "This is allowed with reference to this [case] and is thus allowable; even if there is a discharge from one side or both sides, it is allowable." "Monks, I allow the act of hair-cutting and so forth"...
539:
Because it is said only "for the sake of consenting", it is said "for the sake of consenting to things other than that". The Blessed One did not say only this much: "Monks, I allow the act of cutting hair, etc."; rather, He preached "for the sake of consenting". Therefore, even if that Bhikkhunī has a discharge on both parts due to doubt, she reaches Pārājika through the domain of Pārājika. Thus, this decision is determined in all Commentaries. Since the specific designation has no distinction by other means, that decision alone is the standard. If that were the case, doubt would be allowable for a monk. That word refers only to the time, not to a being. If so, it was preached referring to the time for the Bhikkhunī only. In this way, the Pārājika offense would be made light. In all Pārājikas, the door of opportunity is completely closed. Because it is useless in the Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍala training rule, therefore, based on the sequence of the introductory words "they do not consent", the Blessed One preached "for the sake of consenting", and not otherwise. That Blessed One who prohibited consenting to one's own touch—how would He give opportunity in the domain of Pārājika? However, the wise ones who speak according to what was spoken by the Buddha to the sons of the Buddha and who coordinate the words say: "Only our words are logical here." Because the act of cutting hair, etc., must certainly be done, because of the extreme fickleness of the mind, and because of the completeness of the factors of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, did not the Great Sage act with reference to protecting the Bhikkhunīs and to the absence of doubt?

## 11. Pañcasatikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Commentary on the Introductory Account of the Recital
'Chinnapātaṃ' is a neuter action noun. It means falling in that broken manner. 'Upaddutā ca mayaṃ homa' uses the present tense in the sense of the past; it means 'ahumhā' (we were). Alternatively, it means we were oppressed while that Gautama was alive. Having stated 'pañca bhikkhusatāni' (five hundred monks) by way of number, the designation of persons is made as 'vassaṃ vasantā' (spending the rainy season).

## Commentary on the Account of Minor and Lesser Rules
From the words 'stepping on the rainy-season robe,' it is clear that the Blessed One also had a fourth robe. For that very reason, it was said in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, 'He wore the fourth robe.'

'Api ca yatheva mayā' etc., is said with the intention of not including it in the recital. However, it means, 'Friends, the Dhamma and the Vinaya have been well recited by the elders.' In the place 'api cāhaṃ nāma... dhāressāmi,' it means: just as I heard in the presence of the Blessed One, just as I received in his presence, so too have the elders, upon whom the Blessed One himself conferred the foremost positions, (well recited). Therefore, it means the recital was well-preserved.

## Commentary on the Account of the Brahma-punishment
Although only 'you yourself command' was said, it should be understood that the elders, having imposed the Brahma-punishment, said 'to the monk Channa...' and so forth. In this matter, like the Elder Ānanda, another monk commanded by the Saṅgha is also allowed to speak with the monk who has been given the Brahma-punishment; no one else. 'Ujjavanikāya' refers to a boat going upstream. 'Āgamā nu kho idha', 'āgamā nu khvidha', 'āgamā kho idha', 'te orodhā idha āgamā kho' mean 'Did he come here?', 'Is there a coming here?', 'He has certainly arrived here', 'May your confession certainly come to this place.' 'Bhisicchavi' is written as 'bhisitthavikā' (a bolster case). 'Sabbe vime' means all of them. 'Kulavaṃ gamenti' means they lead to useless destruction. Detestable destruction is called 'kulava'. It means useless destruction. Although it should be called 'Dhamma-Vinaya Recital,' it is specifically called 'Vinaya Recital' here to show that the Vinaya is the root of the Dispensation, to demonstrate that when the Vinaya stands, the stability of the entire Dispensation is accomplished, because it began with the matter of 'this is allowable for you, this is not allowable,' and because this learning is the Vinaya Piṭaka.
