## 12. Sattasatikakkhandhakavaṇṇanā
## Commentary on the Account of the Ten Points
'Nikkhittamaṇisuvaṇṇā' refers to gems and gold that are rejected by the training rule itself. Therein, by the term 'maṇi' (gem), all matters of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) are included; by the term 'suvaṇṇa' (gold), all matters of expiation (pācittiya) are included. 'Bhikkhagga' means by the number of monks.

'Mahikā' means frost. 'Posā' means beings. 'Sarajā' means those who exist with the dust of defilements. 'Magā' means those who are like animals. Because it leads to various sense objects or to existence, it is called 'netti'; this 'netti' is a designation for craving (taṇhā). Because they exist together with that craving, they are called 'sanettikā'.

450-2. 'Ahogaṅga' is the name of a mountain. 'Anumānessāmā' means we will designate. 'Āsutā' means prepared; there is also a reading 'asuttā', meaning young monks who are not late and not yet mature.

'Ujjavimsu' means they went upstream.

'Appeva nāma' means 'it would be good.' The original donors were those who loved virtue. 'Kullakavihārena' is written as 'by a small dwelling.' Because it is merely an incarnation of form, it is called 'kullakavihāra.' How is this known? If a life-long (yāvajīvika) item that has been stored is mixed with a temporary (yāvakālika) item received that day, and the taste is mixed, how is it known that it becomes a 'kālika' received that day and falls under the category of stored food (āmissa)? It is said—because of the words 'Monks, a life-long item [mixed] with a temporary item received that day,' it is established that if a life-long item received previously is mixed with food (āmissa) received that day, it follows the designation of the item received previously. Otherwise, as in the place where it is said 'Monks, a life-long item received with a seven-day (sattāhakālika) item is allowable for seven days,' here too it would say 'Monks, a life-long item received with a temporary item is allowable during the [proper] time,' but it was not said so. Therefore, it should be understood that the life-long item received previously, when mixed with food (āmissa), follows the nature of food (āmissa). In the Gaṇṭhipada, however, it says 'a snack or food that has been stored.' One should not take only the literal expression.
542:
In this text, by the mere words "It is allowable at the proper time (kāla); it is not allowable at the wrong time (vikāla)", if one says "It is allowable at the wrong time", it means it brings the Pācittiya offense of eating at the wrong time. If one says "It is not allowable", it means it brings the Pācittiya offense of eating stored food (sannidhi-bhojana). If there is a mixed liquid, it is written that even if received today, it is "life-long" (yāvajīvika). "In the Suttavibhaṅga" means in the Sutta known as the Mātikā and in the Vibhaṅga known as the Padabhājanīya of that Mātikā. This decision has already appeared. Which decision? This decision: "Chedanaka (cutting off) for one who exceeds [the measure]". If the sitting cloth (nisīdana) is of the measure of three spans and has no fringe, how can it be a sitting cloth? For having a fringe is its characteristic. If that sitting cloth is of the measure of three spans and the fringe therein is one span, because that cloth is named "nisīdana", there should be "chedanaka" (cutting off) therein. It should not be said, "How can there be chedanaka in a cloth not named nisīdana?", because of the three-span measure of the nisīdana. How would the reason "a nisīdana with only a fringe is allowable" be suitable? This cloth with only a fringe does not have the name "nisīdana". Because it is called "nisīdana", because it exceeds the measure, and because of the reason of the permission for that nisīdana, there is "chedanaka" (cutting off) therein. In the rule on gold and silver—gold and silver are prohibited for an individual in the Pāḷi, but not for the Saṅgha. Therefore, if it were entirely allowable for the Saṅgha, and eating at the wrong time is also prohibited for an individual but not for the Saṅgha—if that were so, how would the word "it is allowable for the Saṅgha" be consistent?

## Explanation of the Parivāra
## Homage to Him, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One
## Explanation of the Chapter on Designations
## Explanation of the Sixteen Great Chapters
1-2. It means in the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed One who possesses the body of the Dhamma-aggregates known as virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana). "Parivāra" refers to that Parivāra text which was included in the Council; the designation which is the Vinaya is called the Vinaya-paññatti. Having spoken by the method of dyads (duka) as "one who knows the time of designation", it is said "Furthermore, by means of past lives, etc." to speak by the method of the Suttanta. Therein, "seeing" (passana), having the sense of seeing, is the knowledge and vision of penetration associated with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). "One who sees with the wisdom of teaching" refers to the Blessed One who sees the latent tendencies (āsayānusaya), etc. The word "pucchāya" is in the locative case (sattamī). "Punapi ettha" refers to the questions and answers. "Wrong view" (micchā-diṭṭhi) refers to the view of nihilism (natthika-diṭṭhi) and the view of extremist graspings (antaggāhika-diṭṭhi). Because of the words "designated for the sake of livelihood", it should be understood that, excluding these six training rules, the remaining are called "failure in conduct" (ācāra-vipatti). In this context of "reaching an offense by way of the body", one reaches the offense known as the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) which occurs by producing the intimation known as the bodily door, having made the mind desiring to indulge in the preliminary stage a factor. Although the intimation is produced by the mind, because the meaning intended by the mind is accomplished by the intimation, it is said "one reaches [the offense] by the bodily door"; this is said with reference to this meaning, not with reference to the subsiding of the three things such as quarreling. "Āpāṇakoṭikaṃ" means having made it last as long as life. "By the ancient Great Elders" means they were established at the time when the Great Elders in the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) committed [the scriptures] to books. It is said, "The Council that committed [the scriptures] to books was similar to the Fourth Council."

## Commentary on the Chapter of Committed Offenses (Katāpatti-vāra), etc.

In the Katāpatti-vāra, regarding the Pāḷi "a Saṅgha-owned bed (mañca) or...", because it occurs in the open, and because an offense can be committed even inside a monastery, it is stated by way of exceeding the distance of a stone's throw (leḍḍupāta). In the second training rule, "having spread the bedding" is stated as "exceeding the precinct (parikkhepa)" because, due to it being spread inside, if one goes outside the monastery and does not return on that day, an offense can be committed.

In the phrase "intentionally depriving a living being (pāṇa) of life, there are four offenses," although only animals are intended in that training rule, because the term "living being" (pāṇa) is common usage, it is stated as "four" by way of extracting the meaning. This method also applies to other such instances.

In the training rule on entering a village at an improper time (vikāla-gāma-pavesana), because it is said "with the first step, one exceeds the precinct; there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)," they say that the offense is not committed in the vicinity (upacāra), but the meaning is established that the offense is committed only after exceeding the precinct.

In the Chapter on Conditions (Paccaya-vāra), there is indeed a distinction from the previous chapter. If it is said, "How many offenses does one commit while practicing sexual intercourse (methuna-dhamma)?" there is no occasion for the training rule on the wooden block (jatumuṭṭhaka). However, in this Paccaya-vāra, because it is said "by reason of practicing sexual intercourse," and there is no designation of a person, the training rule on the wooden block is also included. Thus, there is a distinction. It is the same in other such instances.

## The Commentary on the Sixteen Great Chapters in the Mahā-vibhaṅga and the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga is finished.
545:
## Explanation of the Headings of Origination

"Anattā" means devoid of self, as in the case of "alavaṇabhojana" (saltless food) and so forth. He is like the moon because of His cooling nature of compassion. He is like the sun because He dispels the darkness of defilements. Because those Buddhas teach the True Dhamma, He is also called Aṅgīrasa. It means that He taught the three Piṭakas because of being one of those [who teach them].

If the Vinaya stands, it means that the True Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma) and so forth will continue to proceed and endure. If one asks, "How does this Vinaya stand?", He spoke the words beginning with "Ubhato ca" to answer that. It means they stand because they are bound together by the Parivāra. In the Sutta of that Parivāra, the fixed origination (niyata-samuṭṭhāna) is made or stated. "Asambhinna-samuṭṭhāna" means originations that are not mixed or not identical with others.

If the Parivāra exists, the Vinaya stands; if the Vinaya stands, the True Dhamma (the Sāsana) stands. Since the originations are also evident in the Parivāra Pāḷi, it means that one should learn the Parivāra. The words "Dhamma-kāmo supesalo" (one who loves the Dhamma and is well-behaved) were spoken to generate respect for the Parivāra. In that context, "tattha" refers to the word "dissanti". "Arises by one origination" means that the first pārājika offense arises due to one origination. The origination mentioned in the Pāḷi is also very clear. It means that in the previous method, it was said, "The origination of that Parivāra is always fixed and determined." "Yathāñāyaṃ" means according to reality. There is the reading "sañcarittābhāsanañca" as well as "sañcarittānubhāsanañca". "Nayavajjehi" means avoiding the Vinaya (vinaya-vajjehi).

## Explanation of the Origination of the First Pārājika

"Nānubandhe pavattiniṃ" refers to the training rule spoken as: "If a bhikkhunī does not follow for two years the female preceptor (pavattinī) who ordained her." This reading is not found in some books. There are seventy-six originations of the first pārājika.

## Explanation of the Origination of the Second Pārājika

In the phrase "kukkuccaṃ cīvaraṃ datvā," there is a reading: causing remorse, criticizing after giving consent to legal acts, and criticizing after giving a robe. Because the word "datvā" is stated out of order, they say that the reading "kukkuccaṃ dhammikaṃ datvā" is better. This point should be accepted after investigation. "Akataṃ" means new.

## Antarapeyyālaṃ
## Katipucchāvāravaṇṇanā
Paṭiniddesa means repeated explanation. 'Restraints trained by the groups of offenses' means restraints that are forbidden from the groups of offenses. Because it is spoken with the word 'ārakā' (far away) in the sense of removal from these groups of offenses, and wishing to state that essence personally again, He said 'bhusaṃ vā' (or intensely). It destroys the enmity of lust and so forth, just as in 'the house is full of smoke and fumigated.' It destroys by this abstinence (virati). The word 'vela' occurs in the sense of moving. It is called 'setu' (bridge) because it binds the path that leads out of the cycle of suffering. 'Setughāta' (destruction of the bridge) is said to be the abstinence which is the opposite of transgression, or the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that accomplishes the result of that abstinence. 'Dhammassavanagga' is written as the assembly of those listening to the Dhamma. If one does not go, or sits with a distracted mind, bodily impudence (kāyappāgabbhiya) is bodily misconduct. Having said 'pamāda' (negligence), to clarify the meaning of that word, 'sativippavāsa' (absence of mindfulness) is said.

272-3. In one's own continuity or in another's continuity. Those who dispute in such a way do so based on the grounds for causing a schism (bhedakaravatthu). By both senior and junior monks. The word 'naṃ' refers to loving-kindness of bodily action (mettā-kāyakamma). One should remember the Dhamma known as loving-kindness of bodily action for those persons to whom one shows love. The word 'ettakaṃ' (this much) shows the distribution of material things (āmisa). The word 'asukassa ca' (and to such a person) shows the distribution of persons. Because it is said 'it is also proper not to give to an immoral person,' the consumption by shameless persons (alajjī) is forbidden. Some say that by the decision 'it should only be given to all,' it shows the state of giving without making a distinction by one who does not know. In the Commentaries, it is said 'it should only be given to all.' In that regard, it is said 'others say that starting with the consumption by shameless and suspended (ukkhittaka) monks, it should not be given with one's own hand, but one should have it given [by others].' Giving after investigating is called 'viceyyadāna' (discriminating giving). Because this distinction must indeed be made, this monk does it; therefore, it is connected as 'not making a distinction of persons.' Having a dissimilar appearance from the natural appearance, they are called 'aparāmaṭṭhāni' (untouched) because they cannot be reproached by others saying 'he has committed such an offense.' One escapes by making Nibbāna the object with minds having suitable formations (saṅkhāra) as objects.

## Cha-āpattisamuṭṭhānavārādivaṇṇanā
'If asked whether one would fall into a Dubbhāsita offense by the first origin of offenses, it is said that one would not'—this is said because it is to be reached only by the power of speech and mind.
547:
Regarding the phrase 'constructing a hut' (kuṭiṃ karoti), this is stated here to show the sequential occurrence of the offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), grave offense (thullaccaya), and offense entailing a meeting of the Community (saṅghādisesa) in a single case, without mentioning the training rule on communication (sañcaritta). Indeed, it is not that one incurs an offense only in the training rule on communication. It is stated: 'In this way, the reason for not taking them sequentially in all training rules should be understood.'

'One who sees seclusion' (vivekadassī) refers to the Blessed One who sees the five kinds of seclusion, such as 'seclusion by substitution of opposites' (tadaṅgaviveka) and so on.

'One's own gross offense' (attano duṭṭhullaṃ) refers to the offense entailing a meeting of the Community (saṅghādisesa).

'By reason of a legal issue arising from disputes' (vivādādhikaraṇapစ္စယာ) means by reason of others or oneself having previously incurred an offense. 'He insults' (omasati) means that while disputing, 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya,' he insults by saying, 'What do you know?' and so on. It is settled by three ways of settling (samatha): settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya), settlement by admission (paṭiññātakaraṇa), and covering over as if with grass (tiṇavatthāraka). It is stated: 'Since settlement in the presence is desired in all formal acts of the Vinaya, it is also combined with two, such as "by settlement in the presence and by settlement by admission." This method applies everywhere.'

Regarding the phrase 'excluding the seven classes of offenses' (ṭhapeတွာ satta āpattiyo), it is stated: 'Even if the remaining offenses do not exist, the question is asked for the sake of sharpening the intellect in sequence.'

548:
## Explanation of the Distinctions of Settlements
## Explanation of the Section on Legal Issue Categories, etc.
293-4. Because one disputes due to the cause of greed, it is said: 'Greed is the precursor.' The same should be understood for the remaining terms. Terms such as 'basis' (ṭhāna) are synonyms for 'cause.' Because it stands in the cause, it is called 'basis' (ṭhāna); because it dwells in this, it is called 'ground' (vatthu); because it arises in this, it is called 'foundation' (bhūmi). What things stand, dwell, and arise? Legal issues arising from disputes and so on. Because they dispute with wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate thoughts, it is said: 'nine motives' (nava hetū). 'He is angry, he is resentful,' etc., are the twelve roots. Because a monk who reviles accuses with one of the four failures (vipatti), it is said: 'the four failures are the bases.' The twelve roots mentioned in the legal issue arising from disputes, together with body and speech, are called 'the fourteen roots.'

295-6. Regarding 'the seven classes of offenses are the bases,' it is stated that for a monk who incurs an offense and conceals it, whatever offense he has, the offense previously incurred is the basis for that offense. Because of the statement 'There is no wholesome in a legal issue arising from offenses,' there is no wholesome motive for a legal issue arising from offenses; however, a wholesome mind is an auxiliary factor (aṅga). Regarding 'the four formal acts are the bases,' the Pāḷi text that stands as 'this should be done' is called 'the formal act' (kamma). The performance of monks who act according to the established Pāḷi text is called 'a legal issue arising from duties' (kiccādhikaraṇa). Alternatively, the characteristic to be redressed according to the Pāḷi is the formal act; performing it in that way is the legal issue arising from duties. Formal acts with a motion (ñatti), with a motion and a second (ñattidutiya), and with a motion and a fourth (ñatticatuttha) arise from the motion. The formal act of announcement (apalokana) arises from the announcement. It is written that 'a legal issue arising from duties is settled and perfected by a single settlement.' 'Siyuṃ' means 'they are.' 'How would it be?' is a question asking how it occurs. Regarding 'two for a legal issue arising from disputes,' excluding those two, it cannot be settled by other settlements.

'Shared' (sādhāraṇā) means that legal issue arising from disputes should be settled.

'Belonging to that part' (tabbhāgiyā) means having that legal issue arising from disputes as its portion.

Wishing to ask whether all settlements, being in harmony, are capable of settling a single legal issue, he said: 'Settlements are shared with a settlement.' Some settlements are shared with a settlement, and some are not shared.
549:
The same method applies in the section on 'belonging to that part' (tabbhāgiyavāra) where settlements are shared with a settlement. This means: 'These settlements are just settlements, not settlement in the presence.'

Settlements are also called 'Vinaya'; therefore, the section on Vinaya (vinayavāra) should be extracted as 'Vinaya is settlement in the presence.' There may also be cases where settlement in the presence is not extracted. Therefore, excluding settlement in the presence, the remaining settlements such as the verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) and so on are shared.

When there is an admission in the presence of the Community, that admission is called 'presence of the Community' (saṅghasammukhatā). Therefore, referring to the mind of that person who admits, it is said: 'Settlement in the presence is wholesome,' and so on. Regarding 'There is no unwholesome settlement in the presence,' the settlement in the presence which has three factors—presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the person—does not exist apart from these presences. In that settlement in the presence, when performed with wholesome thoughts, it is wholesome. When performed by Arahants, it is indeterminate (abyākata). Since these are the opposites of the unwholesome, the occurrence of the unwholesome is impossible. Therefore, it is written: 'There is no unwholesome settlement in the presence.'

When settling a case by those who speak what is not Dhamma (adhammavādī), if a person who speaks the Dhamma (dhammavādī) causes the voting tickets to be taken, the settlement by majority (yebhuyyasikā) is wholesome. If those who speak the Dhamma also cause the voting tickets to be taken from those who speak what is not Dhamma, it is unwholesome. In all cases, it is indeterminate by power of an Arahant. For one who is not an Arahant, if he gives a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) intentionally, the verdict of mindfulness is unwholesome. If a verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya) is given to one who is not insane, it is unwholesome. If a settlement by admission (paṭiññātakaraṇa) is performed for one who is confused and does not know, it is unwholesome. If a verdict of further misconduct (tassapāpiyasika) is performed for one who is pure, it is unwholesome. It is written that covering over as if with grass (tiṇavatthāraka) is unwholesome if done because of great strife or if done intentionally.

## Explanation of the Section on Questions of 'Where'
'Is it obtained?' (labbhati) is the question (pucchā).

## Explanation of the Section on Answers regarding Settlements
'At the time when by settlement in the presence,' etc., is the answer (vissajjanā) to that question. At the time when a legal issue is settled by settlement in the presence and by settlement by majority, at that place where settlement by majority is obtained, there settlement in the presence is also obtained; thus it should be connected in all terms. In the case where 'where settlement by admission is obtained, there settlement in the presence is obtained,' whether for one, two, or many offenses...
550:
When a monk who has fallen into an offense is asked, "Have you fallen into such-and-such an offense?" and he admits the offense, saying, "Yes, I have," then both Paṭiññātakaraṇa (acting in accordance with the acknowledgement) and Sammukhāvinaya (verdict in the presence) are obtained. In obtaining them, within the Sammukhāvinaya described as Saṅghasammukhatā (presence of the Saṅgha) and Dhammavinayapuggalasammukhatā (presence of the Dhamma, Vinaya, and person), if the acknowledgement is made in the presence of the Saṅgha, it is Saṅghasammukhatā. If the confession (desanā) is made before that very Saṅgha, then Dhammasammukhatā and Vinayasammukhatā are also obtained. If they acknowledge to one another without disputing, it is Puggalasammukhatā. If the confession is made in the presence of that person, then Dhammasammukhatā and Vinayasammukhatā are also obtained. Alternatively, when a single person confesses an offense in the presence of another single person, and when asked, "Do you see [the offense]?" he replies, "I see it," then in that situation, Sammukhāvinaya—comprising Dhammasammukhatā, Vinayasammukhatā, and Puggalasammukhatā—as well as Paṭiññātakaraṇa are obtained.

## Commentary on the Section on Association and Others
The settlement of legal issues (adhikaraṇa) is called samatha. That samatha cannot exist apart from a legal issue. Therefore, it is not possible to separate them and treat them as distinct entities.

309-310. In the phrase "Settlements (samathas) are settled by settlements," the word "settled" (sammanti) means they are accomplished. Or it means legal issues are settled, they are calmed. Therefore, by the Pali text "The majority decision (yebhuyyasikā) is settled by the verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya)," it means it is accomplished together with sammukhāvinaya, but not with sativinaya and so on. This is because sativinaya and the others do not assist that yebhuyyasikā procedure. In the phrase "Settlements are settled by legal issues," it means the settlements reach a state of non-existence.

There is a reading: "The verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya) is not settled by the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa)." Because it is similar to yebhuyyasikā, and because it is stated at the end that "The verdict in the presence is not settled by any settlement" (Pari. 313), it is said with the understanding that the verdict in the presence itself does not need to be settled by either a settlement or a legal issue. The verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) is settled by the legal issue of duties (kiccādhikaraṇa). The verdict of past insanity (amūḷhavinaya), the verdict of further misconduct (tassapāpiyasikā), and the covering over with grass (tiṇavatthāraka) are also settled by the legal issue of duties.

Regarding the statement "The legal issue of dispute is settled by the legal issue of duties," it is settled thus: "Venerable sir, let the Saṅgha listen to me... etc... I first cast the voting ticket." In this way, the legal issue of dispute is settled by the legal issue of duties. The legal issue of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa) and the legal issue of offenses (āpattādhikaraṇa) are also settled by the legal issue of duties. "An act not performed is a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)"—in this way, the legal issue of duties is also settled by the legal issue of duties...
551:
It is written that the reading 'sammati' should be known in this way. In another glossary (gaṇṭhipada), however, it is said: 'In the phrase "settlements (samatha) are settled by legal issues (adhikaraṇa)," since all settlements are settled by the legal issue of duties (kiccādhikaraṇa), the reading "settlements are settled by the legal issue of duties" should be taken.' What legal issue does the legal issue of dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) originate? By merely saying 'this is not the Dhamma,' it does not originate any legal issue.

318-9. There is the reading 'In which legal issue is it included?' 'The legal issue of dispute resorts to the legal issue of dispute' means a later dispute resorts to an earlier dispute. 'The legal issue of dispute resorts to two settlements' means it is like approaching someone saying 'you are able to settle this legal issue,' or it means it is included by two settlements like those saying 'we shall settle that legal issue.'

## Explanation of the Numerical Method (Ekuttarikanayavaṇṇanā)
## Explanation of the Chapter of Ones (Ekakavāravaṇṇanā)
In the Numerical Method, where it is said, "An offense should be known," the question arises: Is what is called an 'offense' (āpatti) an ultimate reality (paramattha) or a nature that is 'not-to-be-declared' (navattabba, i.e., conventional)? It is indeed a nature that is 'not-to-be-declared'. For in the Parivāra, in the detailed analysis of these terms—"The object (vatthu) should be known, the lineage (gotta) should be known, the name (nāma) should be known, the offense (āpatti) should be known"—it is stated: "Sexual intercourse is both the object and the lineage. Pārājika is both the name and the offense."

According to the words "Name and lineage do not decay," name and lineage are merely conventional (sammuti). Therefore, it is said, "It is merely a certain conventional designation (sammuti-paññatti) which is liberated from the Wholesome Triplet and is a nature that is 'not-to-be-declared' (navattabba-dhamma)."

In the Chapter on Settlement (Samathakkhandhaka), the statement "A legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome (akusala) or indeterminate (avyākata)" is spoken figuratively (pariyāya), just as in the statement "A legal issue arising from a dispute (vivādādhikaraṇa) may be wholesome (kusala), unwholesome, or indeterminate." In truth, what is called a dispute is merely a specific conventional designation. Based on the mind of the person endowed with mind, it receives the designation "it may be wholesome" and so on through the figurative use of that mind. A legal issue arising from an offense should be understood in the same way. Thus, it is stated in the Commentary: "A monk committing an offense does so either with an unwholesome mind or with a wholesome or indeterminate mind."

Otherwise, the state of being something to be settled by the Settlements (samatha) would not be possible. Indeed, the Settlements do not proceed by taking wholesome or unwholesome states as their primary object, nor are wholesome states and so on accomplished by the power of the Settlements. It is not the case that a wholesome dispute or a wholesome accusation must be settled by wholesome Settlements; if that were so, their status as legal issues (adhikaraṇa) would not even be possible. Therefore, the wholesome nature and so on of legal issues and Settlements can only be obtained through figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā) and not otherwise. For this reason, the triplet (tika) is not completed in a legal issue arising from an offense, just as in the Settlement in the Presence (sammukhāvinaya).

For a monk who commits an offense while knowing clearly, the volition (cetanā) is strictly unwholesome. In other cases, whether in offenses with intention (sacittaka) or without intention (acittaka), it is called "indeterminate" (avyākata) based merely on the absence of that [unwholesome] volition. Just as in such passages as "If he should have that robe produced after requesting it three times, this is wholesome (kusala)," the word 'wholesome' does not mean 'having happy results' (sukhavipāka); and just as in "For the sake of warding off unwholesome states belonging to the future life," they are not [technically] unwholesome minds; so too in other cases...
553:
...in offenses with intention (sacittaka) or without intention (acittaka), it is called "indeterminate" (avyākata) based merely on the absence of those wholesome or unwholesome states. Indeed, it is like the case where one has a robe produced after requesting it twice (or three times). In this context, regarding the text which says "A legal issue arising from an offense is unwholesome," by the power of that text, seven settled cases (vinītavatthu) should be known from that unwholesome state. Furthermore, because the possession of a robe is possible, monks without robes may also commit intermediate offenses (antarāpatti). One should also know what is called 'fixed' (niyata) by the power of one who has reached the characteristics of an immediate (anantariya) deed. In the conventional description (sammuti-niddesa), descriptions of grave (garuka) and light (lahuka) offenses are also possible. In another way, they are called "obstruction-causing faults by regulation (antarāyika-paṇṇattivajja)" and "faultless faults by regulation (anavajja-paṇṇattivajja)." Offenses regarding hut-building (kuṭikāra) and large dwellings (mahallaka) are called 'obstruction-causing' because they are worldly faults (lokavajja) and blameworthy regulations (sāvajjapaṇṇatti). Deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda) would not be graver than insulting speech (omasavāda) and so on, or this offense is lighter than that offense—all this is the view of some teachers. Others say, "All that is incorrect."

Why? Because if an offense were a nature that is 'not-to-be-declared' (navattabba-dhamma) by the words "Pārājika is both the name and the offense," then the object (vatthu) would also be a nature that is 'not-to-be-declared', because it is spoken of as having the same basis as lineage (gotta). Therefore, the term "sexual intercourse" (methunadhamma) indicates the object which is called 'transgression' (ajjhācāra). Because the name obtained for the offense solely by the power of transgression is a specific name, it is also called "lineage" (gotta). This is the meaning in that text.

Regarding the questions: "What is the precursor of a legal issue arising from an offense? Greed is the precursor, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are the precursors," and "How many roots? Six roots: three unwholesome roots and three indeterminate roots," it is stated directly (nippariyāyena) that "A legal issue arising from an offense may be unwholesome or indeterminate." However, in the Chapter on Settlement (Samathakkhandhaka), it was stated in that manner by way of an intentional utterance (sandhāyabhāsita). Therefore, a legal issue arising from an offense, by its nature and directly, consists of the four unwholesome mental aggregates and indeterminate matter (rūpa-avyākata). Because it is said, "There is no wholesome legal issue arising from an offense," only the wholesome is excluded. For Arahants, there is what is called 'functional indeterminate' (kiriya-avyākata); thus, when the wholesome is excluded, the functional indeterminate is also excluded. When that is excluded, the resultant indeterminate (vipāka-avyākata), which is inactive in every way, is also excluded. Some teachers say there is nothing to be said regarding the indeterminate that is Nibbāna; that statement is incorrect because it is said there are "six roots." Even if it is said in a general sense, nevertheless, only the resultant roots (vipāka-hetu) are intended there, not the functional roots (kiriya-hetu), because those functional roots have a nature similar to the wholesome. Therefore, matter (rūpa) and resultant indeterminate are the grounds for an offense. In that context, the settled cases (vinītavatthu) should be known from the unwholesome offense. For the other [offense] also, it is said that the concealment at the beginning is due to an unwholesome mind.
554:
This is the intended meaning. The state of being a prescribed fault that is obstructive, fixed, and blameworthy should also be understood through synonyms in the context of faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), worldly faults (lokavajja), and the offense committed. Therefore, just as it is said, 'The life faculty (jīvitindriya) may have an object or may not have an object,' so too, worldly faults which are definitely unwholesome or not definitely unwholesome, the reporting of a superhuman state (bhūtārocana) which is definitely indeterminate (abyākata), and the remaining faults by regulation which are not definitely indeterminate—all these are grouped together and it is said: 'A legal question concerning an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome (akusala) or may be indeterminate (abyākata).'

However, in the Samathakkhandhaka, this is said with reference only to faults by regulation. Indeed, it is stated in the Commentary and the Gaṇṭhipada: 'A legal question concerning an offense may be unwholesome, it may be indeterminate; there is no legal question concerning an offense that is wholesome (kusala).' Here, the meaning should be understood according to the intended sense. For instance, in a legal question concerning an offense such as digging the earth, with reference to one unskilled in the Vinaya, when one performs actions like clearing green grass, the wholesome mind is a factor (aṅga), but the physical indeterminate state known as the effort (payoga) of digging, etc., is what gives rise to the offense. This is the intention.

Regarding the statement, 'One with a wholesome mind commits an offense, one with a wholesome mind emerges from an offense,' etc., when such a mind exists, it cannot be said that 'there is no legal question concerning an offense that is wholesome.' Since this was not said with reference to the mind that gives rise to the offense, this statement was not made with reference to the mind that is sufficient as a factor (aṅgappahonakacitta). If it were said with reference to that sufficient mind, it should have been said 'it may be wholesome,' but it was not so said.

Therefore, this is said with reference to the following: Firstly, whatever legal question concerning an offense is a worldly fault (lokavajja), that is definitely unwholesome; there is no alternative such as 'it may be unwholesome.' However, regarding a legal question concerning an offense that is a fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), because it is unwholesome only for one who transgresses intentionally (sañcicca), thinking 'I will transgress this offense,' but for one who commits it unintentionally (asañcicca) without knowing anything, such as through sleeping together (sahaseyya), etc., it is a physical resultant indeterminate state due to the lack of arousal (anuṭṭhāna). Therefore, with reference to this alternative state of the fault by regulation through being intentional or unintentional, it is said: 'A legal question concerning an offense may be unwholesome, it may be indeterminate; there is no legal question concerning an offense that is wholesome.'

If some person unskilled in the Vinaya should say, 'That which one commits with a wholesome mind is called a wholesome legal question concerning an offense,' for such a proponent, even for those origins without consciousness (acittaka) such as sheep's wool (eḷakaloma), etc., at the time when one is endowed with a wholesome mind, those offenses would be committed with a wholesome mind, or else...
555:
...one commits the offense. Why? Because the wholesome mind present at the time of committing that offense is not a factor (aṅga) of the offense. 'Attabhāva' means nature (sabhāva), the natural state. If it is asked, 'What then is the nature of the factor of that offense at that time?' It is said: It is either the body moved by the power of bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) or the speech uttered; one of these two—the moved body or the uttered speech—is the nature of the factor. And because that body and speech are included in the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), they are indeterminate (abyākata). What is meant? It means that at that time, the body and speech are the legal question concerning the offense (āpattādhikaraṇa). Now, at the moment of an unwholesome offense, the indeterminate state of the body and speech is 'non-conventional' (abbhohārika), just like the mental action at the time of bodily or vocal action. In truth, at that time, the body and speech stand in the position of 'producers of offenses' (āpattikara), etc. With reference to this standing, it was said: 'The things that produce offenses should be known. How many are the roots? The six origins of offenses (āpattisamuṭṭhāna) are the roots,' and so on. When the body and speech are indeed the factors of the offense, then, just as in the statement 'The mind is the chief of the mind,' because the preceding efforts are the conditions for the subsequent efforts, they do not abandon the designation of 'producers of offenses,' etc. Even though that state exists, just as it is said, 'How many are the bases of a legal question concerning an offense? The seven classes of offenses are the bases. How many are the planes? The seven classes of offenses are the planes,' so too, even when there is the production of an offense, those things that produce the offense are simply called 'origins of offenses' (āpattisamuṭṭhāna).

By this sequence of words, what is called an 'offense' consists of the four unwholesome aggregates. At the time of intentional transgression, excluding the training rule on reporting a superhuman state (bhūtārocana), all offenses are generally unwholesome. Specifically, however, all offenses are definitely unwholesome (ekanta-akusala). The not-definitely unwholesome (anekanta-akusala) offenses are of ten kinds, such as the training rules on mountain-top festivals (giraggasamajja), picture galleries (cittāgāra), wearing a waist-string (saṅghāṇi), feminine ornaments (itthalankāra), perfumes and unguents (gandhavaṇṇaka), scented oil-cake (vāsitapiññāka), and the various types of massaging or rubbing of bhikkhunīs, etc. These offenses, distinguished by their own names, are unwholesome only at the time of awareness (sacittaka), which is the knowledge of the object. In the absence of that, at the time of lack of awareness (acittaka), for a monk who transgresses those various objects with a wholesome mind—such as meditation, etc.—apart from the legal question concerning the offense, the offense is merely physical indeterminate (rūpa-abyākata).

In this decision, some teachers explain: 'An offense is committed even by a bhikkhunī who wears a waist-string (saṅghāṇi) thinking it is a hip-string (kaṭisuttaka) in an unlit place, or who uses perfumes and unguents (gandhavaṇṇaka), etc., thinking it is fine clay; therefore, it is purely without awareness (acittaka).' Those teachers' views should be rejected by pointing out the absence of a text saying, 'There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for a bhikkhunī who wears a waist-string perceiving it as not a waist-string.' However, the offense of drinking intoxicants (surāpāna), even if without awareness (acittaka), is definitely unwholesome (ekanta-akusala).
556:
Therefore, it was stated (in the Pācittiya Pali): "Even if one drinks an intoxicant thinking it is a non-intoxicant, there is a Pācittiya offense." In this training rule on drinking intoxicants (surāpāna), even if there is a reason such as illness, it is not possible to drink without an unwholesome mind. Thus, unlike in the case of worldly faults (lokavajja) which are not invariably unwholesome as mentioned before, it is not stated here that "there is no offense in drinking intoxicants due to the reason of illness." However, intoxicants used in cooking and such are indeed not intoxicating substances. To dispel the remorse (kukkucca) [of monks] regarding such intoxicants used in cooking, it is stated "there is no offense," just as in the case of water and tooth-sticks. The offense of announcing actual [attainments] (bhūtārocana) is only material indeterminate (rūpabyākata). The offense of sleeping together (sahaseyya) and such, which occurs when one is unconscious (asleep), is only material resultant indeterminate (rūpavipākabyākata). In that offense of sleeping together, the unwholesome state existing during a dream is also negligible (abbohārika) because the factors are not complete. Regarding wholesome states (kusala), there is no need to speak [of offenses], as wholesome states are by nature "no offense" (anāpatti). Functional states (kiriya) are also the same. In this way, it is shown that in all training rules, as may be the case, there are three divisions: unwholesome, pure material, or material with result.

Among those training rules, excluding drinking intoxicants (surāpāna), if a certain training rule is a fault by regulation (paṇṇattivajja) and is also invariably unwholesome, it is only with intention (sacittaka). Announcing actual [attainments] (bhūtārocana) is only without intention (acittaka). The remaining training rules, including drinking intoxicants, are worldly faults (lokavajja) that are not invariably unwholesome, and faults by regulation (paṇṇattivajja) that are not invariably indeterminate; for the most part, all training rules have three divisions as they can be both with intention and without intention. Among these training rules, those that are only with intention (sacittaka) are so only because of the mind that knows the object (vatthu), such as sexual intercourse (methuna). All training rules for training (sekhiya) are with intention only because of the mind that knows the regulation (paṇṇatti), according to the statement "due to disrespect." Thus, there are two kinds of "with intention" (sacittaka). Invariably "without intention" (acittaka) occurs because of the absence of the mind that knows the regulation, not because of the absence of the mind that knows the object. Due to the absence of those two types of mind, drinking intoxicants (surāpāna), which is invariably unwholesome, and the act of acting as a go-between (sañcaritta), which is invariably indeterminate, are "without intention" (acittaka) by way of being without intention due to the absence of both the mind knowing the object and the mind knowing the regulation. However, drinking intoxicants is "with intention" (sacittaka) only by the mind knowing the object. For Noble Ones (ariya) and others, the remaining training rules are both with and without intention due to the presence of both minds or either one. Specifically, they are "without intention" (acittaka) by way of being without intention due to the absence of the mind knowing the object, or due to the absence of the mind knowing the regulation in one who is not proficient in the Vinaya. Among those training rules, both invariably "without intention" and "with intention" are simply called "without intention" (acittaka). This is the decision regarding the phrase "the offense should be known" (āpatti jānitabbā).

"An intervening offense by way of original purification" (mūlavisuddhiyā antarāpatti) refers to an offense committed by one who, having fallen into an intervening offense, is staying while undergoing the act of sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana). This is [the decision] by way of purification of value (agghavisuddhiyā)...
557:
An intervening offense (antarāpatti) refers to an offense committed by a monk who, having fallen into many offenses, is staying while undergoing combined probation (agghasamodhāna) based on the offense concealed for the longest time. The confession is made with an energetic mind, thinking, "I will offend again." It is written that this confession of an offense that enters into the count (gaṇanūpagama) is only for bhikkhunīs. The phrase "it is only a Parājika" (parājikam-eva) is also stated to show it by way of what is evident. Although other teachers say, "In such a confession, any offense without a specific mark does not rise [is not cleared]," it is stated that their word should not be accepted. Because it is stated, "due to not making true a righteous promise," there is no dukkaṭa offense in an unrighteous promise. It is stated that if a monk with a pure mind previously is told, "You all should disrobe," and he agrees saying "Very well," but does not actually disrobe, there is no offense; this same method applies to all agreements. There is also the Pali: "The one who makes it known should be known" (āvikaro jānitabbo). [It should be known] in the fifteen factors such as "I shall speak at the right time, not at the wrong time." One called "capable of offense" (bhabba-āpattika) is one who is liable to fall into an offense.

## Explanation of the Section on Dyads (Duka-vāra-vaṇṇanā)
Placing in the heat of the sun (nidahana). A monk who has an offense stated as "If a monk should stay apart from his triple robe (ticīvara) even for one night... for a maximum of six nights..." and so on, even if he completes the group, he causes the legal act (kamma) to fail because he is of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka). In the phrase "either by a legal act or by taking voting tickets," the recitation (uddesa) and the legal act (kamma) are one and the same. Here, recitation of the Pātimokkha and legal act are identical in meaning. The meaning is that if either of these two is performed, a schism of the Sangha (saṅghabheda) occurs. "Preliminary parts" (pubbabhāga) refers to the parts prior to the schism of the Sangha. In the word "measure" (pamāṇa), it is stated that the schism occurs by either of these two—recitation or legal act—and not by others such as taking voting tickets. "Established in the Vinaya" (vinayasiddhā); "Roman" (romaka) because it is produced in the Roman region; it is mentioned in the Dyads because it is a permitted salt.

## Explanation of the Section on Triads (Tika-vāra-vaṇṇanā)
You should not address (vo tumhehi na samudācaritabbaṃ). "Having performed a physical action associated with speech" means having performed an act of respect with the body. "In destruction" (upaghāte) means it destroys. "Having oppressed" (omadditvā) means having overcome. "Of the one who speaks" (vadato) means of the speaker. Although it comes in the Dyads that "dependence (nissaya) should be given to a fool," here in the Triads it is stated "it should not be given." This refers to not giving it to a person who has many offenses. The meaning is that if it is said, "Do not depart from this monastery to another; go to the experts in Vinaya (vinayadhara) to receive a decision," his word should not be accepted. What is called "eating in a triad" (tikabhojana) is if three monks eat together...
558:
This triad is stated with reference to the non-occurrence of an offense through group meals (gaṇabhojana). "Pasutta" is a word spoken in terms of majority. Or, it means having fallen asleep. When it is requested, "I shall leave this object and go; Venerable Sirs, please lend it to me for a while," it is written that "it is not proper to give it except for the purpose of new construction (navakamma) and so forth." It means that a monk who wears a rainy season robe (vassikasāṭika) that has been assigned (vikappanā) on the first day of the final [month of the season] incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "Apaccuddharitvā" means without having withdrawn [the assignment] (paccuddharaṇa). Because of the statement "Perform the assignment (vikappanā)," it should be understood that it is stated to show that an offense is incurred in the winter season due to the cause of not performing the assignment, and that the assignment must be performed on the full moon day of Kattika. This method is stated with reference to not performing the assignment, while the previous method is stated with reference to the offense arising from the use of a robe that has been assigned. "Vatthapaṭicchādi sabbakappiyatāya" means because covering with cloth is allowable in all respects. Some teachers, without carefully noting this meaning, write "vatthapaṭicchādi sabbakappiyatā tāya paṭicchannena." Since the analysis (vigraha) is "vatthapaṭicchādi" because the cloth itself is the covering, the word "tāya" is inappropriate. It should be "tena." All this is written in a certain glossary (gaṇṭhipada) and should be accepted after investigation.

## စတုက္ကဝါရဝဏ္ဏနာ

In this statement, "One incurs an offense in four ways ... one incurs an offense by a formal act (kammavācā)," if it is assumed that in an offense incurred by a formal act, the body and so forth are not present, then there would be seven factors that produce an offense along with the formal act. If that were the case, it would contradict the statement "six origins of offenses (āpattisamuṭṭhāna)." Only those six are the factors that produce an offense. If, in that offense as well, the body and so forth could be found either collectively or individually, then the statement "in four ways" would be inappropriate, and it should be said "one incurs an offense in six ways." Thus, these sutta-phrases appear contradictory. How are they not contradictory? They are not contradictory because of the distinction between that which is with intimation (saviññattika) and that which is without intimation (aviññattika). There is an offense which is an action (kiriyā) of the body and so forth; some such offenses are incurred by the body with intimation, some by speech with intimation, and some by both body and speech with intimation. There is an offense which is a non-action (akiriyā); some such offenses are incurred by a formal act (kammavācā). Even when incurred by a formal act, it occurs only through the remaining body and speech without intimation; it cannot occur without the body and speech. This is because of the statement: "If he does not relinquish it by body or by speech, at the conclusion of the formal act, he incurs a Saṅghādisesa offense." Or, in a general sense, some offenses are incurred by the body, some...
559: ...by speech, and some by both body and speech. Regarding this, the meaning should be understood as: some offenses are incurred by body and speech alone, and some are incurred through a formal act. In this way, they are not contradictory. Tatra yaṃ samāsato atthavibhāvanā—The brief clarification of the meaning in that sequence of words is: "one incurs an offense by the body" means one reaches some offenses by performing what should not be performed with the body with intimation, or by not performing what should be performed with the body without intimation. Both of these are called bodily action (kāyakamma). In the world, even what is not done is called "done". Just as it is said, "I have done wrong; I have not done good," etc., and in the Dispensation, "Friend Ānanda, this is a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for you, that you did not ask the Blessed One," etc. Similarly, in this Vinaya method, even non-action by the body is called "bodily action". This same method applies to the phrases "one incurs an offense by speech", etc. He is called "purisa" (man) because he goes in front. The word "pura" is used in the sense of going first. He goes in front; he is the leader in all actions. "By way of being first produced" means that in the beginning of the aeon, the male faculty (purisaliṅga) appears first; it means the male faculty, which has reached the designation "purima" (first), arises. In the phrase "and the one hundred and thirty", the unshared (asādhāraṇa) Pārājika offenses are also included. This is because monks who have reached a Pārājika are unfit for monkhood. They also say, "They are extracted by way of the unshared term in a general sense." They also say there is a reading, "one hundred and thirty training rules (sikkhāpada)". Regarding the four Pārājikas shared by monks and nuns, the first question, "There is diversity of basis (vatthu) but no diversity of offense (āpatti)", is here called the second question. There is no difference by this section: "There is similarity of offense but no similarity of basis." "Mantābhāsā" means speech spoken with wisdom. "Those worthy of being saluted" means they salute by raising their heads even while sitting. From the ninth nun onwards, they do not rise from their seats because they should not rise. "Avisesena" (without distinction) refers to anyone who is an elder, whether it be the preceptor (upajjhāya) or another, who approaches a monk who is in the middle of a meal. Even while eating, one should rise and offer a seat. Even one who says, "These are not allowable in this place," while staying in border regions, incurs an offense of wrong-doing for transgressing the Vinaya (vinayātisāra-dukkaṭa). To say "it is not allowable" regarding what is allowable is called destroying the regulation. Similarly, regarding the statement "these are allowable in this place", etc., it means that a monk who is proficient in the Vinaya and says "these are allowable in this place" should not be questioned about the Vinaya.
560:
## Explanation of the Section of Fives (Pañcakavāravaṇṇanā)
The person does not approach. Because of the word, “Being invited and having a meal, without asking a resident monk” (Pācittiya 299), since there is no invitation, it is allowable for a monk who observes the ascetic practice of alms-round (piṇḍapātika) to go about without asking permission (anāmantacāra). Having made an intention with “time of illness” etc., and determining the food, it is called eating. This is not making an assignment (vikappanā) such as, “I give my expectation of a meal to such and such a person.” Speaking ill behind one’s back is called disrepute (ayasa). Blaming to one’s face is called reproach (garahā). Since loss of virtue (sīlavyasana) and loss of view (diṭṭhivyasana) are included in the Vinaya, they are mentioned along with other losses such as loss of relatives (ñātivyasana) to complete the group of five (pañcaka). Because it is said, “by a group with a Vinaya-holder as the fifth,” it becomes a group of five (pañcaka). In a certain monastery, it means one elder. “From the Yonaka country” is decided as being from the region of Cīna (China). “Recollects eight aeons” means he brings about the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa). It means standing in an immediate place. “Reaching the act by the motion (ñatti)” means at the time the motion is set, it reaches the act. Again, the completion of the act is by the formal announcement (kammavācā). Ñattikhetta means the place where only the motion is to be performed, the limit (khetta) of that motion. In acts like the motion-and-one-proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma), the first setting of the motion is called its occasion (okāsa). In living in a forest monastery, one should desire the benefit of forest-dwelling (araññavāsa) such as, “this and that benefit exists.”

## Explanation of the Section of Sixes (Chakkavāravaṇṇanā)
It is said thus because there is a text in the Vibhaṅga: “It should be worn for a maximum of six years.” Fourteen maximums (paramatā) become nine groups of six (chakka). How? First, one group of six; among the remaining eight terms, one with each, thus three groups of six are mentioned in the internal abridgment (antarapeyyāla). How is it mentioned? By the method, “By the fourth origin of an offense, one incurs six offenses,” etc., along with the fifth and sixth origins, there are three groups of six. There are six roots of dispute (vivādamūla) such as greed, etc. Likewise, there are six roots of accusation (anuvāda). The rainy-season cloth is six spans (vidatthi) in length. The robe of the Sugata (the Buddha) is six spans in width. In departing taking an unfinished robe, there are six ways of the Kathina privileges being removed: niṭṭhānantikā (ending in completion), sanniṭṭhāna, nāsana, savana, sīmātikkantikā (ending in crossing the boundary), and sahubbhārā (together with the removal). In the section on taking (samādāyavāra), there are also six, making two groups of six. In the group of seven (sattaka), there are seven including pakkamanantikā (ending in departure).
561:
## Explanation of the Section of Sevens (Sattakavāravaṇṇanā)
The points mentioned in the Section of Sixes should be applied by way of the sevens. Here, the fourteen maximums (parama) mentioned in the Section of Sixes should be applied by way of the sevens. At the dawn of the seventh day, it becomes an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya) means: “That monk should stay apart from that robe for a maximum of six nights; if he stays apart beyond that,” the robe thus mentioned becomes nissaggiya. In the Campeyyakkhandhaka, after the Sugata-cīvara-bhāṇavāra, it should be understood that there are groups of seven mentioned by the method: “But here, monks, there is no offense to be seen for the monk; the Saṅgha or several monks or a single person reproves him,” etc.

## Explanation of the Section of Eights (Aṭṭhakavāravaṇṇanā)
Performing the Uposatha etc. with that monk is a benefit; not performing is a disadvantage; therefore, it means “by seeing these eight benefits clearly.” It is said, “ill-fame (ayasa) and abuse (akkosa).” Before speaking, he has the thought, “I will speak a lie”; while speaking, he has the thought, “I am speaking a lie”; after speaking, he has the thought, “I have spoken a lie.” Covering view, patience, desire, nature, and perception, thus it is made unallowable (akappiya); it is made not-received, etc.—these eight are not exceeded. Ghee etc. becomes nissaggiya at the dawn of the eighth day. The higher ordination (upasampadā) of bhikkhunīs is called aṭṭhavācikā (eight-fold proclamation) because it is a motion-and-fourth-proclamation act (ñatticatutthakamma) in both the male and female Saṅghas. There are eight boons such as giving rainy-season cloths, etc.

## Explanation of the Section of Nines (Navakavāravaṇṇanā)
Nine monks divide it. It is a decision regarding nine types of meat, excluding human flesh. There are nine robes such as the double-layered robe (saṅghāṭī), etc., judged as “good or not good.” The meaning is that those robes should not be assigned (vikappetabbāni) from the time they are determined (adhiṭṭhita), and they should not be assigned without being relinquished (apaccuddharitvā) from the time they are determined. The robe of the Sugata is nine spans (vidatthi). By the method, “He exhorts a group of the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, perceiving them as a group,” etc., two groups of nine in the wrong act (adhammakamma) are mentioned by way of Pācittiya offenses.

## Explanation of the Section of Tens (Dasakavāravaṇṇanā)
By the method, “There is a minor legal issue, and it has not reached a decision,” etc., there are ten unrighteous takings of voting tickets (salākaggāha). The righteous ones, which are the opposite of those, are ten. In the Samathakkhandhaka...
562:
It should be connected as 'he is endowed with the aforementioned factors'. The phrase 'the ten [robes] including the saṃkaccika (breast-cloth) on one side' is stated because those robes are allowable. There are ten types of women, such as those protected by their mothers, and ten types of wives, such as those bought with wealth. The 'agreement for ordination' (vuṭṭhāpanasammuti) should be accepted [with the thought], 'Having given the agreement for training (sikkhāsammuti) to that bhikkhunī of ten years, she herself will be twelve years old at the time she reaches twelve years.' It is written: 'Starting from "he does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense" only for a Vinaya expert, and stating the five factors up to "both Pātimokkhas... in detail (anubyañjanaso)"; and again starting from "he does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense" and stating the five factors up to "he is not skilled in deciding legal issues (adhikaraṇa)"; these five and five factors respectively make ten.' The text 'Dependence (nissaya) is given to a bhikkhunī of ten years' is not found in some palm-leaf manuscripts; however, even if it is not there, the original text (pāṭha) indeed exists.

## Commentary on the Section of Elevens (Ekādasakavāra-vaṇṇanā)
They are not pure; they are not clear. 'Disease' (roga) means the danger of disease (rogātaṅka) or the obstacle of disease.

## The Explanation of the Numerical Method is Finished.

## Commentary on the Questions and Answers regarding the Observance (Uposathādipucchāvissajjanā-vaṇṇanā)
The talk on the Invitation (pavāraṇā), such as 'Venerable Sir, I invite the Saṅgha,' is just like in the verses on the disciplined (vinītagāthā).

## Commentary on the Exposition of the Benefits (Atthavasapakaraṇa-vaṇṇanā)
In the phrase 'depending on the ten benefits,' the excellence of the Saṅgha (saṅghasuṭṭhutā) occurs because of showing the special qualities in laying down each training rule, and because of seeing the disadvantages in not laying them down. In that context, in laying down an inherently wrong (lokavajja) rule that should not be laid down as far as possible, the purity of effort (payogavisuddhi) is the quality. However, regarding an inherently wrong rule of the Sekhiya class which should be laid down...
563:
...in laying down [such a rule], the purity of practice (paṭipattivisuddhi) is the quality. In laying down a rule prohibited by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), the purity of intention (āsayavisuddhi) is the quality because it brings about qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā). Therefore, it was said: 'A monk, being easy to support, easy to maintain, and having fewness of wishes, speaks in praise of one with fewness of wishes...' It should be understood that the purity of a recluse's conduct (samaṇācāra-visuddhi) is also his quality.

Alternatively, in laying down an inherently wrong rule (lokavajja), the excellence of the Saṅgha (saṅghasuṭṭhutā) occurs because the fault is obvious. In laying down a rule prohibited by regulation (paṇṇattivajja), the well-being of the Saṅgha (saṅghaphāsutā) occurs because the benefit is obvious. Likewise, it should be understood that by the first reason, there is the restraint of the shameless (dummanku), and by the second, the comfortable living of the virtuous (pesala). By the first, the taints (āsava) belonging to the future life are warded off; by the second, those belonging to the present life. Likewise, by the first, those who do not have faith are inspired with faith; by the second, those who have faith are further increased in faith. Likewise, by the first, the True Dhamma is made to endure; by the second, it amounts to supporting the Vinaya.

According to the method in the Parivāra, by the first reason, there is the cutting off of the faction of monks with evil desires (pāpiccha), and by the second, there is compassion for the laity. For it was said: 'The Tathāgata laid down training rules for the disciples depending on two benefits: for compassion toward the laity and for the cutting off of the faction of those with evil desires.' Likewise, it should be applied and understood by way of the enmities (vera), faults (vajja), and unwholesome states (akusala) belonging to the present and future lives. For it was said: 'The Buddha laid down... for the warding off of enmities in the present life, for the warding off of enmities in the future life...' and so on.

Furthermore, in this context, all that is connected with unrequested intimation (akata-viññatti), all that is connected with the harassment of the laity, and all that is connected with the protection of their faith and the non-destruction of their wealth, is called 'laid down out of compassion for the laity.' The training rules on the corrupter of families (kulatūsaka) and the group meal (gaṇabhojana) are laid down for the cutting off of the faction of those with evil desires. It should be understood that all inherently wrong rules (lokavajja) are for warding off enmities in the present and future lives, and the rule on making arrangements with a woman (mātugāma) is laid down for the restraint of enmities in the present life. Furthermore, in this context, the decision should be understood based only on the ten benefits from the beginning.

A training rule which is absolutely unwholesome
Due to the transgression of the basis (vatthu),
Is laid down for the excellence of the Saṅgha
Because it is inherently wrong (lokavajja),
Such as the Pārājika and so on.

A training rule where an offense occurs only
By knowing the regulation, and not otherwise,
Is laid down for the endurance of the Dhamma
Or for the purpose of inspiring faith.

The Sekhiya rules connected with the teaching of the Dhamma and others are called 'inherently wrong rules arising from regulation' (paṇṇattisambhava-lokavajja). Except for the rule on drinking intoxicants (surāpāna), all cases where an offense occurs when what is forbidden is done or what should be done is not done—even if there is no intention to transgress the basis or the regulation—should be understood as 'faults by regulation' (paṇṇattivajja). Among those training rules, a Pācittiya offense is incurred due to the transgression of a legal act (ukkoṭanaka). 'If any monk, having given his consent to formal acts that are in accordance with the Dhamma, should later engage in criticism, it is a Pācittiya offense. If any monk, while a discussion for a decision is going on in the Saṅgha...'
564:
If, while a decision of the Saṅgha is being made, one departs from the seat without giving consent, one commits an offense of Pācittiya. If a monk, having given a robe to a harmonious Saṅgha, later engages in criticism, he commits an offense of Pācittiya. Such rules are laid down for the well-being of the Saṅgha. An offense of Pācittiya is committed for prevarication and for harassing. Training rules such as Saṅghādisesa are laid down for accusing with Pārājika offenses and so on, in order to restrain the unvirtuous monks. Training rules such as those regarding intruding, expelling, and eavesdropping are laid down for the comfortable living of the virtuous monks. All 'worldly faults' (loka-vajja) are laid down to ward off the taints (āsavas) that occur in the present life and the future life. All 'faults by regulation' (paṇṇatti-vajja) are laid down to restrain the dangers that occur only in the present life. All training rules related to the laity are laid down to inspire faith in those without faith and to increase the faith of those who already have faith. Specifically, the training rule concerning the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice (samaṇuddesa), and generally, the training rules concerning the limitations of the four requisites, are laid down for the longevity of the True Dhamma. The discourse (sutta) beginning with "This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires" is the evidence in this matter. It should be understood that rules such as "An offense of Pācittiya is committed for disparaging the training rules and for deceiving" are laid down for the support of the Vinaya. If it is asked: For what purpose is this training rule, "An offense of Pācittiya is committed for destroying vegetation (bhūtagāma)," laid down? It is to inspire faith in those without faith and to increase the faith of those who already have faith. How?

Because of the perception of people who have the undistorted view that vegetation is alive,
And because they perceive that the son of the Buddha is destroying that vegetation, faith arises in the Buddha's disciple.
"How can a Sage, who does not even destroy this vegetation which is perceived as lifeless,
Ever take the life of another being, while he is blameless in the allowance of fish and meat?"
Thus, because of the perception that he might be destroying vegetation, faith arises in the Buddha's disciple.
"Since even these teachers of wrong views abstain from destroying vegetation,
The Sage also abstains from it for the sake of guarding the minds of the people."
In this way, there is an increase in the faith of those who already have faith.

Desiring to avoid the great blame that he destroys this tree which is guarded as lifeless,
By the power of craving for the enjoyment of secluded dwellings,
The Buddha laid down the training rule regarding the destruction of vegetation.
565:
Seeing the multitude of people who criticize a monk for eating meat which is lifeless, he abandoned the destruction of vegetation.

Because it is pure in three respects (tikoṭi-parisuddha), in the allowance of fish and meat, it should be understood that the allowance regarding meat was made because of the fear of falling into wrong views regarding the act of killing (pāṇātipāta).

It was laid down for the benefit of the unreflective people, out of compassion for other beings, and because of the fear of falling into the view that destroying vegetation constitutes the act of killing (pāṇātipāta).

In the matter of destroying vegetation, the Blessed One allowed figurative speech (pariyāya-vacana). He rejected meat specifically prepared for a monk because of the fear of falling into the evil of others. In this context, it should be understood that he allowed the monastery and the hut built under one's own direction to make known the absence of evil. In this Vinaya Piṭaka, various benefits known as specific purposes are spread throughout; therefore, this Vinaya Piṭaka should be known as the 'Atthavasa-pakaraṇa' (Treatise on the Reasons/Benefits).

## The Commentary on the Mahāvagga is finished.

## Commentary on the First Summary Verse
## Commentary on the Training Rules Laid Down in the Seven Cities

In another sense, the word 'vā' is a particle (nipāta) in the sense of accepting a statement. 'Aḍḍhuḍḍhasatāni' means three hundred and fifty (350). 'Viggaha' refers to the training rule on human beings (manussa-viggaha). 'Atirekaṃ vā' refers to the training rule on extra robes (atireka-cīvara) kept for more than ten days. 'Kāḷaka' refers to the training rule on black wool mentioned as 'suddhakāḷakānaṃ'. 'Bhūta' refers to the training rule on telling the truth about supernatural attainments (bhūtārocana). 'Paramparabhatta' refers to the training rule on consecutive meals (parampara-bhojana). 'Akkosa' among bhikkhunīs refers to the training rule: 'Whatever bhikkhunī should abuse or revile a bhikkhu'. 'Antaravāsaka' refers to the training rule on receiving a robe from an unrelated bhikkhunī. 'Rūpiya' refers to the training rule on transactions with money (rūpiya-saṃvohāra). 'Sutta' refers to the training rule on asking for yarn oneself and having weavers weave it. 'Ujjhāpanaka' refers to the training rules on complaining (ujjhāpanaka) and criticizing (khīyanaka). 'Pācitapiṇḍa' refers to the training rule on eating alms-food arranged by a bhikkhunī. 'Cāritta' refers to the training rule on going to a family's house without informing an existing monk while being invited for a meal. 'Cīvaraṃ datvā' refers to the training rule on [taking back] a robe after it was given by a harmonious Saṅgha. 'Vosāsantī' refers to the training rule where a bhikkhunī [gives instructions] while monks are eating after being invited to families' houses. 'Giraggacariyā' refers to the two training rules: 'Whatever bhikkhunī should not go to see dancing or singing' and 'Should not wander on tour during the rainy season (vassa)'. 'Chandadāneṇa' refers to the training rule on ordaining a probationer (sikkhamānā) by giving consent while undergoing a penance (pārivāsika).

There are the four Pārājikas, the training rule for bhikkhunīs on building a hut with one's own resources (saññācikakuṭi), the training rule on rugs mixed with silk (kosiyamiassa-santhata), the training rule on lying down with an unordained person, and the training rule on digging the earth. 'Gaccha devate' refers to the training rules on destroying vegetation (bhūtagāma) and pouring water containing living beings. 'Mahāvihāro' refers to the training rule on a large monastery (mahallaka-vihāra). 'Añña' refers to the training rule on prevarication (aññavādaka). 'Dvāra' refers to the training rule on the door-bolts (yāva-dvāra-kosa). There is also a reading: 'Anādariya-pācittīti ca sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno'. 'Payopāna' refers to the training rule on drinking with a 'suru-suru' sound. 'Eḷakalomāni patto ca' refers to the training rule on having sheep's wool washed and the training rule on asking for a bowl with fewer than five mends. 'Ovādo ceva bhesajjaṃ' refers to the training rule on giving exhortation after going to the bhikkhunīs' quarters and the training rule on asking for medicine beyond that. 'Suci araññako' refers to the two training rules: the needle-case made of bone, ivory, or horn, and living in a forest dwelling. 'Ovādo' refers to the training rule where a bhikkhunī does not go for exhortation or for the communal acts (saṃvāsa). The section beginning with 'The four Pārājikas' is a summary of the training rules laid down in the two cities.

## Catu-vipatti-vaṇṇanā

"Ekatiṃsā ye garukā" refers to the 8 Pārājikas common to both (Bhikkhus and Bhikkhunīs), the 13 Saṅghādisesas of Bhikkhus, and the 10 Saṅghādisesas of Bhikkhunīs. By way of common and uncommon, the 8 Pārājikas are called anavasesa (without remainder) offences. "Tadeva" refers only to sīlavipatti (failure in virtue). To show in detail, even the unasked question starting with "Pārājika" is answered. In that Pali, there is the reading "Yo cāyaṃ akkōsati hasādhippāyo". Setting aside the vipatti that comes by way of clarifying duṭṭhulla (gross) offences, he begins to answer the yāvatatiyaka (up to the third time) question according to the order asked. The Bhikkhunī who follows the one who is suspended (ukkhittaka) and the 8 yāvatatiyaka saṅghādisesas are called anantara (immediate) questions because they are asked here.

## Chedanaka-ādi-vaṇṇanā

The bed/couch exceeding measurement, the sitting cloth (nisīdana), the skin-eruption cloth (kaṇḍupaṭicchādi), the rainy-season garment (vassikasāṭikā), the robe measurement of the Sugata (the Buddha), and the water-cloth (udakasāṭikā) of Bhikkhunīs—these 6 are the training rules involving cutting (chedanaka). The 4 rules such as the formal agreement for robe-separation (cīvaravippavāsa-sammuti) are the training rules involving formal agreement (sammuti). The 7 rules that come as "Ayaṃ tattha sāmīcī" are the sāmīciya (proper conduct) training rules.

## Asādhāraṇa-ādi-vaṇṇanā

Finishing only the 14 parama (maximums) mentioned before in the intermediate questions (antara-pañha), he speaks wishing to answer the previous question. The verse "Dhōvanañca paṭiggaho" is a verse of the Teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya). The 2 training rules related to wool are the eḷakaloma tiyojanaparama (wool three-league maximum) training rules.

"Dvevīsati khuddakā" means:
The entire Bhikkhunī-vagga, successive meals (paramparabhojana),
The training rule regarding taking food that is not a remainder (anatiritta), exquisite food (paṇītabhojana), the naked ascetic (acelaka),
Knowingly concealing a gross (duṭṭhulla) offence.
Consulting with a woman (mātugāma) who is deficient (ūna), the king not having departed (anikkhantarājaka),
Entering a village at the wrong time (vikāla) without informing an existing monk.
The training rule on making a sitting cloth (nisīdana), the rainy-season garment (vassikasāṭikā),
These 22 training rules are declared among the minor (khuddaka) ones.
568:
The reading "Kulesu cārittāpatti" should not be taken because that training rule is common (sādhāraṇa). "Sacattārīsā cime" should be split as "Sacattārīsa ime". Because only the training rules taught as "Pārājikas and Saṅghādisesas" are taught by way of analysis, they are called vibhatti (analysis/classification). Sādhāraṇa (common) relates to all eight Pārājikas. The vibhattis that are Pārājikas are called pārājikavibhatti. In the common category, excluding seven Saṅghādisesas, it is called Saṅghādisesa.

In another ganthipada (difficult word commentary): "Alternatively, two Uposathas, two Pavāraṇās, four Kammās, and five Uddesas become four (groups); there is no other way"—this Pali is extracted. In that Pali, because there is no distinction (visesa) for "four Kammās", the original extracted text is better. Previously too, this was said only by way of showing the vibhatti alone. Having said "It is not said by way of settling through samathas", in the analysis of kamma, it was not distinguished as "settled by samathas" because only Uposatha and Pavāraṇā were analyzed. Why? Because here too it is said, "Give the method by distinguishing only Uposatha and Pavāraṇā," and because it leads to the meaning that even offences are settled by unlawful group-acts (vaggakamma), etc. This should be understood and scrutinized. "Accomplishing the task by two, four, three, and one" means: Vivādādhikaraṇa (legal questions of dispute) is settled by two samathas, Anuvādādhikaraṇa (legal questions of accusation) is settled by four, Āpattādhikaraṇa (legal questions of offences) is settled by three, and Kiccādhikaraṇa (legal questions of duties) is settled by one samatha.

## Pārājika-ādi-āpatti-vaṇṇanā

Nibbacanamatta means just a synonym (vevacanamatta). Sesa (remaining) refers to the middle and end remaining from the beginning. Pada refers to the training rule (sikkhāpada). Saddhācitta means a confident mind (pasannacitta), or there is a reading "santācitta". Anāḷiya means a poor person (dalidda). Although this synonym does not exist in the questions like "Garukaṃ lahukañca", it should be known that it is said to clarify the meaning encompassed by the words "Handa vākyaṃ suṇoma te". There is also the reading "Ākāso pakkhinaṃ gatī"; that reading is appropriate by way of class (jāti). Pakkhīnaṃ is just straight (ujuka).
