## Explanation of the Classification of Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇabheda-vaṇṇanā)

## Explanation of the Classification of Reopening [Legal Issues] etc. (Ukkoṭanabhedādi-vaṇṇanā)

In the phrase "to show the reopening of the means of settling (samatha) by reopening the legal issue (adhikaraṇa)," the meaning is that legal issues are settled by the seven means of settling; a monk who reopens those legal issues is said to reopen the seven means of settling. *Pasavati* means it arises or is produced. Regarding the words "They are found in the legal issue of accusation (anuvādādhikaraṇa)," etc., because they are similar to "Dhamma, non-Dhamma," etc., it means they are specifically found in those [categories of] Dhamma, non-Dhamma, etc. *Anihataṃ* refers to what has not been removed by a Sutta, etc. *Avinicchitaṃ* refers to what has not been decided as "an offense, not an offense," etc. "He reopens a legal issue that has arisen in such and such a place... he reopens the settlement by covering over with grass (tiṇavatthāraka)"—only these ten are mentioned. It is written: "Because the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya), the acting according to what is admitted (paṭiññātakaraṇa), and the decision by a majority (yebhuyyasikā) are not mentioned, they cannot be reopened. There is no formal act (kammavācā) for these [three]. Therefore, they say these cannot be reopened." *Pāḷimuttakavinicchayena eva* means only by the power of mere Dhamma teaching, excluding the characteristics of the Vinaya. They show it with the Pali text brought from the Khandhaka or the Parivāra. It means showing "non-Dhamma as Dhamma," etc., for the sake of preceptors (upajjhāya), etc., regarding a legal issue previously decided by the Dhamma and Vinaya. It is called *visamanissita* because it depends on unwholesome (visama) bodily actions, etc. The same applies to the remaining terms.

## Explanation of the Origins of Legal Issues etc. (Adhikaraṇanidānādi-vaṇṇanā)

342-3. *Kiṃsambhāraṃ* means "what requisite?" Here, the word *kiṃ* is an indeclinable (avyaya) of general gender. A dispute that arises later based on a dispute that arose previously is called the origin of a dispute (vivādanidāna). Due to the legal issue of offense (āpattādhikaraṇa), one incurs four kinds of offenses. If a nun knowingly conceals a *pārājika* offense, she incurs a *pārājika* offense. If she conceals it while in doubt, she incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. If a monk conceals a *saṅghādisesa* offense, he incurs a *pācittiya* offense. If he conceals a failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. This refers to the power of activities (kicca) that arise based on activities such as the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) performed previously. What kind of activities? Activities that arise by the power of formal acts of admonishment (samanubhāsana), etc. *Taṃ hi* refers to that legal issue.

In the phrase "by which legal issue they are settled among legal issues," this is said to show that when they are settled by legal issues, they are settled only by the legal issue of business (kiccādhikaraṇa), not...
570:
...it is said to show the meaning that they are not settled by other legal issues. It is not said to show that they are settled exclusively by the legal issue of business.

In the legal issue of offense, the Saṅgha disputes thus: "It is an offense," "It is not an offense."

Because there is no origin (samuṭṭhāna), the six origins of the six [means of settling] such as the settlement through mindfulness (sativinaya), etc., are analyzed without analyzing the performance of the act in the settlement in the presence (sammukhāvinaya), such as "when the act is performed, there is performance," etc. Why is it analyzed so? Because there is no inclusion in the formal act (kammasangaha); the meaning is that there is no such thing as "the state of being a business" (kiccayatā) in the presence of the Saṅgha (saṅghasammukhatā), etc., just as there is none in the settlement through mindfulness, etc.

## The Explanation of the Classification of Legal Issues is finished.

## Explanation of the Inquirer's Practice (Anuvijjakassa-paṭipatti-vaṇṇanā)

*Ṭhānanisajjavatthādinissitā* refers to "one should stand thus, one should sit thus," etc. *Saññājananatthaṃ* means for the purpose of making it known that "one should speak thus." *Anuvidhiyantena* means by keeping it in mind. *Lajjā sā nu kho* means "What is that shame in this assembly?"

## Kathina-atthatādivaṇṇanā
403-4. The meaning of the word 'Kinti' is 'how' (kathaṃ). Giving without prior acceptance is a temporary material object. In the phrase "anāgatavasena anantara hutvā", the effort (payoga) such as fetching water is said to occur after the preliminary act (pubbakaraṇa) such as washing, and also because the effort is made with reference to the act of washing, etc. This effort is understood to be in the sense of the 'pre-arisen condition' (purejāta-paccaya). One cannot obtain even a single dhamma because of the non-existence of the causal object that arose before it.

## Kathinādijānitabbavibhāgavaṇṇanā
'Rūpādidhammesu' refers to the eightfold kalāpas of form, such as color (vaṇṇa) and smell (gandha). Since it is said, "vassānassa pacchimo māso" (the last month of the rainy season), it should be known that it is allowable to spread the Kathina on any day of the last month, Tazaungmon.

Because it is said "Ādiccabandhunā", they say it is the word of the Elders (Theras).

## Palibodhapapañhabyākaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā
415-6. How is the 'Sanniṭṭhānantika' (ending by decision) Kathina removal withdrawn outside the boundary? A monk takes an unfinished robe and departs, thinking, "I will not return." To that monk who has gone outside the boundary, the thought arises, "I will not even have this robe made." Thus, for that monk who has gone outside the boundary, the Kathina is withdrawn. How is it withdrawn inside the boundary? He takes an unfinished robe and departs, thinking, "I will not return." However, not finding a comfortable dwelling there, he returns to that very monastery. For him, the robe-impediment (cīvara-palibodha) still remains. When the thought arises in him, "I will not have this robe made," that impediment is severed. Therefore, it is said, "It is withdrawn inside the boundary." 

There are two types of Sanniṭṭhānantika: one where he severs the residence-impediment (āvāsa-palibodha) thinking "I will not return" but then returns to that monastery and makes the decision "I will not have this robe made"; and another where, staying outside the boundary, the decision is made by the arising of the thought "I will not have this robe made, and I will not return." In the verse, the words "dve palibodhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ" refer only to these two aforementioned impediments. How is the 'Āsāvacchedika' (ending by the cutting off of hope) Kathina withdrawal...
573:
...withdrawn inside the boundary? To a monk who is hopeful, it is said, "You just wish for the monastery; I will send [the robe]." It is written that although he previously departed having severed the residence-impediment (āvāsa-palibodha) thinking "I will not return," when he goes to that monastery again, he is sent word by that person saying, "I am not able to give it." Because it is said, "There is withdrawal (uḍḍhāra) only when there is spreading (atthāra)," withdrawal cannot be obtained without spreading; therefore, it is so stated. The 'former two' refers to 'Antarabbhāra' and 'Sahubbhāra' which were mentioned first in the context where it is said, "The two withdrawals of Kathina arise together and cease together." It does not refer to the two beginning with 'Pakkamanantika.' 'Ceasing together' means they reach the state of being withdrawn (uḍḍhāra).

## Anissitavaggavaṇṇanā
'Kāyika-upaghātikā' means transgression by the body.

## Nappaṭippassambhanavaggavaṇṇanā
'Omaddakāraka' refers to a monk who acts by crushing and overpowering.

## Vohāravaggavaṇṇanā
Disputes (vivādādhikaraṇa) arise depending on the grounds for schism (bhedakaravatthu); thus, it proceeds according to the number. The association with the twelve roots such as anger (kodha) and malice (upanāha) is called 'vivādādhikaraṇa'; the same applies to the remaining cases. In the nine instances such as 'osāraṇā' (restoration), the act is done by 'kamma-ñatti' (formal motion). In the two instances called 'ñattidutiya-kamma' and 'ñatticatuttha-kamma', the act is done by 'kammavācā' (formal act). Since the two Vibhaṅgas (Ubhatovibhaṅga) are not included according to the method stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, therefore, the statement made in the Kurundī should be accepted; thus the connection is made.

## Diṭṭhāvikammavaggavaṇṇanā
It is not allowed to confess an offense together with more than three monks. Only one who holds the view of monks who are of a different communion by act (kammanānāsaṃvāsaka) is called 'laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka' (one of a different communion by view). It is said that the phrase "avippavāsasīmāya ṭhitassa" is stated with reference to the great boundary (mahāsīmā). There is also a variant reading "ummādā cittakkhepā".

## Musāvādavaggavaṇṇanā
'Pariyāyena jānantassa' means a lie (musāvāda) spoken by way of circumlocution to anyone who understands. 'Anuyogo na dātabbo' means one should remain silent without accepting the words spoken by that monk.

In the 'nirutti' (linguistic expression) of usage (vohāra) and the 'nirutti' of sound (sadda), there are nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) such as the reviewing of the path (magga-paccavekkhaṇā).

They also say, "'Yathārattaṃ' means looking at laypeople and novices according to the duration of nights." It is written, "'Yathāvuḍḍhaṃ' means looking at ordained monks [according to seniority]."

Some read "Ekāvaṭṭo"; the meaning of that word is said to be 'angry' or 'overpowered by anger.' Some read "Ekavatthō"; the meaning is said to be 'standing with the upper robe removed.' ## Commentary on the Second Collection of Verses
## Commentary on Bodily Offenses and Others
474-5. Because there are no other recitations (uddesa) except for the recitation of the introduction (nidānuddesa), it is said: "There is a collection of all the Pātimokkha recitations." Those who respect the Vinaya are called vinayagaruka. Although this term appears in two verses, it should be understood as a distinction because it is spoken in combination with other terms. In the phrase "a legal act occurs in nine places," it refers to the legal act and the motion (kammañatti). Vācā means arising from speech (vacīsambhava). Addhānahīno refers to one who is under twenty years of age (ūnavīsativasso). In this matter, it is said to be the view of the Kurundī. Vanappati refers to a "lord of the forest" tree as mentioned in the context of taking what is not given (adinnādāna). Vissaṭṭhichaḍḍana occurs in the emission of semen (sukkavissaṭṭhi). Dukkaṭā katā refers to the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For a nun who asks for and eats raw grain (āmakadhañña), there is a dukkaṭa in the preliminary effort (pubbapayoga) and a pācittiya offense in the act of swallowing (ajjhohāra).

## Commentary on Pācittiya
It is said that the members of the Mahāsaṅghika sect make even novices (sāmaṇera) confess offenses; therefore, it is said: "They should not be made to confess (na desāpetabbā)." However, in the case of such gross transgressions (oḷārikavītikkama), a penalty (daṇḍakamma) should be imposed on those novices.

## Commentary on Persons Not to be Saluted and Others
Dasasataṃ āpattiyo means one thousand offenses. "In the Vinaya case of Campā" means in the Campeyyakkhandhaka. The meaning is that the Blessed One taught only the four legal acts, such as "unlawful and incomplete" (adhammena vagga). It is not only the offenses, but indeed the six settlements (samatha)... are settled by the verdict in the presence (sammukhāvinaya); the meaning is that they reach proper association (sampayoga) through the verdict in the presence. They are settled without the settlements; they reach the state of settlement. When in the sense of prohibition (paṭisedha), "without the settlements" (vinā samathehi) means being devoid of the settlements.

## Commentary on the Sixteen Legal Acts and Others
Asuttaka means that which is devoid of the Sutta; the intention is that there is no usutta (that which is devoid of the Pali text) in that matter.

## Commentary on the Question of Not Living Apart
Tahiṃ means in that person. Akappiyasambhoga refers to sexual intercourse and so forth. In the Garubhaṇḍavinicchaya (Decision on Heavy Goods), it is stated: "It is allowable to relinquish and use [heavy goods] for the purpose of protecting a noble monastery." Among the eleven persons not to be saluted (avandiya), there are eleven to be avoided, such as eunuchs (paṇḍaka). One approaches one's own assembly. It does not live because it is a created form (nimmitarūpa). By the words "I speak of [the area] above the collarbone," it shows the absence of sexual intercourse in the mouth. By excluding the part below the navel, [it refers to] the anus and the urinary tract (not being used).

"Referring to a nun who descends to the opposite bank of a river belonging to another village" is said referring only to the vicinity of the river on that opposite bank belonging to the nun's village. There, on the opposite bank, the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) of a stone's throw is delimited by the edge of the river. Therefore, on that opposite bank, there is no forest even the size of a cubit. Because that forest is covered with grass and so forth, it creates a state devoid of the visual precinct (dassanūpacāra). In that case, there is no offense in one's own village. But on the opposite bank, one sets foot only in the village precinct known as a stone's throw. In between, according to the Abhidhamma method, one is said to have crossed one's own village which has become a forest. Therefore, it should be known that there is a staying behind from the group (ohīyanā) occurred. Even with this much, one should not be satisfied but should investigate and accept it. The five hundred nuns headed by Mahāpajāpatī are those who received ordination in the presence of the monks. Even Mahāpajāpatī is called one who received ordination in the presence of the monks because she accepted the exhortation given by the Elder Ānanda.

## Commentary on Questions on Pārājika and Others
"Referring to a cloth hut" is said because it is possible to transgress along with the cloth. When the gender changes (liṅgaparivatta), because the act of receiving (paṭiggahaṇa) disappears, it is not allowable to take and eat by oneself. "A place where a crow voids" means a place voided by a crow. "Having approached even three men" is the remainder of the text.

## Commentary on Questions on Pācittiya and Others
Due to sexual intercourse means bodily contact (kāyasaṃsagga). For that reason, for a nun who makes an effort in bodily contact which is the preliminary part of sexual intercourse, it is said referring to the fulfillment of the eight grounds (aṭṭhavatthu).
578:
Paribhogappaccayā means due to the cause of use/consumption. Tasmā means because of the cause of use, an offense is committed; therefore, the meaning is that it occurs at the conclusion of the meal. In ancient books, there is the reading "tassā." They say that the statement of the cause is good because it shows the limitation of the meal.

## Kammavaggavaṇṇanā

It is said: "When an insane monk has requested the authorization for the insane (ummattakasammuti) and departed, it is allowable to grant it even in his absence." Even if he is present in that assembly, it is not invalidated because there is no fixed rule. To show that there is no fault in performing it in his absence, it is said: "That which is done in his absence is well done." However, in this legal action, higher ordination (upasampadā) by a messenger cannot be performed in his absence. Because of the specific nature of the kammavācā, legal actions such as the overturning of the bowl (pattanikkujjana) and others must be performed by removing [the object] from arm's reach; therefore, it is said: "That which is done in his absence is well done." "It should be done after questioning, accusing, and reminding; it is done without questioning, accusing, or reminding"—this is the meaning of the words. In the phrase "excluding the month of Kattika," the month of Pavāraṇā is excluded. "The two full-moon days" refers to the two full-moon days of Pavāraṇā for those who entered the first and second rains-retreat (vassa).

It means one omits a word (pada). In the five groups starting with the ka-group, what is called "heavy" (garuka) is a long vowel (dīgha) and a syllable followed by a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga). In the passage "Buddharakkhitattherassa yassa nakkhamati," because it is followed by the conjunct consonants 'ta' and 'ka,' a short vowel (rassa) is spoken where a long vowel (dīgha) should be spoken. It is like saying "so tuṇhi assa" instead of "so tuṇhī assa."

Having clarified the statements made in the other commentaries in the Kurundī, it is said: "They are unable to sit."

487-8. "Four monks of pure virtue" refers to monks who have not committed a Pārājika offense. "Their consent (chanda) or purity (pārisuddhi) does not come" means that while three or two monks are sitting, the consent and purity of one or two, even if brought, is as if not brought.

## Apalokanakammakathāvaṇṇanā

495-6. Physical association, communal giving, sleeping together, receiving, etc., are the occasions for this act of announcement (apalokana-kamma); thus, it means the act of announcement proceeds in this way. Because the act (kamma) itself is the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), it is called kammalakkhaṇa. Like the acts of restoration (osāraṇa), expulsion (nissāraṇa), and the act of shaving (bhaṇḍukamma), etc., it is an act and does not receive another name; being only an act, it should be noted; therefore, it is called kammalakkhaṇa. It is just like the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). For just as all specific conditions that are free from the characteristics of the root condition (hetu-paccaya), etc., are included in that decisive support condition, so too, only the kammalakkhaṇa is included here.
580:
Because it is marked (by the name of the act) just like the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), it is called kammalakkhaṇa. Just as all specific conditions free from the characteristics of the root condition (hetu-paccaya), etc., are included in that decisive support condition, so too it is said: "It is only kammalakkhaṇa." To show the kammalakkhaṇa, the passage beginning with "acchinnacīvara jiṇṇacīvara naṭṭhacīvarānaṃ" (for those whose robes are stolen, worn out, or lost) is stated. The announcement (apalokana) stated as "A monk giving more than that should give after asking permission" is indeed kammalakkhaṇa. In this way, the characteristic should be understood in all instances.

"Iṇapalibodham-pi" means if creditors harass such a monk, it is proper to give from the property arising from that [monastery/garden]. "Antarasannipāto" refers to meetings in between, such as the recitation of auspicious verses (maṅgaluccāraṇa), etc., excluding the great assemblies like Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. "Upanikkhepato" means from what was deposited to protect a cetiya from danger. "Another agreement should be made" is said because these trees are different from those trees for which an agreement was previously made. "If in that original [source]" means that previously, by the words "From now on, distribute and eat [from this tree]," individual use was forbidden. "Anuvicaritvā" means following behind and expecting requisites from them. "Mūlabhāgaṃ" means making a one-tenth portion. Because in former times they gave by making a one-tenth portion, it is called "mūlabhāga." "Akatāvāsaṃ vā katvā" means doing so with the revenue that has arisen. "Jaggitakāleyeva na vāretabbā" means they should not be forbidden when they have been tended and are full of flowers and fruits. "Jagganakāle" means at the time when one begins to tend [them]. "Ñattikammathānabhede pana" means in the specific occasion of the act of motion (ñatti-kamma).

Here is the miscellaneous section (pakiṇṇaka): There is a Saṅgha-kamma (act of the Saṅgha) which only the Saṅgha performs, and not a group (gaṇa) or an individual (puggala). Excluding a portion of the kammalakkhaṇa of the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma), the other four types of acts should be understood as such. There is a Saṅgha-kamma which the Saṅgha, a group, and an individual all perform. This was explained previously. It is also said: "In a monastery where two or three monks reside, the act performed by them meeting together is just like an act performed by the Saṅgha. But in a monastery where there is only one monk, by that monk..." and so on. There is a gaṇa-kamma (act of a group) which the Saṅgha, a group, and an individual all perform. This should be understood by way of the Pārisuddhi-uposatha performed in the presence of others. There is a gaṇa-kamma which only a group performs, and not the Saṅgha or an individual. This should be understood by way of the Pārisuddhi-uposatha performed by way of mutual notification. There is a puggala-kamma (act of an individual) which only an individual performs, and not the Saṅgha or a group. That act...
581:
It should be understood by the power of the Observance by determination (adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha). There is an individual act (puggalakamma) performed by a single person, which is not performed by the Saṅgha or a group (gaṇa). That act should be understood by the power of the Observance by determination. There is also a group act (gaṇakamma) performed by some groups and not by others. Among those acts, an act without a motion (añattika) is performed by only two monks, not three. An act with a motion (sañattika) is performed by only three monks; those fewer or more than three do not perform it. This concludes the explanation of the miscellaneous section of the discussion on the act of announcement (apalokanakamma).

## Commentary on the Chapter of the Unprescribed and Prescribed
The Buddhas Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa alone prescribed the seven classes of offenses (āpattikkhandha). However, the Buddhas such as Vipassī and others only recited the Ovāda-pātimokkha and did not prescribe training rules (sikkhāpada). This concludes the commentary on the Chapter of the Unprescribed and Prescribed.

## Commentary on the Concluding Discussion
There is the teaching of that Vinaya Piṭaka, analyzed through the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra. It is said that the commentary named Samantapāsādikā is completed with the sequence of words stated as "named Samantapāsādikā". That commentary was diligently produced at the monastery named Padhānaghara with complete analytical decisions on meanings and so forth.

It is called samudita because it is well-attained. Those virtues were attained without difficulty. Or, it is endowed with virtues of extraordinary measure. By being thus endowed, the virtues such as faith (saddhā), which are produced by mindfulness (sati) that is said to "seek the destinations of the states that have arisen", are called supremely pure because of being fully protected. Thus, even when mindfulness is present, virtues like faith are also mentioned. In this regard, among the four types of virtue (sīla) mentioned in this Vinaya Piṭaka, faith adorns the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla). Indeed, that pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla is accomplished through faith. It should be understood that the three qualities—mindfulness (sati), energy (viriya), and wisdom (paññā)—adorn the three virtues: restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla), purification of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla), and virtue concerning the use of requisites (paccaya-paribhoga-sīla), as appropriate.

Furthermore, faith without wisdom is impure, because wisdom is the cause of devotion. Wisdoms, however, are called supremely pure by the power of that faith. Wisdom without faith falls into the side of deceit; only wisdom joined with faith is pure. Energy without concentration (samādhi) leads to restlessness, but not when joined with concentration; thus, by mentioning the purity of energy, concentration is also mentioned. In this way, it should be known that the supremely pure virtues like faith also adorn the Pātimokkha virtue. How? Without faith in the Teacher who teaches the practice, in the practice itself, and in the fruit of the practice, it is impossible to undertake virtue or to purify the virtue that has been undertaken. Therefore, faith adorns the Pātimokkha virtue. Among those three, one is able to honor the Buddha with the qualities beginning with "Thus indeed is that Blessed One..."
582: One is able to honor the Blessed One with the qualities beginning with "Itipi so bhagavā". The occurrence of faith in the practice of virtue, and in the results in the present life and the future life arising from the failure or perfection of virtue, should be understood in detail. Having seen the faults and benefits that are the roots of the failure and perfection of virtue, and seeing the means to abandon the faults and to achieve the benefits, the wisdom that arises in such a way adorns the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla). Abandoning laziness (kosajja) that may arise and should not arise, such as "it is too cold", in accordance with what was taught as "he who (disregards) cold and heat", the energy that proceeds by way of not letting unarisen unwholesome states arise, abandoning arisen ones, making unarisen wholesome states arise, and increasing arisen ones, adorns the Pātimokkha virtue. In this same manner, it should be applied to the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties and so forth. Here, conduct (ācāra) should be understood as good behavior consistent with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). By the word "integrity" (ajjava), the disposition of non-greed (alobha) is shown by illustrating the engagement with the quality of rectitude, which is the opposite of crookedness, deception, and hypocrisy in bodily misconduct etc., caused by the desire for gain and honor. By the word "gentleness" (maddava), the disposition of seeking the welfare of others is shown by illustrating the engagement with the gentle qualities such as loving-kindness (mettā), which are the opposite of the resentment (paṭigha) etc. that cause harshness. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the engagement with the qualities taught as "patience, gentleness, kind speech, and hospitality" is shown. The virtues mentioned here, such as integrity and gentleness, are both the cause of the perfection of virtue and the fruit of virtue because they bring about that perfection. "One's own doctrine" (sakasamaya) refers to the four assemblies. By this, the absence of the nature of suffering among monks of similar practice is indicated. Alternatively, "one's own doctrine" refers to the Buddhist Tipitaka. The Tipitaka is called "profound" (gahana) because it is difficult to explain. Decision-making within one's own doctrine, the Tipitaka, is called sakasamaya-gahana. Because it is said, "The four things—Truth, Being, Rebirth, and Dependent Origination—are difficult to see and extremely difficult to teach," just as the connection with the word "profound" is stated for one's own doctrine, the same applies to the doctrines of others (parasamaya). "Skill in wisdom" (paññā-veyyattiya) refers to wisdom whose nature is like a weapon whetted on a stone by sharp intellect. "Distinction of the Tipitaka scriptures" (tipiṭaka-pariyatti-pabheda) refers to the varieties of the scriptures known as the Tipitaka. In that distinction, tanti means the Pāḷi text, its meaning, and the Dispensation (sāsana). Here, some say "the Pāḷi text alone". Since there was no realization-knowledge (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) at the time this commentary was completed, it is said "by the power of unimpeded knowledge" with reference to knowledge consisting in what is heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa). By the perfection of the means (because it has arisen).
583:
Because it produces [sound], it is called speech that comes forth pleasantly. Due to the nature of speech coming forth pleasantly, it is also associated with the beauty of sweet and pure speech. Such speech is pleasant to the ear and also brings about the happiness of a perfect structure. By saying "Mahāveyyākaraṇena" (by the great grammarian) instead of just "Veyyākaraṇena," it indicates the nature of being able to bear texts such as Pāṇini-byākaraṇa, which are unshared with others and adorned with training (sikkhā), linguistics (nirutti), and prosody (chandoviciti), etc. In terms like "Yutta-vādina," it means one who has speech that flows appropriately and freely, or one endowed with instantaneous wisdom (ṭhānuppatti-paññā) or wisdom that arises quickly in various matters.

Regarding the distinction in wisdom (or "ojābhede" in some versions), because the work composed by the teacher, who is a great poet (mahakavi) endowed with powers like the ability to grant longevity (āyusatti-karaṇatā), is vast; and by showing proficiency in these three areas—the Dispensation (Sāsana), the subject matter (hetu-visaya), and linguistics (sadda)—through phrases like "Tipitaka-pariyatti-pabhede," it indicates that the Venerable Buddhaghosa possesses wisdom highly skilled in the Vinaya.

For those individuals in whom the analytical insights (paṭisambidā) etc. are distinct and clear, those qualities are called "pabhinna-paṭisambidā" etc. Those individuals are "surrounded" [by them]. One who is surrounded by the power of producing and increasing [these qualities] in their own continuity, without causing a break in the uplifted sequence, is called "pabhinnapaṭisambidā-parivāra." This "pabhinnapaṭisambidā-parivāra" means being established in superhuman states (uttari-manussadhamma). In the context of being adorned with qualities such as the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā) and the four analytical insights, the six higher powers are indeed superhuman states. Among the four analytical insights, it is only a part of the analytical insight into meaning (attha-paṭisambidā).

If it is asked: "How do these two, being themselves included in superhuman states, adorn superhuman states?" It is said that they adorn them because they are parts of those superhuman states, just as flowers etc., which are parts of a tree, adorn the tree. The knowledge of analytical insight included in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) adorns superhuman states without being a part of them, just as an ornament that is not a part of a man adorns the man. Alternatively, the retinue of sense-sphere analytical insights adorns qualities such as the six higher powers and analytical insights. The word "paṭisambidā" is mentioned again with reference to supramundane (lokuttara) analytical insight.

Arising in the Dispensation and being an ornament of the Dispensation, or being an ornament of the very lineage in which he was born. Because of being endowed with the six qualities of a teacher—such as performing either brevity or detail, causing the arising and increase of faith in those not yet confident and those already confident, and making clear the profound nature of the profound Pali texts that have been taught—he is called "one of vast wisdom" (Vipula-buddhi). Those who let their thoughts run excessively regarding ultimate realities (paramattha) take various extremes such as annihilationism (uccheda); they take it as "all knowable things are merely designations (paññatti)" or "merely ultimate reality." Their wisdom is called "stained" (samala) because it is conditioned by wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). But this teacher's wisdom is called "pure" (visuddha) because it is free from such excessive running of thought regarding the Dhamma. Therefore, it is said:
584: 'One of vast and pure wisdom' refers to [being taught] by teachers endowed with qualities such as 'dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem.' He is called an 'Elder' (Thera) because he has reached a state of firmness through qualities such as virtue. 'Sīlavisuddhi' (purity of virtue) is through virtue or through the purity of virtue. He is the 'Foremost of the World' because he was born first after breaking the eggshell of ignorance (avijjā); or he is called 'Mahesī' (Great Seer) because he sought (esi) the great aggregates of virtue and so forth in the profound world. By this much of the sequence of words, the clarification of difficult points (gaṇṭhiṭṭhāna) has been made by summarizing the collection of decisions in all the words of the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā, which has an extent of more than twenty-seven thousand [stanzas]. Even though this has been done, one should carefully investigate the decisions written in this work, noting the Pali and the Commentary. Those teachers who, noting the great majesty of the Blessed Buddha and the diverse methods and profound meaning of the Vinaya Piṭaka, do not destroy the lineage of the ancient teachers, and setting aside their own opinions, remain explaining the Vinaya Piṭaka solely for the sake of the endurance of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) and out of a desire to help others—one should pay homage at the feet of those teachers, and being endowed with qualities such as patience (khanti) and gentleness (soracca), one should please the minds of those teachers through the fulfillment of duties (vatta), and having them speak the decisions that have come down through the lineage, one should investigate and accept what is consistent with those words, and discard what is inconsistent. In other cases, one should remain silent. One must certainly not cause confusion in the decisions. Why? Because it is a cause for the destruction of the Dispensation (Sāsana). There are these summary verses here: If an ignorant person, without knowing the great majesty of the Buddha and the profound methods and meanings of the Dhamma, should explain that Vinaya, he is a cause for the destruction of the Dispensation, which is difficult to perceive. Indeed, he who, without knowing the Pali and its meaning, nor the method of the Commentary, makes others accept an undecided matter as a decision, being placed at the forefront by them, destroys the Pali, the meaning, and the method of the Commentary.
585:
A monk who considers himself wise (paṇḍita-māni), having been placed at the head and having prospered in due order by the great multitude, remains putting forward the manner of a teacher without causing doubt [in them], even though he is not wise.
